PENTINGNYA KEIKHLASAN DALAM SELURUH AMAL IBADAH

ومَا أُمِرُوْا إِلاَّلِيَعْبُدُاللهَ مُخْلِصِيْنَ لَهُ الدِّيْنَ حُنَفَاءَ

Padahal mereka tidak disuruh kecuali supaya menyembah Allah dengan memurnikan keta`atan kepada-Nya dalam (menjalankan) agama yang lurus…[Al-Bayyinah/98 : 5]

Segala Puji bagi Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala Rabb semesta alam Shalawat dam salam kita sampaikan kepada Nabi Muhammad Shalalllahu ‘alaihi wa sallam Pembawa risalah yang haq ini sebagai rahmat bagi semesta alam kepada keluarganya para shahabatnya dan orang-orang yang setia mengikuti jejaknya hingga akhir zaman.

Berikut ini adalah pembahasan secara singkat hal-hal yang berkaitan dengan pentingnya “keikhlasan” dalam seluruh amalibadah. Sesungguhnya perkara paling mendasar dan terpenting dalam dien ini adalah mengikhlaskan diri kepada Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala dalam setiap amal ibadah yang kita lakukan, hal itu sebagai syarat utama diterimanya amal ibadah. Ikhlas adalah termasuk amalan hati yang perlu mendapatkan perhatian “istimewa” (secara mendalam) dan dilakukan dengan cara “istimrar” (terus menerus) di setiap kita hendak melakukan amalibadah, agar amalan kita menjadi bernilai di hadapan Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala.

Pentingnya Amalan Hati.
Telah kita ketahui bahwa pengertian iman menurut Ahlus Sunah adalah : Keyakinan dengan hati, ikrar dengan lisan, dan amalan dengan seluruh anggota badan, bertambah dengan ketaatan kepada Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala dan berkurang dengan perbuatan maksiat.

Perlu diketahui bahwa ikhlas adalah perkara terpenting dalam amalan hati, yang hal tersebut sangat erat hubungannya dengan pengertian iman tersebut di atas.

Syaikhul Islam Ibnu Taimiyah berkata : “Amalan-amalan hati adalah termasuk pokok-pokok dari keimanan dan tonggak-tonggak agama Islam ini, seperti: mencintai Allah dan Rasul-Nya, bertawakal kepada Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala, mengikhlaskan seluruh macam ibadah hanya kepada Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala semata, bersyukur kepada-Nya atas nikmat-nikmat-Nya dan berlaku sabar di atas hukum-hukum-Nya, khauf (perasaan takut kepada-Nya akan siksa atau adzab-Nya), raja (berharap) kepada-Nya…Semua amalan ini wajib atas seluruh makhluk berdasarkan kesepakatan para imam agama”.[1]

Ibnul Qayim juga menjelaskan keagungan amalan-amalan hati : Amalan–amalan hati ialah pokok adapun amalan–amalan anggota badan adalah pengikut dan penyempurna. Sesungguhnya niat sekedudukan dengan ruh, adapun amalan sekedudukan dengan jasad, sehingga apabila ruh telah terpisah dengan jasad maka binasalah. Oleh sebab itu mengetahui hukum – hukum hati lebih penting dari pada mengetahui hukum-hukum jasad.[2]

Hal inilah di antaranya yang mendorong kami untuk mengulas hal ini agar seluruh aktifitas kita sehari-hari tidak menemui kesia-siaan, yakni hampa, jauh dari berkah Allah atau Ramat-Nya, seolah-olah tiada nilainya aktifitas yang kita laksanakan setiap hari.

Niat berasal dari bahasa Arab, yang berarati tujuan. Sedangkan menurut istilah syara’ memiliki dua arti:

Ikhlash dalam beramal, yaitu semata-mata karena Allah, dan inilah yang sering dibicarakan oleh para Ulama ahli tauhid, suluk (perilaku) dan akhlak.
Membedakan antara ibadah yang satu dengan ibadah yang lain, atau ibadah dengan kebiasaan. Istilah ini sering dipakai oleh ulama-ulama Fiqh.
Niat dipakai untuk membedakan antara ibadah dan adat (kebiasaan yang dilakukan oleh manusia), misalnya : Mandi, apabila dimaksudkan (niatkan) karena Allah semata untuk menghilangkan hadats besar (mandi junub misalnya) maka hal yang semacam itu akan menjadi ibadah, lain halnya apabila mandi semata-mata dimaksudkan untuk membersihkan badan atau mendapatkan kesegaran, maka hal itu menjadi adat (kebiasaan) saja.

Kemudian bahwa niat itu tempatnya di hati dan apabila di lafadzkan menjadi bid`ah.

Kedudukan Ikhlas.
Sesungguhnya ikhlas adalah hakekat dien dan kunci dakwah para rasul, yakni menyembah Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala semata dan menjauhi thagut :

ومَا أُمِرُوْا إِلاَّ لِيَعْبُدُوْا اللهَ مُخْلِصِيْنَ لَهُ الدِّيْنَ حُنَفَاءَ

Padahal mereka tidak disuruh kecuali supaya menyembah Allah dengan memurnikan ketaatan kepada-Nya dalam (menjalankan) agama yang lurus…[Al-Bayyinah/98: 5]

Yang dimaksud dengan ” (حُنَفَاءَ ) agama yang lurus” pada ayat di atas adalah terjauhkan dari perkara-perkara syirik dan menuju kepada tauhid. Di sinilah pentingnya ikhlash dalam selurus amal ibadah, agar amalan tersebut tidak sia-sia, dan tidak mendapat adzab dari Allah, baik di dunia maupun di akhirat kelak.

Kemudian bahwa pengaruh ikhlas terhadap amalan itu sangatlah besar, amal yang kecil dan sedikit jika dilakukan dengan ikhlas dapat memperoleh pahala yang besar. Syaikhul Islam Ibnu Taimiyah dalam perkara ini mengatakan: “Suatu jenis amalan yang dikerjakan oleh manusia dengan menyempurnakan keikhlasannya dan ketundukkannya kepada Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala, terkadang Allah Subahnahu wa Ta’ala akan mengampuni dosa-dosa besar dengan sebab amalan itu, sebagaimana hadits al-bithaqah (seorang yang memiliki satu kartu Laa ilaaha illa Allah, lalu diampuni dosa-dosanya sebanyak 99 lembaran catatan amal keburukan-red)…ini karena dia mengucapkan Laa ilaaha illa Allah dengan ikhlas dan jujur/benar, karena kalau tidak, maka para pelaku dosa besar yang masuk ke dalam neraka semuanya juga mengucapkan tauhid, tetapi perkataan mereka tidaklah lebih berat terhadap dosa-dosa mereka sebagaimana pemilik kartu (Laa ilaaha illa Allah) itu.”

Hadits pemilik kartu Laa ilaaha illa Allah itu, adalah sebagai berikut:

عَنْ أَبِي عَبْدِ الرَّحْمَنِ الْمَعَافِرِيِّ ثُمَّ الْحُبُلِيِّ قَال سَمِعْتُ عَبْدَ الهِb بْنَ عَمْرِو بْنِ الْعَاصِ يَقُولُ قَالَ رَسُولُ الهَِ n إِنَّ اللَّهَ سَيُخَلِّصُ رَجُلاً مِنْ أُمَّتِي عَلَى رُءُوسِ الْخَلاَئِقِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ فَيَنْشُرُ عَلَيْهِ تِسْعَةً وَتِسْعِينَ سِجِلاَّ كُلُّ سِجِلٍّ مِثْلُ مَدِّ الْبَصَرِ ثُمَّ يَقُولُ أَتُنْكِرُ مِنْ هَذَا شَيْئًا أَظَلَمَكَ كَتَبَتِي الْحَافِظُونَ فَيَقُولُ لاَ يَا رَبِّ فَيَقُولُ أَفَلَكَ عُذْرٌ فَيَقُولُ لاَ يَا رَبِّ فَيَقُولُ بَلَى إِنَّ لَكَ عِنْدَنَا حَسَنَةً فَإِنَّهُ لَا ظُلْمَ عَلَيْكَ الْيَوْمَ فَتَخْرُجُ بِطَاقَةٌ فِيهَا أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لاَ إِلَهَ إِلاَّ الهُب وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا عَبْدُهُ وَرَسُولُهُ فَيَقُولُ احْضُرْ وَزْنَكَ فَيَقُولُ يَا رَبِّ مَا هَذِهِ الْبِطَاقَةُ مَعَ هَذِهِ السِّجِلَّاتِ فَقَالَ إِنَّكَ لاَ تُظْلَمُ قَالَ فَتُوضَعُ السِّجِلاَّتُ فِي كَفَّةٍ وَالْبِطَاقَةُ فِي كَفَّةٍ فَطَاشَتِ السِّجِلاَّتُ وَثَقُلَتِ الْبِطَاقَةُ فَلاَ يَثْقُلُ مَعَ اسْمِ الهِق شَيْءٌ

Dari Abdullah bin ‘Amr bin ‘Ash Radhiyallahu ‘anhu , dia berkata: “Saya telah mendengar Rasulullah Shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam bersabda: “Sesungguhnya Allah akan mengadili salah seorang laki-laki dari ummatku di hadapan seluruh makhluk pada hari kiamat. Lalu ditunjukan kepada laki-laki tersebut 99 catatan (amal keburukan), setiap satu catatan panjangnya sejauh mata memandang. Kemudian dikatakan kepada laki-laki tersebut: ”Apakah kau ingkari dari semua ini (kedzaliman yang telah kau perbuat)? Apakah para malaikat-Ku pencatat dan penjaga amalan menzhalimimu? Laki-laki tersebut menjawab: “Tidak Ya Tuhanku!”. Lalu Allah berkata kepada laki-laki tersebut: “Apakah engkau punya alasan (berbuat kezhaliman itu)? Laki-laki tersebut menjawab: “Tidak Ya Tuhanku!”. Kemudian Allah berkata kepada laki-laki tersebut: “Ya benar, tetapi sesungguhnya engkau memiliki satu kebaikan di sisi Kami, dan sesungguhnya tidak ada kedzaliman atasmu pada hari ini. Maka Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala mengeluarkan sebuah kartu kecil yang di dalamnya terdapat : Asyhadu an laa ilaaha illa Allah wa asyhadu anna Muhamadan ‘abduhu warasuluhu (Aku bersaksi bahwa tiada sesembahan yang haq kecuali Allah dan aku bersaksi bahwa Muhammad adalah hamba dan utusan-Nya). Kemudian Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala berkata kepada orang tersebut: “Datangkan timbanganmu”, maka orang tersebut berkata: “Ya Tuhan untuk apa kartu kecil ini dibandingkan dengan catatan (amal keburukan) ini ?”, maka Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala berkata kepada orang tersebut: “Sesungguhnya pada hari ini tiada kedzaliman”. Maka diletakkanlah catatan itu pada salah satu daun timbangan, dan kartu kecil itu diletakan pada satu daun timbangan yang lain. Maka jadi ringanlah catatan-catatan `amal keburukan itu dan beratlah kartu kecil tersebut, maka tiadalah sesuatupun yang menjadi berat dibandingkan dengan nama Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala. [HR. At-Tirmidzi dan An-Nasa’i].

Pengertian Ikhlas dan Batasnya
Ada beberapa pengertian tentang ikhlas yang disebutkan oleh ulama, antara lain :

Diantaranya ada yang mengatakan : Ikhlas ialah “Menjadikan Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala satu-satunya tujuan di dalam menjalankan ketaatan”.
Ada juga yang mengatakan : “Ikhlas ialah membersihkan perbuatan dari mencari pandangan manusia”.
Al-Harawi berkata: “Ikhlas ialah membersihkan amalan dari setiap noda”.
Dan sebagian yang lain ada yang mengatakan: “Orang yang mukhlis ialah orang yang tidak perduli, seandainya hilang seluruh penghormatan kepadanya di dalam hati manusia, untuk kebaikan hatinya bersama Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala. Dan dia tidak suka manusia mengetahui amalannya walaupun seberat debu. Allah.
Tidak diragukan lagi bahwa keikhlasan membutuhkan kesungguhan yang tinggi hingga seorang hamba meraihnya dengan sempurna.

Pengertian Riya’, Sum’ah, Ujub
Telah kita ketahui bahwa keikhlasan dapat dihilangkan oleh beberapa perkara, seperti: mencintai dunia, kemasyhuran, kemuliaan, riya’, sum’ah dan ujub.

Riya ialah melakukan `ibadah dengan tujuan dilihat oleh manusia, sehingga orang yang riya’ itu mencari pengagungan, pujian, harapan atau rasa takut terhadap orang yang dia berbuat riya’ karenanya.
Sum’ah adalah amalan yang dilakukan dalam rangka agar didengar orang lain, misalnya memperdengarkan bacaan Al-Qur’an atau yang lainnya.
Ujub adalah teman riya, yaitu perasaan bangga terhadap diri sendiri atas kemampuan yang dimiliki secara berlebihan.
Syaikhul Islam Ibnu Taimiyah membedakan antara keduanya (antara riya dan ujub ).
a. Riya adalah salah satu bentuk dari syirik kepada makhluk.
b. Adapun ujub adalah bentuk dari pada syirik kepada diri sendiri.[3]

Diantara Bentuk-Bentuk Riya, Ujub dan Sum’ah

Riya dalam ibadah sholat, misalnya : Memperbaiki posisi atau gerakan shalat karena mengetahui bahwa dia sedang diperhatikan oleh orang yang dianggap lebih ‘alim atau lainya.

Riya atau sum’ah dalam kepribadian misalnya : Karena di karuniai oleh Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala suara yang merdu misalnya, maka timbulah penyakit riyaatau ujub ini pada nimat tersebut; Mengeraskan/ menbaguskan bacaan dalam membaca Al-Qur`an atau ketika mengumandangkan adzan dengan harapan ingin mendapatkan pujian atau agar diakui bahwa dia memiliki suara yang bagus atau merdu. Pada hakekatnya membaguskan suara dalam membaca Al-Qur’an, dengan tidak dibuat-buat atau berlebih-lebihan merupakan sunnah Rasulullah Shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam sebagaimana sabadanya:

زَيِّنُوْا اْلقُرْآنَ بِأَصْوَاتِكُمْ.

Baguskanlah (bacaan) Al-Qur`an dengan suara kalian [4]

Ujub atau Riya dalam berdakwah misalnya : Berceramah, menasehati orang, atau mentahdzir (memberi peringatan terhadap seseorang) dengan niat agar dikenal sebagai seorang penasehat, ahli pidato dengan harapan agar semua orang memujinya atau menyanjungnya. Kita berlindung kepada Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala dari semua perkara ini. Hendaklah kita ikhlash dalam berda`wah agar orang yang mendengarnya pun menerima dengan ikhlash (yakni : mendapatkan hidayah dari Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala)

Riya atau Ujub dalam menuntut ilmu : Yaitu berbangga dengan ilmu yang dikaruniakan Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala kepadanya atau menuntut ilmu hanya dalam rangka ingin menjadi seorang yang ahli dalam berdebat, bukan mengharapkan wajah Allah atau mencari berkah dari Allah atas ilmu yang dimilikinya. Sehingga ilmu yang Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala karuniakan tidak mampu membawa dia ke dalam kebahagian di dunia ataupun diakhirat. Padahal rasulullah telah memperingatkan dengan keras bagi para penuntut ilmu dengan ancaman tidak akan mendapatkan bau surga, apabila mempelajari suatu ilmu dalam rangka untuk mencari dunia semata; Rasulullah Shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam bersabada:

مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ عِلْمًا مِمَّا يُبْتَغَى بِهِ وَجْهُ اللهِ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ لاَ يَتَعَلَّمُهُ إِلاَّ لِيُصِيبَ بِهِ عَرَضًا مِنَ الدُّنْيَا لَمْ يَجِدْ عَرْفَ الْجَنَّةِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ يَعْنِي رِيحَهَا

Barang siapa menuntut ilmu yang seharusnya untuk mencari wajah Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala ; tetapi dia tidak mempelajari ilmu itu kecuali untuk mendapatkan harta benda dunia, maka dia tidak akan mendapatkan bau surga pada hari kiamat kelak.[5]

Riya atau Ujub ketika bershadaqah, misalnya : Memperlihatkan harta yang telah dishadaqahkan, atau mengungkit-ungkit kembali pemberian yang telah lalu dengan harapan agar disebut sebagai seorang dermawan.

Penawar Riya
Adapun di antara cara-cara mengobati riya adalah sebagi berikut:

Mengetahui seluk beluk riya itu sendiri dan takut terhadapnya. Sebagaimana hal tersebut adalah perkara yang paling ditakutkan oleh Rasulullah Shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam. Beliau Shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam bersabda:

” إِنَّ أَخْوَفُ مَا أَخَا فُ عَلَيكْمُ الشِّرْكُ اْلأَ صْغَر. قَا لوُا وَمَا الشِّرْكُ اْلأَ صْغَرُ يَا رَسُوْلُ الله ؟ قال : ” الرِّيَاءُ “.يقول الله تعالىيوم القيامة, إذا جازى الناس بأعمالهم : اذهبوا إلى الذين كنتم تراؤون في الدنيا فانظروا هل تجدون جزاء؟”

Sesungguhnya yang paling kutakutkan dari perkara yang aku takutkan atas kalian ialah syirik kecil. Para shahabat bertanya: “Apakah syirik kecil itu wahai rasulullah? Rasulullah Shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam bersabda: “Riya’, Pada hari kiamat , ketika membalas amalan-amalan manusia, Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala akan berfirman: “Pergilah kepada orang yang kamu dahulu sewaktu di dunia berbuat riya’ kepadanya, dan lihatlah apakah kamu dapakan balasan (pahala) darinya? [6]

Memberikan sanjungan atau pujian hanya ditujukan kepada Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala semata, karena Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala sumber dari segala kebaikan; maka hanya Allahlah yang berhaq mendapatkan pujian:

الحمد لله رب العالمين

Segala puji bagi Allah Tuhan semesta alam. [Al-Fatihah/1 :2]

Mengingat mati dan sekaratnya, hari akhir dan kedahsyatan adzabnya, kubur dan kerasnya siksa yang diberikan karena dosa-dosa yang diperbuat selama di dunia. Keadaan di kubur yang sunyi, gelap gulita dan sempit, tidak ada ibu dan bapak atau orang-orang yang dicinta di dekatnya.

Melihat akibat riya’, baik di dunia maupun diakhirat.
Maka perlu diketahui oleh setiap orang bahwa seandainya seluruh manusia berkumpul dalam rangka memberikan manfaat kepada siapapun, maka tiadalah mereka mampu memberikannya kecuali sesuatu itu telah ditentukan oleh Allah Subhanhau wa Ta’ala baginya; Oleh sebab itu sebagian orang-orang salaf mengatakan: “Bersungguh-sungguhlah dalam mencegah timbulnya riya` darimu, anggaplah orang lain bagimu seperti binatang dan anak-anak, janganlah kau bedakan adanya mereka atau tidak adanya, mereka tahu atau tidak tahu, cukuplah Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala saja yang mengetahuinya.

Kemudian singkirkan perasaan ingin dipuji ketika (syetan menggoda), dengan do’a-do’a yang diajarkan Rasulullah Shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam seperti:

أعوذ الله من الشيطان الرجيم

Aku berlindung kepada Allah dari godaan syetan yang terkutuk.

Adapun akibat riya di akhirat antara lain ; sebagaimana sabda Rasulullah Shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam.

مَنْ سَمَّعَ سَمَّعَ الهُ بِهِ وَمَنْ رَاءَى رَاءَى الهُ بِهِ

Barang siapa (yang beramal) ingin didengar maka Allah akan memperdengarkannya dan barang siapa (beramal) ingin dilihat maka Allah pun akan memperlihatkannya.[7]

Artinya : Bila seseorang beramal hanya ingin didengar atau dilihat orang lain maka itulah yang akan dia dapatkan, Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala Maha Sempurna tidak butuh sekutu-sekutu tersebut, Rasulullah Shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam bersabda: bahwa Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala berfirman:

أَنَا أَغْنَى الشُّرَكَاءِ عَنِ الشِّرْكِ مَنْ عَمِلَ عَمَلاً أَشْرَكَ فِيهِ مَعِي غَيْرِي تَرَكْتُهُ وَشِرْكَهُ

Aku adalah Yang paling tidak butuh sekutu, barangsiapa yang mengamalkan suatu perbuatan, yang di dalamnya dia menyekutukanKu dengan selain Aku, maka Aku tinggalkan dia dan sekutunya.[8]

Memohon pertolongan kepada Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala agar senantiasa berlaku ikhlas dalam segala amal ibadah dan berlindung dari-Nya dari riya. Seorang mumin atau muminah hendaklah tunduk, berserah diri kepada-Nya, berusaha semaksimal mungkin menghindarkan diri dari riya, sum’ah dan ujub; dan memperbanyak dzikir (mengingat Allah kapan saja di manapun berada) dan berdo`a kepada Allah Subhanahu wa Ta’ala, sebagaimana do’a-do’a yang diajarkan Rasulullah Shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam antara lain :

الشرك فيكم أخفى من دبيب النمل. وسأدلك على شيءٍ إذا فعلته أذهب عنك صغار الشرك وكبيره . تقول: اَللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَعُوْ ذُ بِكَ أَنْ أُشْرِكَ بِكَ وَأَناَ أَعْلَمُ, وَاسْتَغْفِرُكَ لمِاَ لاَ أَعْلَمُ. 

Kesyirikan yang ada pada kalian lebih tersembunyi merayapnya seekor semut, dan aku akan memberitahukan sesuatu kepadamu apabila hal itu kau kerjakan, maka akan menghilangkan kesyirikan kecil dan besar darimu. Yaitu engkau mengatakan (berdo’a): “Ya Allah aku berlindung kepada-Mu dari mensekutukan-Mu sedangkan saya mengetahuinya dan aku berlindung kepada-Mu dari apa-apa yang aku tidak aku tahu.”[9]

Wallahu A’lam.

A life story shaped by faith, sacrifice, and a lifelong mission for peace, family, and global unity.
Biography of Dr. Hak Ja Han Moon
Distributed to the press as part of her April 1998 speaking tour in the USA.
Childhood and Family Life
Dr. Hak Ja Han Moon, the International President of the Women’s Federation for World Peace, has dedicated her life to the pursuit of peace. Together with her husband, Reverend Sun Myung Moon, she worked alongside heads of state, Nobel Peace Prize recipients, religious leaders, and internationally respected artists to promote God-centered families and global harmony.
Dr. Moon was born in the village of Sinh in the Anju District (now North Korea) on January 6 (lunar), 1943. Her mother, Mrs. Hong, was a devoted Christian, and her father was a disciple of the well-known evangelist Rev. Young Do Lee. Due to their faith, the family faced persecution under the North Korean communist regime. In 1948, at the age of five, Dr. Moon and her mother were arrested and imprisoned for eleven days.
After their release, Dr. Moon, her mother, and grandmother fled under cover of night, eventually settling in Taegu during the Korean War. She was raised in a deeply religious environment and later moved to Choon Chun, where she completed her elementary education. During this period, she and her mother joined the newly formed Unification Church.
On April 11, 1960, Dr. Moon married the church’s founder, Reverend Sun Myung Moon, standing as co-founder of the Unification Church and equal partner in its providential mission. Central to their work has been the sanctification of marriage and the creation of strong, God-centered families. What began with 36 couples in 1961 has expanded to blessings involving tens of millions of couples worldwide.
Dr. Moon is the mother of thirteen children and grandmother to twenty-one grandchildren.
A Sportswoman and Patron of the Arts
Dr. Moon shares her husband’s love for nature and the outdoors, particularly fishing. She was instrumental in founding the Deer Park Equestrian Center in New York, now known for hosting premier equestrian events.
She and her husband are also passionate patrons of the arts. They founded the Little Angels Performing Arts School in Seoul, whose children’s ballet troupe has performed for royalty and world leaders. They also supported the New York City Symphony and established the Universal Ballet Academy in Washington, DC, nurturing world-class dancers and cultural excellence.
A Woman of International Peace and Good Will
Dr. Moon played a vital role in initiatives such as the Professors World Peace Academy and the International Conference on the Unity of the Sciences, bringing together scholars, scientists, and leaders from around the world. Her public speaking emerged naturally through these efforts, especially in addressing women’s gatherings globally.
In 1989, she stepped onto the world stage through international media, followed by historic meetings with global leaders, including Mikhail Gorbachev and President Kim Il Sung, in efforts toward reconciliation and peace.
International President of the Women’s Federation for World Peace
In 1992, Dr. Moon co-founded the Women’s Federation for World Peace and became its International President. Within months, she delivered keynote addresses across multiple continents in several languages. Her global tours reached tens of thousands, including appearances at the United Nations and the U.S. Capitol.
Her efforts contributed to the establishment of National Parents Day in the United States and earned recognition from governments, institutions, and global leaders. Dr. Moon has also presided over large-scale international marriage blessings and received numerous humanitarian awards and honorary doctorates for her lifelong dedication to peace and family values.

SPLM to Hold Joint Caucus Meeting in Juba

The ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM) is set to convene a joint caucus meeting at its headquarters in Juba on Monday, January 12, party officials have announced.

In a notice issued on Saturday, the SPLM Secretary for Culture, Information and Communication, Daniel Badagbu Rimbasa, invited members of the party’s Political Bureau, National Liberation Council, executive and parliamentary caucuses, as well as advisers, secretaries and deputy secretaries, to attend the meeting. The gathering is scheduled to begin at 9:00 a.m. at the SPLM House.

Although the party has not disclosed the agenda, the meeting is widely seen as part of SPLM’s preparations ahead of South Sudan’s planned general elections.

Last month, the presidency and the Council of Ministers approved amendments to key provisions of the 2018 Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan. Among the changes was a decision to delink the December 2026 elections from the permanent constitution-making process, a national population census and other institutional reforms.

The amendments also removed clauses stating that the peace agreement takes precedence over the constitution. However, the proposed changes have yet to be endorsed by the Transitional National Legislative Assembly or the peace monitoring body, the Reconstituted Joint Monitoring and Evaluation Commission (RJMEC).

The 2018 peace deal, signed by President Salva Kiir, opposition leader Riek Machar and other political leaders, has faced repeated delays, with elections postponed several times. Polls are now scheduled for December 2026, despite objections from Machar’s allies, who argue that the presidency-led consultations that produced the amendments excluded key stakeholders.

Saturday, 10 January 2026 | Juba, South Sudan 

Members of the Revitalized Transitional Government of National Unity (RTGONU), comprising the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM) and National Agenda Party, held a consultative meeting with the SPLM Secretary General, Comrade Dr. Akol Paul, at his office at the SPLM Secretariat in Juba on Saturday.

The meeting was convened by the SPLM Secretary General and was attended by representatives from the two political parties. Discussions focused on strengthening cooperation, particularly in the political arena, as the country prepares to declare its readiness to hold general elections scheduled for December 2026.

Speaking to the press after the meeting, Comrade Michael Makuei Lueth, Member of the SPLM National Liberation Council and Minister of Justice and Constitutional Affairs, stated that the parties agreed to establish a joint working group and committee. This body will develop a program agenda to continue dialogue among the participating political parties and engage other political forces as well.

He added that the parties also agreed to formalize their engagement through regular meetings to address emerging issues and ensure a safe, credible, and peaceful electoral process. Furthermore, they agreed to expedite the amendment of the Revitalized Peace Agreement. According to him, the political parties and executive amendments have already been completed, and the process is now moving to the Reconstituted Joint Monitoring and Evaluation Commission (R-JMEC), followed by the Transitional National Legislative Assembly (TNLA) for verification. Thereafter, work will begin on constitutional amendments to ensure full preparedness for the upcoming elections.

Comrade Makuei emphasized that the meeting sent a clear message to skeptics both inside and outside the country that the parties are committed to holding elections in December 2026, with no further extensions.

Meanwhile, the Chairman of the National Agenda Party and Minister of Cabinet Affairs, Hon. Martin Elia Lomuro, encouraged the President to continue leading the country toward sustainable peace. He also urged RTGONU members to work collectively to bring all remaining political parties together in order to guide the country peacefully and inclusively for the benefit of all citizens.

SPLM National Secretariat

Today’s message was super important to me & to my children. It really hit me hard. I’ve been dealing with multiple chronic health issues, plus trying to lose the weight I gained during pregnancy & with nursing my son. I’ve also been dealing with depression caused by multiple things & it’s been worsened by a lot of the negativity on social media. All the ICE corruption & the recent murders plus the Fake UPS Delivery Murder making its rounds in the media again after the convictions of the men responsible. Seeing uncensored footage & the hatred & foolishness in the comments has made my depression worse & it’s also stirred up anger. I watched the multiple videos of the ICE killing of Renee Good on the internet. I’ve seen the deplorable comments & I am guilty of getting “mixed up”, “sucked in”, “entangled in” the nonsense. I’m a very loving person, but I have not behaved lovingly. Today’s message our pastor spoke about “being wise walkers”. “Check our walk”. He said, “I might be wise, but it doesn’t mean I don’t need to check myself or that I am not foolish now & then”. Through him the Lord reminded us to learn to continue to walk wisely. Not get mixed up with fools, with evil. All these people I have responded to on social media I have responded based on my mood at the time. Some of my replies came from a place of trying to be logical with the unreasonable & foolish & other times not being very nice because some of these people are so foolish & hateful that it was so hard not to reply angrily & tell these people how wrong they are. Today’s message was God’s reminder to me that I have enough things on my heart that I need to surrender to him & I need NOT to engage in what is currently a dark place on social media. If I could go back & remove some of the comments I made I certainly would because my heart is refreshed now. Our biggest pieces of scripture today are from Ephesians 5:15-17 where scripture says, “Be very careful, then, how you live—not as unwise but as wise, making the most of every opportunity, because the days are evil. Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the Lord’s will is.” & Romans 16:19, “For your obedience is known to all, so that I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise as to what is good and innocent as to what is evil.”

There’s a lot of focus on reminders of the days being full of evil & foolishness & we need to discern better & walk wisely even when it’s hard. So I am setting boundaries with myself & with social media. I’m “soft-fasting” from social media & will remain available via messenger as my kids’ GG is undergoing major surgery tomorrow & I wish to follow in for updates. I may post occasionally on my wall, but I am going to start turning off notifications for things I may have commented on as to not be tempted to cross my boundaries & engage. Today, I was already depressed & doing my best to pretend everything was okay, but God had a way of reminding me, “No you’re lying to yourself & everyone else. We need to face this today”. The mind is a very powerful force & it can make or break you. Training your mind to elevate in a more healthy manner is something we all need to do.

I’ve already been struggling with the fact that we always tell our children that monsters are not real, but that’s another lie we are telling them. Monsters are real & they aren’t the kind that live under your bed. They are out there in the world. People we are supposed to trust to keep our communities safe from harm are hurting us & I’m deeply depressed about it. I’m angry about it, but I know it’s going to eat me alive if I engage & allow it to consume me on the daily. So with this I will begin my soft-fasting from social media. So I can go back to being a loving person who isn’t perfect, but loves others & wants to see everyone uplifted & happy. It’s just a dark world out there right now. So pursuing, trusting, worshipping the Most High is what I will do my best to keep focusing on.

Lanre was preparing to head to school when the principal knocked on his door, his face red with anger. 

"I heard what happened this morning," he said, his voice stern. "The news has spread everywhere. They said you commanded thunder to strike the masquerades." He shook his head.

"You've drawn the attention of everyone and the oba won't take it lightly. You better leave."

Lanre remained calm.

"I'm not going anywhere, sir. I came for a purpose, and I won't leave until it's fulfilled. I didn't send thunder to anyone. God just delivered me."

"But the news is everywhere... how you raised your hands up and brought down lightning and thunder."

Lanre folded his arms across his chest smiling. He wondered how the whole story was changed.

The principal's expression turned from anger to concern as he placed his hand on Lanre's shoulder.

"My son, I thought you told me you inquired about this kingdom before coming. The Oba is not someone you play with. He is fire and burns anyone that talks about Jesus. How could you be so reckless to have come here? Oba Adewale will kill you, Lanre. Please, run. Follow the path behind the house and run."

He reached into his trouser pocket and pulled out some money. 

"Take this, pack your things, and leave. Don't be foolish, Lanre."

"No, sir. I won't run away because of the Oba. I won't be silenced. People are in bondage, and I can't close my mouth when the Holy Spirit has touched my heart."

The principal sighed, his eyes filled with  frustration and admiration. 

"You're a stubborn one, Lanre, I can see that. But please, be careful. The Oba is not to be trifled with."

"I'm in God's hands, sir. He sent me to do His work, and I won't abandon it."

Sighing deeply, the principal took his leave. Lanre shook his head, picked up his phone and some textbooks from the table and left the house, ready to face whatever lay ahead.

"I don't want to send the guards on a fruitless mission wise one, look far and tell us where Lanre can be found."

The chief priest stood up and smiled before nodding his head. 

"I will require the mirror kabiyesi." He said.

"Keep trying! Call his name. Do whatever you can to make him show himself. He has to appear and tell us where he is."

"Nothing will happen wise one. We're powerful...the power that be are strongly here. Do it!"

"Very well kabiyesi."

The chief priest began the process of touching the mirror with kolanut and just as he started calling Lanre's name, the mirror shattered into pieces. 

For a moment everyone was dazed. It has never happened that the mirror that has been in the palace for decades would shatter. 

"Abomination!" One of the chiefs said. 

The Oba stared at the broken pieces of the mirror scattered on the floor and he was enraged. He rushed out of the chambers and ordered the guards to go look for Lanre. 

"Search for him.Bring him here dead alive." He screamed. " If you don't bring him here...I will kill everyone of you." 

The guards nodded in fear. This is the moment they hate. They rushed in confusion out of the palace.

"Kabiyesi, it seems...it seems he is not like the others. His power is not from the..." One of the chiefs started to say.

"I don't care! I want him here."

The palace fell silent, the only sound was the Oba's heavy breathing. His face twisted in a snarl.

"I don't care what kind of power he has. I will crush him. Bring him to me, and I will show him the true meaning of power!"

The chiefs and chief priest nodded, their faces grim. They knew the Oba's wrath was not to be played with. But they also knew that they had underestimated Lanre, and that this was not going to be an easy battle.

Lanre was in the classroom teaching when the palace guards came to pick him up. Knowing what was coming, he didn't resist them.

Students and teachers ran out of the classrooms, watching as he was being taken out of the school premises. 

In no time Lanre was brought before the angry Oba of Kajola kingdom.

For a long time the Oba stared at him without a word, probably weighing him from head to toe or trying to decipher what kind of man Lanre is.

"Tell me what power you possess that you could command thunder on the masquerades... didn't you know before stepping into this kingdom that Christianity isn't allowed here? Talk to me, he said icily. 

Lanre only stare at him which infuriated the Oba. 

"Do you know who I am? He asked standing up in his full height. "I am Oba Adewale the Great, the mighty and powerful, the ruler of this kingdom and the surrounding lands. I am the one who holds the reins of life and death, the one who commands the spirits and the gods. I am the one who has brought prosperity and peace to this land, and I will not let anyone threaten that. Least of all, a mere preacher like you!"

The king's chest heaved with pride, his eyes blazing with arrogance. 

"You should have known better than to come here, Lanre. You should have known that I am not to be trifled with. But you dared to defy me, to bring your foreign god into my kingdom."

Lanre remained silent, his eyes fixed on the Oba's face. He knew that he was in the presence of a man consumed by his own ego and power, a man who would stop at nothing to maintain his grip on the kingdom.

The Oba''s face turned red with rage, his voice rising to a shout. 

"Speak, Lanre! Tell me what power you possess! Tell me how you dare to challenge me! I have never seen any christian with power."

Lanre stood tall, his eyes locked on the Oba's, and he began to speak in a calm, steady voice. 

"I am a servant of the Most High God, the Creator of the universe. My power comes from Him, and I am here to spread His message of love and redemption. I do not fear you, Oba Adewale, for I know that my God is greater than any earthly king. You may have power over this kingdom, but my God has power over the universe."

The Oba sneered, his face contorted in rage. 

"Your God? Ha! I am the one who holds the power here. I am the one who can crush you like an insect."

Lanre smiled, his eyes shining with conviction. 

"You may think you have power, Oba Adewale, but it is fleeting. My God is the one who can lift up and bring down the proud. He is the one who humbled the proud Nebuchadnezzar, and He is the one who will humble you too, if you do not repent."

The king's face turned purple with rage, and he slammed his fist on the throne. 

"Nebuchadnezzar?"

"Yes! Ask King Nebuchadnezzar." Lanre replied, his voice steady and firm. "Ask him! He was too proud, and the Lord humbled him." 

Oba Adewale snorted.

 "Who is he? Is he as great as I am?" He sneered, his eyes narrowing as he watched Lanre intently. 

"I, Oba Adewale, am the most powerful king in all the land. My reign is unmatched, my wealth unparalleled. What could Nebuchadnezzar possibly have to offer?"

But Lanre remained unimpressed. 

"He was once mighty and arrogant, just like you. He had conquered nations and amassed wealth, but his pride went before a great fall. The Lord humbled him, reducing him to a mere beast, eating grass like an ox for seven years."

Oba Adewale's expression darkened, his face reddening with anger. But Lanre pressed on, his voice unshaken. 

"Yet, Nebuchadnezzar learned his lesson, acknowledging the sovereignty of the Most High God. He emerged from his ordeal a wiser, humbler king, his heart now filled with reverence for the Almighty. In the end, it was his humility that made him truly great." 

Lanre's eyes never left Oba Adewale's face, his gaze a challenge to the Oba''s pride.

"The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are bound."

There was a great murmuring among the people. They couldn't understand why the Oba was listening to Lanre, not taking action against him.

"Oba Adewale, your reign of terror ends now. God has heard the cries of the people of Kajola kingdom, the injustice, the shedding of innocent blood. He has seen the suffering, the oppression, and the pain you have inflicted upon your own people."

The king's face paled, his eyes darting nervously around the room. 

"What are you talking about?" he stammered.

"You have abused your power, Oba Adewale. You have used your throne for selfish gain, crushing those who dare to oppose you. But God is not mocked. He sees all, knows all. And He has had enough."

The king's eyes flashed with anger, but Lanre continued, unstoppable. 

"God is going to take the seat from you, Oba Adewale. He is going to give it to someone who will rule with justice and compassion.  He is going to bring judgment upon you, for all the evil you have done."

Oba Adewale's face contorted with rage, his voice reduced to a snarl. 

"You dare to threaten me? I am the king! I will not be overthrown by some upstart prophet!"

Lanre's gaze never wavered. 

"It is not I who threaten you, Oba Adewale. It is God Himself and His judgment is inevitable. Repent, repent.

Oba Adewale snorted, rolling his eyes. "What does that have to do with me?" he sneered
"Enough! You dare to insult me in my own palace? Guards, take him away. Lock him up.

The guards moved forward, their eyes full of malice, but Lanre did not flinch. He knew that he was in God's hands, and that was all that mattered. 

As they dragged Lanre away, he prayed for the Oba and his subjects, that they might come to know the true power of God.

Today, Monday, January 12th, the second training session in the series of workshops within the "Empowering Women Peacebuilders" project, organized by Nabdh Libya for Childhood and Youth, and generously sponsored by the Canadian Embassy, ​​commenced.
The training is being conducted by the young trainer, Dr. Abdulbasit Al-Hanqari, at the Al-Shajara Hotel in Al-Dhahra, Tripoli, with the participation of a group of women activists and peacebuilders.
Training topics include:
Effective communication skills.
Communication in stressful situations and managing interactions during crises.
Community leadership in times of conflict.

Practical and applied aspects of the acquired skills.

Not every day feels easy, and not every chapter makes sense while you’re living it 🤍🌧️ Some days test your patience, your strength, and even your faith in yourself. Yet, even in the middle of the chaos, there are soft moments that quietly remind you why you keep going — a gentle smile, a deep breath after a long day, a heart that still hopes 🌿💫
Life has a way of teaching us that perfection isn’t the goal. Growth is 🌱💖 It’s in the lessons learned through tears, the strength built in silence, and the courage it takes to keep showing up even when you’re tired 😔➡️💪 The beauty isn’t always loud or obvious; sometimes it’s hidden in the small victories, the healing you don’t announce, and the peace you slowly reclaim ✨🤍

Myšlienka, že ľuďom stačí kolektívne sa prebudiť a systém padne, je veľmi utopická... 

Vedomie sa nemení deklaráciami, heslami ani symbolickými gestami... 

Mení sa až vtedy, keď sa mení spôsob, akým jednotlivec vníma realitu a ako v nej koná…

Žiadny systém nemôže skončiť, pokiaľ ľudia, ktorí v ňom žijú, rozmýšľajú, reagujú 
a rozhodujú sa rovnakým spôsobom ako predtým... 

Neexistuje žiadny náhly evolučný skok, ktorý by nás vytrhol zvonka, ani kolektívne prebudenie, ktoré by nahradilo osobnú zodpovednosť... 

Skutočná zmena nevzniká čakaním ani vierou, že sa niečo samo zlomí... 

Vzniká cez vedomú prácu s pozornosťou, cez voľby, ktoré robíme, a cez každodenné konanie...

Message from the Chairperson
“Terrorism and narco-terrorism are among the most dangerous challenges confronting our world today. These forces thrive on fear, division, and exploitation—destroying innocent lives, destabilizing nations, and pushing our youth toward violence and addiction. Peace cannot prevail unless humanity stands united against these evils.”
Dr. Fayaz Ahmad Bhat further highlighted that narco-terrorism fuels extremist activities while simultaneously corroding societies through drug abuse, crime, and moral decay.
“The fight against terrorism must also be a decisive fight against drug trafficking and illegal networks that finance violence. Peace is not merely an idea—it is a shared global responsibility that requires cooperation beyond borders, religions, and ideologies,” he added.
Peace Foundation Global calls upon governments, international institutions, civil society organizations, religious leaders, educators, and youth movements to work collectively to:
Promote peace education, tolerance, and dialogue
Counter extremist ideologies through awareness and understanding
Strengthen action against drug trafficking and terror financing
Empower youth as ambassadors of peace and unity
The Foundation believes that lasting peace is built on justice, compassion, and collective action. Through unity and sustained global cooperation, terrorism and narco-terrorism can be defeated, paving the way for a safer and more peaceful future.
Peace Foundation Global remains committed to raising its voice for peace, humanity, and global solidarity.

Sometimes I wonder if I’m too sensitive.
If I’m reading too much into people’s words, their tone, their pauses.

But then I remember what life as a blind woman is actually like.
It’s living under constant observation.
Like being an insect under a microscope.
You stand out, so everything you do is noticed, interpreted, and quietly measured against a norm.

Most ableism isn’t cruelty.
It’s kindness tangled with ignorance and fear.

When people meet disability, three things happen inside them.
First, it reminds them that bodies are fragile and control is temporary. That creates discomfort.
Second, they feel a strong pull to be “a good person”, so they rush to soften, help, praise, or protect — often to regulate their own unease.
Third, to feel stable again, they quietly place you into a category: brave, tragic, special, dependent, inspiring — anything except simply another adult human.

That’s how microaggressions are born.

Not insults.
Not hatred.
Small, repeated distortions in how you are treated.

People talk to the person with me instead of to me.
They assume I have a carer.
They explain how something works to whoever I’m with, even when I’m the one buying it.
They lower expectations without realising they’re doing it.

None of it is meant to hurt.
All of it changes how you are seen.

And the impact isn’t in any single moment.
It’s in the accumulation.

Psychologists call this chronic minority stress — the ongoing load of being subtly reminded that you don’t belong to the default version of the world. It makes you alert, jumpy, and tired of being watched.

Disability isn’t just in the body.
It’s in the world that body has to move through.
When I travel in places with poor access, I feel far more disabled than in places built with inclusion in mind. My blindness doesn’t change. The environment does.

Ableism also isn’t limited to non-disabled people.
It happens between disabilities too, often driven by ignorance and quiet hierarchies — the assumption that one way of being is more normal, more capable, more valid than another.

Ramps, Braille, and access matter.
But the real starting point is internal.

It’s whether we can truly accept the full diversity of human minds and bodies as part of what being human is.

Legal Analysis of Allegations of Supposed Leadership Coups and Conflicts in South Sudan (2013–2026)

By Dr. Luke Kerding, PhD  
Tuesday, 13 January 2026

I. Introduction
Since gaining independence in 2011, South Sudan has experienced recurrent allegations of coups involving His Excellency President Salva Kiir Mayardit and senior leaders of the Sudan People's Liberation Movement (SPLM) and South Sudan People's Defense Forces (SSPDF). Between 2013 and 2025, such claims have contributed to political instability, fueled armed rebellions, and challenged the stability of the Government of National Unity. Judicial proceedings have consistently resulted in the dismissal of coup-related cases due to insufficient evidence, raising concerns about potential misuse of legal language and the undermining of due process rights. This analysis situates these allegations within the framework of the Transitional Constitution of South Sudan (2011, amended 2015), the Comprehensive Peace Agreement (CPA, 2005), the Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan (ARCSS, 2015), and the Revitalized ARCSS (R-ARCSS, 2018).

II. Constitutional Framework
- Sovereignty: Article 3 of the Transitional Constitution affirms that sovereignty resides with the people, exercised through legitimate institutions.  
- Rule of Law: Article 19 guarantees the right to a fair trial, emphasizing that allegations such as coups must be investigated and adjudicated by competent courts.  
- Checks on Executive Authority: The Constitution prohibits dismissals based solely on unproven allegations; due process must be observed.  
- Peace Agreements as Constitutional Supplements: The CPA, ARCSS, and R-ARCSS incorporate mechanisms for power-sharing and national reconciliation, mandating disputes be resolved through dialogue and established institutions rather than through force.

III. Historical Context
- 2012 SPLM Convention: Internal disagreements over leadership nominations caused divisions within the party.  
- 2013 Allegations of Coup: Several SPLM members were detained by the South Sudan National Security Service (SSNS) and military intelligence; courts subsequently dismissed charges for lack of evidence, exposing fragility in leadership cohesion.  
- Consequences: The dismissals contributed to rebellions and ongoing instability, undermining the government’s efforts at national unity and leading to cycles of violence.

IV. Notable Cases of Leadership Disputes
1. President Kiir and Vice President Machar (2013 & Peace Agreement):  
   - The dispute originated from succession disagreements following the death of Dr. John Garang.  
   - Machar claimed he was assured the presidency after five years of implementing the CPA.  
   - No constitutional evidence substantiated a coup; the conflict was primarily a dispute over leadership succession.

2. Gen Paul Malong versus Gen Akol Koor:  
   - Malong’s influential role in military operations led to suspicion among rivals.  
   - Allegations against Malong were politically motivated and were dismissed without formal trial.

3. Hon. Nhial Deng Nhial versus Gen Akol Koor:  
   - Framed as a coup plot, these rivalry claims resulted in Nhial Deng Nhial’s dismissal following accusations allegedly engineered by Akol Koor.  
   - No judicial determination of misconduct was made.

4. Gen Dr. Paul Ngang versus Gen Dr. Bol Mel:  
   - Mutual accusations of collaborating with rebel forces emerged.  
   - President Kiir dismissed Ngang, but the allegations lacked legal substantiation and reappointed him and fired Dr. Bol Mel based on the same accusations of coup allegations as a payback.

V. Legal Implications
- Due Process Violation: Dismissals founded on unproven allegations without judicial proceedings contravene constitutional guarantees of fair hearings.  
- Institutional Erosion: Repeatedly baseless allegations diminish public trust in the judiciary, security apparatus, and leadership.  
- Leadership Disputes as Constitutional Challenges: Framing political rivalries as coups undermines constitutional governance and fosters instability.  
- Violation of Peace Agreements: Neglecting dispute resolution provisions in the CPA, ARCSS, and R-ARCSS hampers efforts toward reconciliation and peace.

VI. Pathways for Constitutional Reconciliation
To promote national stability and restore trust, South Sudan should adhere to constitutional principles by:  
- Conducting Transparent Investigations: Allegations should be thoroughly and impartially examined.  
- Ensuring Judicial Adjudication: Courts must rule based on substantive evidence, not rumors or political pressure.  
- Fostering Reconciliation through Accountability: Addressing past grievances within a legal framework supports national healing.  
- Enforcing Peace Agreements: The provisions of ARCSS and R-ARCSS should be fully implemented to uphold power-sharing arrangements and conflict resolution mechanisms.

VII. Conclusion
The future stability of South Sudan depends on adherence to constitutional processes and justice. Resolving leadership disputes through lawful procedures, rather than unfounded allegations, is essential for sustainable peace and development. The nation’s sovereignty and unity can only be strengthened through lawful reconciliation, respect for due process, and a commitment to constitutional integrity.

“Do your duty as the older sister,” Dad said. “For once in your life, be useful to this family.”

I walked out of that room without saying another word.

I told Detective Morris the truth about everything.

The Statement
Raven had called me that night, hysterical, begging me to come to the police station for support. She’d been driving drunk, hit Mrs. Patterson in a crosswalk, and panicked. Our parents had arrived before me, already formulating their plan.

The look on my mother’s face when I gave my statement has fueled me through everything that came after.

My hands shook as I answered Detective Morris’s questions. He was patient, methodical, writing everything down in careful detail. Behind the glass of the interview room, I could see my parents’ faces contorted with rage. Dad was pacing like a caged animal. Mom had her arm around Raven, who had stopped crying but stared at me with pure hatred.

“Let me make sure I understand,” Detective Morris said, reviewing his notes. “Your sister called you at approximately 11:47 p.m., asking you to meet her at this station. She didn’t explain why over the phone.”

“She just kept saying she needed me, that something terrible had happened.” I wrapped my arms around myself, suddenly cold despite the stuffy room. “I thought maybe she’d been attacked or robbed. She sounded terrified.”

“And when you arrived, your parents were already here.”

“They pulled Raven into a private room. When I walked in, Dad immediately started explaining their plan.” The memory made my stomach turn. “They’d already decided everything. They just needed me to agree.”

Detective Morris set down his pen, studying me with an expression I couldn’t quite read. “Ms. Morgan, what you’re doing takes courage. Family cases are always the hardest.”

“They’re not my family anymore,” I heard myself say.

The words felt true as soon as they left my mouth.

The formal statement took another two hours. They asked me to repeat details multiple times, probing for inconsistencies. I understood what they were doing—verifying that I was telling the truth, that this wasn’t some vindictive fabrication born of sibling rivalry.

“Had there been any recent conflicts between you and your sister?” Sergeant Hayes asked.

“There’s always been conflict,” I admitted. “But not fighting exactly. More like… she existed in the sun and I existed in her shadow. That was just how our family worked.”

“Can you elaborate?”

I took a breath, trying to find words for dynamics that had always simply been. “Raven was the pretty one, the smart one, the one with potential. I was just… there. My parents made that clear in a thousand small ways. Better clothes for her, nicer birthday parties, more attention to her problems. I learned to be invisible.”

“That must have been painful.”

“It was normal,” I said. “At least I thought it was. Maybe every family has a scapegoat and a golden child. I just happened to be born into the wrong role.”

Sergeant Hayes exchanged a look with Detective Morris. “And tonight, when they asked you to take responsibility for your sister’s crime—was that the first time they’d asked you to sacrifice something for her?”

The question opened a door I hadn’t expected. Memories flooded through, sharp and painful despite their age.

“I was fifteen when I got my first job, bagging groceries at the supermarket downtown. I saved every dollar for almost a year because I wanted to go on the school trip to Washington D.C. It cost $800.”

“Did you go?”

“Raven’s car broke down two weeks before the trip. She was seventeen, had just gotten her license. Dad said the family couldn’t afford both the repair and my trip. He took my savings to fix her car.” The old hurt felt distant now, like something that had happened to someone else. “Raven went to prom in that car. I watched the school trip photos on Facebook.”

“Did your parents pay you back?”

“They said I was being selfish for asking. That family means sacrifice.”

I told them about the college fund that had existed for both of us until Raven decided she wanted to go to an expensive private university. My fund had been absorbed into hers. I’d been told community college was perfectly adequate for someone with my grades.

I told them about the time I’d won a regional art competition in high school, the only thing I’d ever been genuinely good at. My parents had missed the award ceremony because it conflicted with Raven’s volleyball game. When I came home with my ribbon and a $50 prize, Mom had barely looked up from cooking dinner.

“That’s wonderful, sweetheart,” she’d said absently. “Can you set the table? We’re eating early because Raven has practice.”

The ribbon had gone into a drawer. Raven’s volleyball trophies lined the mantle.

“Why didn’t you leave?” Sergeant Hayes asked. “Once you were eighteen, you could have walked away.”

“Where would I go?” The question sounded naive even to my own ears. “I had no money, no car, no support system. And there was a part of me that kept thinking if I just tried harder, did better, proved myself somehow… they’d finally see me.”

“And tonight?”

“Tonight I finally understood they’ll never see me, not the way I needed them to.” I met her eyes directly. “They looked at me and saw someone disposable. So I’m disposing of them instead.”

After I finished my statement, they asked me to wait while they interviewed my sister. I sat in a different room drinking terrible coffee from a vending machine and watching the minutes crawl by on the wall clock. It was past 3:00 in the morning.

Detective Morris found me around 4:30. He looked exhausted but satisfied.

“Your sister has confessed. The evidence was overwhelming—traffic camera footage, paint transfer on her vehicle, her own blood alcohol test from tonight. Her story kept changing, but eventually she admitted to everything.”

Relief flooded through me so powerfully I felt dizzy. “What happens now?”

“She’ll be formally charged. Given the severity—DUI, hit-and-run, fleeing the scene of an injury accident—she’s looking at significant prison time. Your testimony will be crucial at trial.”

“I’ll be there,” I promised. “Whatever you need.”

He studied me for a moment. “Your parents are still in the building. We can escort you out through a back entrance if you prefer to avoid them.”

I considered this, then shook my head. “I’ll walk out the front. I’m not hiding anymore.”

They were waiting in the lobby. Dad standing with his arms crossed while Mom sat in a plastic chair looking hollowed out. Raven was nowhere to be seen—likely already processed and held pending arraignment.

Dad’s eyes locked onto me with an intensity that would have terrified the younger me.

“You’ve destroyed this family.”

“You destroyed it yourself when you decided one daughter was worth more than the other,” I replied calmly. “I just refused to go along with it.”

Mom finally looked up. Her face had aged a decade in one night. “She’s your sister. How can you do this to her?”

“She’s a drunk driver who left someone to die in the street. How can you defend her?”

“We’re your parents,” Mom’s voice cracked. “After everything we’ve done for you—”

“Like what?” The question came out sharper than I’d intended. “Fed me? Gave me a room? That’s the bare minimum of parental responsibility, not some debt I owe you.”

Dad stepped closer, his voice dropping to a threatening whisper. “You walk out that door, you’re dead to us. No more family, no more support. You’ll have nothing.”

I smiled, and I could tell the expression unsettled him.

“I already have nothing from you. At least now I’m free.”

I walked past them into the early morning darkness. The sky was just beginning to lighten at the edges, that deep blue that comes before dawn.

My car sat alone in the parking lot, and I drove home through empty streets, feeling lighter than I had in years.

The Trial
The next few weeks were a blur of court appearances, paperwork, and increasingly hostile messages from my parents. They hired a lawyer who tried to discredit my testimony, painting me as a jealous, vindictive sister who’d fabricated evidence out of spite.

The traffic camera footage made that narrative impossible, but they tried anyway.

Mrs. Patterson’s family reached out through the prosecutor’s office, asking if they could meet me. I agreed, terrified of facing the woman whose life my sister had nearly ended.

Mrs. Patterson was in a wheelchair when I met her, her daughter Patricia pushing her into the victim services office where we’d arranged to talk. She was smaller than I’d imagined, with silver hair and hands that trembled slightly, but her eyes were sharp and kind.

“You’re Morgan,” she said, studying my face. “You look like you haven’t slept in weeks.”

“Neither do you,” I responded, then immediately regretted my bluntness.

But she laughed—a sound like rustling leaves. “I like honesty. Sit down, dear. Let’s talk.”

We spent two hours together. She told me about the accident from her perspective: crossing the street after her book club meeting, the sudden impact, waking up in the hospital unable to move her legs, the months of physical therapy, the financial devastation, the nightmares that still woke her at 3:00 in the morning.

“I’m so sorry,” I kept saying, as if I could somehow apologize on behalf of my sister’s actions.

“You didn’t do this,” Mrs. Patterson said firmly. “And according to the police, you’re the only one in your family who tried to make it right.”

She paused, then added quietly: “Your parents actually approached my daughter. Did you know that?”

I felt my blood run cold. “What?”

Patricia pulled out her phone, showing me a saved voicemail. My father’s voice filled the small room:

“Mrs. Patterson, this is Robert Sheffield. I’m calling to discuss a settlement. My daughter made a terrible mistake, but she’s young and has her whole future ahead of her. I’m prepared to offer substantial compensation if you’d be willing to speak to the prosecutor about reducing the charges.”

“He tried to buy her silence,” I whispered.

“I told him to go to hell,” Patricia said flatly. “Your sister nearly killed my mother and drove away. No amount of money changes that.”

Mrs. Patterson reached across and took my hand with her trembling one. “But you told the truth. In a family that clearly values image over integrity, you chose to do the right thing. That takes a kind of courage most people never need to find.”

Her words stayed with me through the trial, through watching my sister sentenced to four years, through my parents’ final vicious message telling me I was no longer their daughter.

The New Life
I packed up my studio apartment the day after the sentencing. My phone had been ringing constantly with calls from my parents, which I sent straight to voicemail.

The first one from Mom was almost conciliatory: “Morgan, we need to talk about this. You’ve made your point.”

By the fifth, her true feelings emerged: “You’ve destroyed your sister’s life out of spite. I always knew you were jealous of her, but I never thought you’d be this vindictive.”

Dad’s messages focused on practicality: “What Raven did was wrong, but your stubbornness has cost this family hundreds of thousands in legal fees. Your sister’s future is ruined. I hope you can live with that.”

I could. I slept better than I had in years.

I moved to Portland, three states away from my family in Ohio. I enrolled in community college using the money I’d saved working double shifts at the grocery store. The plan had always been there, buried under years of their low expectations and my own defeated acceptance.

Now nothing held me back.

My academic advisor, Dr. Patricia Walsh, became the first person who ever saw potential in me. She reviewed my placement tests with growing interest.

“Have you considered majoring in computer science? These analytical scores are exceptional.”

“I barely graduated high school,” I admitted. “My family always said I wasn’t college material.”

Dr. Walsh removed her glasses, studying me with sharp brown eyes. “Your family was wrong. I’ve been doing this for thirty years. You have aptitude.”

Those words changed everything.

I threw myself into my coursework with obsessive focus. Programming languages made sense to me in a way nothing else ever had. There were rules, logic, problems with clear solutions. Work produced results. Effort mattered.

The first semester was brutal. I’d been out of school for ten years, and my study skills were nearly non-existent. Everything my classmates seemed to know instinctively—how to take notes, how to prepare for exams, how to manage multiple deadlines—I had to learn through trial and error.

I failed my first programming midterm. Sat in my car afterward and cried for twenty minutes, convinced my parents had been right about me all along.

Then I dried my eyes, went to Dr. Walsh’s office hours, and asked for help.

“You’re behind,” she said, not sugarcoating it. “Your fundamentals are weak. But you’re also one of the most determined students I’ve encountered. Determination can overcome a lot.”

She connected me with a tutor, a graduate student named Kevin who had infinite patience for my stupid questions. We met three times a week in the library, working through problems until the concepts clicked.

Slowly, painfully, I started to understand.

The second midterm, I got a B. The final exam, I got an A.

Kevin high-fived me when grades posted. “You know what the difference was? You stopped being afraid of being wrong. You just kept trying until you got it right.”

His observation hit deeper than he knew. I’d spent my entire life afraid of being wrong because being wrong meant proving my parents right about me.

But here, in this new life I was building, being wrong just meant I hadn’t learned something yet. There was no shame in it, just opportunity.

Within a year, I transferred to Portland State University with a full scholarship. I worked part-time at a tech startup, debugging code and learning everything I could absorb.

The owner, Marcus Carter, saw the same thing Dr. Walsh had seen.

“You’re wasted doing grunt work,” he told me after I’d solved a problem that had stumped their senior developers for weeks. “I’m moving you to the development team.”

My new supervisor, Tyler, made his skepticism clear from day one. “Marcus likes to give people chances. But this is professional-level work. If you can’t keep up, speak up before you drag down the whole team.”

I kept my mouth shut and my head down, letting my work speak for itself.

When Tyler assigned me what he clearly thought was a grunt task—documenting legacy code that nobody wanted to touch—I found three critical security vulnerabilities hidden in the ancient functions.

Marcus called an emergency meeting when I submitted my report. The vulnerabilities could have cost the company everything if exploited. I’d not only found them but proposed elegant solutions that would patch the holes without breaking existing functionality.

Tyler’s face when Marcus praised my work in front of the whole company was almost worth the sleepless nights I’d spent combing through that code.

“Good catch,” Tyler muttered afterward, unable to quite meet my eyes.

“Just doing my job,” I replied evenly.

But something had shifted. The other developers started coming to me with questions, asking my opinion on design decisions, including me in casual conversations around the coffee machine.

I was becoming part of the team, earning respect one problem solved at a time.

My neighbor, Ruth, became an unexpected friend. She was a retired teacher who reminded me of what a mother could be—interested, supportive, critical when necessary, but always kind.

She taught me to cook real food, not just ramen and frozen dinners.

“You’re too thin,” she declared, showing up at my door one Saturday with bags of groceries. “Come on, I’m teaching you to make lasagna.”

Her kitchen was warm and cluttered with the accumulation of a long life. Photos of children and grandchildren covered the refrigerator. Plants thrived on every windowsill.

“Cooking is chemistry,” she said. “You understand code. You can understand this.”

She was right. Following a recipe was like following an algorithm: precise measurements, specific steps, predictable outcomes.

The lasagna turned out perfectly. Ruth sent me home with half of it and a promise that next week we’d tackle bread from scratch.

“You’re good for my ego, Morgan,” she said, patting my hand. “I’m glad you moved in next door.”

The comment touched something raw in me. Someone was glad I existed in their space. Such a simple thing, but I’d never had it before.

The Messages
My parents called a few times during the first year. I changed my number, but they somehow kept tracking down my new contact information.

Then, about eighteen months after I’d moved to Portland, Mom managed to catch me during a moment of weakness. I’d just finished a brutal exam and wasn’t paying attention when I answered an unknown number.

Her voice was tight with anger.

“Raven writes to us about how terrible prison is. She cries every day. She’s having panic attacks. The other inmates are cruel to her. And you’re out there living your life like nothing happened.”

“She hit someone with her car and left them to die in the street,” I said calmly. “Mrs. Patterson spent three months in the hospital. She still can’t walk without assistance. But please, tell me more about how hard prison is for Raven.”

“You could have prevented all of this,” Mom’s voice cracked. “One small sacrifice. That’s all we asked.”

“You asked me to go to prison for a crime I didn’t commit. You told me I was worthless compared to her. You wanted me to throw away my life because you decided hers was worth more.” I kept my voice steady, clinical. “So I made a choice too. I chose myself.”

“You’re not the daughter I raised.”

“Good. Your daughter was miserable.”

I hung up and blocked the number.

That was two years ago, and I haven’t spoken to them since.

The Vindication
Last month, I got a message on LinkedIn from someone named James Fitzgerald. The name was familiar—then I remembered. James, Raven’s fiancé, the one she’d supposedly been planning a future with.

His message was brief:

I hope this reaches you. I know we’ve never met. I wanted you to know that I ended my engagement to your sister about six months after her conviction. Your parents told her you’d been spreading lies about what happened that night, that you’d sabotaged her out of jealousy. I want you to know I never believed them. I contacted Mrs. Patterson’s family and heard the truth. I’m sorry for what you went through. You did the right thing.

I stared at that message for a long time. The vindication felt distant, like something happening to someone else. I’d stopped needing their validation years ago.

But I responded anyway: Thank you for reaching out. I hope you’re well.

His reply came an hour later: I married someone else last year. She’s a public defender. Works with people the system failed. Meeting her helped me understand why you made the choice you did. Some things matter more than family loyalty.

I smiled at that. Some stranger’s husband understood me better than my own parents ever had.

The years in Portland transformed me in ways I’m still discovering. That initial struggle through community college led to my transfer to Portland State, where I graduated summa cum laude with a degree in computer science.

The girl who’d barely graduated high school finished university with a 3.9 GPA and job offers from three different companies.

I chose to stay with Marcus. Loyalty mattered to me, and he’d given me a chance when I was nobody.

Two years after graduation, I was promoted to lead developer. My salary was now six figures. I purchased a small house in a quiet neighborhood with a garden I was learning to cultivate.

Last week, Raven was released on parole. She’d served three and a half years of her four-year sentence with credit for good behavior.

I knew because she’d found my email address somehow and sent me a message.

The subject line read: “We need to talk.”

The email itself was long and rambling, swinging between rage and self-pity. She’d lost her graduate school acceptance. James had abandoned her. She had a criminal record that made employment nearly impossible. Our parents had depleted their retirement savings on legal fees and appeals.

And somehow, all of this was my fault.

You destroyed my life because you were jealous. You always hated that I was prettier, smarter, more successful. You saw one chance to tear me down and you took it. I made a mistake. People make mistakes. But you had a choice and you chose to be cruel.

I read it three times, waiting for some feeling to surface. Anger, guilt, satisfaction—anything.

But there was just a distant recognition of who she’d always been and who I’d finally stopped being.

I crafted my response carefully:

Raven, you were driving drunk. You hit a 62-year-old woman in a crosswalk and drove away while she lay bleeding in the street. Mrs. Patterson survived, but she’ll never fully recover. She had to relearn how to walk. She still has chronic pain. Her medical bills bankrupted her family’s savings.

Our parents asked me to go to prison for your crime. They told me I was worthless, ugly, and that my life mattered less than yours. They asked me to sacrifice my freedom so you could keep your opportunities.

I chose not to. That’s the extent of my crime against you.

You’re angry because you faced consequences for your actions. You believe you deserve special treatment because our parents spent your whole life telling you that you were exceptional.

I hope you rebuild your life. I genuinely do. But you’ll have to do it the same way I did mine—through work, accountability, and the understanding that nobody owes you anything just because you want it.

I won’t be responding to future emails. I wish you well, but I’m not part of your life anymore.

I sent it and immediately blocked her email address. Then I blocked my parents’ emails too, severing the last threads that connected us.

The relief was overwhelming.

The Letter
Two days ago, I received a letter via certified mail. No return address, but the postmark was from Ohio.

Inside was a handwritten note from my father:

Morgan, your mother is very ill. The doctors say she doesn’t have much time left. She’s asking for you. Whatever grievances you have with this family, she’s still your mother. She raised you, fed you, gave you a home. You owe her at least a visit. Set aside your pride and do the right thing. Dad.

I held the letter for a long time, sitting on my porch swing as the evening light faded from my garden. Ruth was watering her flowers next door, humming something tuneless and cheerful.

The woman who was dying was not my mother in any way that mattered. She’d stopped being that the moment she looked at me with cold calculation and decided I was expendable.

The biological connection between us was just an accident of genetics, no more meaningful than sharing a blood type with a stranger.

I thought about the mother I’d wanted—the one who would have protected both her daughters, who would have insisted Raven face her consequences while still offering love and support, the one who would have seen worth in both of us.

That mother had never existed. I’d finally accepted that truth.

I went inside and drafted a brief response:

Dad, I hope Mom gets the care she needs. I won’t be visiting. Morgan.

I mailed it the next morning.

Three weeks later, another certified letter arrived. I knew what it would say before I opened it.

The funeral notice was brief and formal. My mother had passed away. Services would be held at the church where I’d been baptized as an infant, a building I hadn’t entered in over a decade.

I was listed among the survivors, as if I’d been present in her life.

I threw the notice in the recycling bin and went to work.

The Promotion
Yesterday, Marcus called me into his office. I’d been working on a major security contract that could take the company to the next level. My work had been meticulous, anticipating problems before they developed, solving them with elegant efficiency.

“The client was impressed,” Marcus said, grinning. “They want you to lead the implementation team. It’s a promotion—significant raise, your own department.”

We discussed the details for an hour. The position would make me one of the youngest department heads in the company. The salary was absurd, the kind of number I’d never imagined applying to my life.

I accepted on the spot.

Walking to my car afterward, I called Dr. Walsh. She’d become a friend over the years, someone I checked in with quarterly to share progress and seek advice.

“I got the promotion,” I told her.

Her delighted laughter filled the phone. “I knew you would. You’ve earned this a thousand times over.”

“I keep thinking about that first meeting in your office when you told me I had aptitude.”

“You did. You do.” She paused. “I’ve watched a lot of students pass through my programs. Very few of them have your combination of intelligence and drive. But I’ve noticed something—the ones who succeed wildest are usually the ones who had something to prove. You had more to prove than most.”

“I don’t anymore,” I realized, saying it out loud. “I’m not trying to prove them wrong anymore. I’m just living.”

“That’s when you’ve really won,” Dr. Walsh said gently.

I drove home through Portland’s evening traffic, watching the city lights flicker on against the darkening sky. My phone buzzed with texts from coworkers offering congratulations.

I thought about Raven in Ohio, recently released and probably struggling. I thought about Dad, alone with the daughter he’d tried to save and the one he’d thrown away. Mom was gone now, buried three weeks ago without my presence.

And I felt nothing but a distant hope that they’d eventually find peace with their choices the same way I’d found peace with mine.

My house glowed warmly as I pulled into the driveway. Ruth waved from her porch, calling out something about bringing over zucchini bread tomorrow.

Inside, my home office held the evidence of my real life: framed degrees on the wall, awards from work, photographs of colleagues who’d become friends.

No family photos. I’d stopped displaying those years ago.

I made dinner and worked in my garden until the light failed completely. The tomatoes were finally thriving, heavy with fruit that would ripen in the coming weeks.

My phone buzzed one final time. An email from an unknown address. I almost deleted it without reading, but something made me open it.

Dear Miss Morgan, my name is Patricia Patterson. My mother was the victim of the hit-and-run involving your sister. I wanted to reach out because my mother asked me to contact you.

She wanted you to know that she forgives your sister for what happened. But more than that, she wanted me to tell you that your testimony, your honesty about what happened that night, gave her faith in people again.

She’d been struggling with anger and bitterness, feeling like justice didn’t exist. Learning that someone had chosen truth over family loyalty, even at great personal cost, helped her heal in ways medicine couldn’t.

My mother is 71 now. She still has pain and uses a cane, but she’s made peace with it. She wanted you to know that your choice mattered to her, that it helped.

Thank you for your integrity. Sincerely, Patricia Patterson.

I read it twice, then a third time. Tears blurred the words, surprising me with their intensity. I hadn’t cried about any of this in years.

But these weren’t tears of sadness or anger. They were something cleaner, something that felt almost like closure.

I wrote back:

Dear Patricia, please tell your mother that her message means more than she could know. I hope she continues to heal. I hope she has many good years ahead. Thank you for reaching out. With gratitude, Morgan.

I sent it and closed my laptop.

The house was quiet around me, filled with the life I’d built from nothing. No family legacy, no parental support, no sister’s shadow to live in.

Just my own work, my own choices, my own stubborn refusal to accept their version of who I was supposed to be.

I walked through my home, turning off lights, locking doors, preparing for sleep. In my bedroom, I caught my reflection in the mirror.

The face looking back wasn’t ugly. It had never been ugly.

It was just mine—lived in and earned, marked by struggles my family would never understand because they’d never bothered to see them.

Tomorrow, I’d go to work and start building my new department. I’d hire people who showed potential the way Marcus and Dr. Walsh had seen it in me. I’d create something worthwhile from nothing but effort and vision.

My phone was silent now. No more letters from Ohio. No more guilt trips or attempts at manipulation.

My mother was dead, buried without my tears. My father had Raven back, the daughter he’d chosen. They could rebuild whatever relationship they wanted without me in the way.

Ruth’s zucchini bread would arrive at some point. Work would be challenging and rewarding. My garden would need tending. My life would continue—built on foundations I’d laid myself, sustained by effort I’d chosen to make.

They’d wanted me to sacrifice everything for Raven because they decided I was worth less.

Instead, I’d walked away and discovered what I was actually worth when measured by my own standards instead of theirs.

The math worked out better than they’d ever imagined.

I climbed into bed and slept deeply, dreamlessly—the sleep of someone who had finally stopped carrying weight that was never hers to bear.

Tomorrow would bring new challenges, new victories, new evidence that the person they’d thrown away was exactly the person who deserved to be kept.

But they’d never know that.
