My mother locked my children in the freezing basement of my own villa in Pozuelo just to give their room to my nephew. What she didn’t know was that I had installed cameras—and the eviction had already begun.
My mother locked my children in the freezing basement of my own villa in Pozuelo—just to give their bedroom to my nephew.
What she didn’t know was that every hallway, every door, every stair in that house was covered by cameras.

And that the eviction had already begun.

My name is Inés. I’m thirty-nine years old, and until that moment, I truly believed I had built a flawless life. I had climbed to a senior position at a financial firm on Paseo de la Castellana. I earned more in a year than my parents had ever imagined possible. I had two children—my entire world—and a modern villa in Pozuelo de Alarcón, one of the safest, most exclusive areas in Madrid.

I had even bought that house with a specific purpose: to give my parents dignity after the bank seized the small apartment they had lived in their entire lives in Carabanchel.

I thought I was doing everything right.

I thought I was honoring my family while protecting my own.

While I was managing multimillion-euro portfolios and closing deals that moved markets, my parents were quietly moving my children’s clothes, toys, and schoolbooks out of their rooms.

Downstairs.

Into the basement.

Cold. Damp. Unfinished.

Why?

Because my brother’s son—the golden grandson—needed a “proper bedroom.”

When I found my children sitting on the concrete floor, shaking, their lips tinged purple from the cold, my mother didn’t apologize. She didn’t even look uncomfortable.

She straightened her back, crossed her arms, and said with the authority only a traditional Spanish matriarch can summon:

“This is my house, Inés. You should be grateful.”

I smiled.

Not a warm smile. Not forgiveness.

The kind of smile you give when you’ve just stopped explaining—and started planning.

She had no idea that the villa was legally registered only in my name.
She had no idea that she had no tenant rights.
And she had no idea that I had already documented everything.

Before I go on, let me ask you something honestly:

Have you ever had to choose between unquestioning loyalty to your parents… and the physical safety of your children?

Because that choice changes you.
The sound of the security lock echoed through the travertine marble foyer at exactly 9:00 p.m. I had just finished a twelve-hour day buried in market forecasts and risk models, my mind still buzzing with numbers. All I wanted was to kiss my children goodnight and pour myself a glass of Ribera del Duero.

Instead, I walked into betrayal.

And that night marked the beginning of an eviction that no one in my family saw coming.

Not even my mother.

The house was silent. Too silent.

Normally, when I walked in, I was greeted by the sound of Sofia and Marcos arguing over the game console or laughing at a video on the tablet. Tonight, nothing. Just the constant whirring of the American-style refrigerator in the kitchen.

A knot tightened in my stomach, that maternal intuition that rarely fails.

I called out loud, my voice bouncing off the stucco walls: “Sofia! Marcos! Mom is home!”

Only silence answered.

Then I heard it. A faint, muffled sound.

A sob.

It wasn’t coming from their bedrooms upstairs. It was coming from under my feet.

From the basement.

My blood ran cold. I dropped my Loewe leather briefcase onto the marble floor, not caring if it got scratched, and ran.

I yanked open the heavy oak basement door and practically tumbled down the stairs. The air down there was different; it didn’t have the central heating of the rest of the house. It smelled damp, musty, like cold concrete.

The sight that greeted me knocked the air out of my lungs like a physical punch.

My children—Sofia, my bright 10-year-old, and Marcos, my sweet 8-year-old—were huddled together on a bare mattress. It was one of the old guest mattresses, thrown directly onto the freezing tile floor.

Around them, like the wreckage of a shipwreck, lay their belongings. Their open suitcases. Their toy chests. Marcos’s Lego box, Sofia’s painting easel. All piled against the damp concrete wall.

The basement wasn’t habitable. It was where we kept the Christmas decorations, empty suitcases, and the old water heater. It was cold, a damp cold that chilled you to the bone.

Sofia looked up. Her face was streaked with tears and her nose was red.

“Mom,” she whispered, as if she were afraid to speak. “Grandma Lourdes… told us we had to move down here.”

I ran towards them, wrapping them in my arms. They were freezing. They were trembling.

—What do you mean, darling? What happened?

My little Marcos buried his face in my wool coat. His voice was small and broken.

—He said our room is now for cousin Leo. He packed our things while we were at school. He said Leo is the real grandson, the boy, and that he deserves the best room. He said… he said we were making too much noise.

I looked over their heads at the single dim lightbulb illuminating the gloomy room. I saw the mist of their breath in the cold air.

The real grandson.

The words echoed in the cold, awakening echoes of my own childhood.

A sharp, icy rage, unlike anything I’d ever felt, shot down my spine. It wasn’t just anger. It was a terrifying, sudden clarity. It was over.

I kissed them both on the head.

—Stay here for a minute. Don’t move. I’m going to fix this.

I clenched my jaw so hard that my teeth hurt.

I turned around and didn’t walk. I stormed up the stairs, my heels striking the wood like a judge’s gavel. I was ready for war.

I walked past the main floor and took the upper stairs two at a time, heading straight for my children’s wing.

Her room—or what used to be her room—was at the end of the hall. It was the second-best suite in the house, right after the master suite. It had its own private bathroom and a large window overlooking the rose garden, and in the distance, the lights of Madrid could be seen.

I saw it even before I got to the door.

The door was wide open, and the room was unrecognizable.
All of Sofia’s drawings had been torn from the walls. Marcos’s star-patterned curtains were gone. Their twin beds were no longer there.

In its place was a brand-new, enormous double bed with a duvet that looked incredibly expensive. Football pennants were crudely tacked to the freshly painted walls. A huge 80-inch television—one we didn’t have this morning—was mounted on the wall opposite the bed. A new video game console was already plugged in, its cables snaking across the floor.

And there, in the middle of the new bed, jumping around with his shoes on, was my 9-year-old nephew, Leo.

He jumped up and down, laughing wildly, oblivious to the suffering of his cousins ​​downstairs.

My mother, Lourdes, was there. At 63, she maintained that austere elegance of a lady from the Salamanca district, her face permanently hardened by years of perceiving offenses where none existed. She hummed, her back to me, as she meticulously unfolded a new set of linen sheets.

-Mother.

He didn’t turn around.

“Ah, you’re home now,” she said, her voice light and carefree. “I’m just getting things organized. Your sister Alicia and Carlos are on their way from the airport. They’re staying with us for a while, and little Leo needs a proper, quiet space.”

My voice was trembling. I could barely get the words out.

—A quiet space. And you decided that the best way to do that was to throw my eight- and ten-year-old children into the basement?

I made a wild gesture toward the hallway.

—You didn’t even call me. You didn’t think to ask me.

That made him stop.

He turned around, his face contorting in a mask of indignation, as if I had just insulted the Pope.

—What kind of tone is that, Inés? I’m your mother. I don’t need permission to rearrange things in my own house.

He spat out the words.

— My own house . Your children can stay anywhere. They’re young, they’re resilient. They’ll be fine. Stop being so selfish. Honestly, you’re 39 years old. When are you going to learn to behave and respect your elders?

My house.

The words hit me like a physical slap, taking my breath away.

The trembling in my voice, the hot tears of anger that threatened to spill… all vanished, replaced by a sudden, chilling ice.

I remembered being 18. I remembered running home with the full scholarship letter for college, thinking that this was it. Thinking that I had finally made her proud.

My mother was on the porch talking to a neighbor. I handed her the letter. She barely glanced at it. She just waved her hand dismissively and said, “She got lucky. You know how they are these days, giving things away.” Then she looked at me and said, “Now you have to learn how to earn real money to take care of this family, not just chase silly dreams with your books.”

And now, 21 years later, standing in the six-bedroom, 500-square-meter villa I had paid for in cash, nothing had changed. To her, I was still the utilitarian daughter, the one who pays the bills but has no voice.

The shock in my system evaporated. The trembling in my hands stopped. I felt my face settle into a calm, cool mask. My breathing became deep and even.

She mistook my silence for submission.
She snorted, satisfied.

—Good. Now that that’s settled, go tell your children to lower their voices. Leo needs to rest before his parents arrive.

I looked at her. I really looked at her.

I watched the spoiled child jumping on the bed with his dirty shoes. I thought of my own children freezing in the damp basement.

I took a long, slow breath, and smiled.

In the corner by the door, my father, José, 64 years old, who had spent his entire life indulging my mother’s whims, did what he always did. He found a spot on the wall to stare at, avoiding my gaze, wishing he could be invisible. His silence was his agreement.

I looked away from my father’s cowardice and focused again on my mother. She was still expecting the usual fight, the crying, the pleading.

I let a slow, cold smile spread across my face. It didn’t reach my eyes.

“You’re right, Mom,” I said. My voice was suddenly calm, clear, and devoid of all emotion. “You’re absolutely right. Leo deserves the best room.”

Lourdes’ eyebrows shot up in genuine surprise. She hadn’t anticipated this. Her victory had been too easy. After a second, her surprise melted into pure, gleeful triumph. “I thought I’d broken,” she thought.

“Well,” he said, puffing himself up like a peacock. “It’s about time you saw things clearly.”

I didn’t say another word.

I turned my back on her, on my father’s silence, and on the desecrated room.

I went out into the hallway and down the stairs straight back to the cold, dark basement.

My children were exactly where I had left them. Sofia was trying to be brave for her little brother, but fresh tears were streaming down her face. Marcos was simply shivering, his small hands tucked under his armpits for warmth.

I heard my mother’s footsteps following me. She was basking in her victory. She appeared at the top of the stairs, a triumphant silhouette against the light in the hallway.

“See, children?” Lourdes said, her voice dripping with condescension. “Your mother finally understands. I told you, Grandma knows what’s best for this family.”

I completely ignored her.

I walked over and knelt on the concrete floor right in front of my children. I took out my handkerchief and gently wiped Sofia’s face, then Marcos’s.

—Sofia. Marcos— I said, my voice soft and full of a warmth I hadn’t felt a moment ago. —Don’t cry anymore, my loves.

Sofia sniffed.

—But… but Grandma said…

“I know what Grandma said,” I interrupted gently.

I looked them both in the eyes, and smiled, a real smile just for them.

—Now, I need you to listen to me very carefully. Pack your bags.

I pointed to Sofia’s Lego cube and art supplies.

—And that bucket of toys too. We’re going somewhere much, much better.

The change was instantaneous. Lourdes’ triumphant pose on the stairs vanished.

“What?” she shrieked, her voice echoing in the concrete space. “What did you just say?”

I stood up slowly, turning to face her. The smile I gave her wasn’t the one I gave my children. This one was pure ice.

“What are you talking about, Inés?” she stammered, turning red. “You’re leaving? You’re going to pack your bags and leave over this, over a silly room? Your sister is about to walk through that door. Are you going to embarrass me in front of Alicia?”

I took a step toward her. Instinctively, she took a step back.

“Oh, I’m not going anywhere, Mom,” I said, my voice barely a whisper, but it cut through the cold air. “Not tonight, at least.”

I let the silence hang for a second, watching confusion and panic fight for space in her eyes.

“But I promise you,” I continued, “you’re about to learn exactly what it feels like to have nowhere to go. Very, very soon.”

Lourdes’ mouth opened and closed, but no sound came out. She was completely baffled. She had no script for this. She didn’t know this side of herself.

And right at that moment, as if summoned by the tension, a sound echoed throughout the house from above.

The doorbell.

My sister, the golden girl, had arrived. The real drama had just begun.

Before I could even process the doorbell, I heard the front door slam open. There was no knock, no polite entrance, just the sound of the heavy oak door slamming against the foyer wall.

“We’re here!” a voice squealed.

Alicia. My 37-year-old sister. The eternally spoiled girl.

I took a deep breath, got ready, and led my children upstairs. We emerged into the foyer just in time for the main event.

Alicia burst into the living room like a hurricane. Designer sunglasses (even though it was nighttime), dramatic sighs, and leaving a trail of chaos in her wake. Right behind her was her husband, Carlos. Carlos, 40 years old, a man with the undeserved confidence of someone who has never worked a real day in his life but always has a “business project.” He was dragging four enormous and ridiculously expensive suitcases.

“Finally,” Alicia announced to the room, taking off her glasses as if she were a celebrity honoring us with her presence. “The flight was brutal.”

Carlos, meanwhile, didn’t bother to lift the suitcases. He dragged them. He dragged them across the polished oak parquet floor of the living room, leaving four long, pale scratches in his wake. My father, José, who spent every Saturday waxing that floor, shuddered. I saw his hands clench at his sides, but as always, he said nothing.

“God, I’m exhausted,” Alicia declared, collapsing onto the velvet sofa. “Inés, why are you just standing there? Go get the rest of the bags from the car. And someone bring me a glass of wine. A Rioja, please.”

She hadn’t even really looked at me. She was busy inspecting her acrylic nails.

Carlos, oblivious to the damage he had just caused to the floor, patted my father on the shoulder with a broad and presumptuous smile.

“José, what a place. Seriously, what a mansion. So spacious,” he boomed. “I told Alicia there was no need to worry. I told her your parents would definitely take care of us.”

My mother Lourdes was radiant, all her previous panic forgotten. She ran towards Alicia, showering her with compliments.

—Oh, my sweet girl. You must be so tired. Of course… Inés, go get some wine for your sister. Don’t just stand there.

“And Mom,” Alicia shouted in a squeaky voice, “is Leo’s room ready? You bought the new mattress, right? And the air purifier. You know he can’t sleep without his HEPA filter.”

My mother nodded enthusiastically.

—Of course, darling. Everything is ready. The best room in the house, just as I promised.

“The best room,” I said.

My voice was calm, but it cut through the room like a ham knife.

Everyone froze.
Alicia’s head turned slowly toward me. Her eyes traveled down, noticing for the first time that Sofia and Marcos were standing beside me, clutching their coats, their faces pale and streaked with tears. She saw us standing at the top of the basement stairs.

A slow, malicious smile spread across his face. It was the same smile he’d worn his whole life, right before saying something cruel.

“Well,” she said, her voice dripping with false sweetness. “There you are. You and the children stay in the basement. That’s perfect.”

He laughed, a short, dry sound.

“It’s actually great. The basement’s basically soundproof, right, Mom? At least Leo won’t be bothered by all your shouting and running around when he’s trying to study. You know how gifted he is. He needs his peace and quiet.”

I looked at my sister, the golden girl who had dropped out of two different university degrees paid for by my parents. I looked at her husband, a man whose entire career was a series of failed startups funded by my parents’ retirement account.

And I thought of my “gifted” nephew.

I let out a short, dry laugh.

—Study? —I asked.

Alicia’s smile faltered.

—What’s so funny?

“I don’t know, Alicia,” I said, walking slowly toward the living room, my children staying close behind me. “It just strikes me as odd that Leo suddenly needs so much silence to study, because the last I heard, he wasn’t studying much. The last I heard, he was expelled from that private school for theft. Something about stealing other children’s medicine and selling it.”

Alicia’s face went white. My mother gasped.

—Inés, how dare you?

I ignored my mother and turned my cold gaze towards Carlos, who was still standing near the striped floor.

—So, Alicia, Carlos, how long do you plan to mooch off this time? Or is “staying for a while” the new term for indefinitely? Tell me, Carlos, what happened? Did that revolutionary cryptocurrency startup of yours finally go bust again? Or was it the NFT market this time? I’ve lost count.

The air in the room was so thick I could barely breathe. The battle lines were drawn, and I had just fired the first shot.

Carlos and Alicia exchanged a glance: a quick, panicked blink. Carlos’s smug smile dissolved into a tense, angry line. He was the first to recover, letting out a forced laugh.

“Oh, sister-in-law,” she said, trying to regain her composure. “That’s a bit sensitive, don’t you think?” She picked an imaginary piece of lint from her designer polo shirt. “It’s not bankrupt. It’s called a transition phase. The market is just correcting itself. We just need a place to regroup for a few months, that’s all.”

Alicia, seeing her husband falter, immediately switched to her most effective tactic: playing the victim. She ran towards my mother, burying her face in Lourdes’s shoulder.

“Mom,” she moaned, her voice thick with fake tears. “Are you going to let her talk to me like that? Look at her. She’s being so mean. We’re family, Inés. We’re struggling, and you’re so rich, working at your big financial firm. Why are you counting pennies with your own sister? You have this huge house all to yourself and your children. The least you can do is share.”

My mother reacted as if I had physically hit Alicia.
“Inés!” she shouted, trembling with rage. “Shut your mouth right now. Your sister is in trouble. You’re going to help her. This house is more than big enough for everyone. God knows you’ve been living here rent-free long enough. The least you can do is share some of this space with your family, you ungrateful, selfish girl.”

 

The words landed one by one like stones in a deep well. The injustice of it—the sheer, astonishing hypocrisy—left me breathless.

—We lost it, Inés. The bank. They took the apartment. We’ve been evicted. We’re on the street.

They had given everything. Their entire nest. Five hundred thousand euros earned over forty years of work, vanished. Handed over to a con man with a friendly smile, Carlos, all because he was married to his golden girl.

I, the ungrateful daughter, drove in the rain, picked them up from the sidewalk with their few belongings, and took them to my apartment. A week later, I liquidated my bonds, my savings, everything. And I bought this house.

This villa in Pozuelo. Cash only. My name, and only my name, on the deed.

I bought it so my parents wouldn’t be homeless. I bought it so my family, the ones who had only taken from me, would have a safe place. And now they were calling me ungrateful.

The last fragment of filial obligation within me withered and died.

I looked at Carlos, who was now trying to intimidate me with his height.

“Listen, Inés,” he growled. “Stop acting like a know-it-all. I know how you financiers are. Creative accounting. We’re family. I know you’ve been hiding money. How would you like a call from the tax authorities? A full audit. I bet they’d love to see how you organized your ‘investments.’ You wouldn’t want to lose this big house and your children, would you?”

Alice lit up with malicious glee.

—Yes, Inés. You should be nice to us, or you’ll go to jail and then maybe we’ll be the ones raising your children in this house.

I stared at them.

“Are you threatening me, Carlos?” I asked quietly. “Are you threatening me with a financial crimes investigation? It’s a bold move, especially in a house that, from this moment on, is recording audio on at least four different high-definition security cameras.”

The color drained from Carlos’s face. My mother sneered.

—He’s lying. This house doesn’t have cameras. I live here. I would know.

I gave him that same cold smile.

—Oh, Mom. That’s just what I let you think.

Before they could say anything else, I took my children by the hand and led them to my study. I closed the solid wood door and locked it.

The sound of the click was the loudest in the world.
I sat down in my leather chair, took out my laptop, and looked for an email from two years ago.

Subject: Pozuelo Agreement – ​​Highlighted.

It was time.

While they were banging on the door and shouting insults, I opened the PDF file sent by my lawyer, David.

I turned the 32-inch monitor on my desk towards them.

“You told me it was for taxes…” my mother stammered.

“I lied to you to save your pride,” I said coldly. “But look at Clause 12B, highlighted in yellow: ‘The Tenant agrees not to allow any other person to occupy the premises for more than 48 hours without written consent. And agrees not to disturb the living spaces of the Landlord’s minor dependents, Sofia and Marcos.’”

The silence was absolute.

—Mom, Dad, you’re in breach of contract. You kicked my children out to bring in these parasites. And that’s grounds for immediate eviction.

At that moment, the doorbell rang. Delivery men were bringing the €3,000 mattress my mother had ordered (hoping I would pay for it). I went outside, stopped them, and told them the truth: “This woman is a tenant facing eviction and doesn’t have authorization.” They took the mattress.

My mother, humiliated, resorted to her final weapon: she called the Parish Priest and Aunt Clara, the village gossip, to say that I was throwing my elderly parents out onto the street.

The phone rang. It was Father Juan. I put it on speakerphone.

“My daughter, you shall honor your father and your mother…” the sermon began.

“Father,” I interrupted. “My parents have thrown my 8- and 10-year-old children into a damp basement so that my brother-in-law, who stole 500,000 euros from them, can sleep in a suite. Is that honoring the family?”

The silence on the other end was deafening. The Father hung up.

Carlos, cornered, tried to physically attack me. And then I called the police.

The National Police arrived quickly. I showed them the security camera footage: Carlos admitting to the financial fraud and conspiring with Alicia.

They were taken away in handcuffs. The sound of the handcuffs clicking was heavenly music.

A court officer served my parents with an immediate eviction order for allowing criminal activity on the property.

“You have 24 hours to get your things out,” he told them.

My mother cried and begged, but I felt nothing anymore. I picked up my children and took them to the kitchen.

Three weeks have passed. The house is quiet. We’ve baked muffins. For the first time, this house feels like home.

I learned that you can’t choose the family you’re born into, but you have a duty to protect the one you create.

ဂမ်ဘီယာ ရှေ့နေက ဗုဒ္ဓဘာသာ ဆရာတော်ကြီးနှစ်ပါးကို အကြမ်းဖက်အဖြစ်စွတ်စွဲတာနဲ့ပါတ်သက်လို့ သီတဂူဆရာတော်ကြီးလို ဓမ္မစေတီတော်ကြီးထိုက်တဲ့ ဆရာတော်ဘုရား ပါဝင်နေမှုဟာ သည်းခံနိုင်စရာ အကြောင်းလုံးဝမရှိပါဘူး။

လမင်းခွေးဟောင်တာတွေဘာတွေမလိုပါ လမင်းခွေးဟောင်တာက အိပ်ရေးပျက်ယုံပဲရှိပေမဲ့ အခုဟာက ခွေးလိုက်ဆွဲနေတာဖြစ်ပါတယ်။

ကမ္ဘာသိ စွတ်စွဲနေတာကို သည်းခံတယ်ဆိုရင်တောင်  စွတ်စွဲတာထက် ပိုတဲ့ တရားစွဲတဲ့အဆင့်ဆိုရင်တော့ icj မှာ ဘာဖြေရှင်းချက်မှ ပေးစရာမလိုတော့သလို ယခင် ဂျီနိုဆိုက်နဲ့ နိုင်ငံကို တရားစွဲထားတဲ့အမှုကိုလည်း ဆက်လက်ရင်ဆိုင်စရာ အကြောင်းမရှိတော့ပါဘူး။

လူစိတ်ရှိလို့ ဂမ်ဘီယာနဲ့ icj ကို လူတွေလို့ထင်လို့ နိုင်ငံရေးအရ ဂုဏ်သိက္ခာအရ အမှန်တရားကိုရှင်းလင်း ထုချေဘို့ နိုင်ငံရဲ့ကိုယ်စား ဒေါ် အောင်ဆန်းစုကြည် နိုဘယ်ဆုရှင် တယောက်အနေနဲ့ ကိုယ်တိုင် တက်ရောက်ဖြေရှင်းခဲ့ပါပြီ။

သမာသမတ်ကျကျ လူလိုသူလို ဆုံးဖြတ်မယ်ဆိုရင် လက်ခံလို့ရပေမဲ့ အခုလို ဘာသာရေး ဆရာတော်ကြီး (ဗုဒ္ဓဘာသာမှာ ခေါင်းဆောင်ဟုမခေါ်ဝေါ်ပါ) အများကြည်ညိုလေးစားရတဲ့ နိုင်ငံတော်ဩဝါဒစရိယ လည်းဖြစ်တဲ့ ဆရာတော်ကြီးကို အကြမ်းဖက်အဖြစ် စွတ်စွဲတာ တရားစွဲဘို့ကြိုးစားတာဟာ ဘာသာရေး ပဋိပက္ခ ဖြစ်အောင် ဘာသာရေး အထိကရုန်းနဲ့ ဆူပွက်အောင်လုပ်တာဖြစ်တယ်လို့ တထစ်ချ ယုံကြည်တယ်။

ဘာသာတရားတိုင်းမှာ ဘာသာတခုခုကို သက်ဝင်ယုံကြည်မှုမရှိတဲ့ အခြားဘာသာဝင်က နားမလည်နိုင်တဲ့ စည်း/ကျင့်ဝတ်/ဓလေ့ထုံးတမ်း/သက်ဝင်ယုံကြည်မှု ဆိုင်ရာတွေ များစွာရှိတယ်။

ငါတို့ဟာ ခရစ်ယာန်ရဲ့ ပုပ်ရဟန်းမင်းကြီးကို မဝေဖန်သလို အစ္စလာမ်ရဲ့ အာလင်မ်၊ ဟာဖိဇ်၊ ဝလီ ဘယ်သူ့ကိုမှ မပုတ်ခတ်ဘူး ဒီလိုပဲ အခြားဘယ်ဘာသာရေးခေါင်းဆောင်ကိုမှ မကဲ့ရဲ့ မရှုံ့ချဘူး။ 

မြန်မာနိုင်ငံနဲ့ပါတ်သက်ပြီး ဂမ်ဘီယာရှေ့နေတွေနဲ့ ဂမ်ဘီယာနိုင်ငံရဲ့ ပြောဆိုလုပ်ကိုင်မှု အားလုံးကို ပြစ်တင်ရှုံချပါတယ်။ 

နိုင်ငံတကာတရားရုံးလို့သာခေါ်ပြီး အရေးယူထားပါတယ်ဆိုတဲ့ အမေရိကန် အစ္စရေး ရုရှားလို နိုင်ငံကြီးတွေက $အဖက်မလုပ်တဲ့အဖွဲ့ကြီးကို တလေးတစားသွားရောက်ဖြေရှင်းနေစရာအကြောင်း မရှိတော့ပါကြောင်း လေးနက်တည်ကြည်စွာဖြင့် မိမိအမြင်ကိုဖေါ်ပြလိုက်ပါတယ်။

I had two failed relationships last year. 
It was a major emotional breakdown. 
One almost had me lost my sanity. 
I questioned so many things. But I never wanted to blame anyone. I’m good at taking self evaluations. My mental health was attacked. You know what? I didn’t run to anyone for healing. I made peace with myself. I reminded myself of who I’m and what I’ve. 
Depression did me dirty! But I had to stay focused. At some point, I was getting uninterested in any conversation that looks like relationship. And if you know me well, I can’t make a post a day without talking about relationships. 

I was battling with that, handling work. 
I tried in my most possible way not to allow my experiences determine my future. 
Love will always come when we least expect. 
And often, God takes us through route to teach us certain things. 
Breakups can lead to many things, one of it can be lost identity. You start to question yourself, your worth and your potentials. Sometimes, it feels like you’re the problem. 
But here is why I’m sharing this, I want you to heal as much as it broke you. I want you to take back the YOU that was broken. I want you to understand that it didn’t happen to you, it happened for you. 

There is no timetable to your healing. It’s a personal journey. Heal as much as it broke you. 
While in the healing process, be much aware of who you’re. 
Love is a beautiful thing! It’s not a cliche! 
It’s a proven reality. And because your father in heaven wants you to enjoy good things, He will surely give you one. 
Don’t loose track of who you’re!
Don’t shrink because you got jilted!
Don’t succumb to societal pressures! 
When the time is RIGHT, the Lord will make it happen.

A reflection.
A reminder of where we come from and how we heal, connect, and transform together.

Manuel scolaire pour les soutiens de Bazoum sur le net. Ceux qui aiment Bazoum plus que même ceux qui ont mis des millards sur lui pour qu'il devient président.  Il y a une manière à faire et on va vous la démontrer 

Face à un pouvoir militaire issu d’un coup d’État, la demande de libération d’un dirigeant détenu exige une approche réaliste, respectueuse et stratégique. L’objectif n’est pas de provoquer l’affrontement, mais de créer les conditions d’un geste d’apaisement qui serve à la fois la dignité humaine, la stabilité nationale et les intérêts des autorités en place.

1. Reconnaître le rapport de force sans le légitimer

S’adresser au CNSP suppose de prendre acte de sa position de fait, sans pour autant valider le renversement de l’ordre constitutionnel. Le langage doit être pragmatique : éviter les accusations publiques frontales, préférer une reconnaissance factuelle de l’autorité exercée, afin de maintenir un canal de dialogue ouvert.

2. Mettre en avant la dimension humaine et sanitaire

L’argument le plus difficile à rejeter reste l’humanité. Insister sur l’âge, la santé, les conditions de détention et le respect de la dignité de Mohamed Bazoum permet de déplacer le débat du terrain politique vers celui des valeurs universelles. Une libération, même conditionnelle, peut être présentée comme un acte de responsabilité morale.

3. Parler le langage de la stabilité et de la sécurité

Les autorités militaires se définissent souvent par la recherche de stabilité. Il est donc stratégique de souligner que la détention prolongée alimente les tensions internes, isole le pays et complique la normalisation internationale. À l’inverse, un geste d’ouverture peut réduire les pressions, favoriser la confiance et renforcer le contrôle sécuritaire par l’apaisement.

4. Proposer une issue honorable

Plutôt qu’exiger une libération immédiate et sans condition, il est souvent plus efficace de suggérer des options graduelles :
 • résidence surveillée allégée,
 • accès régulier à la famille et aux soins,
 • libération pour raisons humanitaires,
 • engagement public à ne pas intervenir dans la vie politique.

Ces options offrent au CNSP une sortie honorable, sans impression de recul sous contrainte.

5. Privilégier la médiation discrète

Les demandes publiques trop dures peuvent pousser à la rigidité. Les médiations silencieuses (chefs religieux, notabilités, anciens responsables, partenaires africains) sont souvent plus efficaces. Elles permettent d’exprimer la demande avec respect et de sauver la face de toutes les parties.

6. Insister sur l’intérêt supérieur du Niger

Enfin, le message central doit rester le bien du Niger. Présenter la libération de Mohamed Bazoum comme un pas vers la réconciliation nationale, la levée progressive des sanctions et la restauration de la confiance internationale peut transformer la demande en opportunité politique pour les militaires eux-mêmes.

Conclusion

Face aux militaires du CNSP, demander la libération de Mohamed Bazoum ne peut relever ni de la confrontation directe ni de la soumission. La voie la plus efficace repose sur un discours calme, humaniste, sécuritaire et stratégique, laissant aux autorités la possibilité d’un geste fort sans perdre leur crédibilité. Dans ce type de contexte, la patience et la diplomatie pèsent souvent plus que la pression brute.

প্রধান উপদেষ্টা অধ্যাপক মুহাম্মদ ইউনুস মঙ্গলবার পুনর্ব্যক্ত করেছেন যে, তাঁর নেতৃত্বাধীন সরকার নির্ধারিত সময় অনুযায়ী আগামী ১২ ফেব্রুয়ারি জাতীয় সংসদ নির্বাচন ও গণভোট (রেফারেন্ডাম) আয়োজন করতে বদ্ধপরিকর। ঢাকার রাষ্ট্রীয় অতিথি ভবন যমুনায় ডোনাল্ড ট্রাম্প প্রশাসনকালে দায়িত্ব পালন করা যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের দুই সাবেক শীর্ষ কূটনীতিক অ্যালবার্ট টি. গম্বিস ও মরস ট্যানের সঙ্গে এক ঘণ্টাব্যাপী বৈঠকে তিনি এই অঙ্গীকার পুনরায় স্পষ্ট করেন। গুরুত্বপূর্ণ নির্বাচনকে সামনে রেখে তারা বাংলাদেশ সফর করছেন।

বৈঠকে আসন্ন নির্বাচন ছাড়াও জুলাই বিপ্লব ও তার পরবর্তী পরিস্থিতি, তরুণ আন্দোলনকারীদের উত্থান, জুলাই চার্টার ও গণভোট, নির্বাচনকে ঘিরে ভুয়া খবর ও অপপ্রচার, রোহিঙ্গা সংকট এবং জুলাই-পরবর্তী বাংলাদেশের সত্য ও পুনর্মিলনের সম্ভাবনা নিয়ে বিস্তৃত আলোচনা হয়।

এরই ধারাবাহিকতায় ১১ জানুয়ারি রবিবার দুপুর ২টায় বাংলাদেশ জামায়াতে ইসলামীর কেন্দ্রীয় কার্যালয়ে জামায়াতে ইসলামীর আমীর ডা. শফিকুর রহমানের সঙ্গে তারা সৌজন্য সাক্ষাৎ করেন। বৈঠকে পারস্পরিক আগ্রহের বিভিন্ন বিষয় নিয়ে মতবিনিময় হয়।

এছাড়াও তারা ডাকসু ও জাকসুর নেতৃবৃন্দের সঙ্গে সাক্ষাৎ করেন এবং সরাসরি তাদের কাছ থেকে জুলাই বিপ্লবের অভিজ্ঞতা ও বাস্তবতা সম্পর্কে অবগত হন। পাশাপাশি তারা দেশের বিভিন্ন নাগরিক সমাজের প্রতিনিধিদের সঙ্গেও মতবিনিময় করেন।

সব মিলিয়ে, এই কূটনৈতিক তৎপরতা বাংলাদেশের চলমান রাজনৈতিক রূপান্তর, গণতান্ত্রিক প্রক্রিয়া এবং ভবিষ্যৎ পথচলা নিয়ে আন্তর্জাতিক আগ্রহ ও সম্পৃক্ততার একটি গুরুত্বপূর্ণ বার্তা বহন করে।

In Memory of Renee Nicole Good — A Call for Justice, Compassion, and an End to Hate 🕊

On January 7, 2026, 37-year-old Renee Nicole Good, a loving mother, partner, and neighbor, was fatally shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent in Minneapolis. She was an American citizen — not someone being pursued for a crime or immigration violation — and at the time of the shooting she was near federal agents conducting a search in her neighborhood. 

Footage and multiple eyewitness accounts show her in her vehicle as the encounter unfolded; federal officials have claimed the agent acted in self-defense, but videos and civic leaders dispute that narrative and raise serious questions about the use of lethal force. Thousands in her community and across the country have protested the killing and called for accountability.  

Renee’s loved ones remember her not for controversy, but for her kindness, compassion, and devotion to her family — her mother described her as “one of the kindest people I’ve ever known.”  

This was not an isolated incident. Across the world, LGBTQ+ people are still too often met with anti-LGBTQ+ laws, discrimination, hate crimes, unjust violence, and even murder simply for living. Laws that target our identities, rhetoric that dehumanizes us, and violence that stems from prejudice create an environment where tragedies like this don’t feel distant — they feel personal.

To our LGBTQ+ siblings, families, allies, and all people of conscience:

Hate must not and will not prevail.
No person should fear violence for who they are or who they love.

Love is stronger than hatred.
Every act of compassion breaks down fear and builds a more just world.

We are stronger together.
Standing in unity against discrimination, whether in immigration enforcement, policing, or in laws that strip dignity from LGBTQ+, is how we protect each other and demand accountability.

From a spiritual perspective , we also affirm that no act of hatred is justified in the eyes of a loving God — and that justice, peace, and respect for human dignity are values worth holding onto, even in the darkest moments.

Let Renee’s life and tragic death remind us not to turn away from pain, but to speed toward justice with love, truth, and courage.

🕯 🕊️ Rest in peace, Renee. Your life matters. Your memory calls us to do better.

In a powerful demonstration of unity and cultural harmony, the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF) Visayas Regional Office successfully conducted the Peace Building Forum 2025 last December 17, 2025, at the Bai Hotel.

Under the theme “Voices for Peace: Insights that Inspire Harmony,” the forum served as a strategic platform for dialogue between Muslim community leaders, religious figures, and government stakeholders to strengthen the foundations of peace in the region.

The event was spearheaded by Acting Regional Director Hanefah M. Sultan, alongside the Peace Building and Conflict Resolution Division (PBCRD) led by Acting Chief Atty. Al-Emir Yusoph J. Balt.

The forum drew high-level support from across the Central Visayas governance, featuring messages of solidarity from:
• Hon. Gerald Anthony V. Gullas, Jr. (Mayor, City of Talisay) - Representative
• Hon. Cynthia K. Chan (Mayor, City of Lapu-Lapu) - Representative
• PBGen Redrico Atienza Maranan (Regional Director, PNP-PRO 7) - Representative
• Director Leocadio T. Trovela (DILG-VII) - Representative
• PLTCOL. Janette Rafter (Police Regional Office - Central Visayas)
• Mr. Erwin Alviola (NICA-7)

Cebu Governor Hon. Pamela S. Baricuatro, serving as the Keynote Speaker via a special audio-visual presentation, reminded the audience that peace is a daily practice. “𝘓𝘦𝘵 𝘶𝘴 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘶𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦 𝘷𝘰𝘪𝘤𝘦𝘴 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘱𝘦𝘢𝘤𝘦, 𝘯𝘰𝘵 𝘰𝘯𝘭𝘺 𝘪𝘯 𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘶𝘮𝘴 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴, 𝘣𝘶𝘵 𝘪𝘯 𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘥𝘢𝘪𝘭𝘺 𝘭𝘪𝘷𝘦𝘴. 𝘛𝘰𝘨𝘦𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳, 𝘭𝘦𝘵 𝘶𝘴 𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘵𝘦𝘤𝘵 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘶𝘯𝘪𝘵𝘦𝘴 𝘶𝘴 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘩𝘰𝘯𝘰𝘳 𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘮𝘢𝘬𝘦𝘴 𝘶𝘴 𝘶𝘯𝘪𝘲𝘶𝘦." Governor Baricuatro emphasized, reaffirming the Province's commitment to interfaith dialogue and mutual respect.

A highlight of the afternoon was the Recognition of Muslim Community and Religious Leaders, led by Shariah Counselor at Law Abubacar S. Gunang.

The forum culminated in a historic moment as National Commission on Muslim Filipinos Secretary Hon. Sabuddin N. Abdurahim officiated the Pledge of Commitment for Peace and Order. Leaders from various groups signed the manifesto, symbolizing a collective vow to uphold harmony and conflict resolution within their respective communities.

In his closing remarks, Acting Chief Atty. Al-Emir Yusoph J. Balt expressed gratitude to the participants, noting that the "insights shared today are the seeds for a more harmonious tomorrow." The program was seamlessly moderated by Master of Ceremonies Fateen Al- Jonara D. Pangarungan-Bao.

The NCMF Visayas remains steadfast in its mission to bridge gaps and build a future where every voice contributes to a symphony of peace.

PEACE SCIENTIST HAILS MATURITY IN CHAWAMA BY-ELECTION

Peace, Leadership, and Conflict Resolution Scientist Tom Njovu has described the ongoing Chawama Parliamentary by-election as a powerful demonstration of Zambia’s democratic maturity, unity, and commitment to peace.  

Njovu, who holds a Master of Science in Peace, Leadership, and Conflict Resolution from the University of Zambia (UNZA), expressed satisfaction with the calm and respectful atmosphere that has characterised the campaigns.  

“It is truly gratifying and encouraging to witness the peaceful conduct of campaigns during the ongoing Chawama Parliamentary by-election,” Njovu stated.  

“This is how democracy should be practised—through tolerance, mutual respect, and peaceful engagement rather than hostility and violence.”  

He emphasised that Zambia’s reputation as a beacon of peace on the African continent must be preserved, cautioning that political competition should never descend into physical confrontations or sow seeds of hatred and division.  

“Elections are a competition of ideas, visions, and leadership styles—not a battlefield,” he added.  

Njovu highlighted the cordial interactions between the ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) and opposition parties, noting that supporters exchanged greetings, flashed party symbols, and chanted slogans peacefully—scenes he described as “heart-warming” and reflective of political maturity.  

He recalled that in previous elections, encounters between rival political camps had sometimes escalated into violence, destruction of property, and tragic loss of life.  

In contrast, the peaceful atmosphere in Chawama stands out as both refreshing and commendable.  

“This development sends a powerful message that peaceful co-existence is possible, even in highly competitive political environments,” Njovu said.  

“It affirms the enduring relevance of Zambia’s founding motto, ‘One Zambia, One Nation.’”  

He acknowledged the efforts of political leaders, campaign teams, and supporters for choosing peace over provocation, underscoring that leadership is not only about securing votes but also about protecting national unity and social cohesion.  

Njovu expressed hope that the peaceful spirit witnessed in Chawama will be maintained throughout the remainder of the by-election and serve as a model for future local and national polls.  

“Peace, unity, and oneness are what Zambia needs to strengthen its democracy and ensure a stable future for generations to come,” he said.

He discovered how old the Earth was. Then he discovered something that could destroy us all.
For thousands of years, humanity wondered about the age of our planet. Religious texts offered one answer. Philosophers debated another. Scientists made educated guesses based on fossils and rock layers. But nobody actually knew.
Until a quiet scientist named Clair Patterson figured it out in 1953.
He should have become instantly famous. His name should have appeared in every textbook. Instead, what he discovered next turned him into a target. He found himself standing alone against one of the most powerful industries on Earth, fighting a battle that would determine whether millions of children would grow up with damaged minds.
And for decades, almost nobody knew his name.
Patterson's journey began in the late 1940s at the University of Chicago. He was a young geochemist with an impossible assignment: measure the precise amount of lead isotopes in a meteorite fragment called Canyon Diablo. The theory was elegant—if he could measure these specific lead ratios accurately, he could calculate when the solar system formed, and therefore, when Earth was born.
But there was a problem that nearly broke him.
Every time he tried to measure the lead in his samples, the numbers were wildly inconsistent. One day high, the next day higher, never stable. His equipment seemed fine. His calculations were correct. Yet the data was chaos.
Most scientists would have given up or blamed the methodology. Patterson was different. He possessed an almost obsessive attention to detail and patience that bordered on stubborn madness.
One day, he realized something shocking: the problem wasn't his rock sample. The problem was everything else.
There was lead everywhere. On the lab benches. In the air. Tracking in on people's shoes. Floating as invisible dust particles. The entire world was contaminated, and it was sabotaging his measurements.
So Patterson did something unprecedented. He built the world's first ultra-clean laboratory.
He scrubbed every surface until his hands bled. He sealed cracks in walls with tape. He installed specialized air filters. He made his assistants wear protective suits and wash repeatedly before entering. For years, he cleaned and refined and eliminated every possible source of contamination.
Finally, in 1953, he achieved it. He got a clean reading. He ran the numbers through a mass spectrometer, performed the calculations, and suddenly held an answer that no human in history had ever known:
4.55 billion years.
The Earth was 4.55 billion years old.
It's said that in his excitement, he drove straight to his mother's house in Iowa and told her he'd solved one of humanity's oldest mysteries. The weight of not knowing had finally lifted.
But while building his clean room, Patterson had stumbled onto something far more disturbing.
Where was all this lead coming from?
Lead is naturally rare on Earth's surface. It stays locked deep underground in mineral deposits. It doesn't float freely in the air. It doesn't coat laboratory tables. Yet it was everywhere—in quantities that made no sense.
Patterson began testing the world outside his lab. Ocean water. Mountain snow. Everywhere he looked, lead levels were hundreds of times higher than natural background levels.
And then he understood.
Since the 1920s, oil companies had been adding a compound called tetraethyl lead to gasoline. It prevented engine knock and made cars run smoother. But every car on every road was functioning as a poison dispersal system, spraying microscopic lead particles into the air with every mile driven.
Lead is a neurotoxin. It damages developing brains. It lowers IQ. It causes behavioral problems, aggression, and cognitive impairment. And an entire generation of children was breathing it every single day.
Patterson had to make a choice.
He was a geochemist. His job was studying rocks and isotopes, not fighting corporations or advocating for public health. He had stable funding and a promising academic career. He could have simply published his Earth-age discovery and moved on to the next project.
But he couldn't unsee what he'd found.
In the mid-1960s, he published papers warning that industrial lead contamination was poisoning the environment and harming human health.
The response was swift and brutal.
The lead industry was massive, wealthy, and had no intention of losing billions in revenue. Their chief scientific defender was Dr. Robert Kehoe, who had spent decades assuring the public that environmental lead was natural and harmless. Kehoe was polished, well-funded, and had the backing of powerful corporations.
When Patterson challenged this narrative, the industry attempted to buy his silence. Representatives visited him offering generous research grants and institutional support. All he had to do was redirect his focus elsewhere.
Patterson refused.
So they tried to destroy him professionally.
His funding from petroleum-connected sources was immediately cut. The industry pressured his university to dismiss him. They used their influence to block his papers from peer-reviewed journals. They publicly dismissed him as an overzealous geologist stepping outside his expertise.
For years, it worked. Patterson was marginalized, labeled an alarmist, and isolated from mainstream scientific discussions.
But Patterson had something the industry couldn't counter: evidence from before the contamination began.
He realized he needed a time machine—a way to prove what Earth's atmosphere was like before automobiles. So he traveled to one of the most remote places on the planet: Greenland.
In brutal, freezing conditions, Patterson and his team drilled deep into ancient glaciers, extracting long cylinders of ice. These ice cores were frozen time capsules. Snow that fell in 1700 was preserved deep in the ice. Snow from 1900 was higher up. Snow from the 1950s was near the surface.
Back in his clean lab, Patterson carefully melted layers of ice from different time periods and measured their lead content.
The results were devastating to the industry's claims.
For thousands of years, atmospheric lead levels were essentially zero. Then, starting precisely in the 1920s—exactly when leaded gasoline was introduced—the levels shot upward like a rocket. The graph was unmistakable. The contamination wasn't natural. It was recent, man-made, and accelerating.
Armed with this irrefutable proof, Patterson returned to the fight.
He testified before congressional committees, sitting across from industry lawyers who tried to confuse the science. He wasn't comfortable with public speaking. He was nervous, awkward, and preferred the quiet predictability of his laboratory. But he refused to back down.
He told legislators they were poisoning their own children. He showed them the ice core data. He made the invisible visible.
Slowly, reluctantly, the truth broke through.
Other scientists began supporting his findings. Public health advocates took notice. Parents started demanding action. The tide turned.
In the 1970s, the United States passed the Clean Air Act and began the slow process of removing lead from gasoline. It took years of regulatory battles, but eventually, unleaded gasoline became the standard.
The results were nothing short of miraculous.
Within years, blood lead levels in American children dropped by nearly 80%. An entire generation was saved from cognitive impairment, behavioral disorders, and reduced intelligence. Millions of lives were protected from lead-related health problems.
Clair Patterson had won.
Yet when he died in 1995, few outside the scientific community knew his name. He never received a Nobel Prize. He never became wealthy. He simply returned to his laboratory and continued studying the chemistry of the oceans and the history of the Earth.
Patterson's story is a reminder of what integrity looks like when nobody's watching.
It's easy to do the right thing when the crowd is cheering. It's infinitely harder when powerful interests are trying to ruin you, when your career is threatened, when taking the money would be so much easier.
He could have stayed silent. He could have enjoyed a comfortable, well-funded career studying rocks while children's minds were damaged. He could have said, "Not my problem."
But he looked at the data, looked at the world, and decided truth mattered more than comfort.
He gave us the age of the Earth—a number that changed our understanding of time itself.
And then he gave us a future—a world where children could grow up without poison in their lungs.
We often imagine heroes as soldiers, activists, or celebrities. But sometimes a hero is just a stubborn man in a white lab coat, scrubbing a floor over and over, refusing to accept a convenient lie.
He cleaned the room.
And then he cleaned the world.

Why Some Connections Are Meant to Teach, Not to Stay

Not every connection comes to last forever.
Some come to wake something in us.
They arrive gently — sometimes passionately — and for a moment, they feel like home. We think, this is it. We plan, we hope, we imagine permanence. But over time, the connection begins to change. Not because it was fake. Not because it failed. But because it has done its work.
Some people come into our lives to teach us things we wouldn’t learn alone.
They teach us how to love deeply.
How to communicate honestly.
How to open our hearts — or protect them when needed.
They show us our patterns, our wounds, our softness, our strength.
And sometimes, they leave right after that lesson is learned.
It hurts because we mistake purpose for permanence.
We assume that if something feels meaningful, it must stay forever. But meaning isn’t measured by duration. Some of the most powerful connections last briefly — yet shape us permanently.
A teaching connection often feels intense. Because lessons are never gentle.
They push us to grow.
They challenge our expectations.
They force us to confront what we ignore about ourselves.
And when the growth is complete, the relationship can no longer stay the same. Holding on would mean refusing the lesson.
So the connection loosens.
Distance enters.
Silence replaces closeness.
Not as punishment — but as transition.
What makes it painful is not the loss of the person.
It’s the loss of the version of ourselves we were when they were still there.
But if we look closely, we realize: They weren’t meant to stay — they were meant to prepare us.
For healthier love.
For clearer choices.
For deeper self-awareness.
Letting go doesn’t erase what was shared.
It honors it.
Because some connections don’t come to walk the whole journey with us.
They come to point us in the right direction… and then release our hand.

“Not everyone who matters is meant to stay; some are meant to wake parts of you you didn’t know existed.”

Memphis, TN - The Tennessee Highway Patrol released dash camera footage to refute claims that a state trooper struck a protester at this weekend’s anti-ICE demonstration.

The video shows a man stepping into the roadway as a trooper was maneuvering through traffic and protesters. After briefly blocking the vehicle’s path, the man moves to the side and returns to his vehicle.

Tennessee Highway Patrol officials said the footage was released to clarify what it called “false” accusations that an individual had been hit by a trooper during the protests.

“We respect and protect the right of people to protest peacefully. That right, however, does not include entering active roadways or placing themselves in danger,” the Tennessee Highway Patrol said in a statement.

The agency added that its priority is public safety for all involved, including motorists, protesters and its troopers.

Tyler Foster is the vice president of the Memphis Interfaith Coalition for Action, a local social justice organization. He says that the video released by troopers does not paint the entire picture of what happened.

“It’s not surprising that they released a selected clip of what they claim transpired,” Foster said. “The reality is that there is a lot more to the story. A lot more video footage, and we have been calling on them to release that video footage.”

Foster says he was at the protest, and it only escalated when troopers arrived just as the protest was about to end. He says a vehicle may have run over the foot of a woman who was arrested during the protest after an altercation with state troopers.

That woman has been identified by authorities as Rebecca Ann Leathers. Troopers said Leathers stood in front of a Tennessee Highway Patrol cruiser as officers tried to maneuver through the crowd, and that she struck the vehicle’s windows.

Police say Leathers did not cooperate during her arrest and became violent, but Foster says she was peacefully protesting.

“When THP aggressively showed up, drove into the crowd and got out and snatched [Leathers], who was peacefully protesting and threw her in the back of the patrol car, brandished their Tasers, shouted at people, advanced aggressively toward people, that naturally escalated the situation,” Foster said.

Leathers was charged with disorderly conduct, resisting official detention and additional charges.

It is unclear at this time whether the man seen in the dash camera footage is facing any charges.

Il y a quelques mois, j’ai fait une publication par ici parlant de ma participation à la mission des jeunes observateurs de la #CEDEAO en Côte d’Ivoire. 

Mais cette fois ci, je vous emmène dans la sphère de formateur des observateurs électoraux.
Eh oui, pour les élections législatives et communales de mon pays, j’ai eu l’immense plaisir de me positionner en tant que formatrice des OE dans les communes :Bohicon et Abomey-Calavi.

Le 25 décembre 2025, contrairement à la plupart, je me déplaçais sur Bohicon pour être formé à la formation des formateurs.
Trois jours d’activités intenses, de mise en situation, d’échanges et de partage de connaissances.

Repartis en binôme, nous avons eu à outiller 12000 observateurs sur le cadre légal des élections au Bénin, les principes d’une mission d’observation, les mesures et dispositions sécuritaires à prendre pendant la mission d’observation et pour finir le mode de rapportage des informations collectées. 

Il n’a pas uniquement été question d’être formateur mais également de superviser les observateurs durant la mission d’observation : veille, jour et lendemain du scrutin.

THE HEART: WHERE FOREVER MEETS NOW

Your heart isn’t just a muscle keeping time.
It’s a signal tower.

Every beat sends invisible ripples through your body and beyond it. Science can measure its field, but it can’t measure its message. What your heart truly carries goes far deeper than instruments can reach.

Its greatest gift is harmony.

When your heart finds its natural rhythm, the body remembers how to repair itself. The nervous system settles. The cells respond. The inner chaos quiets. Even time seems to move differently. Your very biology starts listening to balance instead of stress.

The heart doesn’t live inside straight lines or simple timelines.
It holds memory that isn’t bound to one moment.

It remembers connections, missed roads, old dreams, and stories older than this lifetime. That’s why emotional pain can feel so huge — it isn’t only about now. It touches many layers of you at once.

Real healing doesn’t come from thinking harder.
And it doesn’t come from forcing yourself to be okay.

Healing begins where the unseen and the physical finally meet.

In deeper traditions, the heart is seen as the crossing point — where active and receptive, light and depth, motion and stillness come together. It’s where separation ends and unity begins. Where the soul decides to fully live inside the body.

Every heartbeat is a quiet call back to yourself.
A gentle correction.
A reminder of who you really are.

When you bring your attention to your heart and breathe there, you leave survival mode. You start to remember. Your presence becomes a tuning instrument for calm, for clarity, for love.

Stop for a moment.
Place your awareness in your chest.
Notice the rhythm underneath everything else.

That rhythm is life itself moving through you.

You are not trying to reach something divine.
You are expressing it — from the center of your being into the world.

And the longer you stay there, something very old stirs awake.

The mind softens. The body opens. Time feels less rigid.

You remember you were never meant to live split — torn between thinking and feeling, between spirit and flesh. Your heart was made to be the bridge. The doorway. The place where the infinite learns your name.

Every breath you take into your heart brings you back into alignment. Every beat subtly reshapes your experience. This is how real change happens — not by pressure, but by vibration. Not by struggle, but by attunement.

When your heart is clear, you don’t hunt for meaning.
You embody it.
You don’t look for truth.
You move as it.

That’s why your presence can shift a space before you speak. Why real love, when lived, rearranges everything.

Stay with the rhythm.
Let it ground you.
Let it both calm and strengthen you.

You are not turning into something else.
You are remembering what you have always been.

The doorway was never somewhere outside you.
It has always been your heart.

Midsayap Declared LTG/CTG-Free as 34th Infantry Battalion Bids Farewell, 33rd IB Takes Over in Historic Transition

MIDSAYAP, Cotabato — The Municipality of Midsayap was officially declared Local Terrorist Group/Communist Terrorist Group (LTG/CTG)-free on January 14, 2026, marking a major milestone in the government’s peace and security campaign, as the Philippine Army simultaneously held the Send-Off Ceremony of the 34th Infantry (Reliable) Battalion at its headquarters in Barangay Salunayan.

The historic activity was led by Brigadier General Ricky P. Bunayog, PA, Commander of the 6021st Brigade, 6th Infantry Division, who served as keynote speaker. He was joined by top civilian and military leaders, including Maguindanao del Norte Governor Datu Tucao O. Mastura, North Cotabato Governor Emmylou J. Taliño-Mendoza (represented by Board Members Rose Cabaya and Sittie Eljorie Antao Balisi), SGADA Administrator Butch P. Malang, and Midsayap Mayor Renz Tukuran, along with officials from various LGUs of SGA BARMM and North Cotabato.

The program opened with the singing of the National Anthem and interfaith prayers, followed by the welcome message of Lt. Col. Edgardo B. Batinay, Battalion Commander of the 34th Infantry Battalion. This was highlighted by the formal signing of the declaration proclaiming Midsayap as LTG/CTG-free—an affirmation of the municipality’s improved peace and order situation after years of security operations, community engagement, and cooperation between the military, LGUs, and residents.

As a strong symbol of peace, surrendered loose firearms were formally turned over, followed by a symbolic release of doves, signifying freedom, healing, and a new chapter for the community.

In his message, Lt. Col. Batinay admitted that leaving Midsayap was not easy, but stressed that their departure is part of the Army’s mission to sustain peace in other areas. “Ang pamamaalam ay hindi madali, ngunit ito ay mahalaga para sa pagpapatuloy ng kapayapaan at kaayusan,” he said.

Local officials and residents expressed deep gratitude to the 34th Infantry Battalion for its years of dedicated service in securing communities, dismantling insurgent threats, and helping bring stability to the area.

The second part of the ceremony featured the readiness report and awarding of troops, followed by the inspection and send-off of the 34IB by BGen Bunayog and other key leaders. The event concluded with the singing of the Unit Hymn and “Pilipinas Kong Mahal” by the 34IB troops, led by PFC Jaime T. Coyme and PFC Reyvin W. Requillos as Masters of Ceremony.

As part of the official command swapping, Lt. Col. German Legada, PA, from Rajah Buayan, was introduced as the incoming Commanding Officer-in-Charge of the 33rd Infantry (Makabayan) Battalion, which formally assumed responsibility for the area. He replaced Lt. Col. Batinay, a native of Barangay Salunayan, Midsayap, who in turn took over as Commanding Officer of the 33rd Infantry Battalion.

The smooth transition highlighted the professionalism, discipline, and continuity of leadership within the Philippine Army, ensuring that security gains in Midsayap will be sustained.

Earlier this week, on January 12, 2026, the 34th Infantry Battalion was formally welcomed back into the 1st Infantry (Tabak) Division during a flag-raising ceremony at the Division Grandstand, marking its reintegration into the “Tabak family” following a unit realignment ordered by the Philippine Army Headquarters to enhance operational effectiveness.

In his message, Major General Yegor Rey P. Barroquillo Jr., Commanding General of the 1st Infantry Division, said the return of the 34IB was not merely a reassignment but “a homecoming,” noting that the battalion traces its roots to Fort Magsaysay, the former headquarters of the 1st Infantry Division.

Activated on February 18, 1974, the 34th Infantry Battalion has served for over five decades across Mindanao, Samar, and the Bangsamoro region, playing a crucial role in counter-insurgency, stability operations, and community peacebuilding.

“Matapos ang mahigit limampung taon ng paglilingkod, ang 34th Infantry Battalion ay tuluyan nang nakauwi,” Barroquillo said, praising the unit’s sacrifice, resilience, and unwavering dedication to the Filipino people. He assured full divisional support as the battalion begins its new chapter under the Tabak Division.

The ceremony also saw the donning of the Tabak Patch to 32 newly graduated Second Lieutenants and 70 Privates, symbolizing their formal entry into the Division, as well as the promotion to Colonel of Terence P. Ylanan (G3), Andy John R. Tupas (G2), and Christopher V. Dayag, Commanding Officer of Kuta Cesar Sang-an Station Hospital.

The twin events—the declaration of Midsayap as LTG/CTG-free and the redeployment of the 34th Infantry Battalion—stand as powerful proof of the effective partnership between the government, the Armed Forces, and local communities in advancing peace, stability, and development in Cotabato and the wider region.

As Midsayap turns a new page in its history, officials emphasized that sustaining peace will require continued vigilance, unity, and cooperation—ensuring that the hard-won gains will translate into lasting progress and prosperity for the people.

Post-Chroma
 
Inner Vibes’26 was a large-scale monochrome exhibition curated by Deepak Sonar at Lalit Kala Akademi, Chennai, bringing together 54 artists working exclusively in black, white, and grey. I encountered the exhibition not in the gallery but through social media, PDFs, and digital images and that distance felt appropriate. Black-and-white is the language of mediation: archives, newspapers, legal records, evidence. It is how images travel when they want to be taken seriously. Viewed this way, the exhibition did not lose meaning online; it found its natural register.

What the show staged was not a collection of monochrome works but a field of shared pressure. The restriction of black and white functioned as a governing climate rather than a stylistic choice. Every artist worked under the same chromatic law, and that law became active, it shaped, limited, and sharpened what could be said visually. Colour was not removed; it was replaced by discipline.

Without colour, everything else grew louder. Structure, density, pacing, surface, and silence were exposed. Each work negotiated how much it could hold and how much it had to release. Meaning emerged between the works, through adjacency, tension, and contrast, rather than through individual signature.

This is also why the exhibition translated so well to screens. Black and white are highly sensitive to mediation; small shifts in contrast or compression can remake an image. Rather than weakening the works, this revealed their nature as responsive surfaces that change as they are seen.

The deepest charge lay in the greys. Grey is where binaries collapse, neither black nor white, neither certainty nor negation. In a world increasingly driven by rigid oppositions, this insistence on nuance felt quietly resistant. Black and white carry the authority of documents and truth; grey unsettles that authority, refusing closure.

Deepak Sonar’s curatorial vision was central. By enforcing a single chromatic condition, he created a shared ground that sharpened difference rather than flattening it. Temperament, intensity, and visual intelligence became more visible precisely because colour was absent. Inner Vibes’26 should not remain static. It deserves to travel and grow, absorbing new artists wherever it lands, becoming a living monochrome ecology. Ultimately, this exhibition was not about the absence of colour, but the presence of attention, what remains when excess is stripped away, and which truths can survive in that stark light.

Frédéric Bastiat’s complaint about half-truths feels painfully current because the tactic has been perfected. 

A political actor utters a sentence so compact, so morally flattering, that it lands before anyone can ask a second question. “The government will fix it.” “This costs nothing.” “It helps ordinary people.” 

By the time the audience exhales, the half-truth has already been accepted as common sense.

The problem is not that the statement is false. 

It’s that it is incomplete by design. The missing half — the costs, incentives, trade-offs, and behavioral distortions — cannot be shouted back in a soundbite.

This is not confined to politics. 

Corporations deploy the same maneuver daily. “This will improve efficiency.” “We’re future-proofing the business.” “This is industry standard.” 

Once spoken, the room subtly shifts from inquiry to compliance. 

Questioning the claim feels obstructive, even disloyal.

So what can be done immediately, in real time, when a potent half-truth is released?

First, interrupt the narrative before it settles. Do not argue conclusions; demand completion. The fastest counter is a neutral clarifier: “Under what assumptions?” or “What must be true for this to work?” Half-truths depend on silence after the statement.

Second, force instant cost visibility. The most effective response is not a rebuttal but a bill: “Who pays, when, and in what form?” If the speaker cannot answer in the same time span as the claim, the asymmetry becomes visible to the audience.

Third, translate abstraction into displacement. Ask: “What stops or gets worse as a result?” Benefits that cannot name casualties are almost always overstated.

Fourth, anchor the claim in time. Require a concrete prediction: “What will success look like in 12 months?” Vague promises hate calendars.

Finally, document the moment. Half-truths thrive on institutional amnesia. Recording the claim, its assumptions, and its promised outcomes converts rhetoric into a testable hypothesis.

The Negev has entered a dangerous phase. A surge of violence within Bedouin communities, alongside growing friction and attacks affecting nearby Jewish towns, reflects more than local criminality. It signals a deeper erosion of state authority in Israel’s south, one that threatens public safety, social cohesion, and national security alike.
Polygamy is one of the clearest indicators of this breakdown. Long treated as a social issue, a women’s rights concern, or a cultural practice best handled delicately, it has been systematically misdiagnosed. What is unfolding in the Negev is not a private family matter, but a structural phenomenon with direct implications for governance and sovereignty. At its most dangerous edge, polygamy has become a vehicle for cross-border infiltration, demographic distortion, and the erosion of loyalty to the state.
Polygamy is illegal in Israel. Yet in the Negev it persists at scale, expands with minimal deterrence, and is routinely tolerated by state authorities. This failure is not benign. It has enabled the large-scale importation of women from Gaza and other Palestinian controlled areas through unregistered and polygamous marriages, often bypassing immigration controls, civil registration, and meaningful security screening.
Under Israeli law, a child born to one Israeli parent is entitled to Israeli citizenship, even when the other parent has no legal status. In isolation, this reflects a humane citizenship framework. In the context of widespread polygamy, however, it creates a multiplying effect.
In parts of the Bedouin sector where unregistered marriages are common, a single Israeli citizen can lawfully transmit citizenship to multiple family units, dramatically amplifying the demographic and civic impact of each case.
While precise data are lacking, security officials and policymakers increasingly warn that this legal structure is being deliberately exploited, with Palestinian families marrying daughters to Israeli Bedouin men as a pathway into Israeli society through citizenship transmission. The absence of figures does not negate the concern; it exposes a structural blind spot the state has failed to address.
This is not theoretical. Ismail Haniyeh, Hamas’s leader until his assassination in 2024, had close family members living in the Negev, including sisters who were Israeli citizens residing in Tel Sheva. Several relatives were arrested over the years on serious criminal and security-related charges.
The issue is not guilt by association, but vulnerability by design: the leader of a genocidal terror organization maintained intimate family networks inside Israel, embedded in communities where law enforcement is already weak.
Security professionals have long warned that family ties are among the most powerful loyalty-forming mechanisms in Middle Eastern societies. When those ties extend into Gaza and Hamas-controlled environments, the implications are obvious. In times of escalation, familial loyalty can come into direct conflict with national loyalty, particularly where state authority is already contested and illegal norms are entrenched.
Polygamy does not exist in isolation. It is embedded in a broader ecosystem of illegality: illegal construction on state land, welfare fraud, falsified or absent civil registration, harboring of illegal residents, weapons offenses, and chronic non-compliance with planning and security authorities.
These are not random violations. They form a coherent system sustained by the expectation of non-enforcement. Areas where the law is optional quickly become areas where sovereignty is challenged.
Demography magnifies the threat. Polygamous households drive exceptionally high birth rates, particularly in illegal or unrecognized settlements, producing population growth far beyond state planning assumptions. The result is a rapidly expanding population concentrated in areas with weak infrastructure, poor educational outcomes, low labor-market participation, and limited integration into Israeli civic life. This is not merely a socioeconomic failure; it is a long-term security risk.
Public funds unintentionally deepen the problem. Polygamous households rely disproportionately on welfare transfers rather than earned income. Child allowances, unemployment benefits, and disability payments often sustain illegal family structures. When the state systematically subsidizes illegality, it ceases to be neutral and becomes complicit.
This is often framed as a humanitarian dilemma: enforce the law or harm vulnerable populations. That framing is false. The absence of enforcement has not protected women or children; it has entrenched their vulnerability. Women brought into Israel through illegal polygamous marriages, often without legal status, live under extreme dependency and control. Children raised in these environments face neglect, poor schooling, and social alienation, making them more susceptible to criminal and extremist influence.
Culture is frequently invoked as a shield against intervention. But sovereignty cannot be outsourced to tradition. Practices that violate criminal law, undermine gender equality, distort demographic planning, and weaken national security are not cultural expressions deserving immunity.
Israel has convened committees, commissioned reports, and issued recommendations. Yet the central failure remains unchanged: deterrence has been absent. Social services without enforcement function as incentives. Education without accountability cannot compete with a system that rewards illegality.
This is not a call for collective punishment. It is a call to restore the basic premise of statehood: that the law applies everywhere, to everyone, consistently. Enforcement, paired with protection, legal pathways, and exit options for women and children, is not repression, it is governance.
Polygamy in the Negev is no longer a marginal social issue. It is a security stress test for Israel’s ability to maintain sovereignty over a strategic region, prevent internal erosion driven by cross-border hostile networks, and uphold the rule of law.
Israel still has the capacity to act. What remains in question is whether it has the will to treat polygamy not as a cultural inconvenience, but as what it has become: a strategic liability and threat.

Informed choice is not ignorance. Bodily autonomy is not dangerous. And truth does not need permission to be spoken.

What is dangerous is blind trust without research. What is dangerous is conditioning parents to believe that questioning authority is ignorance while obedience is intelligence. What is dangerous is dismissing injured children and adults as coincidences, genetics, or bad luck instead of listening, investigating, and taking responsibility. What is dangerous is telling families their lived experience is not valid because it makes others uncomfortable.

What is dangerous is a system that shields manufacturers from liability while families shoulder the consequences. What is dangerous is medical decisions influenced by incentives, percentiles, and compliance metrics instead of individualized care. What is dangerous is normalizing chronic illness, developmental regression, neurological damage, and lifelong dependence on medications as “just how it is now.”

What is dangerous is suppressing the body’s natural detox mechanisms while introducing substances that require detoxification. What is dangerous is telling parents to premedicate children with drugs that deplete glutathione while claiming safety has been fully studied. What is dangerous is refusing to acknowledge biological reality in favor of rigid narratives.

Truth is not dangerous. Education is not dangerous. Informed consent is not dangerous. Parents protecting their children are not dangerous. People who read inserts, question ingredients, understand safety testing, and choose differently are not dangerous.

What is dangerous is a world where asking questions gets you attacked, threatened, or silenced. And what is truly terrifying is how many people confuse compliance with care and obedience with science.

Medical freedom means the right to make informed decisions about your own body and your children’s bodies without coercion, punishment, or fear. It means consent that is freely given, not consent obtained through pressure, threats, shame, or withheld access to care. Medical freedom exists so individuals and families can weigh risks and benefits, ask questions, seek second opinions, and choose the path that aligns with their health, values, and lived experience.
Medical freedom does not mean forcing others to agree with you. It does not mean denying care. It does not mean ignorance. It means autonomy. It means the acknowledgment that bodies are not identical, risk is not uniform, and medicine is not one size fits all. It recognizes that informed adults and parents have the right to say yes, no, or not right now without being labeled reckless or dangerous.

Without medical freedom, informed consent does not exist. Choice becomes compliance. Healthcare becomes control. History has shown us repeatedly what happens when people are stripped of the right to question medical authority. That is why medical freedom is not optional. It is foundational.
You do not have to agree with someone’s medical decisions to respect their right to make them. Freedom only works when it applies to everyone, not just those who follow the majority.

Medical freedom is not extremism. It is a human right.

One last thing that needs to be said is that medical freedom also protects minorities and the medically vulnerable. People with prior injuries, genetic differences, autoimmune conditions, neurological sensitivities, or a history of adverse reactions are often the first to be harmed by one size fits all medicine. Medical freedom exists so those individuals are not forced into protocols that ignore their unique biology.

Medical freedom also protects the right to delay. Not every decision has to be yes or no forever. Sometimes the most responsible choice is not right now. A system that does not allow space for timing, readiness, and individualized pacing is not practicing care, it is enforcing compliance.
Another overlooked truth is that coercion erodes trust permanently. When people feel pressured, silenced, or punished for asking questions, they disengage entirely. Medical freedom keeps people involved, curious, and accountable. Fear based compliance creates silence, not safety.

Medical freedom also safeguards parental responsibility. Parents are legally and morally responsible for the outcomes of decisions made for their children. Removing their authority while keeping their liability is unethical. You cannot demand responsibility while denying choice.
And finally, medical freedom exists because medicine is practiced on humans, not machines. Humans have variability. Humans have history. Humans have intuition. A system that does not honor that reality will always cause harm.
Medical freedom is not the problem. The absence of it is.

At the end of the day, this is not about division. It is about honoring choice. Medical freedom means allowing every person to decide what is right for their own body and their own family without hatred, judgment, or harm. That goes both ways. You do not have to agree with someone’s choices to respect their right to make them.

Everyone deserves autonomy. Everyone deserves dignity. Everyone deserves the freedom to choose what they believe is best for their health without being attacked, threatened, or dehumanized. Love does not disappear because we disagree. Compassion does not require conformity.

We can stand firmly in our beliefs while still honoring the humanity of others. Medical freedom only works when it applies to all of us equally. Choice is not dangerous. Respect is not weakness. And allowing people the space to decide for themselves is how true freedom exists.

Love y'all,
Alissa 🫶🏼
