Saint Savva, First Archbishop of Serbia, in the world Rostislav (Rastko), was a son of the Serbian king Stephen Nemanya and Anna, daughter of the Byzantine Emperor Romanus. From his early years he fervently attended church services and had a special love for icons.

At seventeen years of age, Rostislav met a monk from Mount Athos, secretly left his father’s house and set off for the Saint Panteleimon monastery. (By divine Providence in 1169, the year of the saint’s birth, the ancient monastery of the Great Martyr and healer Panteleimon was given to Russian monks.)

Knowing that his son was on Athos, his father mobilized his retainers headed by a faithful voevod and wrote to the governor of the district which included Athos, saying that if his son were not returned to him, he would go to war against the Greeks. When they arrived at the monastery, the voevod was ordered not to take his eyes off Rostislav. During the evening services, when the soldiers had fallen asleep under the influence of wine, Rostislav received monastic tonsure (in 1186) and sent to his parents his worldly clothes, his hair and a letter. Saint Savva sought to persuade his powerful parents to accept monasticism. The monk’s father (in monasticism Simeon, commemorated on February 13) and his son pursued asceticism at the Vatopedi monastery. On Athos they established the Serbian Hilandar monastery, and this monastery received its name by imperial grant. At Hilandar monastery, Saint Savva was ordained to the diaconate and then presbyter. His mother Anna became a nun with the name Anastasia (June 21).

For his holy life and virtuous deeds on Mount Athos, the monk was made an archimandrite at Thessalonica. At Nicea in the year 1219 on the Feast of the Dormition of the Most Holy Theotokos, the Ecumenical Patriarch Germanus consecrated Archimandrite Savva as Archbishop of Serbia. The saint petitioned the Byzantine Emperor to grant permission for Serbian bishops to elect their own Archbishop in future. This was a very important consideration in a time of frequent wars between the eastern and western powers.

Having returned to the Holy Mountain from Nicea, the saint visited all the monasteries for the last time. He made prostrations in all the churches and, calling to mind the blessed lives of the wilderness Fathers, he made his farewells to the ascetics with deep remorse, “leaving the Holy Mountain, as if from Paradise.”

Saddened by his separation from the Holy Mountain, the saint went along the path from Athos just barely moving. The Most Holy Theotokos spoke to the saint in a dream, “Having My Patronage, why do you remain sorrowful?” These words roused him from despondency, changing his sorrow into joy. In memory of this appearance, the saint commissioned large icons of the Savior and of the Mother of God at Thessalonica, and put them in a church.

In Serbia, the activity of the Hierarch in organizing the work of his native Church was accompanied by numerous signs and miracles. During the Liturgy and the all-night Vigil, when the saint came to cense the grave of his father the monk Simeon, the holy relics exuded fragrant myrrh.

Being in charge of negotiations with the Hungarian King Vladislav, who had declared war on Serbia, the holy bishop not only brought about the desired peace for his country, but he also brought the Hungarian monarch to Orthodoxy. Thus he facilitated the start of the historical existence of the autonomous Serbian Church. Saint Savva also contributed to strengthening the Serbian state. In order to insure the independence of the Serbian state, Archbishop Savva crowned his powerful brother Stephen as king. Upon the death of Stephen, his eldest son Radislav was crowned king, and Saint Savva set off to the Holy Land “to worship at the holy tomb of Christ and fearsome Golgotha.”

When he returned to his native land, the saint blessed and crowned Vladislav as king. To further strengthen the Serbian throne, he betrothed him to the daughter of the Bulgarian prince Asan. The holy hierarch visited churches all across Serbia, he reformed monastic rules on the model of Athos and Palestine, and he established and consecrated many churches, strengthening the Orthodox in their faith. Having finished his work in his native land, the saint appointed the hieromonk Arsenius as his successor, consecrating him bishop and giving his blessing to all.

He then set off on a journey of no return, desiring “to end his days as a wanderer in a foreign land.” He passed through Palestine, Syria and Persia, Babylon, Egypt and Anatolia, everywhere visiting the holy places, conversing with great ascetics, and collecting the holy relics of saints. The saint finished his wanderings at Trnovo in Bulgaria at the home of his kinsman Asan, where with spiritual joy he gave up his soul to the Lord (+ 1237).

At the time of transfer of the holy relics of Saint Savva to Serbia in 1237, there were so many healings that the Bulgarians began to complain about Asan, “because he had given up such a treasure.” In the saint’s own country, his venerable relics were placed in the Church of Mileshevo, bestowing healing on all who approached with faith. The inhabitants of Trnovo continued to receive healing from the remnants of the saint’s coffin, which Asan ordered to be gathered together and placed in a newly built sarcophagus.

The legacy of Saint Savva lives on in the Orthodox Church traditions of the Slavic nations. He is associated with the introduction of the Jerusalem Typikon as the basis for Slavic Monastic Rules. The Serbian Hilandar monastery on Mt. Athos lives by the Typikon of Saint Savva to this day. Editions of The Rudder (a collection of church canons) of Saint Savva, with commentary by Alexis Aristines, are the most widely disseminated in the Russian Church. In 1270 the first copy of The Rudder of Saint Savva was sent from Bulgaria to Metropolitan Cyril of Kiev. From this was copied one of the most ancient of the Russian Rudders, the Ryazan Rudder of 1284. It in turn was the source for a printed Rudder published in 1653, and since that time often reprinted by the Russian Church. Such was the legacy of Saint Savva to the canonical treasury of Orthodoxy.

বাংলাদেশের অনির্বাচিত সরকারকে গুরুত্বহীন মনে করে ভারত,

ভারতের সেনাপ্রধানের সাম্প্রতিক মন্তব্য বাংলাদেশের অনির্বাচিত বা অস্থায়ী সরকারকে ভারত গুরুত্ব দেয় না দুই দেশের সম্পর্কের ক্ষেত্রে একটি স্পষ্ট ও তাৎপর্যপূর্ণ রাজনৈতিক বার্তা বহন করে। এটি নিছক কোনো সামরিক বা কূটনৈতিক মন্তব্য নয় বরং দক্ষিণ এশিয়ার শক্তির ভারসাম্য, গণতন্ত্রের প্রশ্ন এবং আঞ্চলিক স্থিতিশীলতার বাস্তবতার সঙ্গে গভীরভাবে সংযুক্ত।
ভারত দীর্ঘদিন ধরেই নিজেকে বিশ্বের বৃহত্তম গণতন্ত্র হিসেবে উপস্থাপন করে আসছে এবং প্রতিবেশী রাষ্ট্রগুলোর সঙ্গে সম্পর্কের ক্ষেত্রে “স্থিতিশীল ও নির্বাচিত সরকার”-কেই সহযোগিতার প্রধান ভিত্তি হিসেবে বিবেচনা করে। সেই দৃষ্টিকোণ থেকে অনির্বাচিত বা অস্থায়ী সরকারের প্রতি ভারতের অনাগ্রহ কৌশলগতভাবে অস্বাভাবিক নয়। দিল্লি ভালোভাবেই জানে, অস্থায়ী সরকার সাধারণত স্বল্পমেয়াদি, নীতিনির্ধারণে সীমাবদ্ধ এবং প্রায়ই অভ্যন্তরীণ বৈধতার সংকটে ভোগে। এমন সরকারের সঙ্গে দীর্ঘমেয়াদি নিরাপত্তা, বাণিজ্য কিংবা অবকাঠামো সংক্রান্ত চুক্তিতে যাওয়া ঝুঁকিপূর্ণ।
বাংলাদেশের প্রেক্ষাপটে এই বক্তব্যের তাৎপর্য আরও গভীর। বাংলাদেশ-ভারত সম্পর্ক কেবল আনুষ্ঠানিক কূটনৈতিক সৌজন্যের মধ্যে সীমাবদ্ধ নয় সীমান্ত নিরাপত্তা, সন্ত্রাসবাদ দমন, পানি বণ্টন, বাণিজ্য ও ট্রানজিট সবকিছুই এই সম্পর্কের সঙ্গে ওতপ্রোতভাবে জড়িত। ফলে অনির্বাচিত সরকারকে গুরুত্ব না দেওয়ার ভারতের ঘোষণা ঢাকার জন্য একটি পরিষ্কার সংকেত বহন করে রাজনৈতিক বৈধতা দুর্বল হলে আঞ্চলিক আস্থাও টেকসই হয় না।
এই প্রেক্ষাপটে আরেকটি গুরুত্বপূর্ণ বিষয় বিবেচনায় আসে। দক্ষিণ এশিয়ায় চীন ক্রমশ প্রভাব বিস্তার করছে, বিশেষ করে রাজনৈতিক অনিশ্চয়তা ও ক্ষমতার শূন্যতার সুযোগ নিয়ে। অনির্বাচিত বা দুর্বল সরকারগুলো অনেক সময় বিকল্প শক্তির দিকে ঝুঁকে পড়ে। ভারতের এই বক্তব্য সেই প্রবণতার বিপরীতমুখী একটি কৌশলগত অবস্থানও নির্দেশ করে দিল্লি স্পষ্ট করে দিচ্ছে, তারা স্থিতিশীল, গণতান্ত্রিক ও বৈধ অংশীদারের সঙ্গেই দীর্ঘমেয়াদি সম্পর্ক গড়ে তুলতে আগ্রহী।
বাংলাদেশের জন্য বার্তাটি তাই দ্বিমুখী। একদিকে এটি অভ্যন্তরীণ রাজনীতিতে গণতান্ত্রিক প্রক্রিয়ার গুরুত্ব নতুন করে স্মরণ করিয়ে দেয়, অন্যদিকে আঞ্চলিক ও আন্তর্জাতিক রাজনীতিতে গ্রহণযোগ্যতা অর্জনের বাস্তব শর্তও স্পষ্ট করে তোলে। শুধু ক্ষমতায় থাকা নয়, জনগণের ম্যান্ডেট ও রাজনৈতিক বৈধতাই আন্তর্জাতিক সম্পর্কের প্রধান ভিত্তি এই সত্য আবারও সামনে আসে।
 ভারতের সেনাপ্রধানের মন্তব্য কোনো আকস্মিক বা বিচ্ছিন্ন উচ্চারণ নয় এটি সময়ের বাস্তবতায় দাঁড়িয়ে দেওয়া এক সুস্পষ্ট কূটনৈতিক ইঙ্গিত। বাংলাদেশের ভবিষ্যৎ রাজনৈতিক পথচলায় এই বার্তাকে উপেক্ষা করার সুযোগ সীমিত। গণতন্ত্র, স্থিতিশীলতা ও বৈধতার সমন্বয়ই কেবল একটি রাষ্ট্রকে শক্ত, সম্মানজনক ও বিশ্বাসযোগ্য আঞ্চলিক অবস্থানে পৌঁছে দিতে পারে।

Celebrating the Good Mother

On Sunday, November 23, the feast of Christ the King and the anniversary of the passing of our Foundress, Henriette Aymer de la Chevalerie, the SS.CC. brothers and sisters of the Rome communities gathered at the General House on Via Rivarone. They held especially in their hearts the SS.CC. sisters, brothers, and lay members throughout the world, as well as a special intention for peace. They began with the Eucharist, presided over by Enrique Ramírez Capetillo sscc, who highlighted the following in his homily:

“The Good Mother was a promoter of community solidarity. She encouraged the sharing of personnel, goods, and fraternal services.
However, she knew that solidarity was not only about money or resources but about giving something of oneself—presence, time, and love. It is about offering one’s own life. Her vows of February 1801 end with these words: ‘I have offered my life… I dared, despite my unworthiness, to offer myself as a victim for all. God accepted this holocaust; the sufferings, illnesses, and mortifications imposed on his servant as compensation for sinners are proof of this.’ She offers herself to God as a victim of expiation and reparation for souls in general.
‘I have vowed to be crucified in everything, meaning that from the heart, spirit, will, and action, I must not only accept all crosses, all sufferings, all adversities that come my way, but say: even more, Lord! … so that in the smallest details of life, something indifferent in itself—if it displeases me—I must not refuse it.’
The central axis of her interior life with God could be summarized in one word: surrender—total, free, without reserve or compensation. She expresses this in short and varied formulas that continually flow as advice to others or as desires for herself: ‘all for God,’ ‘do not think so much about yourself,’ ‘here I am, my God.’

Today, as we celebrate the anniversary of the Good Mother’s death, we celebrate her life, which in so many ways became a sign of the Kingdom to come. Enriqueta, through her self-giving, becomes herself a proclamation of the Love that lives.”
After the Eucharist, an aperitif and a fraternal meal followed.

Célébrer la Bonne Mère
Le dimanche 23 novembre, fête du Christ Roi et anniversaire de la Pâque de notre Fondatrice, Henriette Aymer de la Chevalerie, les frères et sœurs des communautés sscc de Rome se sont réunis à la Maison Générale de la Via Rivarone. Ils ont porté dans leur prière les sœurs, frères et laïcs sscc du monde entier, ainsi qu’une intention particulière pour la paix. Ils ont commencé par l’Eucharistie, présidée par Enrique Ramírez Capetillo sscc, qui a souligné dans son homélie ce qui suit :

« La Bonne Mère fut une promotrice de la solidarité communautaire. Elle encourageait le partage du personnel, des biens et des services fraternels.
Cependant, elle savait que la solidarité ne se limitait pas à l’argent ou aux ressources, mais qu’elle impliquait de donner quelque chose de soi : présence, temps et amour. Il s’agit d’offrir sa propre vie. Ses vœux de février 1801 se terminent par ces mots : ‘J’ai offert ma vie… j’ai osé, malgré mon indignité, m’offrir comme victime pour tous. Dieu a accepté cet holocauste ; les souffrances, maladies et mortifications qu’il a imposées à sa servante comme compensation pour les pécheurs en sont la preuve.’ Elle s’offre à Dieu comme victime d’expiation et de réparation pour les âmes en général.

‘J’ai fait vœu d’être crucifiée en tout, c’est-à-dire que, du cœur, de l’esprit, de la volonté et de l’action, je dois non seulement accepter toutes les croix, toutes les souffrances, toutes les contrariétés qui se présentent, mais dire : encore plus, Seigneur ! … De sorte que, dans les plus petits détails de la vie, une chose indifférente en soi, si elle me contrarie, je ne dois pas la refuser.’
L’axe central de sa vie intérieure avec Dieu pourrait se résumer en un mot : abandon — total, gratuit, sans réserves ni compensations. Elle l’exprime dans des formules brèves et variées qui reviennent sans cesse comme conseils aux autres ou comme souhaits pour elle-même : ‘toute à Dieu’, ‘ne pense pas tant à toi’, ‘me voici, mon Dieu’.

Aujourd’hui, alors que nous célébrons l’anniversaire de la mort de la Bonne Mère, nous célébrons sa vie, qui de multiples façons est devenue un signe du Royaume qui vient. Enriqueta, par son don de soi, devient elle-même une annonce de l’Amour vivant. »
Après l’Eucharistie a suivi un apéritif et un repas fraternel.

Trust is so important for relationships because we need to know that we can rely on, depend on, and count on someone in order to have a healthy relationship.

What do you do when you’re in a relationship in which trust has been broken, but you have a desire to rebuild that trust?

Forgiving a person who has sinned against us means that we will no longer hold the sin against the offender. It does not mean that the relationship returns to where it was before.

There are three key ingredients to start rebuilding trust in a relationship after trust has been broken. Repentance. Forgiveness. And Reconciliation.

Betrayal is a bitter experience and produces a range of emotions: fury, resentment, heartbreak, numbness, humiliation, rejection, hurt, insecurity, and feeling unsafe. Betrayal can shatter the world you live in.

It would be safer to live in isolation with no pain or crying from broken relationships, but the problem is that we are designed by God to live in a relationship with each other. We thrive by living in relationships and wilt in isolation.

When trust is broken, restoration can be a long process determined by changing attitudes and actions of the offender. Words and tears are not enough and will never restore trust.

When an offender genuinely repents, there is an acceptance and understanding that rebuilding trust will take time.

Restoration in these situations requires clarity of confession from the offender, authentic repentance, taking responsibility, and providing restitution as appropriate. Amen

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen listed the EU’s five priorities for a peace process to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.

🎤“I would like to outline some of the core priorities for Europe as we work with Ukraine, the United States and the Coalition of the Willing on the way forward. The first priority is that any agreement should deliver a just and lasting peace. And it should ensure real security for Ukraine and Europe,” von der Leyen said, speaking at a plenary debate of the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Wednesday.

🛡️Ukraine as a sovereign nation can have no cap on the size of its military, she said.

🔒“Ukraine needs robust, long-term and credible security guarantees as part of a wider package to dissuade and deter any future attacks from Russia. And it is equally clear that any peace agreement needs to ensure that European security is guaranteed for the long-term,” von der Leyen said.

🏛️The second priority is to uphold Ukraine’s sovereignty, she continued.

🗺️“If today we legitimise and formalise the undermining of borders — we open the doors for more wars tomorrow. And we cannot let this happen,” she said, adding that “Ukraine’s future lies in the European Union” and that it is an “essential part of any security guarantee framework.”

💶The third priority, according to von der Leyen, is to secure Ukraine’s financial needs.

📑“In the last European Council, we committed ourselves to cover the financial needs of Ukraine for 2026 and 2027. On this topic we, the Commission, have presented an options paper. This includes an option on immobilized Russian assets. The next step is that the Commission is ready to present the legal text,” she said.

🤝The fourth priority is summed up in a phrase: “Nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine. Nothing about Europe without Europe. Nothing about NATO without NATO.”

👶“The last priority I would like to focus on is one that cannot be forgotten — and that is the return of each and every Ukrainian child abducted by Russia,” von der Leyen said.

🏛️The EU Commission continues to work on a draft proposal to use Russia’s immobilized assets to finance a reparations loan for Ukraine in 2026-2027. The EU leaders are expected to make a final decision at the EU summit in December.

IRCS J&K Imparts 8-Day First Aid Training to the commercial vehicle drivers and others

The Indian Red Cross Society, Jammu & Kashmir-UT successfully conducted an intensive eight-day First Aid Training Programme for the commercial vehicle drivers and others aimed at strengthening safety preparedness and equipping participants with essential life-saving skills.

The training covered a comprehensive range of First Aid procedures including CPR (Cardio-Pulmonary Resuscitation), management of bleeding, fractures, burns, choking, shock, and various medical emergencies. The sessions were designed with a strong focus on practical demonstrations and hands-on learning to ensure participants could confidently respond during real-life situations.

The training was imparted by Dr. Rita Kumari and Dr. Manpreet Kour, Medical Officers, IRCS J&K, who delivered detailed demonstrations and interactive learning sessions. They were assisted by Sh. Joginder Kumar, Pharmacist, Smt. Mohna Devi, FMPHW and Sh. Manjeet Singh supported by Ms. Vironica Marwah, Field Officer, who coordinated, assisted, and facilitated the overall training programme.

On the concluding day, Sh. Rohit Khajuria, General Secretary, IRCS J&K, personally interacted with all participants in a one-on-one conversation, reviewed their feedback, and appreciated their enthusiastic involvement throughout the eight days. He also distributed provisional certificates to the trainees as a recognition of their successful completion of the course.

Participants expressed their gratitude to the Indian Red Cross Society for providing such valuable training and shared that the skills learned would prove crucial in enhancing safety measures. The IRCS J&K reiterated its dedication to enhancing First Aid awareness and empowering individuals with the confidence to act promptly during emergencies.

Let’s talk about a question I get all the time:
“If I forgive someone… does that mean I have to reconcile with them?”

Forgiveness is vertical.
It’s between you and God.

Jesus commands us to forgive (Matthew 6:14–15) and to pray for those who mistreat us (Matthew 5:44).

He never commands us to stay in harm’s way.

Reconciliation is horizontal—and it requires repentance, safety, and truth on both sides. If those aren’t present, reconciliation isn’t restoration… it’s self-destruction.

I know this because my family has lived it.
I have a sibling who put my parents and me through decades of chaos—poor choices, addiction, manipulation, and a pattern of character that left scars on all of us.

We didn’t cut ties because his life was constantly imploding.
We cut ties because his constant implosions were detonating inside ours.

One day he crossed a line—hateful, insidious, and harmful enough that I had to call law enforcement. I was ready to send my own brother to jail.

And afterward?
He twisted grace like a weapon.
“If you all don’t let me back in, you’re not forgiving. You’re fake Christians.”

Some people become experts at turning your faith into their loophole.

So we faced an impossible choice:
Reconcile—and open the door to more abuse.

Or forgive him, genuinely pray for his healing… but refuse access to our lives.

We chose protection.
And it still took me nearly two years to forgive him fully.

Not to excuse him—
but to keep my own heart from hardening.

Forgiveness changed me.
It freed me.
That vertical work with God softened my spirit.

But reconciliation?
There’s no repentance. No safety. No fruit of transformation (Matthew 7:17).

And God does not call us to submit ourselves to unrepentant harm.

You may be living your own version of this story.

And maybe you’ve been manipulated to doubt your pain, your discernment, or even your faith.

If you wrestle with forgiveness vs. reconciliation—good.

Wrestling is evidence of an active, honest faith.

Let God shape your heart with both love and wisdom.

And remember this:
Forgiveness sets you free.
Reconciliation requires change.
Only one of those is commanded.

RJMEC warns deteriorating security threatens peace agreement, elections

The Reconstituted Joint Monitoring and Evaluation Commission (RJMEC) has warned that South Sudan’s political and security situation significantly deteriorated in the last quarter, putting the implementation of the 2018 Revitalised Peace Agreement and the conduct of the 2026 elections at serious risk.

Presenting the RJMEC Quarterly Report to the Transitional National Legislative Assembly (TNLA) on Tuesday, Ambassador Berhanu Kebede, RJMEC Chief of Staff, said the latest findings—covering 1 July to 30 September 2025—show worrying regression.

“During the reporting period, the political and security situation continued to deteriorate significantly, undermining the implementation of the revitalized peace agreement,” he told lawmakers.

Kebede said the situation worsened following the Nasir incident, describing it as a major violation of the permanent ceasefire.

“The agreement faced renewed pressure following the Nasir incident, a major violation of the permanent ceasefire, and its aftermath, which triggered arrests, prolonged detention, and judicial process, as well as several political actions detrimental to trust building between the parties to the peace agreement and its implementation,” he stated.

While the RJMEC quarterly report warned of serious violations, it also acknowledged some positive steps, especially in governance, where the legislature managed to pass a number of bills into law.

“The TNLA resumed sittings after a six-month recess and made some progress on its legislative priorities, and this is a welcome development,” Kebede noted, adding that RJMEC appreciated being invited to present its report for the third consecutive time.

However, he raised concerns about the slow pace of judicial reforms.

“The implementation of the judicial reforms as contained in the recommendations of the Ad hoc Judicial Reform Committee, the report is still pending,” Kebede said.

He added that although new judges had been appointed to the Supreme Court and Court of Appeal, deeper reforms require “the review and implementation of the judiciary act, and the reconstitution of the judicial service commission, both of which are still pending.”

The report further warned that preparations for the December 2026 elections remain far behind schedule.

“The election-related institutions, such as the National Election Commission and the Political Parties Council, continued with institutional strengthening and capacity building activities, but lacked subject funding to discharge their mandates with time, fast running out,” Kebede stated. “If urgent steps are not taken to expedite progress, then holding elections as scheduled in December 2026 may be extremely difficult.”

“We appeal to this August House to prevail upon RTGoNU to provide funding to expedite the implementation of the critical pending elections-related tasks,” he added.

Maya Angelou's poignant quote, "Hate, it has caused a lot of problems in the world, but has not solved one yet," encapsulates a profound truth about the futility and destructiveness of hatred as a force in human affairs. While the exact origin of this specific phrasing isn't tied to one of her major published works like her seminal autobiography *I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings* (1969)—where she explores themes of racism, trauma, and resilience through her own experiences of childhood abuse and segregation in the American South—it aligns seamlessly with her lifelong philosophy of empathy, forgiveness, and human connection. Angelou, born Marguerite Annie Johnson in 1928, rose from a tumultuous early life marked by racial prejudice, sexual assault at age seven (which led to years of selective mutism), and single motherhood as a teenager, to become a celebrated poet, memoirist, civil rights activist, and the first Black woman to recite a poem at a U.S. presidential inauguration (Bill Clinton's in 1993). Her words often drew from personal and collective Black experiences under systemic oppression, yet she consistently advocated for transcending hate through love and understanding, as seen in her broader oeuvre, including essays, speeches, and interviews. This quote, frequently cited in compilations of her wisdom, likely emerged from her reflections on civil rights struggles, where she worked alongside figures like Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X, witnessing how hatred fueled violence but never yielded lasting justice. It serves as a timeless rebuke to those who wield hate as a tool, reminding us that it perpetuates cycles of suffering without offering resolution.

To unpack the quote's layers, consider first how hate "has caused a lot of problems in the world." History is replete with examples where hatred—rooted in fear, ignorance, or power imbalances—has ignited catastrophic conflicts and injustices. On a global scale, the Holocaust during World War II stands as a stark illustration: Nazi ideology's virulent antisemitism and racial hatred led to the systematic murder of six million Jews and millions more, devastating Europe and scarring humanity's conscience, yet it solved no underlying societal issues like economic inequality or national insecurities; instead, it birthed the United Nations and human rights frameworks as reactive measures against such horrors. Similarly, colonial imperialism, driven by racial and cultural hatred, ravaged continents like Africa and Asia, extracting resources and subjugating populations, only to leave legacies of poverty, division, and post-colonial strife that persist today—problems exacerbated, not alleviated, by the initial hate. In the American context, which deeply informed Angelou's worldview, the transatlantic slave trade and subsequent Jim Crow laws were fueled by dehumanizing hatred toward Black people, resulting in centuries of lynching, segregation, and economic disenfranchisement. The 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre, where white mobs destroyed the prosperous Black Wall Street out of envy and racism, killed hundreds and displaced thousands, solving nothing but intensifying racial tensions that echoed into the civil rights era. Even in modern times, as of 2025, hate-driven events like the rise of extremist groups, cyberbullying epidemics, or geopolitical conflicts—such as ongoing tensions in the Middle East where ethnic and religious hatred prolongs wars without diplomatic breakthroughs—continue to breed refugees, economic ruin, and generational trauma. Angelou's quote underscores that hate acts as a multiplier of misery, often manifesting in violence, discrimination, and social fragmentation, but it lacks the constructive power to address root causes like inequality or misunderstanding.

Yet, the quote's core insight lies in its second clause: hate "has not solved one yet." This highlights hatred's inherent impotence as a problem-solver, contrasting it with positive forces like compassion, education, and dialogue that Angelou championed throughout her life. For instance, in the civil rights movement, while hate from segregationists led to bombings like the 1963 Birmingham church attack that killed four Black girls, it was the nonviolent resistance inspired by love and justice—embodied in King's "I Have a Dream" speech and Angelou's own advocacy—that dismantled legal apartheid through the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and Voting Rights Act of 1965. These victories didn't erase hate, but they demonstrated that solutions emerge from empathy, not enmity. On a personal level, Angelou's own story exemplifies this: After her rapist's murder following her testimony against him, she fell silent for five years, internalizing guilt and pain, but it was through literature, mentorship, and self-expression—acts of love and healing—that she found her voice, eventually becoming a global icon. She often spoke of forgiveness not as weakness but as liberation, arguing in interviews that holding onto hate poisons the hater more than the hated, a sentiment echoed in psychological research showing how chronic resentment leads to stress-related illnesses without resolving interpersonal conflicts. In contemporary society, movements like #MeToo or Black Lives Matter reveal how exposing hate (sexual harassment, police brutality) can spark change, but only when channeled into systemic reforms rather than reciprocal animosity. Angelou's wisdom here is pragmatic: Hate might rally the aggrieved temporarily, but it blinds us to nuanced solutions, fostering division over unity. Instead, she urged building bridges, as in her poem "On the Pulse of Morning," where she envisions a diverse America united by shared humanity.

This quote's enduring relevance in 2025 stems from a world still grappling with polarized politics, social media-fueled echo chambers, and rising hate crimes—reportedly up 12% in the U.S. alone last year, targeting groups based on race, religion, or orientation. Angelou, who passed in 2014, would likely see parallels to her era in today's debates over immigration, AI ethics, or climate justice, where hate-mongering scapegoats vulnerable populations without tackling complexities like resource scarcity or technological displacement. By framing hate as a cause without a cure, she invites introspection: What if we redirected that energy toward understanding? Her life, marked by triumphs over adversity without bitterness, models this—transforming pain into art that inspires millions. Ultimately, the quote is a call to action, reminding us that true progress demands love's labor: educating the ignorant, empathizing with the other, and forging equitable systems. In a divided age, it's a beacon that hate's legacy is merely more problems, while solutions bloom from its antithesis.

Peace comes when you stop taking responsibility for things that are beyond your control or not meant for you to fix.

Here’s a deeper breakdown:
   •   “Peace begins”
Peace isn’t something you find outside yourself; it starts internally, with a shift in mindset.
   •   “The moment you stop trying to control”
Much of our stress comes from the urge to manage outcomes, people, or situations. Control often creates anxiety because life is unpredictable.
   •   “What isn’t yours to carry”
This refers to burdens that don’t belong to you—other people’s choices, emotions, expectations, past mistakes, or the future’s uncertainty.

When you carry what isn’t yours—other people’s problems, guilt you don’t deserve, or outcomes you can’t influence—you drain yourself emotionally. Letting go doesn’t mean you stop caring; it means you recognize your limits and respect the boundary between what you can influence and what you must accept.

In practice, this can mean:
   •   Allowing others to make their own choices, even when you disagree
   •   Releasing the need for constant approval or perfection
   •   Accepting that some things unfold without your permission
   •   Choosing self-compassion over self-blame

Ultimately, the sentence teaches that peace is not control—it’s acceptance with wisdom. When you carry only what is truly yours, your mind becomes lighter, and peace naturally follows.

Humans have a much longer childhood than other mammals — so we can learn the nuances of social cohesion and how to work within different groups. Kids and teens need many, many hours, days, months and years *in the company* of other people in order for their brains to wire up properly.

Washington Welcomes Release of 18 Cambodian Soldiers, Backs Cambodia–Thailand Peace Process

Washington, D.C., 31 December 2025 — The United States has welcomed the continued efforts of the governments of Cambodia and Thailand to uphold the ceasefire agreement reached on 27 December 2025, underscoring the importance of dialogue and restraint in advancing lasting peace and regional stability.

In an official press statement issued on 31 December, Mr. Thomas “Tommy” Pigott, Principal Deputy Spokesperson of the U.S. Department of State, affirmed that the sustained observance of the ceasefire reflects the firm commitment of both Cambodia and Thailand to peace through the full and faithful implementation of the Kuala Lumpur Peace Accords.

The United States further welcomed Thailand’s release of 18 Cambodian soldiers as a constructive and confidence-building measure, describing the move as a positive step toward restoring neighborly relations and rebuilding mutual trust between the two countries.

Washington reiterated its readiness to continue supporting both governments as they move forward with the critical implementation measures agreed upon under the Joint Declaration of 26 October 2025, emphasizing that consistent adherence to these commitments remains essential for consolidating peace and ensuring long-term stability along the Cambodia–Thailand border.

Media literacy is the ability to access, analyze, evaluate, and create media thoughtfully, which is essential in a world where information spreads quickly through news, videos, and social media. It helps people determine what to trust, what to question, and what to share responsibly. Media literacy is important because not all online information is accurate or complete, algorithms can amplify misinformation, and poor evaluation skills can lead to being misled. By being media literate, individuals are better equipped to make informed decisions and think critically about the content they consume every day.

Practicing media literacy involves checking the credibility of the source, looking for evidence supported by reliable data, being aware of bias or emotional language, and verifying information through other trusted outlets. For example, a claim that drinking lemon water cures serious illnesses may come from an unreliable personal blog, lack scientific evidence, use exaggerated language, and be unsupported by reputable health organizations. This makes the claim untrustworthy and not worth sharing. Overall, media literacy empowers people to pause, question information, and choose wisely before believing or spreading it.

My side of the story doesn't matter now. Life happened, it hurt, I recovered, but most importantly I learned who deserves a seat at my table and who will never sit there again. This is the energy you reach when you've truly healed. You stop needing people to understand your perspective. 

You stop trying to explain yourself to those who refused to listen. You stop caring whether they know the truth or believe their own narrative. Your side of the story doesn't matter now because you've moved past needing validation from people who never valued you in the first place. You've made peace with what happened, and that peace doesn't require anyone else's approval.

Life happened. It brought betrayal, disappointment, heartbreak, loss. It hurt deeply. There were moments you thought you wouldn't survive, moments you questioned everything, moments you felt completely broken. But you did survive. You recovered. You put yourself back together, learned from the pain, and became stronger because of it. 

And through that healing process, you gained the most valuable gift: discernment. You learned who actually showed up for you and who disappeared when things got hard. You learned who celebrated your growth and who secretly hoped you'd stay broken. You learned who deserves access to your life and who lost that privilege permanently.

Now you protect your peace fiercely. You know who deserves a seat at your table, the people who showed up, who stayed loyal, who supported you without conditions, who proved their place in your life. And you know who will never sit there again, the ones who betrayed you, abandoned you, disrespected you, took advantage of your kindness, or showed you their true colors when you needed them most. 

You're not angry anymore. You're not bitter. You're just clear. Crystal clear about boundaries, about standards, about who gets access to your energy, your time, your space, your heart.

So to everyone who's reached this level of healing, this level of clarity, protect that peace. Your side of the story doesn't need to be told, understood, or validated by people who already decided what to believe. 

What matters is that you know your truth, you've recovered from the pain, and you've learned who deserves to be in your life moving forward. Some people lost their seat at your table, and that's okay. Your table is more peaceful without them. Keep it that way.

IRCS J&K Imparts 8-Day First Aid Training to the commercial vehicle drivers and others

The Indian Red Cross Society, Jammu & Kashmir-UT successfully conducted an intensive eight-day First Aid Training Programme for the commercial vehicle drivers and others aimed at strengthening safety preparedness and equipping participants with essential life-saving skills.

The training covered a comprehensive range of First Aid procedures including CPR (Cardio-Pulmonary Resuscitation), management of bleeding, fractures, burns, choking, shock, and various medical emergencies. The sessions were designed with a strong focus on practical demonstrations and hands-on learning to ensure participants could confidently respond during real-life situations.

The training was imparted by Dr. Rita Kumari and Dr. Manpreet Kour, Medical Officers, IRCS J&K, who delivered detailed demonstrations and interactive learning sessions. They were assisted by Sh. Joginder Kumar, Pharmacist, Smt. Mohna Devi, FMPHW and Sh. Manjeet Singh supported by Ms. Vironica Marwah, Field Officer, who coordinated, assisted, and facilitated the overall training programme.

On the concluding day, Sh. Rohit Khajuria, General Secretary, IRCS J&K, personally interacted with all participants in a one-on-one conversation, reviewed their feedback, and appreciated their enthusiastic involvement throughout the eight days. He also distributed provisional certificates to the trainees as a recognition of their successful completion of the course.

Participants expressed their gratitude to the Indian Red Cross Society for providing such valuable training and shared that the skills learned would prove crucial in enhancing safety measures. The IRCS J&K reiterated its dedication to enhancing First Aid awareness and empowering individuals with the confidence to act promptly during emergencies.

HOW TO PROCESS YOUR FEELINGS (Without Being Controlled by Them)

Feelings are not problems to fix.
They are messages to understand.

Most suffering doesn’t come from emotions themselves —
it comes from resisting them, suppressing them, or becoming lost inside them.

Here’s how to process your feelings with awareness, not avoidance:

1. PAUSE
Before reacting, pause.

Take a breath.
Slow your body down.

This pause creates space between what you feel and what you do.
In that space, wisdom can arise.

In Buddhism, this moment of pause is mindfulness —
the ability to see clearly instead of acting blindly.

Not every emotion needs an immediate response.
Some only need your attention.

2. NAME IT
Give the feeling a name.

Anger.
Sadness.
Fear.
Disappointment.
Joy.

Naming an emotion takes away its power to overwhelm you.
What is named becomes observed, not possessed.

You are not “angry.”
Anger is arising within you.

This subtle shift reminds you:
You are the observer, not the emotion.

3. FEEL IT (WITHOUT JUDGMENT)
Sit with the emotion instead of pushing it away.

Don’t label it as good or bad.
Don’t rush to escape it.
Don’t shame yourself for feeling it.

Feelings are like waves —
they rise, peak, and fall if you don’t fight them.

In Buddhist practice, this is equanimity:
allowing what is, without clinging or aversion.

What you resist persists.
What you allow, softens.

4. ASK WHY
Gently explore the root.

What triggered this feeling?
What expectation was unmet?
What attachment was touched?

Often, emotions reveal hidden truths —
unhealed wounds, unmet needs, or false stories we tell ourselves.

This is not about blaming yourself or others.
It’s about understanding.

Awareness turns pain into insight.

5. RELEASE
Once understood, let it move through you.

Breathe deeply.
Write it out.
Speak to someone you trust.
Sit quietly and watch it fade.

Feelings are energy.
If they are not expressed or released, they become stored tension.

Release does not mean forgetting.
It means not carrying unnecessary weight.

6. SHIFT
After release, gently redirect your energy.

Toward calm.
Toward kindness.
Toward something constructive.

Not as an escape —
but as a conscious choice.

This is wisdom in action:
choosing peace over rumination, growth over repetition.

FINAL TRUTH.

Feelings are temporary guests.
They come to teach, not to stay forever.

Suffering begins when you cling.
Freedom begins when you observe, understand, and let go.

You don’t need to control your emotions.
You need to befriend them — and know when to let them leave.

🧘‍♂️ Nothing that arises is meant to be held onto forever.
HAPPY GOOD DAY

Reconciliation — Message for the Collective

This energy comes forward gently, not to reopen wounds, but to soften them.

Reconciliation isn’t always about returning to what once was. Sometimes it’s about making peace with what happened so it no longer has power over you. For some, this is an actual reunion… a conversation long avoided, an apology finally offered, a bridge slowly being rebuilt. For others, it’s an internal reconciliation: forgiving yourself for choices made in survival, not failure.

The collective is being asked to release pride, fear, and the need to be “right.” Healing flows when the heart leads instead of the mind keeping score. This does not mean forgetting, excusing, or allowing old patterns to repeat. It means choosing peace over punishment.

If reconciliation is meant to happen externally, it will come with accountability, honesty, and changed behavior… not empty words. If those elements are missing, the reconciliation is with your own heart, allowing yourself to move forward without carrying resentment as a shield.

A reminder for you now:
✨ You are allowed to heal without reopening every door.
✨ You are allowed to accept an apology…even if it comes from within.
✨ Peace is not weakness; it is power reclaimed.

I’m learning this alongside my children — and trying to teach it as I go.

That being loving doesn’t mean giving until there’s nothing left.
That kindness doesn’t require hurting yourself.
That you don’t have to set yourself on fire to keep others warm.

As a mum, it’s tempting to believe we’re meant to absorb everything.
Every feeling. Every need. Every mess.
To be endlessly available, endlessly patient, endlessly self-sacrificing.
But I don’t want my children to grow up thinking love should feel like exhaustion.

I want them to know they can care deeply and have boundaries.
That it’s okay to say no without guilt.
That their needs matter too — even when they’re kind, generous, and empathetic people.

So I’m trying to model it.
Resting without apologising.
Saying “that’s too much for me right now.”
Choosing steadiness over burnout.

Because one day, they’ll be adults navigating relationships of their own.

And I want them to know this, in their bones:
You are allowed to protect your peace.
You are allowed to stay whole.
Love should never require you to disappear.

🐺 Denmark | Wolf encounter near homes highlights limits of coexistence
On the evening of 10 January 2026, a 14-year-old girl encountered a wolf just meters from her home in Oksbøl, south-west Jutland. The wolf appeared suddenly on the road, fewer than 200 metres from the forest edge. The girl, understandably frightened, filmed the animal as it remained close for several moments before retreating.
Following the incident, Danish authorities immediately activated the local wolf protection and monitoring group. Tracks were examined, the video was reviewed by authorities, and fox lights (flashing deterrent lights) were installed to push wolves back toward the forest. Camera traps are now being deployed to monitor movements and confirm whether the wolf remains in the area.
The Danish Minister for the Environment, Jeppe Bruus, stated that the incident is taken seriously and confirmed that lethal control is an option if the wolf shows further problematic behaviour. 
Experts later described the wolf as likely young, inexperienced and recently dispersed from its pack, stressing that such animals can behave unpredictably and show reduced flight distance when stressed or disoriented. Authorities acknowledged that the situation was extremely unpleasant for the girl, even if it was not officially classified as “dangerous”.
Read more here: https://jyllands-posten.dk/
⚠️ Why dismissing concerns is irresponsible
It is also important to be honest about recent European experience.
In the Netherlands and other countries, wolves have approached people, attempted attacks and, in some cases, injured humans. These incidents are documented and investigated by authorities — they are not hypothetical scenarios.
Against this background, it is irresponsible to simply label close encounters with children near homes as “normal” or “unproblematic”. Normal behaviour for a stressed or disoriented wolf does not automatically mean an acceptable risk for society.

Our vision is simple. To inspire kids to see coexistence as a way of life.

By teaching respect, curiosity, and understanding from an early age, we can build a generation of Canadians who see predators as valued, respected members of our ecosystems.

Despite decades of scientific research, policy interventions, and public awareness campaigns aimed primarily at adults, fear-based narratives and misinformation continue to dominate public discourse around apex predators. This has resulted in reactive decision-making, polarized debates, and repeated cycles of conflict that undermine both conservation outcomes and community safety.

Across Canada, human–wildlife conflict remains one of the greatest barriers to conservation. While science and policy play critical roles, lasting change begins with education and with reshaping the stories we tell our children about the wild.

Even with growing environmental awareness, most provincial curricula barely touch on predator ecology or coexistence. Children often grow up fearful or misinformed about the species that maintain ecological balance.

Meanwhile, the mental health crisis and disconnection from nature among youth is deepening. Evidence shows that time in nature improves emotional regulation, empathy, and cognitive development. This is key to building resilient, environmentally literate communities.

What we know: 

🔹 Early nature experiences build empathy and ecological literacy.

🔹 Students in outdoor learning programs show higher wellbeing and stronger stewardship values.

🔹 Education is one of the most powerful tools for long-term conservation.

With this in mind, EWC is developing an innovative education initiative designed to inspire a new generation of coexistence leaders across Western Canada. This multi-faceted program will connect children, youth, and educators to the landscapes and species that define Canada’s ecological identity.

Leaders of the Moru Congregation of the Episcopal Church of South Sudan say churches belonging to them were attacked in Juba during Sunday prayers, and they blame the Juba Diocese for the violence.

Speaking at a press conference in Juba on Monday, Canon Oneil Yosia Daima said Moru churches in Nyakuron, Munuki and Gudele were attacked on January 11, 2026. He said police and security officers were involved and worshippers were beaten while praying.

According to Daima, pastors linked to the Juba Diocese went to Nyakuron Moru Church with the aim of forcing back church leaders whom the Moru Congregation had already rejected, including Rev. Gibson Ali Roba.

He explained that the Moru Congregation has existed for 88 years and that its churches were built by members on land they acquired themselves, without any support from the Juba Diocese.

Daima said the congregation never accepted a 2008 decision by the Juba Diocese to dissolve it, saying churches cannot be dissolved by orders. He added that the Moru Congregation officially returned to its original status on May 10, 2025.

He said church leaders had received information days earlier that an attack was being planned and wrote letters to the Archbishop of Juba Diocese and state authorities to stop it, but no action was taken.

On the morning of January 11, Daima said pastors accompanied by Central Equatoria State police officers forcefully entered Nyakuron Moru Church and started beating worshippers with sticks, hoes and iron bars. Many people, including women and youth, were badly injured.

He said 15 injured people were taken to Juba Teaching Hospital, including four in critical condition. However, police later removed them from the hospital and detained them at Mauna Police Station instead of allowing them to continue treatment.

Daima also said attempts were made to forcefully enter Moru churches in Munuki and Gudele, but church members resisted and stopped the attacks.

The Moru Congregation said it has a letter dated January 7, 2026, which allegedly requested security support for the operation. Daima said one officer even threatened worshippers with a grenade and a pistol.

The congregation said it may take legal action against those involved in the attacks and will use all legal means to seek justice.

While remaining open to dialogue, the Moru Congregation said it wants its independence in managing its church affairs and finances to be respected. It called on church leaders to stop violence and resolve issues peacefully, warning that such incidents damage the image of the church.

The office of the Primate of the Episcopal Church of South Sudan said it would respond to the allegations at a later time.

Coexistence with wolves isn’t a theory, it’s already working all over the world when we choose prevention over punishment.

Globally ranchers are using range riders, human presence, and proactive monitoring to prevent conflict: reducing farm animal losses without killing wolves. We see the same tools succeed:

• Livestock guardian dogs protecting herds in Portugal & northern Spain
• Indigenous stewardship guiding coexistence in Canada and beyond
• Adaptive herding in Mongolia
• Collaborative management in British Columbia

The lesson is simple, and applicable here:
👉 Conflict drops when we invest in prevention, partnership, and people on the ground.
👉 Killing wolves doesn’t solve conflict, it escalates it.
👉 Nonlethal tools work when they’re prioritized.

The question isn’t whether coexistence works, it’s whether we’re willing to apply what already work.

🐺 Let’s fund prevention.
🤝 Let’s support ranchers who choose coexistence.
🌱 Let’s stop repeating failed solutions.

Respect of Culture, Religion, and Ethnicity is the unshakable foundation of sustainable Peace and Unity in South Sudan: A case of Mundari Festival. 

By: Guot G. Akol 
Juba, 16th January 2026. 

South Sudan’s greatest strength lies in the richness of its people—diverse cultures, vibrant traditions, deep-rooted beliefs, and resilient communities. In a nation shaped by many identities, true unity emerges not when differences disappear, but when every group’s heritage is honored and respected.

Recent cultural celebrations across the country continue to prove this truth. The current Mundari Cultural Festival has brought people together through music, dance, cattle culture, traditional arts, and communal ceremonies. These gatherings invite South Sudanese from different regions and ethnicities to witness, appreciate, and celebrate Mundari heritage. Such a festival becomes more than a cultural showcase—it becomes a bridge, strengthening understanding and reducing the misconceptions that fuel division.

Similarly, the Pojulu Cultural Festival, held previously, highlighted the songs, rich history, and values of the Pojulu people. It reminded the nation that every community contributes something essential to the identity of South Sudan. Both festivals serve as living proof that respect for cultural expression encourages harmony and reinforces national cohesion.

For South Sudan to achieve lasting unity, sustainable development, and shared prosperity, we must fully embrace the diversity that defines us. Respecting one another’s cultural values, traditional customs, ethnic identities, and religious beliefs is not optional—it is the foundation upon which peace must be built. When every citizen feels seen, valued, and protected, trust grows. With trust comes cooperation, and with cooperation comes progress.

As a nation, we have the opportunity to transform our diversity into a source of strength rather than division. By promoting cultural festivals, supporting inter-community dialogue, and teaching younger generations to honor differences, we strengthen the social fabric that binds South Sudan together.

Together, in unity and mutual respect, we shall build a peaceful, prosperous, and unified South Sudan.

Chapter 1: The True Love Movement Bringing Salvation to Asia and the World
This speech was given at the founding assembly of the Women's Federation for Peace in Asia, held on September 17, 1991 at the Tokyo Bay Hotel, in Tokyo, Japan.
Distinguished president of the rally, members of the Women's Federation for Peace in Asia, and my fellow women leaders who have gathered here from all parts of Japan:
Today we stand at a turning point on the road marking great and historic changes. I offer my heartfelt congratulations to the Women's Federation for Peace in Asia for its rapid growth in the five years since its inauguration to the point that you are now able to host this splendid rally.
In little more than forty years since you emerged from the ruins of a devastating war, your nation, Japan, has accomplished the greatest economic turnaround in the world. This feat, which may well be termed a miracle of modern times, is now the envy of people throughout the world. More laudable still is the fact that, even while achieving such amazing industrial developments, Japan has endeavored to sustain the traditional values particular to the East and has shown a great commitment and effort in family and social education.
Underlying such wonderful success is the efforts you women have made, as kind and self-sacrificing mothers and devoted wives. It is you, more than anyone else, who made your families healthy and strong while you nurtured and watched over them. Since it is your work as women that stands as the basis of this success, I as a woman also feel proud.
Leaders of the Women's Federation for Peace in Asia! The world is now on the brink of a great historic transition period. The wartime policies of communism caused bloodshed ravaging millions of human beings. In the seventy years since the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917, communism came to rule more than half of the world, plunging all humanity into the pits of fear and anguish.
New leaders finally have lowered that red flag, and we are watching it disappear into the mists of history. This shows that the worldview based on atheism, with state policies that deny God, has come to ruin. The philosophy of conflict, struggle, and hatred has revealed its limits, and the one-party dictatorial structure of communism is now facing its own demise.
However, this event leads to an important realization: the downfall of communism does not mean the victory of the free democratic world. Just as communism, which asserted economic equality, was brought to its end by the collapse of its own economy, society in the free democratic world, which cries out for freedom, is also on the verge of breakdown due to extreme confusion regarding values.
Corruption, sexual immorality, violence, and addiction are multiplying under the shadow of so-called freedom. They are causing the dissolution of that free society.
The Cold War era that lasted for more than forty years after the Second World War is coming to an end. It was a game with losers on both sides and no victor. This makes us realize that now is the time for a new salvation to reach both the communist world and the free democratic world.
Capitalism and communism originated from the West and were based on material values. They have revealed their limited ability to satisfy the true desires of human beings, who have both a spirit and a physical body. We are living in an age when it has become absolutely necessary for Eastern society, with its emphasis on spiritual values, to play a central role.
Historically, the Asian continent has served as the cradle of spiritual civilization, and the time has finally arrived for the East to fulfill its global mission as the prime mover of spirituality. That is why this age has come to be called the Asia-Pacific era and why it is another great historic transition period.
Most respected women leaders! I believe that this society was able to do an excellent job of protecting its historical values during the past half century. While Japanese industry developed and the nation became economically affluent, women voluntarily declined the opportunity for special treatment. Instead, they protected their families with devotion and sacrifice.
In truth, the most important of all traditional values are the values centered on the family. There is an old saying to the effect, “When one's family is harmonious, all goes well.” What this means is that the family is the basis of peace. And the most important factor in forming such a family is true love.
The word love has various meanings. However, I am speaking here about true love, which refers to absolute love centered on God. In other words, true love is to love even someone who seems impossible to love. In true love, one must love even one's enemies. Furthermore, true love is the sacrificial love of giving one's life for others. Therefore, in true love, antagonisms and conflicts among individuals, societies, and nations are transcended and dissolved.

L’épuration ethnique des communautés juives du monde musulman de 1948 à 2025 ! 🤔✡️☪️

✡️ Pendant plus de treize siècles sous la domination musulmane, s’est développée dans le monde arabo-persan une forme unique de coexistence entre juifs et musulmans. Ces communautés juives constituaient des éléments organiques et anciens, des sociétés du Moyen-Orient et d'Afrique du Nord. Leur présence datait parfois de l’Antiquité, précédant même l'arrivée de l'Islam. En 1948 ils étaient encore près de 900.000, aujourd’hui ils ne sont plus que quelques milliers, une disparition démographique aussi rapide que radicale.

✡️ Contrairement à l’Europe chrétienne médiévale, marquée par des expulsions massives, des pogroms et l’accusation de déicide, le monde musulman offrait un cadre juridique de protection aux « Gens du Livre » (juifs et chrétiens), le statut de dhimmi. En échange d’un impôt (jizya) et d’une position sociale subordonnée, les communautés juives jouissaient d’une autonomie juridique et religieuse importante. Elles prospérèrent dans le commerce, l’artisanat, la finance et la vie intellectuelle, produisant des figures majeures comme Maïmonide.

✡️ Juifs et musulmans vivaient côte à côte, partageant la langue, la cuisine et de nombreux aspects de la culture matérielle. Les périodes de tensions existaient, mais elles n’atteignirent jamais l’échelle ni la nature systématique des persécutions européennes. La violence anti-juive était plus souvent liée à des crises politiques ou économiques ponctuelles, qu’à un antisémitisme théologique structurel.

✡️ Le 19e siècle avec la colonisation européenne et les réformes de l’Empire ottoman, introduisit des changements profonds. Le statut de dhimmi fut officiellement aboli, ouvrant la voie à une émancipation légale. Cependant cette période vit aussi la montée d’un nationalisme arabe et, plus tard d’un islam politique, qui allaient redéfinir la place des minorités.

✡️ La création de l’État d’Israël en 1948 et la guerre qui s’ensuivit, constituèrent un point de rupture cataclysmique. L’établissement d’un État juif souverain, fut perçu comme un acte de guerre. Dans de nombreux pays, les juifs désormais identifiés à l’« ennemi sioniste », passèrent du statut de minorité tolérée à celui de cinquième colonne. Une vague de violence, de lois discriminatoires, et d’expulsions se déclencha.

✡️ Les cartes et les chiffres sont implacables, ils racontent l’histoire d’une disparition presque totale en l’espace d’une génération, des communautés juives du monde musulman. Entre 1948 et le début des années 1970, environ 820 000 à 885 000 juifs quittèrent ou furent contraints de fuir les pays musulmans.

✡️ Cet exode fut massif, rapide, et forcé par les violences et les discriminations :
- Irak : l’une des communautés les plus anciennes et prospères, 140.000 âmes en 1948, il ne reste aujourd’hui que quelques individus.
- Maroc : la communauté est passée de 265.000, à moins de 2.000 âmes aujourd’hui.
- Égypte, Libye, Syrie, Yémen, Algérie : des présences multimillénaires, ont été réduites à zéro ou presque.
- Iran : la communauté juive iranienne est la plus importante de la région hors Israël, elle a été considérablement réduite de 100.000, à environ 8.500 personnes.

✡️ La majorité des réfugiés juifs séfarades des pays arabes (près de 650.000) s’installèrent en Israël, où ils constituèrent environ la moitié de la population juive. Leur intégration fut souvent difficile, marquée par des discriminations de la part de l’establishment ashkénaze (européen). Ce n’est que récemment, que leur héritage culturel et leur récit historique ont commencé à être pleinement reconnus.

✡️ Cet exode provoqué par cette épuration ethnique, est longtemps resté un « récit oublié », éclipsé dans le discours international par la question des réfugiés palestiniens. Aujourd’hui il est de plus en plus revendiqué en Israël, comme un élément central du conflit, servant parfois d’argument pour contrer les demandes palestiniennes de « droit au retour ».

✡️ L’effacement quasi total des juifs du monde arabe en moins de trois décennies, constitue l’un des bouleversements démographiques et culturels les plus brutaux du 20e siècle. Il marque la fin tragique d’un modèle de coexistence séculaire, vulnérable aux soubresauts de l’histoire et des nationalismes. Il raconte comment une relation complexe faite de protection, de subordination, d’échanges et de tensions, a pu se briser sous le poids de l’idéologie et de la géopolitique.

Timeline of New Media 

New media began with early computers and the internet, especially with the introduction of the World Wide Web in the 1990s. It grew rapidly in the 2000s with email, blogs, and social media. Today, smartphones, streaming platforms, and artificial intelligence make information easily accessible anytime and anywhere.

Impact on Media and Information Literacy 

New media changed how people communicate, learn, and access information. While it makes information more accessible, it also increases misinformation. Media and Information Literacy helps individuals evaluate sources, think critically, and use media ethically and responsibly.

Insights and Reflections 

This lesson shows that new media is powerful and influential. It offers many benefits but also requires awareness and responsibility. Being media literate means using media wisely, thinking critically, and making informed decisions online.

As new media continues to evolve, Media and Information Literacy becomes more important. It helps individuals adapt to digital changes, avoid misinformation, and use media in a positive and meaningful way.

Accountability vs. Enabling

Accountability isn’t punishment.
It’s love with boundaries.

When we constantly make excuses for people, cover for their mistakes, or shield them from consequences, we think we’re helping. But what we’re really doing is enabling. And enabling doesn’t heal—it delays growth.

Every time poor choices are rescued instead of addressed, responsibility is transferred. The person no longer learns to stand on their own; they learn to depend on the ones who keep saving them. Over time, that dependence turns into entitlement, resentment, and stagnation—on both sides.

True accountability says:
I care enough about you to let you feel the weight of your decisions.
It allows discomfort so growth can happen. It encourages ownership, maturity, and change.

Enabling says:
I’ll carry this for you,
until both people are exhausted and nothing improves.

Growth requires honesty. Healing requires boundaries. And love sometimes means stepping back—not because you don’t care, but because you care enough to stop participating in patterns that keep everyone stuck.

Accountability builds independence.
Enabling builds dependence.

Choose wisely. 🫶🏼

Moru Congregation Condemns Closure of Nyakuran Church in Juba

Juba, South Sudan | January 19, 2026

The leadership of the Moru Congregation of the Episcopal Church of South Sudan (ECSS) has strongly condemned the sudden closure of Nyakuran Moru Congregation Church in Juba, describing the action as unlawful, unprofessional, and a violation of freedom of worship.

In a press statement issued on Monday, the church said armed security personnel arrived in three vehicles on Sunday, January 18, 2026, shortly after the conclusion of English and Arabic services, and ordered the immediate closure of the church. The officers allegedly claimed they were acting on instructions from the Juba City Mayor but failed to present any official written authorization.

According to the statement, the service had ended peacefully and no violence or clashes had occurred inside or around the church. Church leaders said some of the security officers later admitted that they had acted on false information alleging unrest within the congregation.

The church reported that the abrupt intervention caused panic and emotional distress among worshippers, with several women collapsing from shock and residents of the surrounding neighborhood left in tears. Requests to allow prayers to conclude peacefully, even for an additional 30 minutes, were reportedly rejected.

The Moru Congregation described the incident as a serious criminal offense under national law, noting that the disruption of a peaceful religious gathering is punishable under the Penal Code. The leadership further alleged that the closure may have been carried out in collaboration with elements within the Juba Diocese seeking to take over Moru churches by force while refusing dialogue with the lawful owners of the congregations.

While reaffirming its commitment to peace and nonviolence, the church stated that it reserves the right to pursue legal action against those responsible.

The statement appealed to the Juba City Council to maintain neutrality and impartiality, respect freedom of worship, and uphold the administrative and financial autonomy of churches. It also called on the leadership of the Juba Diocese to cease inflammatory actions and engage in dialogue based on Christian principles.

The Moru Congregation urged city authorities to reopen Nyakuran Moru Congregation Church immediately, stressing that there was no legal or moral justification for its closure.

The statement was signed by Canon Onil Yosia Daima, Chairperson of the Moru Congregation Church in Juba.

להתיחס לפתרון שתי המדינות. אבל כל עוד אין הבנה בין הרבה ישראלים שיש דרך בטוחה לשלום  כל איזכור של פתרון שתי מדינות הוא רעיל. לכן אין תמה שזהו המצב.

הנה הפוסט של שאול אריאלי:

מי מאמין בשתי מדינות, ומי רק מזכיר את זה כשזה לא עולה לו קולות ?!

קצת עובדות מאיסוף רבעוני שיטתי של הציוצים של ראשי המפלגות  פה ברשת הזו

הגרף שואל שאלה פשוטה: מי באמת תומך בפתרון שתי המדינות, ומי רק מזכיר אותו כשנוח.
אצל איימן עודה ומנסור עבאס אין דרמה. יש עמדה. רציפה, עקבית, כזו שלא נעלמת כשמתקרבים לשלטון ולא מתאדה מול סקרים. אפשר לא להסכים, אבל אי אפשר להתבלבל.
אצל לפיד וגולן התמונה אחרת. התמיכה קיימת, אבל היא קופצת ונעלמת לפי עונות פוליטיות. באופוזיציה מדברים על אופק מדיני; ליד שולחן הממשלה האופק מתקפל. לא שקר, יותר תמרון פוליטי.
ואז גנץ ובנט. שנים של אפסים, עם הבהובים נדירים שנראים כמו תקלה בגרף. לא חזון, לא תהליך, בעיקר ניסוחי ביניים זהירים שמכוונים החוצה, לא פנימה.
המסקנה לא אידיאולוגית אלא אמפירית: בישראל יש מי שמחזיק פתרון שתי מדינות כעמדה, יש מי שמחזיק אותו כאפשרות, ויש מי שמחזיק אותו רק כזיכרון עמום מהרצאות בחו״ל.
זה לא עניין של ימין ושמאל, אלא של אומץ פוליטי: לומר עמדה, להתמיד בה, ולשלם מחיר ציבורי במקום להתחבא מאחורי עמימות, גם כשזה לא נוח פוליטית עכשווית.

Johnson Olony Thebo, who simultaneously serves as Deputy Chief of Defence Forces for Mobilization and Disarmament and as a commander of the Agwelek militia. Lt. Gen. Olony publicly ordered forces under his command not to spare any life—including women, children, or livestock—in Nyirol, Uror, Akobo, Fangak, and Ayod. The directive represents a grave violation of international humanitarian law (IHL) and poses an immediate and serious danger to civilian populations. Specifically, it:

1. Orders the collective and forced displacement of civilians from their habitual residences without lawful justification or provision of protection, shelter, or humanitarian assistance;

2. Effectively declares civilians legitimate military targets based on vague and arbitrary criteria, including mere proximity to opposition-controlled areas;

3. Orders the withdrawal of NGOs and UNMISS personnel, deliberately stripping civilians of protection and independent monitoring.

These actions violate the Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocols, the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, and the Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan (R-ARCSS).

The SPLM-IO warns that this directive constitutes an early indicator of genocidal intent, including forced displacement, extrajudicial killings, and collective punishment against civilian populations.

The SPLM-IO reiterates its unwavering commitment to the protection of civilians and calls on the United Nations, African Union, IGAD, and the international community to take urgent action and ensure accountability for all violations of international law.

IS THE SOUTH SUDAN COUNCIL OF CHURCHES MONETIZED OR POLITICIZED? Examining Its Silence amidst the Ongoing Turmoil in the Country.
25-1-2026
Torit

The Call to Serve
Religious institutions have historically played a critical role in defending human dignity, advocating for justice, and mediating peace during times of political crisis. In Uganda, for example, the Interreligious Council of Uganda (IRCU) demonstrated this moral responsibility when, three days after the recent presidential elections, its leaders visited the raided home of opposition figure Robert Kyagulanyi (Bobi Wine). Their public act of solidarity, offering encouragement and prayer to the affected family, affirmed the Church’s pastoral and prophetic mandate, even as political persecution persisted.

The Sudan Council of Churches, established around 1964, was founded on core principles that included advocacy for good governance, equitable representation, and peace and reconciliation. For decades, the Council upheld these values and played a visible role in national struggles, including the liberation movement that culminated in South Sudan’s independence in 2011. Today, however, questions arise regarding the Council’s diminished public voice amid the country’s prolonged crisis.

The Rhythm of Conflict
The South Sudan Council of Churches (SSCC) continues to organise workshops and forums on peace and reconciliation. While these initiatives are important, they appear increasingly disconnected from the lived realities of citizens who endure recurring cycles of violence, displacement, and insecurity. Since the outbreak of conflict in 2013, there has been limited public condemnation by the churches of the widespread abuses committed against civilians, despite their proximity to communities directly affected by the war.

This perceived silence contrasts sharply with the moral clarity the Church once demonstrated during the struggle for self-determination, raising concerns about whether its influence and resolve have weakened over time.

Political Persecution and Governance
South Sudan is also experiencing continued political repression, particularly against opposition figures who are legitimate stakeholders in the nation’s future. As these actors face intimidation, detention, and exclusion, the absence of a strong ecclesiastical response is striking, especially given the Council’s stated commitment to principles of justice, accountability, and good governance.

Fragile Peace
Repeated collapses of peace agreements suggest deeper structural and leadership failures. As a recognised moral guarantor and custodian of peace, the SSCC is uniquely positioned to urge political leaders to prioritise dialogue and respect for the rule of law. Its limited engagement in publicly challenging actions that undermine peace invites scrutiny and concern from citizens who look to the Church for moral leadership.

A Call to Renewed Moral Leadership
For many believers, scriptural mandates such as those found in Psalm 82:1–4, calling for the defence of the poor, the weak, and the oppressed, remain central to the Church’s mission. These principles demand not only pastoral care but also courageous public witness in times of injustice.

In light of ongoing war rhetoric, population displacement, and the persecution of critics and political opponents, there is a growing expectation that the South Sudan Council of Churches will more assertively exercise its moral authority. This includes speaking out against violence, condemning actions that violate human dignity, and engaging all parties to accelerate a sustainable and inclusive peace process.

Recent events, including the killing of clergy members and public statements by senior officials that endorsed indiscriminate violence coded “SPARE NO ONE”, further underscore the urgency of a clear and principled response from the Council.

The question, therefore, is not whether the South Sudan Council of Churches possesses moral authority, but whether it is prepared to exercise it fully and independently in the service of peace, justice, and national healing.

اتهمت الحركة الوطنية الديمقراطية، إحدى الاطراف الموقعة على اتفاقية السلام المُنشّطة لعام 2018 في جنوب السودان، يوم السبت، الحركة الشعبية لتحرير السودان الحاكمة بالاستيلاء الممنهج على المناصب المخصصة لأحزاب المعارضة، واصفةً ذلك بأنه “خرق جوهري” للاتفاقية.

وفي بيان صدر عقب اجتماع لجنتها التنفيذية الوطنية، سردت الحركة الديمقراطية الوطنية – بقيادة السياسي المخضرم الدكتور لام أكول أجاوين – عدة إجراءات اتخذتها الحركة الشعبية لتحرير السودان مؤخراً، والتي قالت إنها تنتهك اتفاقية السلام المُنشّطة لعام 2018 في جمهورية جنوب السودان.

وأوضحت الحركة أن الحركة الشعبية لتحرير السودان قامت من جانب واحد بعزل اثنين من محافظي المقاطعات المعينين من قبل الحركة الوطنية الديمقراطية في ولايتي أعالي النيل والوحدة – أحدهما هذا الشهر والآخر في نوفمبر/تشرين الثاني – واستبدلتهما بأعضاء من الحركة الشعبية لتحرير السودان. 

كما اتهمت الحركة الوطنية الديمقراطية الحزب الحاكم بتعيين أحد أعضائها في منصب استشاري لشؤون النوع الاجتماعي والرعاية الاجتماعية، وهو منصب كان مخصصًا للحركة بموجب اتفاقية السلام.

ووفقًا للبيان، فقد أُقيل مصطفى قاي، محافظ مقاطعة فانيكانق في ولاية أعالي النيل، في 23 يناير/كانون الثاني، وعُيّن مكانه عضو في الحركة الشعبية لتحرير السودان.

 وجاء ذلك عقب إقالة ماركو جونق ماقوك قاتلواك، محافظ مقاطعة ميانديت في ولاية الوحدة، في 21 نوفمبر/تشرين الثاني 2025، في ظروف مماثلة.

وأشارت الحركة الوطنية الديمقراطية أيضًا إلى إقالة حاكم ولاية جونقلي، الذي رشحته الحركة في فبراير/شباط 2025، وتعيين ريك قاي كوك، عضو الحركة الشعبية لتحرير السودان، مكانه.

وفي مارس/آذار 2025، أُقيل محجوب بيل توروك، أحد كبار قادة الحركة الوطنية الديمقراطية، من منصبه كحاكم لولاية جونقلي بمرسوم رئاسي بعد أن قضى عشرة أشهر في منصبه.

يوم الجمعة، أشار مفوضية مراقبة السلام (RJMEC)، خلال إحاطة قدمها لمجلس السلام والأمن التابع للاتحاد الأفريقي، إلى إجراءات أحادية الجانب من جانب الحزب الحاكم، قائلاً إن إقالة الحكومة لشخصيات معارضة من مناصب وزارية وتشريعية تقوض ترتيبات تقاسم السلطة التي تُعدّ جوهر اتفاق السلام.

وقال كاي تاب قاتشانق، المتحدث باسم الحركة الوطنية الديمقراطية “إن استيلاء الحركة الشعبية لتحرير السودان (SPLM-IG) على المناصب المخصصة لأطراف أخرى في اتفاق السلام يُشكل خرقًا جوهريًا لاتفاقية السلام المنشطة (R-ARCSS)، التي تُعدّ مصدر شرعية حكومة الوحدة الوطنية الانتقالية الحالية”.

وأضاف الحزب أن توصياته بشأن تغييرات في مناصبه داخل الحكومة الانتقالية، والتي قُدّمت وفقًا للاتفاق، لم تُلبَّ، وفي بعض الحالات لأكثر من 43 شهرًا.

ووفقًا للحركة الوطنية الديمقراطية، فإن هذه الإجراءات تُخالف بنود اتفاق السلام المتعلقة بنسب تقاسم السلطة وسلطة الترشيح للأطراف الموقعة، وتُهدد بتقويض الثقة والتعاون.

وجاء في البيان “تُظهر هذه الإجراءات والتقصيرات نية واضحة ومقلقة لاستبعاد الحركة الديمقراطية الوطنية من المشاركة الفعّالة”.

وأكد الحزب أنه أثار هذه القضية على أعلى مستويات الحكومة دون أي إجراء تصحيحي، مضيفًا أنه لا “يستجدي امتيازات” بل يطالب “بحقوقه المشروعة بموجب الاتفاقية”.

وتُعدّ الحركة الوطنية الديمقراطية جزءًا من تحالف معارضة جنوب السودان، وهو ائتلاف مُدرج في حكومة تقاسم السلطة المُشكّلة بموجب اتفاقية السلام لعام 2018 التي أنهت حربًا أهلية دامت خمس سنوات.

وقد أسفرت اتفاقية السلام لعام 2018 عن تشكيل حكومة وحدة وطنية هشة، إلا أن تنفيذها تعثّر مرارًا وتكرارًا وسط نزاعات سياسية وأعمال عنف متفرقة. ومن المقرر إجراء الانتخابات العامة في ديسمبر/كانون الأول 2026.
