In 1967, a drunk driver killed her husband while she was pregnant, leaving a disabled Black woman to raise a son alone in the Jim Crow South.

There are lives that get remembered in history books with monuments and plaques, and then there are lives like Pearline McClendon's that shaped communities through quiet determination and everyday courage. She lived 87 years, from 1934 to 2021, in Pensacola, Florida, proving that resilience isn't about grand gestures but about showing up, adapting, and refusing to let circumstances define your limits.

Pearline was born on August 6, 1934, into a world that was already hostile to Black people and would prove even more hostile to disabled Black people. She was born during the Great Depression, during Jim Crow's iron grip on the South, into a reality where being Black meant navigating daily humiliation and violence.

In the 1930s, polio was a terrifying disease that swept through communities with devastating randomness. It didn't care about race or class or geography.

It attacked children primarily, leaving some dead and others permanently disabled. Parents lived in fear during summer months when outbreaks peaked, keeping children away from public pools and crowded places.

Pearline contracted polio as a young child, just two years before Dr. Jonas Salk's vaccine would begin protecting children from the disease that had terrorized a generation. Two years.

That's how close she came to being spared. But timing is cruel sometimes, and Pearline's childhood happened just before the medical breakthrough that would have saved her from a lifetime of disability.

Polio attacked her nervous system, damaged her ability to walk, left her body changed in ways that would never fully heal. She would use a wheelchair for the rest of her life, navigating a world that wasn't built for her, that didn't consider her needs, that saw disability as something to hide rather than accommodate.

Being a disabled Black girl in 1930s Florida meant facing compounded discrimination. Jim Crow didn't make exceptions for wheelchairs.

Segregation applied whether you could walk or not. The racism that told Black people where they could sit, where they could eat, where they could exist didn't soften because you had polio.

Pearline grew up learning to navigate both ableism and racism simultaneously. She attended segregated schools that were already underfunded and under-resourced for able-bodied Black children, let alone children with disabilities.

She learned early that the world wouldn't accommodate her, that she'd have to accommodate the world while demanding it do better. She grew up at 810 West Gregory Street in Pensacola, and that address would remain her home for her entire life.

There's something profound about staying rooted in one place, about claiming a spot on the map and saying "this is mine, I belong here, I'm not going anywhere." In middle school, Pearline met a boy named Randolph McClendon.

Young love in segregated Pensacola, two Black teenagers finding each other and building dreams despite everything working against them. Randolph would join the Army, serving a country that didn't fully recognize his humanity, wearing a uniform that supposedly represented freedom while Black people back home couldn't vote or eat at lunch counters.

Pearline and Randolph married, building a life together with the stubbornness that Black love requires. They created home and family while navigating racism, while managing Pearline's disability, while Randolph served in the military and came home on leave whenever he could.

Their love story had the sweetness of middle school sweethearts who made it work, who chose each other repeatedly, who built something real. In 1967, Randolph came home on leave from the Army.

He was a veteran, had served his country faithfully, was visiting his wife and preparing to meet the child they were expecting. Pearline was pregnant with their first and what would be their only child.

A drunk driver killed him. Just killed him, destroyed him, took him away from Pearline and from the baby he would never meet.

One moment of someone else's recklessness, one decision to drive while intoxicated, and Randolph McClendon was gone. Pearline was left widowed and pregnant at 33 years old, grieving a husband while preparing to become a mother.

She had to bury the love of her life while her body was growing new life. She had to figure out how to survive overwhelming loss while preparing to bring a child into the world without his father.

And she had to do all of this as a disabled Black woman in 1967 Florida, without her partner, without the person who'd been her support system. Some griefs are compounded by circumstance in ways that feel unbearable.

Pearline's grief included losing her husband, losing her child's father, losing her future as she'd imagined it. It included knowing that drunk driving deaths were often treated casually, that justice for victims' families was inconsistent, that the person who killed Randolph might face minimal consequences.

She gave birth to Michael Earl McClendon, carrying him into the world alone. Single motherhood by choice is hard enough.

Single motherhood by tragedy, by having your partner stolen, is something else entirely. Pearline had to be mother and father both, had to provide financially and emotionally, had to raise Michael while navigating her own disability and her own grief.

She managed. Not because managing was easy or natural or anything other than exhausting, but because her son needed her and giving up wasn't an option she allowed herself.

She raised Michael at 810 West Gregory Street, the same home she'd known her whole life. She created stability for him despite everything being unstable.

Pearline found joy where she could. She loved fishing, loved being outdoors despite a world that wasn't designed for wheelchair users to access nature easily.

She joined the Pensacola Penwheels, an organization for disabled people who refused to let wheelchairs limit their activities. They held fishing rodeos, competitions that celebrated skill and community, that proved disabled people could do everything able-bodied people could if given the opportunity and accommodation.

Pearline didn't just participate. She won.

She earned recognition for her fishing skills, proved she was excellent at something she loved. Those victories mattered not just because winning always feels good, but because they were proof that disability doesn't determine capability.

The Penwheels gave Pearline community. Other disabled people who understood the daily navigation of an inaccessible world, who got the frustration and the exhaustion and the small victories that able-bodied people never think about.

They fished together, competed together, existed together in spaces they'd claimed for themselves. But Pearline's legacy extends beyond fishing trophies and community participation.

She became an advocate for civil rights and accessibility, fighting battles that would benefit people she'd never meet. In a time when disability rights were barely acknowledged, when accessibility was an afterthought if it was thought about at all, Pearline pushed for change.

She made history as the first disabled person to use the handicap ramp at the Federal Courthouse in downtown Pensacola. That might seem like a small thing to people who've never needed a ramp, who've never faced stairs as an insurmountable barrier.

But for disabled people, ramps are freedom. They're access, inclusion, acknowledgment that you belong in public spaces.

That courthouse ramp existed because people like Pearline demanded it. And Pearline being the first to use it was a statement: disabled people have business in courthouses, in government buildings, in every public space.

We belong here. Accommodate us.

Building that ramp required advocacy, required disabled people and their allies pushing officials to recognize their legal and moral obligation to make public buildings accessible. The Americans with Disabilities Act wouldn't pass until 1990, but local activists were fighting for accessibility long before federal law required it.

Pearline's willingness to be first, to be visible, to literally roll up that ramp while people watched, was an act of courage. She was claiming space, demonstrating need, proving that accommodation works and matters.

Every person who used that ramp after Pearline benefited from her willingness to go first. Her advocacy work happened alongside her daily life as a single mother, as a fisherwoman, as a community member.

She didn't have the luxury of being a full-time activist. She had a son to raise, bills to pay, a life to maintain.

But she made time anyway because she understood that fighting for accessibility wasn't optional. It was necessary for her and for everyone else navigating the world in wheelchairs.

Being a Black disabled woman doing civil rights work in Florida meant navigating multiple forms of discrimination simultaneously. The civil rights movement of the 1960s primarily focused on racial justice, often overlooking disability.

The emerging disability rights movement was often dominated by white disabled people whose experiences and needs were different from disabled people of color. Pearline existed at an intersection that neither movement fully addressed, but she fought anyway.

She lived through Pensacola's entire civil rights era. She saw segregation, saw the fights for integration, saw the slow, painful progress toward equality that was always incomplete.

She saw how accessibility got left out of those conversations, how civil rights for Black people didn't automatically include civil rights for disabled Black people. She understood that liberation had to be intersectional before that word became common.

Pearline raised Michael to be proud, to understand his father's sacrifice, to honor his mother's strength. She gave him stability and love despite navigating single parenthood and disability simultaneously.

Michael grew up watching his mother refuse to be limited, watching her fish and advocate and live fully. That example shaped him, taught him resilience and determination.

Pearline lived until 2021, reaching 87 years old. She survived polio before the vaccine.

She survived Jim Crow. She survived her husband's death and single motherhood.

She survived decades in a world that wasn't built for disabled people. She didn't just survive, she thrived in the ways she could, created joy where possible, fought for change where necessary.

When she died on March 7, 2021, Pensacola lost a legend. Not the kind of legend who gets national recognition or textbook mentions, but the kind who shapes communities through persistence and presence.

She was buried at Barrancas National Cemetery, resting alongside other veterans and their families. Randolph had served, and Pearline's connection to him gave her that burial right.

They're together again now, the middle school sweethearts who built a life, who were torn apart by drunk driving, who spent 54 years separated by death. Her legacy lives through Michael, through the son she raised alone, who carries both his parents' memory.

It lives through every person who's used that courthouse ramp, who's benefited from accessibility she helped create. It lives through the Penwheels and the fishing competitions she won, through the community she built.

Pearline McClendon's story asks us to remember that heroism looks like showing up every day despite everything. It looks like raising a child alone while grieving a murdered husband.

It looks like fishing from a wheelchair because you refuse to let disability steal your joy. It looks like rolling up a courthouse ramp first because someone has to go first and you're willing to be visible.

Her story reminds us that intersectionality isn't academic theory, it's lived reality. Being Black and disabled and a woman and a widow and a single mother meant navigating multiple oppressions simultaneously, meant fighting battles on multiple fronts.

It reminds us that accessibility is a civil right. That ramps and accommodations aren't special treatment, they're basic inclusion, they're recognizing that disabled people deserve full participation in public life.

It reminds us that love persists through tragedy. That Pearline carried Randolph's memory for 54 years, raised their son to know his father's story, kept their middle school love alive through decades of widowhood.

It reminds us that communities remember their own. That Pensacola calling her a legend and an angel matters, that local recognition honors lives that national history overlooks.

It reminds us that joy matters even during struggle. That Pearline fishing and winning competitions wasn't frivolous, it was necessary, it was proof that disabled people deserve leisure and hobby and fun.

It reminds us that representation matters. That Pearline being first to use that ramp showed other disabled people they belonged, that visibility creates possibility.

It reminds us that two years timing can change everything. That polio vaccine coming just two years after Pearline contracted the disease meant she lived 87 years with disability that could have been prevented, that timing is cruel and arbitrary.

It reminds us that drunk driving destroys families. That Randolph's death wasn't just his loss but Pearline's and Michael's, that one person's irresponsibility creates ripples of pain.

It reminds us that single mothers are warriors. That Pearline raising Michael alone while disabled, while grieving, while facing racism and ableism, required strength most people never have to access.

It reminds us that staying rooted matters. That Pearline living her entire life at 810 West Gregory Street meant claiming space, refusing displacement, saying "I belong here" through presence.

It reminds us that organizations like Penwheels create community. That disabled people gathering, competing, existing together builds the support systems society often denies.

It reminds us that winning feels good. That Pearline's fishing trophies mattered not just as objects but as validation, as proof of skill, as visible achievement.

It reminds us that advocacy requires courage. That being first means being watched, being judged, carrying the weight of representation for everyone who comes after.

It reminds us that civil rights work is ongoing. That accessibility fights Pearline waged in Pensacola connected to national movements, that local activism creates change.

It reminds us that veterans' families sacrifice too. That Randolph served and died, that Pearline raised their son alone, that military service affects entire families.

It reminds us that burial locations carry meaning. That Pearline resting at Barrancas National Cemetery with Randolph reunites them, honors their connection, completes their story.

It reminds us that 87 years is simultaneously a long life and not long enough. That Pearline saw so much change but deserved to see more, lived fully but was limited by circumstances beyond her control.

It reminds us that legends aren't always famous. That Pearline being a Pensacola legend matters more than national recognition, that community memory honors people mainstream history forgets.

It reminds us that angels walk among us. That calling Pearline an angel recognizes her grace, her strength, her impact on everyone who knew her.

It reminds us that disability history is American history. That Pearline's story connects to polio's devastation, to disability rights movements, to accessibility fights that continue.

It reminds us that Black women carry impossible burdens. That Pearline navigating racism and ableism and widowhood and single motherhood simultaneously required resilience that shouldn't be necessary but was.

It reminds us that love stories include tragedy. That Pearline and Randolph's middle school romance ending in drunk driving death doesn't erase their love, makes it more poignant.

It reminds us that children inherit legacies. That Michael carries both parents' stories, that Pearline's strength shaped him, that family history matters.

It reminds us that ramps change lives. That infrastructure and accessibility aren't abstract policy but concrete inclusion that determines who can participate in public life.

It reminds us that fishing is freedom. That Pearline loving the outdoors, competing in rodeos, winning recognition shows disabled people deserve leisure and nature access.

It reminds us that first times matter. That someone has to be first to use the ramp, first to demand access, first to be visible, and Pearline was willing.

It reminds us that March 7, 2021 took someone irreplaceable. That Pearline's death left holes in her family and community, that her absence is felt.

It reminds us that August 6, 1934 gave us someone extraordinary. That Pearline's birth began a life of impact, that celebrating her birthday honors her existence.

It reminds us that rest is earned. That telling Pearline "rest easy" acknowledges her life's work is done, that she fought enough, that peace is deserved.

Rest in power, Pearline McClendon. Pensacola legend, civil rights advocate, disability rights pioneer, devoted mother, talented fisherwoman, beloved community member, widow who carried love through decades, woman who refused to be limited.

You rolled up that courthouse ramp first so others could follow. You raised your son alone after tragedy stole your husband.

You caught fish and won competitions and proved disability doesn't limit capability. You lived 87 years of quiet heroism, daily courage, persistent advocacy.

You stayed at 810 West Gregory Street your entire life, claiming Pensacola as yours, refusing to be displaced or erased. You loved Randolph from middle school until death separated you, and now you're together again at Barrancas National Cemetery.

You are remembered. You are honored.

You are a legend and an angel. Pensacola is better because you were here.

The disability community is stronger because you fought for access. Michael knows his mother's strength and his father's sacrifice because you made sure he understood both.

Thank you for being first up that ramp. Thank you for showing disabled Black people we belong everywhere.

Thank you for fishing and winning and living fully despite everything working against you. Thank you for raising your son with love and strength.

Thank you for 87 years of resilience. Rest easy, Pearline.

You've earned it.

While thousands of children were sent to death camps, one quiet Austrian woman went into those horrors and brought 10,000 children back out.
During World War II, the Holocaust brought suffering across Europe in many ways. In the Nazi-controlled Independent State of Croatia, the Ustaše regime set up concentration camps where Serbs, Jews, Roma, and political opponents were systematically killed. Thousands of children were taken from their families and faced death.
Most people who knew about these camps turned away. It seemed too dangerous, too difficult, and too late to help.
Diana Budisavljević chose to pay attention.
Diana Obexer was born in Austria in 1891. She married a Croatian Serb doctor and moved to Zagreb. As a mother and a trained nurse, she believed that staying silent in the face of evil was a kind of participation. When she learned that thousands of innocent children were dying in camps like Jasenovac and Stara Gradiška, she made a choice that would shape her life.
She decided to save them.
In 1941, Diana started organizing what became known as "The Action of Diana Budisavljević." She quietly gathered a group of brave volunteers, mostly women, who believed these children's lives were important. They collected food, medicine, and clothing. They forged documents, bribed officials, and used every connection and act of kindness they could find in a world filled with hate.
Then Diana did something few could imagine: she negotiated access to the camps themselves.
With persistence, persuasion, and great courage, she managed to enter some of the regime's most notorious camps. She went into places meant for death and came out with life. Sometimes she carried children in her arms, sometimes she secured their release through paperwork, and she always kept careful records of every name, every family, and every child who might one day be reunited with loved ones.
The work was extremely dangerous. If discovered, Diana and everyone in her network could be executed immediately. Still, they continued, month after month and year after year, through the darkest days of the war.
By the end of World War II in 1945, Diana Budisavljević and her network had saved more than 10,000 children from certain death.
Ten thousand lives were saved from destruction.
Ten thousand futures that would have been lost.
But after the war, Diana's remarkable heroism was deliberately hidden.
In the new communist Yugoslavia, authorities wanted to focus on unity and move beyond ethnic violence. Diana's work, which highlighted the systematic killing of Serbian children, was considered politically inconvenient. Her story was suppressed, her name removed from official histories, and the notebooks where she recorded every rescued child's name were taken and hidden in archives.
Diana Budisavljević lived until 1978 and died in obscurity in Zagreb. She never looked for fame or recognition. She did what she believed was right, and that was enough for her.
For many years, the world forgot her name.
But the truth eventually came out. Historians found her notebooks, and survivors shared their stories. The children she saved, now elderly, began to talk about the quiet woman who had saved their lives.
In 2017, seventy-two years after the war ended, Diana Budisavljević was finally recognized by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations. This honor is given to non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews during the Holocaust.
In Croatia, her story is now taught in schools. Documentaries have been made, and memorials have been built. The woman who never asked for anything is finally getting the recognition she deserved.
Diana Budisavljević proved that a single person, armed with compassion and courage, can defy systematic evil and prevail. She showed that even when the world turns away, one determined soul can save thousands.
She entered concentration camps and left with children.
She remembered their names when the world tried to forget them.
She saved 10,000 lives and never asked for anything in return.
And for many years, almost no one knew her name.

Now, at last, her name is remembered.

While many claimed powerlessness, Diana proved that "impossible" is often just a veil for fear. She worked in the shadows and died in obscurity, content with the knowledge that 10,000 lives continued because of her. Though political regimes may suppress the facts for decades, the legacy of a life saved is a living testimony that cannot be permanently erased.

*Bulan Ramadhan adalah bulan yang penuh dengan barakah dan penuh dengan keutamaan.* Allah subhanahu wa ta’ala telah mensyariatkan dalam bulan tersebut berbagai macam amalan ibadah yang banyak agar manusia semakin mendekatkan diri kepada-Nya. Akan tetapi sebagian dari kaum muslimin berpaling dari keutamaan ini dan membuat cara-cara baru dalam beribadah. Mereka lupa firman Allah ta’ala, “Pada hari ini Aku telah menyempurnakan agama kalian.” (QS. Al-Maidah: 3). Mereka ingin melalaikan manusia dari ibadah yang disyariatkan. Mereka tidak merasa cukup dengan apa yang telah dicontohkan oleh Rasulullah shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam dan para sahabat beliau ridhwanullahi ‘alaihim ajma’iin.

Oleh sebab itu pada tulisan ini kami mencoba mengangkat beberapa amalan bid’ah yang banyak dilakukan oleh kaum muslimin, yaitu amalan-amalan yang dilakukan akan tetapi tidak diajarkan oleh Nabi kita shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam maupun para sahabat beliau, semoga dengan mengetahuinya kaum muslimin bisa meninggalkan perbuatan tersebut.

*🛑 BID'AH BERZIKIR DENGAN KERAS SETELAH SALAM SHALAT TARAWIH*

Berzikir dengan suara keras setelah melakukan salam pada shalat tarawih dengan dikomandani oleh satu suara adalah perbuatan yang tidak disyariatkan. Begitu pula perkataan muazin, “assholaatu yarhakumullah” dan yang semisal dengan perkataan tersebut ketika hendak melaksanakan shalat tarawih, perbuatan ini juga tidak disyariatkan oleh Rasulullah shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam, tidak pula oleh para sahabat maupun orang-orang yang mengikuti mereka dengan baik. Oleh karena itu hendaklah kita merasa cukup dengan sesuatu yang telah mereka contohkan. Seluruh kebaikan adalah dengan mengikuti jejak mereka dan segala keburukan adalah dengan membuat-buat perkara baru yang tidak ada tuntunannya dari mereka.

*🛑 MEMBANGUNKAN ORANG-ORANG UNTUK SAHUR*

Perbuatan ini merupakan salah satu bid’ah yang tidak pernah dilakukan pada masa Rasulullah shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam, beliau tidak pernah memerintahkan hal ini. Perbedaan tata-cara membangunkan sahur dari tiap-tiap daerah juga menunjukkan tidak disyariatkannya hal ini, padahal jika seandainya perkara ini disyariatkan maka tentunya mereka tidak akan berselisih.

*🛑 MELAFAZKAN NIAT*

Melafazkan niat ketika hendak melaksanakan puasa Ramadhan adalah tradisi yang dilakukan oleh banyak kaum muslimin, tidak terkecuali di negeri kita. Di antara yang kita jumpai adalah imam masjid shalat tarawih ketika selesai melaksanakan shalat witir mereka mengomandoi untuk bersama-sama membaca niat untuk melakukan puasa besok harinya.

Perbuatan ini adalah perbuatan yang tidak di contohkan oleh Rasulullah shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam juga orang-orang saleh setelah beliau. Yang sesuai tuntunan adalah berniat untuk melaksanakan puasa pada malam hari sebelumnya cukup dengan meniatkan dalam hati saja, tanpa dilafazkan.

*🛑 IMSAK*

Tradisi imsak, sudah menjadi tren yang dilakukan kaum muslimin ketika ramadhan. Ketika waktu sudah hampir fajar, maka sebagian orang meneriakkan “imsak, imsak…” supaya orang-orang tidak lagi makan dan minum padahal saat itu adalah waktu yang bahkan Rasulullah menganjurkan kita untuk makan dan minum. Sahabat Anas meriwayatkan dari Zaid bin Sabit radhiyallahu ‘anhuma, “Kami makan sahur bersama Rasulullah shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam kemudian beliau shalat. Maka kata Anas, “Berapa lama jarak antara azan dan sahur?”, Zaid menjawab, “Kira-kira 50 ayat membaca ayat al-Qur’an.” (HR. Bukhari dan Muslim)

*🛑 MENUNDA ADZAN MAGRIB DENGAN ALASAN KEHATI-HATIAN*

Hal ini bertentangan dengan perintah Nabi shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam yang menganjurkan kita untuk menyegerakan berbuka. Rasulullah bersabda,

لاَ يَزَالُ النَّاسُ بِخَيْرٍ مَا عَجَّلُوا الْفِطْرَ

“Manusia senantiasa berada dalam kebaikan selama mereka menyegerakan berbuka.” (HR. Bukhari Muslim)

*🛑 TAKBIRAN*

Yaitu menyambut datangnya ied dengan mengeraskan membaca takbir dan memukul bedug pada malam ied. Perbuatan ini tidak disyariatkan, yang sesuai dengan sunah adalah melakukan takbir ketika keluar rumah hendak melaksanakan shalat ied sampai tiba di lapangan tempat melaksanakan shalat ied.

*🛑 BADUSAN*

Yaitu Mandi besar pada satu hari menjelang satu ramadhan dimulai. Perbuatan ini tidak disyariatkan dalam agama ini, yang menjadi syarat untuk melakukan puasa ramadhan adalah niat untuk berpuasa esok pada malam sebelum puasa, adapun mandi junub untuk puasa Ramadhan tidak ada tuntunannya dari Nabi kita shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam.

*🛑 MENDAHULUI PUASA SATU HARI ATAU DUA HARI SEBELUMNYA*

Rasulullah telah melarang mendahului puasa ramadhan dengan melakukan puasa pada dua hari terakhir di bulan sya’ban, kecuali bagi yang memang sudah terbiasa puasa pada jadwal tersebut, misalnya puasa senin kamis atau puasa dawud. Rasulullah bersabda, “Janganlah kalian mendahului puasa ramadhan dengan melakukan puasa satu hari atau dua hari sebelumnya. Kecuali bagi yang terbiasa melakukan puasa pada hari tersebut maka tidak apa-apa baginya untuk berpuasa.” (HR. Bukhari dan Muslim)

*🛑 PERAYAAN NUZUL QUR’AN*

Yaitu melaksanakan perayaan pada tanggal 17 Ramadhan, untuk mengenang saat-saat diturunkannya al-Qur’an. Perbuatan ini tidak ada tuntunannya dari praktek Rasulullah shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam, begitu pula para sahabat sepeninggal beliau.

*🛑 BERZIARAH KUBUR KARENA RAMADHAN*

Tradisi ziarah kubur menjelang atau sesudah ramadhan banyak dilakukan oleh kaum muslimin, bahkan di antara mereka ada yang sampai berlebihan dengan melakukan perbuatan-perbuatan syirik di sana. Perbuatan ini tidak disyariatkan. Ziarah kubur dianjurkan agar kita teringat dengan kematian dan akhirat, akan tetapi mengkhususkannya karena even tertentu tidak ada tuntunannya dari Rasulullah maupun para sahabat ridhwanullahi ‘alaihim ajma’iin.

Inilah beberapa bid’ah yang dilakukan oleh sebagian kaum muslimin, khususnya di negeri kita, semoga Allah ta’ala memberikan kita ilmu yang bermanfaat, sehingga kita bisa meninggalkan perkara-perkara tersebut dan melakukan perbuatan yang sesuai dengan tuntunan Nabi kita Muhammad shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam.

Oleh sebab itu pada tulisan ini kami mencoba mengangkat beberapa amalan bid’ah yang banyak dilakukan oleh kaum muslimin, yaitu amalan-amalan yang dilakukan akan tetapi tidak diajarkan oleh Nabi kita shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam maupun para sahabat beliau, semoga dengan mengetahuinya kaum muslimin bisa meninggalkan perbuatan tersebut.

*🛑 BID'AH BERZIKIR DENGAN KERAS SETELAH SALAM SHALAT TARAWIH*

Berzikir dengan suara keras setelah melakukan salam pada shalat tarawih dengan dikomandani oleh satu suara adalah perbuatan yang tidak disyariatkan. Begitu pula perkataan muazin, “assholaatu yarhakumullah” dan yang semisal dengan perkataan tersebut ketika hendak melaksanakan shalat tarawih, perbuatan ini juga tidak disyariatkan oleh Rasulullah shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam, tidak pula oleh para sahabat maupun orang-orang yang mengikuti mereka dengan baik. Oleh karena itu hendaklah kita merasa cukup dengan sesuatu yang telah mereka contohkan. Seluruh kebaikan adalah dengan mengikuti jejak mereka dan segala keburukan adalah dengan membuat-buat perkara baru yang tidak ada tuntunannya dari mereka.

*🛑 MEMBANGUNKAN ORANG-ORANG UNTUK SAHUR*

Perbuatan ini merupakan salah satu bid’ah yang tidak pernah dilakukan pada masa Rasulullah shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam, beliau tidak pernah memerintahkan hal ini. Perbedaan tata-cara membangunkan sahur dari tiap-tiap daerah juga menunjukkan tidak disyariatkannya hal ini, padahal jika seandainya perkara ini disyariatkan maka tentunya mereka tidak akan berselisih.

*🛑 MELAFAZKAN NIAT*

Melafazkan niat ketika hendak melaksanakan puasa Ramadhan adalah tradisi yang dilakukan oleh banyak kaum muslimin, tidak terkecuali di negeri kita. Di antara yang kita jumpai adalah imam masjid shalat tarawih ketika selesai melaksanakan shalat witir mereka mengomandoi untuk bersama-sama membaca niat untuk melakukan puasa besok harinya.

Perbuatan ini adalah perbuatan yang tidak di contohkan oleh Rasulullah shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam juga orang-orang saleh setelah beliau. Yang sesuai tuntunan adalah berniat untuk melaksanakan puasa pada malam hari sebelumnya cukup dengan meniatkan dalam hati saja, tanpa dilafazkan.

*🛑 IMSAK*

Tradisi imsak, sudah menjadi tren yang dilakukan kaum muslimin ketika ramadhan. Ketika waktu sudah hampir fajar, maka sebagian orang meneriakkan “imsak, imsak…” supaya orang-orang tidak lagi makan dan minum padahal saat itu adalah waktu yang bahkan Rasulullah menganjurkan kita untuk makan dan minum. Sahabat Anas meriwayatkan dari Zaid bin Sabit radhiyallahu ‘anhuma, “Kami makan sahur bersama Rasulullah shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam kemudian beliau shalat. Maka kata Anas, “Berapa lama jarak antara azan dan sahur?”, Zaid menjawab, “Kira-kira 50 ayat membaca ayat al-Qur’an.” (HR. Bukhari dan Muslim)

*🛑 MENUNDA ADZAN MAGRIB DENGAN ALASAN KEHATI-HATIAN*

Hal ini bertentangan dengan perintah Nabi shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam yang menganjurkan kita untuk menyegerakan berbuka. Rasulullah bersabda,

لاَ يَزَالُ النَّاسُ بِخَيْرٍ مَا عَجَّلُوا الْفِطْرَ

“Manusia senantiasa berada dalam kebaikan selama mereka menyegerakan berbuka.” (HR. Bukhari Muslim)

*🛑 TAKBIRAN*

Yaitu menyambut datangnya ied dengan mengeraskan membaca takbir dan memukul bedug pada malam ied. Perbuatan ini tidak disyariatkan, yang sesuai dengan sunah adalah melakukan takbir ketika keluar rumah hendak melaksanakan shalat ied sampai tiba di lapangan tempat melaksanakan shalat ied.

*🛑 BADUSAN*

Yaitu Mandi besar pada satu hari menjelang satu ramadhan dimulai. Perbuatan ini tidak disyariatkan dalam agama ini, yang menjadi syarat untuk melakukan puasa ramadhan adalah niat untuk berpuasa esok pada malam sebelum puasa, adapun mandi junub untuk puasa Ramadhan tidak ada tuntunannya dari Nabi kita shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam.

*🛑 MENDAHULUI PUASA SATU HARI ATAU DUA HARI SEBELUMNYA*

Rasulullah telah melarang mendahului puasa ramadhan dengan melakukan puasa pada dua hari terakhir di bulan sya’ban, kecuali bagi yang memang sudah terbiasa puasa pada jadwal tersebut, misalnya puasa senin kamis atau puasa dawud. Rasulullah bersabda, “Janganlah kalian mendahului puasa ramadhan dengan melakukan puasa satu hari atau dua hari sebelumnya. Kecuali bagi yang terbiasa melakukan puasa pada hari tersebut maka tidak apa-apa baginya untuk berpuasa.” (HR. Bukhari dan Muslim)

*🛑 PERAYAAN NUZUL QUR’AN*

Yaitu melaksanakan perayaan pada tanggal 17 Ramadhan, untuk mengenang saat-saat diturunkannya al-Qur’an. Perbuatan ini tidak ada tuntunannya dari praktek Rasulullah shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam, begitu pula para sahabat sepeninggal beliau.

*🛑 BERZIARAH KUBUR KARENA RAMADHAN*

Tradisi ziarah kubur menjelang atau sesudah ramadhan banyak dilakukan oleh kaum muslimin, bahkan di antara mereka ada yang sampai berlebihan dengan melakukan perbuatan-perbuatan syirik di sana. Perbuatan ini tidak disyariatkan. Ziarah kubur dianjurkan agar kita teringat dengan kematian dan akhirat, akan tetapi mengkhususkannya karena even tertentu tidak ada tuntunannya dari Rasulullah maupun para sahabat ridhwanullahi ‘alaihim ajma’iin.

Inilah beberapa bid’ah yang dilakukan oleh sebagian kaum muslimin, khususnya di negeri kita, semoga Allah ta’ala memberikan kita ilmu yang bermanfaat, sehingga kita bisa meninggalkan perkara-perkara tersebut dan melakukan perbuatan yang sesuai dengan tuntunan Nabi kita Muhammad shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam.

She earned a black belt, played rugby at the Air Force Academy, and became a military pilot. Seven months after giving birth, she was killed on a refueling mission—leaving behind a baby who will only know her mother through stories.
May 3, 2013. Kyrgyzstan. A KC-135 Stratotanker refueling aircraft took off from Manas Air Base on a routine mission. The massive jet—essentially a flying gas station that keeps combat aircraft airborne—carried three crew members conducting operations supporting the war in Afghanistan.
Captain Victoria "Tori" Pinckney was aboard as one of the pilots.
Shortly after takeoff, something went catastrophically wrong. The aircraft crashed, killing all three crew members instantly.
Tori was 27 years old. She'd been a mother for seven months.
Her daughter would never remember her face, her voice, her laugh. She'd grow up knowing her mother only through photographs, stories from family, and the knowledge that she died serving her country before her first birthday.
That's the tragedy that hits hardest—not just that Tori died, but when. Seven months after giving birth. Still in that overwhelming early phase of motherhood where exhaustion and joy mix together, where every day brings new milestones, where you're learning how to be a parent while trying to maintain your identity as everything else you are.
Tori was a military pilot. She was a new mother. She was trying to balance both—and she was killed before she could see which kind of woman her daughter would become.
Let's talk about who Victoria Pinckney was before that day.
She wasn't someone who lived cautiously. She wasn't someone who chose the easy path. From early on, Tori gravitated toward challenges that tested her limits.
She earned a black belt in karate—not just a colored belt, not just "dabbled in martial arts," but achieved black belt rank, which requires years of dedicated training, physical discipline, and mental toughness. It's a commitment most people never make because it's too hard.
Tori did it.
Then she went to the United States Air Force Academy.
The Air Force Academy isn't a normal college. It's a four-year military training institution where students are cadets, where academics combine with military discipline, where physical fitness standards are mandatory, and where the goal is producing military officers, not just graduates.
The acceptance rate is typically under 15%. You need congressional nomination. You need exceptional grades, test scores, and leadership experience. You need to be physically fit and mentally tough.
Thousands apply. A tiny fraction are accepted.
Tori got in.
And then she played rugby.
Rugby is a brutal sport—full-contact, high-speed collisions, no protective gear beyond a mouthguard. It requires toughness, strategic thinking, teamwork under pressure, and the willingness to throw your body into situations where you're going to get hurt.
Women's rugby is especially intense because it's often played by women who've chosen the sport specifically because they want that level of physicality and challenge.
Tori played rugby at the Air Force Academy while simultaneously handling academic coursework, military training, and the constant pressure of cadet life.
She graduated. She commissioned as an Air Force officer. She trained to become a pilot.
Not all Academy graduates become pilots. Flight training requires passing stringent physical exams, aptitude tests, and a demanding training pipeline. Many cadets want to fly but can't make it through the program.
Tori made it. She became qualified to fly the KC-135 Stratotanker—a modified Boeing 707 that serves as an aerial refueling tanker, extending the range of fighters, bombers, and other aircraft by refueling them mid-flight.
Flying a refueling tanker requires precision. You're connecting a fuel boom to aircraft flying at high speed, often in rough weather, sometimes over hostile territory. One mistake can cause collisions, fuel spills, or crashes. It's technical, demanding work that keeps Air Force operations functioning worldwide.
Tori flew these missions. And at some point during her military career, she became a mother.
Having a child as a military officer—especially as a pilot—creates impossible tensions. The military demands deployments, training exercises, long hours. Motherhood demands presence, consistency, the exhausting round-the-clock work of caring for an infant.
Tori was trying to be both. A pilot. A mother. A military officer. A parent.
Seven months into motherhood, she deployed to support operations in Afghanistan from Manas Air Base in Kyrgyzstan.
Manas was a critical hub for Afghanistan operations—a staging ground where aircraft refueled, supplies were moved, and personnel rotated. It was technically outside the war zone, but it directly supported combat operations.
May 3, 2013, Tori's KC-135 crashed shortly after takeoff. The investigation revealed mechanical failure—something broke, something critical, something that turned a routine refueling mission into a catastrophe.
All three crew members died. Captain Victoria Pinckney, age 27, was one of them.
Back home, a seven-month-old baby would grow up without her mother.
Tori's grandfather later said: "Family was everything to Tori. She loved her family, her country, and the Air Force."
In that order. Family first. Then country. Then service.
And she died trying to balance all three.
Here's what's heartbreaking: Tori made every "right" choice. She worked hard. She earned admission to the Air Force Academy. She excelled at challenging pursuits—karate, rugby, aviation. She served her country. She became a mother.
She did everything we tell people to do—pursue excellence, serve something larger than yourself, build a family, balance career and personal life.
And she died at 27 in an aircraft crash caused by mechanical failure.
There's no lesson here about making better choices. Tori made excellent choices. There's no moral about avoiding risk—military service requires risk. There's no comfort in "she died doing what she loved" because she loved being a mother too, and she didn't get to keep doing that.
Sometimes life is just unfair. Sometimes excellent people die for no good reason. Sometimes mothers of seven-month-olds don't come home.
Tori's daughter is 11 years old now. She's approaching middle school age—old enough to understand that her mother died, old enough to ask questions about who she was, old enough to feel the absence keenly.
She'll grow up knowing her mother was tough—black belt in karate, rugby player, military pilot. She'll know her mother graduated from one of the most prestigious military academies in America. She'll know her mother served her country.
But she won't remember her mother holding her. Won't remember her mother's voice singing to her. Won't remember the smell of her mother's hair or the feeling of being rocked to sleep in her mother's arms.
Because Tori died when her daughter was seven months old.
That's the loss that's impossible to calculate. Not just what was lost, but what never got to be. The childhood moments Tori missed. The teenage conversations they'll never have. The adult relationship that would have developed.
All gone because a refueling plane crashed in Kyrgyzstan on May 3, 2013.
Military service asks families to sacrifice alongside service members. Partners who deploy know their loved ones face danger. Children of deployed parents grow up with absences, with fear, with the knowledge that not everyone comes home.
But Tori's daughter didn't get the chance to understand that sacrifice. She was seven months old. Too young to know her mother was deploying. Too young to understand military service. Too young to remember anything about the woman who gave her life.
She'll spend her entire childhood—and adulthood—knowing about her mother without knowing her mother.
Captain Victoria Pinckney left behind more than a seven-month-old child. She left behind a family who loved her. A grandfather who talked about how much family meant to her. Friends who remembered her toughness and warmth. Military colleagues who'd flown missions with her.
She left behind a legacy of service, of achievement, of balancing multiple demanding roles and doing all of them well.
But mostly she left behind a baby girl who will never remember her mother's face.
That's the tragedy beyond the crash. Beyond the service. Beyond the honor and the sacrifice.
A child growing up with photographs instead of memories. Stories instead of experiences. Knowledge about her mother without knowing her mother.
May 3, 2013. Captain Victoria "Tori" Pinckney. Age 27. Black belt. Rugby player. Air Force Academy graduate. Military pilot. Mother of a seven-month-old daughter.
Killed in a KC-135 crash in Kyrgyzstan.
Her country honors her service. Her family grieves her loss. Her daughter will carry her name and her legacy.
But that seven-month-old baby deserved more than legacy. She deserved her mother. She deserved to grow up with the woman who earned a black belt, played rugby, flew military aircraft, and loved her family above everything else.
Tori wanted to be both—a pilot and a mother. She was trying to serve her country and raise her daughter.
She died before she could finish doing either one.
Rest in peace, Captain Pinckney. Your service mattered. Your sacrifice was real. Your family carries your memory.
And your daughter will grow up knowing she had a mother who was strong, accomplished, dedicated—and who left too soon, far too soon, to watch her grow.
Family was everything to Tori. And she didn't get enough time with the family she'd just started building.
That's not just a military loss. That's a human tragedy that echoes across a lifetime—for a daughter who will always wonder what it would have been like to actually know her mother, instead of just knowing about her.

The monks frequently refer to "loving-kindness" in their talks. Where did this composite word come from? It's actually a translation of the Pali word Metta. And there is a brief discourse called the Karaniya Metta Sutta where the Buddha instructs the monks to practise it. It is memorised and chanted often. 

Karaniya Metta Sutta: The Buddha's Words on Loving-Kindness
translated from the Pali by The Amaravati Sangha

This is what should be done 
By one who is skilled in goodness, 
And who knows the path of peace: 
Let them be able and upright, 
Straightforward and gentle in speech, 
Humble and not conceited, 
Contented and easily satisfied, 
Unburdened with duties and frugal in their ways. 
Peaceful and calm and wise and skillful, 
Not proud or demanding in nature. 
Let them not do the slightest thing 
That the wise would later reprove. 
Wishing: In gladness and in safety, 
May all beings be at ease. 
Whatever living beings there may be; 
Whether they are weak or strong, omitting none, 
The great or the mighty, medium, short or small, 
The seen and the unseen, 
Those living near and far away, 
Those born and to-be-born — 
May all beings be at ease! 
Let none deceive another, 
Or despise any being in any state. 
Let none through anger or ill-will 
Wish harm upon another. 
Even as a mother protects with her life 
Her child, her only child, 
So with a boundless heart 
Should one cherish all living beings; 
Radiating kindness over the entire world: 
Spreading upwards to the skies, 
And downwards to the depths; 
Outwards and unbounded, 
Freed from hatred and ill-will. 
Whether standing or walking, seated or lying down 
Free from drowsiness, 
One should sustain this recollection. 
This is said to be the sublime abiding. 
By not holding to fixed views, 
The pure-hearted one, having clarity of vision, 
Being freed from all sense desires, 
Is not born again into this world.

The Unsung Contributors in the History of the SPLM 

By William Sunday D. Tor  

A careful exploration of the history of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM) and its military wing, the Sudan People’s Liberation Army (SPLA), since their inception, reveals the decisive roles played by countless individuals, institutions, and even nations in sustaining the movement—both materially and morally. Many of these contributors, however, remain anonymous to this day. Among the few who knew them all was the late Dr. John Garang, the SPLM Chairman and Commander-in-Chief, who maintained precise knowledge of every single supporter, both within Sudan and abroad, including those across the Middle East.  

Among these hidden supporters were thousands of South Sudanese expatriates working across the Arab world and the Gulf States. Throughout the 1990s, they quietly sent portions of their monthly earnings to fund the movement’s activities. Although many of them have since risen to senior government positions or influential roles in society, their contributions remain largely unacknowledged. Some of their relatives were also part of this discreet network of solidarity.  

One compelling example of such unsung heroes is **Mr. Mohamed Ali Wol Makuac, a native of Atar. A Muslim intellectual and a graduate of the College of Law, Sharia, and Education, he currently serves in a senior capacity within the Islamic Council of Upper Nile State, South Sudan. Mr. Mohamed Ali has been a prominent community leader whose home remains open to all, regardless of faith or tribe. Multilingual and deeply respected, he has long been a bridge among the diverse communities of his region.  

Mr. Mohamed Ali was among the earliest supporters of the SPLM during the 1990s. While working as a teacher in Yemen, he maintained his membership and continued to contribute financially and morally to the movement until the signing of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement in 2005. His steadfast loyalty, despite his distance from home, exemplified the spirit of quiet dedication that sustained the movement during its most challenging years.  

Despite his distinguished experience in education, diplomacy, and community service, the SPLM leadership did not directly tap into his skills in these fields, nor award him a ministerial or diplomatic role. This, in turn, mirrors a broader truth: that the movement's success often rested on the unrecognized efforts of thousands of committed supporters whose names were never publicly honored.  

The story of Mr. Mohamed Ali embodies enduring loyalty, discreet service, and the harmonization of religious devotion with patriotic and social engagement. The history of these overlooked contributors highlights an essential dimension of the SPLM’s struggle — that the movement’s resilience and eventual triumph were built, in large part, upon the sacrifices of those who worked in silence and anonymity.

From Dialogue to Action: Standing Together to End FGM

Yesterday, I had the honour of moderating a powerful and timely virtual panel discussion commemorating the International Day of Zero Tolerance to Female Genital Mutilation, convened by Global Peace Let’s Talk International (GPLT) in partnership with the Young African Women Congress (YAWC) Network, Cameroon Chapter.

The conversation brought together passionate voices and experts committed to protecting the dignity, health, and future of women and girls. I was privileged to engage with an incredible panel: Joan Tambelin, Wamei Gladys Ndem, and Dr. Mugisho Ndabuli, who shared valuable insights on the realities of FGM, its consequences, the cultural and social drivers behind the practice, and the collective responsibility required to end it.

From understanding how FGM manifests in communities, to discussing youth-led advocacy, sustainable grassroots solutions, and the importance of policy and education, the dialogue reminded us that ending FGM is possible when awareness meets action.

What stood out most was the shared commitment among participants and speakers alike — a reminder that silence sustains harm, but conversation drives change. Together, we reaffirmed that protecting women and girls is not the responsibility of a few, but of all of us.

I am grateful to GPLT, YAWC Cameroon Chapter, our panelists, and every participant who contributed their voice to this important conversation.

The work continues, and so must our collective commitment.

KENYAN POLICE PEACEKEEPERS AWARDED UNITED NATIONS MEDALS IN JUBA, SOUTH SUDAN

The Inspector-General of Police, Mr.Douglas Kanja, on Saturday, 7th February 2026, applauded the Kenyan police contingent serving under the United Nations Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS) during a medal-pinning ceremony held at the UNMISS compound in Juba, South Sudan.

In remarks delivered on his behalf by the Kenyan Contingent Commander, Mr.Mbatian Kantai,SSP, the Inspector-General commended the officers for their professionalism, discipline, and unwavering dedication to duty in a complex operating environment. He noted that the contingent has continued to make a significant contribution towards the UNMISS mandate through the protection of civilians, facilitation of humanitarian assistance, securing key installations, and supporting peace efforts at the community level.

“You have facilitated humanitarian assistance, protected key sites, and fostered dialogue at the grassroots level. Each day, through your actions, you have embodied the core principle of UNMISS: to protect civilians and build durable peace,” read the Inspector-General’s message.

The colourful ceremony brought together senior UNMISS leadership, members of the diplomatic community, and distinguished guests, underscoring the strong partnership between Kenya and the United Nations in advancing peace and stability in South Sudan. A total of 27 Kenyan police officers were awarded the United Nations Service of Peace Medals in recognition of their outstanding service as part of the International Police Component in UNMISS.

The medals were presented by the Guest of Honour, the Officer-in-Charge (OIC) Police Commissioner, Mr.Jeremiah Togba Massaqoui. Also in attendance were the Representative of the Kenyan Ambassador, Mr.Benedict Watamba; Major General (Rtd) Aggrey Owino (Chairman, RJMEC); UNPOL senior leadership; and the Defence Attaché at the Kenyan Embassy in South Sudan, Col Martin Owino.

Among the recipients were the UNMISS UNPOL Gender Adviser, Ms.Millicent Alambo,SSP, and the UNPOL Team Leader of the Anti-Cattle Raiding Specialized Police Team, Mr.Kioko Munyambu,SSP 

Others included, Mr.Magongo Amadiva,SSP, Mr.Kipsang Kipkazi,SP, and Mr.Silas Kiptoo, ASP, among others, whose roles reflect Kenya’s continued contribution to specialised policing, protection, and community-focused interventions within the mission.

The award of the medals marks a major milestone for the contingent and affirms the National Police Service’s commitment to international peacekeeping. The successful event celebrated not only individual achievement but also the collective dedication of Kenyan officers to promoting peace, security, and the protection of civilians in South Sudan.

CEPO Condemns Alleged Killing of Prisoners of War

Mr. Edmund Yakani, Executive Director of the Community Empowerment for Progress Organization (CEPO), has stated that after closely tracking and verifying information regarding the alleged killing of prisoners of war from the SSPDF while under the custody of SPLA-IO, the findings are deeply disturbing.

Killing prisoners of war constitutes a war crime under international humanitarian law. CEPO strongly condemns any form of human rights violations and war crimes committed by any party to the conflict.

CEPO urges the leadership of SPLA-IO to provide accurate, evidence-based information on what exactly happened that led to the deaths of the SSPDF prisoners of war during the recent armed clashes between SSPDF and SPLA-IO forces.

The organization further calls on all warring parties to strictly respect international humanitarian law. Exploiting or implicating humanitarian actors in conflict situations for political or military advantage is unacceptable and must stop immediately.

Mr. Yakani emphasized the urgent need to end the ongoing senseless violence. He warned that continued armed confrontation risks pushing the country toward mass atrocities if political leaders from the conflicting parties fail to resolve their differences through peaceful dialogue.

He stressed that using military approaches to resolve political disputes is one of the gravest political mistakes in South Sudan’s current situation. Sustainable peace can only be achieved through genuine political dialogue and commitment to national stability.

SPLM-IO POSITION ON GRASSROOTS PEACE AND THE LEGACY OF THE WUNLIT PEACE CONFERENCE 

BY THE SPLM-IO CATTLE CAMP NEWS DESK 

The Sudan People’s Liberation Movement/Army–In Opposition (SPLM-IO) affirms that sustainable peace in South Sudan must be rooted in the will, agency, and reconciliation of grassroots communities, not imposed solely through elite political agreements detached from social realities. The 1999 Wunlit Peace Conference stands as the most powerful historical evidence that people-to-people peace is both possible and effective in South Sudan.

The Wunlit Peace Conference, formally known as the Dinka–Nuer West Bank Peace and Reconciliation Conference, was a landmark grassroots initiative held from 27 February to 8 March 1999 in Wunlit, South Sudan. After eight years of devastating inter-communal conflict west of the Nile, ordinary citizens, chiefs, elders, women, youth, and spiritual leaders, demonstrated that reconciliation could be achieved through truth-telling, accountability, cultural legitimacy, and collective commitment to coexistence.

What Happened at Wunlit: A People-Centered Peace 

Wunlit was fundamentally different from elite-driven political negotiations. Organized and facilitated by the New Sudan Council of Churches (NSCC) with support from international partners, the conference prioritized traditional authority, moral leadership, and inclusive participation, with women constituting nearly one-third of the delegates. The process restored dignity to local peace-making institutions that had been marginalized by militarization and political fragmentation.

The conference culminated in the Wunlit Covenant, sealed through the culturally significant sacrifice of a white bull (Mabior), symbolizing the cleansing of past grievances and the restoration of moral order. This was not symbolism alone; it was a binding social contract anchored in community norms.

Core Resolutions and Practical Outcomes

The Wunlit Conference produced concrete, enforceable resolutions, including:

 An immediate and comprehensive ceasefire between the Dinka and Nuer communities west of the Nile.
 Amnesty for past offenses to enable reconciliation and reintegration.
 The return of abducted women and children.
 Guarantees for the shared and peaceful use of grazing lands, water points, and fishing grounds.
 Mechanisms for dispute resolution led by traditional authorities.

These outcomes were respected and implemented because they emerged from the people themselves, not from coercion or external pressure.

Strategic and Political Significance 

The SPLM-IO recognizes that Wunlit had far-reaching political consequences beyond community peace. By stabilizing the southern front and healing internal divisions, grassroots reconciliation exerted decisive pressure that contributed to the 2002 reunification of the SPLM/A factions. This unity was instrumental in paving the way for the 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement (CPA) and, ultimately, South Sudan’s independence in 2011.Wunlit proves that national political settlements are fragile without social reconciliation, while grassroots peace can reshape national political trajectories.

Contemporary Relevance and SPLM-IO Commitment

Today, as South Sudan faces renewed inter-communal violence, cattle raiding, political exclusion, and the erosion of trust, the spirit of Wunlit remains urgently relevant. Recent initiatives, including follow-up dialogues in the so-called “Wunlit Triangle,” reaffirm that unresolved local conflicts continue to threaten national peace.

The SPLM-IO therefore:

 Reaffirms its commitment to grassroots-led peace processes to address communal violence at grassroots uniformly across South Sudan as a central pillar of national reconciliation.
 Calls for the protection and empowerment of traditional institutions, women, and faith-based actors in peacebuilding.
 Rejects the militarization and politicization of community conflicts.
 Enacting community resolutions into national law called Community Communal Violence Act of South Sudan; and 
 Advocates for the integration of people-to-people peace mechanisms into the implementation of the Revitalized Peace Agreement.

Conclusion 

Wunlit was not an accident of history, it was a deliberate choice for peace made by ordinary South Sudanese under extraordinary circumstances. The SPLM-IO holds that lasting peace cannot be decreed from presidential palaces or negotiated solely in foreign capitals. It must be rebuilt from villages, cattle camps, and communities. The future of South Sudan depends on reviving the Wunlit model: truth before power, reconciliation before revenge, and people before politics.

John Wayne and Robert Mitchum — With Their Mothers: The Quiet Roots of Two Western Legends
Both John Wayne and Robert Mitchum came from modest, hardworking backgrounds where mothers were the steady, guiding forces shaping boys into men of quiet strength and unbreakable resolve.
Wayne (born Marion Robert Morrison in 1907) was raised in Glendale, California, by his mother Mary Alberta Brown. After his parents’ separation and his father’s struggles, it was Mary who kept the family together, instilling discipline, self-reliance, and a deep sense of duty. She worked tirelessly and expected the same from her son. That foundation of resilience and moral clarity became the core of Wayne’s on-screen persona — the man who stood tall when others faltered.
Mitchum (born Robert Charles Durman Mitchum in 1917) grew up in Bridgeport, Connecticut, and later Delaware. His mother Ann Harriott Mitchum was a Norwegian immigrant who raised her children alone after his father’s death in a railroad accident when Robert was just two. Ann worked multiple jobs, moved the family across the country, and taught her children independence through example. Mitchum’s laid-back defiance, dry humor, and refusal to bow to authority — traits that defined his anti-hero roles — were born from a mother who never let hardship break her spirit.
Their paths crossed in Hollywood’s overlapping orbits. Wayne, already the towering icon of the Western, recognized Mitchum’s raw, authentic intensity early. Mitchum, in turn, admired Wayne’s work ethic, quiet leadership, and refusal to compromise on principle — not just as an actor, but as a man who commanded respect without demanding it.
That mutual respect found its perfect expression in El Dorado (1967), directed by Howard Hawks. Wayne played Sheriff J.P. Harrah, a once-great lawman fighting alcoholism and doubt. Mitchum was the drunken deputy Cole Thornton, a man of lethal skill and dry wit. There was no competition between them — only balance. Wayne’s seasoned, authoritative presence paired naturally with Mitchum’s relaxed, coiled menace. Each gave the other room to exist fully in the frame, something only truly confident actors can do. The film’s chemistry felt effortless because the men themselves were comfortable in each other’s company — two legends who didn’t need to outshine one another.
Both carried the lessons their mothers taught: strength is not loud, dignity is earned, and family (blood or chosen) is what matters most when the dust settles. Wayne’s mother shaped his unshakeable moral compass; Mitchum’s mother forged his refusal to let the world define him.
Their friendship was never flashy — no tabloid scandals, no grand gestures. It was built on shared respect, shared values, and the quiet understanding that comes from men who knew what it meant to carry weight without complaint.
Rest in peace to John Wayne and Robert Mitchum — two icons whose mothers gave them the foundation to become legends, and whose on-screen partnership reminded us that true strength is best shown in partnership, not rivalry.
The West still feels their presence — steady, silent, and forever true.

Some of you may have seen Josie Gibson on the “This Morning”recently, discussing her struggles with a condition called Lipedema: A condition I’ve had for many years. I wanted to share my experiences, in the spirit of helping raise awareness of one of the most under diagnosed diseases that affects around 1 in 10, (mostly) women. I know there will be many ladies out there that identify with the symptoms: If I can help one person realise they’re not alone, that it’s not their fault, and that there are things you can do to manage symptoms, then it’s worth sharing I feel.

So, what it is? In a nutshell, it’s a chronic, painful, progressive disease characterised by an abnormal distribution of adipose tissue (fat), affecting the lower limbs and sometimes arms. The diseased tissue becomes fibrotic, nodular, and it doesn’t respond to diet or exercise. The arms and legs look disproportionate in relation to the rest of the body. 

It can cause joint and even mobility issues over time. We know that, while there’s no specific gene responsible, patients are predisposed via genetics and seems to be triggered by hormonal changes (puberty, pregnancy, menopause). In the UK there is little to no funding for research - so no official test exists for it, and so no help whatsoever via NHS.

For me,  it was disproportionality large, heavy and painful thighs and upper arms.  I bruised super easily - simply scratching an itch would leave me bruised. I’ve lost count of the number of doctors I’ve seen over the years, only to be told to lose weight, to exercise more. Basically that it’s me to blame, despite a (mostly) healthy diet, managed weight, regular exercise and a physical job. Soul destroying to be healthy with diet & exercise, sometimes obsessively so over the years, to still be over the “ideal weight and BMI for my height”. And the embarrassment and hatred of my own body for the way it looked.

If you any questions or would like to know more about the condition, where to go for help & support, things you can do to help manage it, etc, feel free to message me direct  🤗🥰

How Bitterness & Hatred Quietly Damage Your Body

Bitterness and hatred don’t just stay in your heart — they attack your body silently.

When you hold on to anger for too long, your body stays in stress mode. This triggers hormones like cortisol and adrenaline, and over time, they cause real damage.

💔 Heart problems – Increased blood pressure, higher risk of heart disease and stroke
🧠 Mental exhaustion – Anxiety, depression, poor concentration, insomnia
🦠 Weak immune system – You get sick more often and heal slower
🍽️ Digestive issues – Ulcers, stomach pain, poor appetite
😴 Poor sleep – Racing thoughts, shallow sleep, constant fatigue
🧬 Faster aging – Chronic stress accelerates aging inside and out

The truth is:

The person you hate is resting, but your body is paying the price.

💡 Forgiveness is not weakness.
It’s a health decision.
It frees your mind, protects your heart, and restores your body.

✨ Choose peace.
✨ Choose healing.
✨ Choose yourself. 
I know it's hard but try and let go please 🙏 

Your health is worth more than bitterness. ❤️

Serious Questions Surround the Handling of the Judy Deen Death Investigation

BRUNSWICK GA - On Friday, we spoke directly with the Glynn County Coroner, Marc Neu regarding the death of Judy Deen. While we have long held respect for the Coroner and his office, we were concerned by what we perceived as evasive and inconsistent responses regarding the status of Ms. Deen’s death report.

Our concern is straightforward: if the coroner’s report is altered, heavily redacted, or withheld without lawful justification, it raises serious questions about transparency and public trust. More troubling is the possibility that this case may not be isolated. If one report can be delayed or modified, the public has a right to ask whether other cases have been handled similarly, including cases such as Tom Sublett and others that remain unresolved or controversial.

What we know as fact is limited, but significant. Ms. Deen’s daughter, Lisa Rayfield, burned her mother’s body. According to available information, very little remains were recovered. Experts widely acknowledge that open fires do not reach temperatures sufficient to fully destroy human bone without mechanical processing, such as what occurs in a crematorium. This naturally raises questions about whether remains were moved or whether a secondary crime scene may have existed. Despite these circumstances, no criminal charges have been filed.

We have exhausted all lawful avenues to obtain public records, including submitting multiple Open Records Requests (ORRs). The police report that was released is heavily redacted. The Coroner’s Office has refused to release its narrative, stating most recently that the report is now considered to be in “draft” form—despite credible information indicating the report was completed by Mr. Fox and uploaded into the system some time ago.

This contradiction is difficult to reconcile.

Adding to the confusion, multiple independent contacts have told us there is no active investigation. If that is true, then the justification for withholding or redacting public records becomes unclear. Officials have repeatedly stated there was “no foul play.” If that conclusion has been reached, what remains under investigation?

These unanswered questions naturally lead to a larger one: Why the secrecy? Are charges forthcoming, or is the case effectively closed? No agency involved has been willing to answer that directly.

Our city has never had a sustained investigative media presence willing to challenge official narratives. We understand the law. We understand public records policy and procedure. Transparency should not be viewed as a threat—yet the behavior we are seeing suggests otherwise.

We will continue to ask questions. However, it appears unlikely that meaningful answers will be provided until the case is formally marked closed, which—based on available information—we believe may have already occurred.

The public deserves clarity. The family deserves peace. Public officials have a duty not just to follow the law, but to demonstrate integrity through transparency.

We are demanding the release of all lawfully available documents so the public can evaluate the facts for themselves. Silence and secrecy only further damage confidence in local law enforcement and now, increasingly, the Coroner’s Office.

This is not about making friends. It is about accountability.

Finding peace. Forgiving my father. Letting go of anger. Hoping for reconciliation. A new chapter begins.

Nimule’s Border, Trade Ambitions, and the Cost of Delay

By Emmanuel Patrick Laku | Nimule Town, Eastern Equatoria State | February 9, 2026

By sunrise, Nimule Town is already awake to the rumble of diesel engines. Long queues of cargo trucks line the roads, stretching from customs yards into residential areas, their drivers waiting—sometimes for weeks —for clearance. At South Sudan’s busiest commercial gateway, congestion has become both a symptom and a symbol of a border under strain.

On Sunday, senior government officials gathered in Nimule to confront the challenges head-on. At the center of the discussions was the long-awaited One Stop Border Post (OSBP), a regional trade project designed to modernize border management, reduce delays, and integrate South Sudan more fully into East African trade corridors.

But before construction can begin, one obstacle remains: residents occupying land allocated for the project.

Racing Against Development Timelines

Minister of Trade and Industry Atong Kuol Manyang used the high-level inter-ministerial meeting with the government agencies operating at the border to request Nimule’s municipal leadership to relocate the residents.

“The issue of the One Stop Border Post is well known. Construction is expected to start soon, yet people are still occupying the site,” Atong said, addressing the Mayor of Nimule Municipal Council. “This falls within your jurisdiction, and it is important that the relocation is done in a timely manner.”

Her request carried urgency. Development partners supporting the OSBP operate within fixed timelines, she said, and failure to meet preconditions could derail the project entirely.

“If we do not fulfill our responsibilities, we risk losing the project altogether. Funds could be diverted, timelines may elapse, and this is a development that is critical to all of us,” she cautioned.

For Nimule, the OSBP is more than infrastructure. It represents the promise of faster clearance, reduced costs for traders, and improved revenue collection for a country heavily dependent on imports.

A Gateway Under Pressure

Nimule handles the bulk of South Sudan’s imports, linking the country to Uganda, Kenya, and the wider region. Every delay at this border ripples across the economy, affecting food prices, fuel supply, and business confidence.

Mayor Cearar Longa Fuli framed the OSBP as a turning point.

“This represents a bold leap into the future of trade,” he said. “We are moving away from manual delays toward digital efficiency.”

Yet outside the meeting hall, the scale of the challenge was visible. Trucks packed into narrow streets, parked along highways,  underscored how far reality remains from digital ambition.

Congestion and the Politics of Compliance

Addressing the congestion, the Commissioner General of the South Sudan Revenue Authority (SSRA), William Anyuon Kuol, said the backlog is driven less by infrastructure and more by resistance to reform.

“We will not allow any vehicle to move without paying E-Tax,” Kuol said. “This must be clear to customs officers and clearing agents.”

According to Kuol, the electronic permit (E-Permit) system—introduced to increase transparency and curb revenue leakages—has disrupted long-standing informal practices.

“Our system is international. It detects where goods originate and calculates customs duties based on actual purchase prices, whether goods come from China, India, or Dubai,” he explained.

The result, he said, has been pushback from traders accustomed to under-declaration and political interference.

“The congestion you see is not accidental,” Kuol added. “Some people are trying to create pressure so that trucks are released without paying tax.”

 Gaps That Smugglers Exploit

Even as he defended stricter enforcement, Kuol acknowledged serious operational challenges. Nimule lacks cargo scanners and heavy-handling equipment, making inspections slow and, at times, ineffective.

“Some containers are declared as carrying sugar, but inside there are high-value goods like cigarettes,” he said. “Without scanners, it becomes difficult to detect these practices.”

These gaps, he argued, have encouraged false declarations, smuggling, and the commercialization of tax exemptions—further compounding congestion.

Kuol was unequivocal in his response: trucks that entered Nimule without due process would either be turned back or required to pay full tax before proceeding. “There will be no compromise,” he said.

Traders, Drivers, and Conflicting Accounts

Clearing agents at the border disputed claims that new policies were to blame for the delays. Deng, representing clearing agents, said the E-Permit system has been in place for over a year.

“The trucks you see here are not here because of new charges,” he said. “They were smuggled in from Mombasa and Uganda without due process, and now they are stuck.”

Truck drivers offered yet another perspective. Adam Jallas, who represents drivers operating across the region, said congestion is being worsened by delays in processing E-Permits and the lack of designated parking space.

“Parking along the road is dangerous,” Jallas warned. “If a fire breaks out, all these trucks will be affected.”

He appealed to authorities to redirect trucks to larger parking areas such as Corona while documentation is processed, arguing that safety risks are growing by the day.

 More Than a Border

The debates in Nimule go beyond traffic jams and paperwork. They reflect a broader struggle facing South Sudan: how to enforce laws in a system long shaped by informality, while still facilitating trade in a fragile economy.

For the government, the OSBP and digital customs reforms represent a chance to reset the system—to improve efficiency, increase revenue, and restore confidence among regional partners.

For traders and drivers, the transition has come with uncertainty, delays, and rising pressure.

And for residents living on land earmarked for the OSBP, development now carries the personal cost of displacement.

A Test of Political Will

As timelines tighten and trucks continue to queue, Nimule stands at a crossroads. The success or failure of the One Stop Border Post will signal whether South Sudan can translate policy into practice—and whether it can align enforcement with facilitation.

For now, the engines idle, the paperwork piles up, and the future of South Sudan’s most important gateway hangs on decisions made not just at the border, but in the balance between reform, accountability, and urgency.

CEPO Raises Concern Over Traffic Disruptions During Court Trial of Suspended First Vice President

Mr. Edmund Yakani, Executive Director of the Community Empowerment for Progress Organization (CEPO), has expressed concern over the worsening traffic congestion in Juba during the court trial sessions of the suspended First Vice President and his party co-accused.

According to Mr. Yakani, the repeated roadblocks and diversions implemented on trial days have caused significant disruption to public movement, creating stress and frustration among drivers and road users. He described the situation as disturbing, noting that court trial days have increasingly become difficult and exhausting for residents navigating the city.

He further highlighted the absence of adequate traffic police officers to guide and manage vehicle movement during peak congestion. Mr. Yakani observed that while traffic builds up across major roads, some traffic police officers appear to be more focused on collecting fines from drivers rather than facilitating the smooth flow of vehicles.

“This is a disturbing and stressful moment for citizens in the town,” he stated, emphasizing that trial days consistently result in heavy traffic and unnecessary hardship for the public.

On behalf of stressed drivers and road users, CEPO is urging the Honorable Minister of Interior, the Inspector General of Police (IGP), and the Director of Traffic Police to urgently intervene and address the situation.

Mr. Yakani proposed that the most practical solution would be the proper deployment of traffic police officers to effectively manage and control road usage in an organized and professional manner during court proceedings.

CEPO calls for immediate measures to ensure public convenience, reduce congestion, and restore order on Juba’s roads during high-profile court sessions.
