Two of the ancient world's greatest superpowers, Egypt and the Hittite Empire, ended decades of war with a peace treaty that looks surprisingly modern.

This agreement, known today as the Treaty of Kadesh, was finalized around 1259 BC between Pharaoh Ramesses II of Egypt and King Hattusili III of the Hittites.

It came about 15 years after the massive but indecisive Battle of Kadesh. Both sides realized that endless fighting was getting them nowhere.

The treaty wasn't just a promise to stop fighting. It was a complete defensive alliance. 📜

Both empires agreed to come to each other's aid if attacked by an outside enemy. It even included a clause for returning political fugitives to their home countries.

What makes it so incredible is that we have written versions from both empires. The Egyptians carved it in hieroglyphs on temple walls, while the Hittites inscribed it in cuneiform script on clay tablets.

A replica of the Hittite tablet is even displayed at the United Nations headquarters in New York, a testament to its place as the earliest surviving peace treaty. 🤝

This agreement brought stability to the region for decades, proving that even the bitterest of enemies can find common ground through diplomacy.

We brought home our new rescue Maine Coon just three days ago. The shelter was honest with us — her past had been harsh. She’d been returned twice, misunderstood over and over, and deeply afraid of men after suffering neglect and mistreatment from a former owner.

Whenever a man came too close, her large, gentle body would tense. She’d tremble, hide, and retreat completely. Once, she even hissed — not from aggression, but from pure fear. We were told she might never fully trust again, that healing could take months… maybe even longer.

With all of that in mind, my husband chose to let her lead. He didn’t reach for her or force contact. Every evening, he simply sat quietly on the floor, calm and still, giving her the space to share the room without any expectations. The first night, she stayed hidden. The second night, she edged a little closer, watching him carefully with those wise Maine Coon eyes, her fluffy tail wrapped close as she observed from a safe distance.

And then last night… everything changed.

She walked slowly over to him, curled up beside him, and gently rested her head against his — like she had finally found somewhere safe.

I took the photo through tears. Seeing her choose him, after all she’d endured, reminded me exactly why I fell in love with this man. He didn’t move an inch for nearly an hour, even as his neck stiffened and his arms went numb, because he refused to risk breaking that moment or scaring her away.

We bought cozy beds and her favorite toys. But in the end, none of that mattered most. What mattered was patience. What mattered was kindness. What mattered was someone willing to earn her trust at her pace, not their own.

She’s still wary of most men and hides when visitors come over. But she follows my husband from room to room. At night, she sleeps curled beside him, her soft purr filling the quiet, like she finally found the person she’d been waiting for all along.

Sometimes the greatest gift you can offer a wounded soul — human or animal — is time, compassion, and the freedom to heal in their own way.

The disengagement from Gaza proved something painful but important: territorial withdrawal on its own does not create peace when a society is deeply fragmented internally and dominated by a narrative of struggle until Israel’s elimination. When the prevailing mindset is that the fight continues until “return” and the removal of Israel from the map, every area that is vacated turns into an additional arena of confrontation – not a foundation for a functioning state.

In the reality that emerged after the withdrawal, the only path to improvement is neither another unilateral pullout nor continued stalemate, but structural change: dismantling Hamas’s military power, creating conditions for stable civilian life, and building Palestinian leadership oriented toward a functioning state rather than permanent conflict.

That requires three things in parallel:
 1. A clear definition of the final status – an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel, not an endless interim arrangement.
 2. A transitional period that allows for real political and social change within Palestinian society, including leadership, institutions, and economy.
 3. A narrative shift – moving from the “right of return” as a practical goal to a model of compensation, rehabilitation, and a focus on building a future state.

Without a clear horizon, the violence continues. Without time and conditions for internal change, no moderate leadership can emerge. And without replacing the narrative that defines the conflict as an existential struggle to the end, any agreement will remain on paper only.

The goal is not to impose a reality on the Palestinians, but to create a path in which their own interest becomes clear: that independent, stable, sovereign lives are preferable to a constant war with no real purpose.

Amma Houri was the name of resistance and a mother who never stopped resisting. Since 2012, after her beloved son was taken by the state, her life has been a journey of grief and unanswered questions. A widow for over thirty years, she carried her pain to the streets, roads, camps, and protests, knocking on every door in search of her son. She faced baton charges, threats, hunger, and exhaustion, yet never stepped back. She witnessed violence at the Baloch National Gathering and in 2023, joined the camp alongside Dr. Mahrang Baloch, travelling even to Dalbandin for the jalsa. For thirteen years she searched, and in 2025 in Islamabad, she was still demanding justice for her leaders and whispering her son’s name in every prayer.

And today, Amma Houri has passed away waiting. She died carrying that same ache in her chest. She died without holding her son one last time. She died without knowing where he was. She couldn't hug his son one last time. And even today, as her eyes have closed, her resistance has not ended. It lives in every mother who stands with a photograph in her hands. It lives in every voice that still demands truth and justice.

Amma Houri did not leave this world defeated. She left it as she lived in it, waiting, loving, and resisting. May her restless heart finally find peace. And may the son she waited for know that his mother never stopped calling his name not even in her final breath. As Amma Houri tirelessly demanded justice for her son and for all forcibly disappeared sons. We urge the immediate and safe return of all those held in detention and torture cells, so that the long and painful waiting of mothers may finally come to an end.

Mutfwang: Orange Economy Holds the Key to Nigeria’s Sustainable Future

The Executive Governor of Plateau State, Barrister Manasseh Caleb Mutfwang, has described the Orange Economy as a strategic pathway to Nigeria’s economic diversification and sustainable development, urging senior executives to reposition creativity and entrepreneurship at the centre of national policy thinking.

Represented by the Deputy Governor, Ngo Josephine Chundung Piyo, at the inauguration of the Senior Executive Course, (SEC) 48, of the National Institute for Policy and Strategic Studies, the Governor congratulated the 105 nominees on their selection and charged them to maximise the opportunity to deepen their strategic leadership capabilities.

He noted that the study theme, “Orange Economy and Entrepreneurship for Sustainable Development in Nigeria,” is timely, particularly as the country confronts unemployment, youth restiveness, and the urgent need to diversify from resource-dependent growth models. According to him, sectors such as culture, tourism, media, fashion, film, music, and digital innovation must now be treated as serious economic drivers capable of creating jobs, strengthening social cohesion, and expanding Nigeria’s global competitiveness.

The Governor further observed that Plateau State, with its rich cultural heritage, tourism assets, and vibrant creative landscape, offers practical insights into how creativity, governance, and peace-building can intersect to drive development.

In his welcome address, the Director-General of the Institute described the inauguration as the commencement of a rigorous ten-month intellectual and leadership engagement designed to sharpen strategic thinking and deepen policy insight among senior executives  ￼. He emphasised that participation in the Course is not merely an academic exercise but a call to national service that demands intellectual discipline, ethical leadership, and commitment to the collective good.
The Director-General stressed that the Orange Economy challenges traditional development paradigms anchored predominantly on extractive resources. Instead, it requires policymakers to recognise creativity, ideas, talent, and cultural heritage as strategic economic assets and to develop coherent policies that protect intellectual property, incentivise innovation, and promote entrepreneurship .
He reminded participants that the NIPSS experience is deliberately demanding, involving intensive academic sessions, interdisciplinary research, structured debates, and field studies aimed at producing policy options that are practical, evidence-based, and implementable  ￼.

The formal swearing-in of the nominees marked their transition into full participants of SEC 48. Over the next ten months, they are expected to interrogate national challenges critically and generate policy recommendations capable of advancing Nigeria’s creative economy and strengthening sustainable development outcomes.

🔴 OPINION | Peace Betrayed: How Leadership Failure Is Stealing South Sudan’s Future.

The failure to fully implement the Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan (R-ARCSS) has once again placed the nation at a dangerous crossroads. When peace agreements are dishonored, war becomes inevitable, not always with guns, but through the slow destruction of hope, institutions, and the future of a generation.

Years after the signing of R-ARCSS, South Sudanese citizens continue to witness political delays, broken promises, and a leadership unable or unwilling to deliver its mandate. Security arrangements remain incomplete, reforms are stalled, and national priorities are sacrificed for political survival. This incompetence has robbed the people of peace dividends and weakened trust in the state.

Yet we are now in 2026, a modern world where real battles are no longer fought in the bushes but in classrooms, laboratories, farms, and digital spaces. Nations rise through education, technology, science, agriculture, and artificial intelligence, not endless political games. South Sudan has the potential to compete, but only if its people reclaim their power and demand accountable leadership.

It is time for South Sudanese to wake up, stand up, and take responsibility for the future. Peace cannot survive on paper alone; it must be defended by citizens who refuse to accept failure as destiny. The choice is clear: continue down the path of broken agreements and stagnation, or rise to match our potential and build the nation we deserve.

Two long-standing community education centers in Pankisi and Akhmeta are currently facing closure following the non-renewal of their municipal lease agreements after 20 years of continuous operation.

For two decades, these centers have served as critical space for education, women’s empowerment, youth engagement and social cohesion in one of Georgia’s most diverse regions.

Their programs have included:

• Free university preparatory courses for rural students
• Academic support and educational camps for children
• Vocational training and certified nursing courses for young women
• Grant funding for women entrepreneurs, farmers, and local initiatives
• Free legal aid for refugees and socially vulnerable groups
• Crisis support for survivors of violence
• Civic education programs and community dialogue spaces

More than 20 women are directly employed through these initiatives and thousands of residents from Pankisi Valley (17 villages) and Akhmeta Municipality (120 villages, including Tusheti) have benefited over the years.

These centers represent long-term, community-rooted development and inclusive regional growth. Their closure would mean the loss of a trusted educational and civic infrastructure in a rural and historically sensitive region.

We call on international partners, development agencies and foundations supporting education, gender equality and civil society to closely follow this situation and explore ways to safeguard the continuity of these programs.

YOUR MISTAKE IS NOT A LIFE SENTENCE. YOU DONT HAVE TO BE STUCK IN THE PRISON OF SHAME … THE PRISON DOOR IS ALREADY OPEN
Some of you are living inside a cell that has no lock — only memory.

You wake up rehearsing your mistake. You sleep replaying your regret. The walls of the room are not made of iron; they are made of accusation. And because the voice has been speaking so long, it sounds like your own.

Failure happened.

But shame moved in and unpacked its bags.

You tell yourself, “If I punish myself long enough, maybe I can pay the debt.”

You tell yourself, “If I stay small, I will not disappoint again.”

You tell yourself, “If I never forgive myself, at least I am being honest.”

But honesty without mercy becomes cruelty.

There are people reading this who feel like they have been given a life sentence. Not by a judge. Not by a court. But by their own thoughts. A lifelong prison of “I should have known better.” A lifelong prison of “I ruined it.” A lifelong prison of “God must be disappointed.”

Look at the scene in John 8.

A woman dragged into public humiliation. Accused. Exposed. Surrounded. Stones in hand. Religious certainty in the air.

Jesus does not debate her history.

He confronts the accusers.

“Let the one without sin cast the first stone.”

Silence falls. One by one, the stones drop.

Then He turns to her — not with condemnation, not with disgust — but with authority wrapped in mercy.

“Neither do I condemn you. Go, and sin no more.”

He did not call her mistake righteousness.

He simply refused to call her identity shame.

You have confused repentance with self-hatred.

They are not the same.

Repentance turns.

Self-hatred chains.

It is time to walk out of the dark room. The sentence you are serving was never signed by Heaven.

THE LORD IS SAYING

“Why are you repeating a verdict I never spoke?

I disciplined you to mature you, not to erase you. I exposed weakness so you could grow in strength, not so you could hide in humiliation.

You confessed. I forgave. Why are you still prosecuting yourself?

Return the stones. Return the borrowed voices. Return the lies you placed upon your own shoulders.

I am not asking you to deny what happened. I am asking you to rise from it.

Your failure is not the final word. I am.”

MENTAL HEALTH REVELATIONS

When shame embeds itself, it fuses to identity. The mind begins to interpret every new opportunity through the lens of past error.

Self-condemnation feels like control. “If I criticize myself first, no one else can hurt me.” But constant inner criticism activates chronic stress patterns in the brain, reinforcing fear and paralysis.

Growth requires safety. The nervous system cannot evolve while it is under constant internal attack.

Jesus corrected behavior without crushing identity. That is the psychological miracle of the Gospel. You cannot hate yourself into holiness.

Freedom begins when you say, “Yes, I failed. And I am still worthy of restoration.”

PROPHETIC DECLARATIONS

I declare:

— I will not confuse my humanity with disqualification.

— I release the prison of lifelong regret.

— My past mistakes do not hold governing authority over my future.

— I reject internalized shame and receive divine correction.

— I will not prosecute myself for what Christ has already forgiven.

— I choose transformation over torment.

— I rise from error with wisdom and clarity.

— I will not rehearse accusation more than I rehearse truth.

— My joy will not be held hostage by yesterday.

— I step out of condemnation and into restoration.

10 HEAVENLY WHISPERS

 1. Your failure revealed your humanity; it did not revoke your calling. Wisdom is often born in the soil of mistakes.

 2. Shame tries to freeze you in one chapter; grace turns the page. You are allowed to become someone wiser than your worst decision.

 3. The cross absorbed the penalty; you are not required to keep paying emotional interest. Mercy already settled the account.

 4. When you replay regret, you rehearse a story that Heaven has closed. Release the memory from its throne.

 5. You cannot build a future while bowing to yesterday. Lift your head; destiny does not grow in self-contempt.

 6. Correction is an invitation upward, not a sentence downward. God’s discipline refines identity; it does not destroy it.

 7. Accusation demands punishment; truth produces change. You are being transformed, not condemned.

 8. The lesson is sacred; the shame is not. Keep the wisdom, discard the self-hatred.

 9. You are not the only one who has fallen short. The ground at the cross is level for all.

 10. Freedom begins the moment you agree with grace more than with guilt. The door is open — walk through it.

PRAYER

Dear Lord Jesus,

I bring You my failures without disguise. I acknowledge the places where I chose wrongly, where I lacked maturity, where I hurt myself or others.

But I refuse to live under condemnation. You did not shame the woman in the dust, and You are not shaming me.

Remove every borrowed lie that became my inner voice. Break the prison of regret I built with my own thoughts. Teach me to own my mistakes without enslaving myself to them.

I receive Your correction. I receive Your mercy. I receive restoration.

In Jesus’ name, Amen.

SCRIPTURES TO ANCHOR

“Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her.” — John 8:7

“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.” — John 8:11

“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1

“For though the righteous fall seven times, they rise again.” — Proverbs 24:16

He handcuffed a grieving Black mother at her son’s open grave, but when the police station discovered who she really was, their panicked scramble to fix it was already too late for everyone involved.

"The cold Chicago air felt thinner today, like it couldn't hold the weight of our grief. I stood beside the hole in the earth that was waiting for my son, my Malik, and focused on my breath. In, out. A rhythm to anchor me while my world had none. The pastor’s words about mercy were a distant hum, a soundtrack to the silent film of my own heartbreak.

My hands were clenched so tight my knuckles were white. Control. That’s what grief had taught me. Not the loud, shattering kind, but a quiet, brittle control. The kind you use when you’re a Black mother in a world that’s always watching, waiting for you to fall apart.

Then, a sound that didn't belong. The crunch of tires on gravel, too fast, too aggressive.

A patrol car.

It stopped just feet from the mourners, a jarring intrusion of blue and white into our sea of black. The car door swung open, and an officer stepped out. He wasn't there to pay respects. His eyes swept over us, my family, my friends, like we were a problem to be solved.

— ""Who owns the black Mercedes?""

His voice was a blade, slicing through the sacred quiet. My sister, confused, raised a hand.

— ""It’s ours.""
— ""We’re in the middle of a funeral.""

He walked forward anyway, his gaze zeroing in on my family. He was looking for a fight.

— ""License plate was flagged.""
— ""Stolen vehicle. I need to see everyone's ID. Now.""

The pastor stepped forward, a gentle hand raised in peace.

— ""Officer, please.""
— ""This is a graveside service for her son.""

He ignored the pastor, his eyes landing on me. The mother. The one standing closest to the casket. Something in his stare hardened.

— ""You.""
— ""Step away from the grave. Show me your ID.""

My voice came out steadier than I felt. My son was lying in a box at my feet, and this man was demanding I prove I belonged here.

— ""Officer, my identification is in the car.""
— ""We are in the middle of my son’s burial.""

He let out a short, ugly laugh.

— ""Convenient.""

He saw my nephew lift a phone to record and his face twisted with anger.

— ""Put that away. Now.""

I held my ground, my feet rooted in the cold dirt next to my child. I would not be moved.

— ""You can do your check.""
— ""But you will not disrupt this service further. I am cooperating.""

His personal space violation came next. One step closer, his breath a foul puff in the chilled air.

— ""You’re obstructing my investigation.""

I met his glare, my own voice dropping to a near whisper, heavy with the full weight of the moment.

— ""I am grieving.""
— ""Please. Lower your voice.""

It wasn't my fear that broke his patience. It was my lack of it.

— ""Turn around.""
— ""Put your hands behind your back.""

The world went silent. The pastor’s Bible fell from his hands. My sister gasped.

— ""Officer, this is completely unnecessary.""

He didn't answer with words. He answered with force, grabbing my arm. Cold metal bit into my wrist, tight and unforgiving. The click of the handcuffs echoed in the stunned silence, a sound more final than the dirt hitting a casket. He was pulling me away from my son.

My voice, when it came, was no longer quiet. It was the sound of a mother’s heart breaking for the second time in a week.

— ""You are arresting me.""
— ""At my own child’s funeral.""

He leaned in, his voice a venomous hiss in my ear.

— ""Maybe you should've thought about that before breaking the law.""

He had no idea who I was. He had no idea what he had just done. But he was about to find out.

To those who do not understand the conflict here is a very succinct explanation which shows how it happened without any villain. Just history pitting stateless jewish refugees seeking a safe heaven for jews In the land where the Jewish nation was formed against the Arabs of Palestine unable and uninterested in understanding what is happening.
 Zionism was never realistically implementable without an Arab minority inside whatever Jewish political framework emerged. The land was already inhabited. Even the most modest versions of a Jewish national home assumed coexistence, not empty space.

Mainstream Zionist leadership repeatedly stated that the future Jewish state would include Arab residents with civil and political rights. This was written into early proposals and later into Israel’s Declaration of Independence. And in practice, despite discrimination and the ongoing conflict, a large Arab minority did remain and became citizens with voting rights, parties, courts, and representation.

But from the Arab perspective at the time, that promise was extremely hard to believe.

They were watching:
   •   a growing national movement seeking sovereignty in their country
   •   immigration changing demographics
   •   open discussions among some Zionist thinkers about transfer or separation
   •   imperial backing from Britain

To them, “equal rights in a Jewish state” sounded like permanent minority status in a polity defined by another people’s national project. Many assumed — not irrationally — that this would eventually lead to marginalization or displacement.

So the core problem was not simply rejectionism or hatred.
It was a collision between two perceptions:

Zionist perception:
A small, vulnerable people returning to their homeland, prepared to share it and grant rights.

Arab perception:
A foreign-backed national movement arriving to take political control and reduce them from majority to minority.

Both were grounded in real fears.
Both made compromise psychologically difficult.

That gap in perception still shapes the conflict today. Israelis often point to equal rights inside Israel as proof coexistence was possible. Palestinians and the broader Arab world remember loss of control, displacement, and minority status as proof the promises were not credible.

Until that gap is addressed — not rhetorically but through structures people trust — the argument just keeps repeating itself across generations.

🔥 Je Suis… Jesus… I Am

Here’s something that stopped me in my tracks once I really saw it.

In French, “je suis” means… I am.

Say it out loud slowly.
Je suis.

Sound familiar?

Now step back and feel into this.

The one many were taught to worship outside themselves… spent his entire life pointing people back inside. He didn’t just perform miracles. He reminded people of what they carried within. He kept saying things that made the authorities uncomfortable because they shifted power back to the individual.

“The Kingdom of Heaven is within you.”
“You will do greater works than these.”
“I and the Father are one.”

Not statements of separation. Statements of unity.

Then you go back even further. To the moment when the Creator is asked for a name and responds:

“I Am That I Am.”

Not a title. Not something owned by one religion or language. A state of being. Existence itself speaking.

I Am.

Je suis.

Whether by coincidence, poetic echo, or something deeper… the resonance is undeniable. The realization is simple but life-changing. The divine was never meant to be seen as something only outside of you. It’s something expressed through you.

Not your ego. Not your personality.
Your awareness. Your presence. Your ability to create, love, choose, and become.

When you start to really feel that, you stop living small. You stop waiting for permission. You start operating from the quiet knowing that life itself is moving through you… as you.

Maybe the message was never about worshipping a man.
Maybe it was about remembering the state of being he embodied.

I Am.

And once you truly understand that… you begin to live differently.

A mother screams as a stranger walks away with her baby into the darkness — knowing if caught, both the child and the woman carrying him will be executed."Will my child live?" the mother cries desperately.The woman pauses, turns. "I cannot promise you that. But if your child stays here, I can promise you death."This impossible choice repeated itself hundreds of times in the Warsaw Ghetto between 1942 and 1943. And the woman who walked into that darkness — carrying sedated infants in toolboxes, hiding toddlers in coffins and potato carts — would carry those moments with her forever."In my dreams," Irena Sendler said decades later, "I still hear the children crying as they left their parents."She stood barely 4'11" tall with a gentle, round face — nothing about her suggested the resistance leader who would outwit Nazi guards again and again, smuggling 2,500 Jewish children to safety.Her courage had roots. When she was seven years old, her father — a doctor who treated poor Jewish patients for free — died of typhus after refusing to abandon them during an epidemic. Before he died, Dr. Stanisław Krzyżanowski told his daughter something she would never forget:"If you see someone drowning, you must jump in to save them — even if you cannot swim."When the Nazis sealed 400,000 Jews inside the Warsaw Ghetto in 1940, Irena saw an entire community drowning. She didn't hesitate.She forged thousands of documents. She found ways past Nazi checkpoints. When the underground resistance formed a division to save Jewish children in 1942, she led it — directing a network of mostly women who risked death every single day.The Nazis had made the law clear: anyone helping Jews, even a baby, would be executed. Sometimes entire families paid the price. In one village, the Nazis murdered a pregnant mother, her husband, their six children, and the eight Jews they were hiding.Still, Irena's network found families willing to die for someone else's child. They coached children to memorize new names and stories. They sedated infants so they wouldn't cry. They smuggled them out in ambulances with false bottoms, in burlap sacks, beneath loads of potatoes.And Irena insisted on one thing: these children would be returned to their people after the war. She wrote each child's true identity on tissue paper and buried the lists in glass jars beneath an apple tree — so they might one day remember who they really were.The hardest part wasn't the danger. It was convincing parents to let go — to trust a stranger with everything they loved, with no guarantee of reunion.In October 1943, someone broke under torture and gave the Gestapo her name. As Nazi officers ransacked her apartment, she threw a bundle containing children's names out the window to a friend below. The full record was already buried beneath the apple tree.At Gestapo headquarters, they shattered both her legs and feet, demanding names and locations. She gave them nothing.She was sentenced to death and sent to Pawiak prison, where almost no one survived. But the resistance bribed her executioner. A Nazi officer led her out one morning, and by the next day, posters across Warsaw announced that Irena Sendler was dead.Reading her own death notice, she realized being officially dead had its advantages. Within weeks, under a new name, she was back at work — finding hiding places, delivering money, forging papers. She continued until the war ended.After liberation, she dug up the jars beneath the apple tree and began searching for families. Almost all the parents had been murdered at Treblinka. Of the 2,500 children she saved, some stayed with adoptive families, some joined the Jewish diaspora overseas. Hundreds were never found — some may still be alive, unaware of their true identity.Irena never accepted the word "hero." It irritated her. "I could have done more," she insisted. "This regret will follow me to my death."Who were the real heroes? "The mothers," she said, "who gave what was most dear to their hearts to unknown strangers."For decades, Communist authorities suppressed her story. Then in 1999, something extraordinary happened. A Kansas high school teacher named Norm Conard showed three students a news clipping mentioning a woman who saved 2,500 children. Thinking it must be a typo, the students investigated.They discovered Irena Sendler wasn't dead — she was 90 years old, living in poverty in Warsaw. The students wrote a play about her life called "Life in a Jar" and raised money selling candy bars to meet her. The play has since been performed hundreds of times.At one performance in Warsaw, a man sat clutching something throughout the show. Afterward, he opened his palms to reveal his own medal for saving Jews during the war. "I buried this in my basement for sixty years," he said through tears. "I told only my wife. Now, because of these American students, I can show this proudly. It was the finest thing I ever did."In 2003, Poland awarded Irena its highest honor. In 2007, she was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize. She died in May 2008 at age 98.Before her death, she wrote to the Polish Senate: "Every child saved with my help is the justification of my existence on this earth, and not a title to glory."Irena Sendler saw children drowning and jumped in — 2,500 times. She carried them through darkness in toolboxes and coffins. She buried their names in jars. She endured torture and near-execution. And she kept going, because some things matter more than survival.Her father was right. When you see someone drowning, you jump in — even if you cannot swim.#NeverForget #RighteousAmongTheNations ~Ifestory

The first question people ask is, “What are twin flames?”
And the most honest answer is, it's a mystery. It's not something that can be fully captured in words. Anyone who claims to have fully grasped this divine bond is likely limiting its depth. Because some connections are known not through logic but through experience.

Yet one thing is clear—energy patterns.

Two people living in different corners of the world, who have never met, wake up at the same time. They feel the same vibration in their chests. They have the same dreams—which seem like memory, not imagination. Suddenly, someone's name resonates within them. An invisible pull, difficult to explain in words.

It doesn't feel like just a romantic feeling—it feels like a resonance of consciousness. As if two souls vibrating at the same frequency.

Humanity has been experiencing this mystery since ancient times. Plato told the story of the splitting of the soul—as if one original consciousness had split into two forms.  Hinduism has the principle of Shiva and Shakti—where not man and woman, but consciousness and energy, are incomplete without each other. In Egyptian tradition, the bond between Isis and Osiris transcends death.

Different civilizations. Different centuries. Yet the same essence—some souls are connected on a deeper level.

Spiritually, a twin flame is not a "perfect love story." It's a process of awakening. When you meet such a soul, it brings to light every hidden wound, every unfinished lesson, every unresolved karma within you. This union can be both joyful and painful—because it's not just love, it's purification.

The fundamental purpose of a twin flame relationship is often inner unity rather than external union. When you balance the feminine and masculine, Shiva and Shakti, consciousness and energy within you—you come closer to wholeness.

And there's also a subtle truth—

energy is never one-sided.

 If you feel a soul so deeply that it inhabits your meditation, your dreams, your heartbeat—chances are that somewhere, the same vibration is running through the other side.

Twin flame is perhaps not a label, but a state of consciousness—where love becomes unconditional, where distance is merely physical, and where souls communicate beyond time and space.

It's a mystery.

But perhaps some mysteries are not meant to be understood, but to be experienced. 🔥✨

FACT CHECK: Is Iran Really One of the World’s Most Corruption-Free and Crime-Free Countries?
A viral claim suggests that Iran has become one of the world’s most crime, corruption, and bribe-free countries while building a $20 billion defense industry without Western support.
Here’s what verified data shows:
🔹 According to Transparency International’s global corruption index, Iran does not rank among low-corruption countries. In fact, it scores relatively low in global transparency rankings.
🔹 However, it is true that Iran has significantly developed its domestic defense industry despite decades of Western sanctions.
Iran has expanded missile systems, drone technology, and naval capabilities largely through indigenous production.
🔹 Independent global institutes confirm Iran’s growing military manufacturing capacity, but there is no widely verified international data confirming the exact "$20 billion" valuation.
📊 Conclusion:
Iran has made notable progress in defense self-reliance under sanctions, but the claim that it is one of the world’s most corruption-free and crime-free countries is not supported by international data.

The Story of a Son Who Turned His Home into a Crime Scene

On September 6, 2011, at around 1PM, life in Karen, Nairobi was moving slowly.

Lunch was being prepared.
Gardens were being watered.
Drivers were washing cars.

Peace everywhere.

Except in one house…
where betrayal was loading its gun.

This is the story of David Tett.

PART 1: Raised Like Royalty

David was not abandoned.

When his mother died, his aunt, Betty Tett, took him in without hesitation.

Together with her husband, William Mulready Tett, they raised him as their own.

Same schools at the international school of Kenya 
Same comfort.
Same privileges.

No “stepchild” treatment.

To David, poverty was just something he saw on TV.

PART 2: The First Fall

At 17, life tested him.

A pregnancy. Kijana kapachika msichana Na akakimbia. 
School dropped.
Dreams collapsed.

Instead of facing it, David ran.

No apology.
No explanation.

Just disappearance.
Nairobi taught him fast:
Hakuna mchezo.

PART 3: The Second Chance

Years later, he returned.
Like the prodigal son.

No anger from home.
No rejection.

Only forgiveness.

His father gave him KSh 70,000 to start afresh.

“Build yourself.”

But money without discipline is like fuel in a burning house.

It vanished.

No business.
No progress.

Only regret.

PART 4: When “No” Became Poison

When he failed, he returned again.
This time, demanding land.
His father refused.

Firmly.

That “no” entered his heart like a slow poison.
In his mind, it translated to:

 “You are not really one of us.”

Resentment grew quietly.
Like rust on metal.

PART 5: The Devil’s Business Plan

Instead of rebuilding himself…
David chose darkness.

His plan was simple and deadly:

Rob them.
Kill them.
Blame carjackers.
Disappear rich.

Get rich or die trying.

PART 6: From Ngara to Karen

That morning, David picked up two criminals in Ngara, Nairobi.

They carried an AK47.
He carried betrayal.
They drove to Karen.

The gate opened.
The maid trusted him.

Nobody suspected that death had just walked in.

PART 7: “My Son, Why?”

When his father came downstairs, he saw visitors.

He smiled.

He had no idea he was standing before his execution squad.
Outside, he asked about the loan.
David asked him to return inside.

Inside was a trap.
The gun appeared.
Hands were tied.
Hope disappeared.

His father whispered:

“My son… why?”

David heard nothing.
Greed had blocked his ears.

He slapped him.

Demanded keys.

Started tearing the bedroom apart.
Looking for money.
Looking for escape.
Looking for a future built on blood.

PART 8: A Mother’s Instinct

While this was happening, Betty tried calling home.

No answer.

She sent the gateman.
He was tied too.
Alarm bells started ringing.
She called police.
Minutes later, officers arrived.
The alarm went off.

Suddenly, a car shot out of the compound like a bullet, VROOOM VROOOM.

Then the gunmen appeared.

AK47 in hand.

The police responded instantly.

Gunfire.
Silence.
Both criminals fell.

Dead.

PART 9: The Truth Comes Out

Only the driver escaped.

And the father identified him.

David.
His own son.
The betrayal was complete.

PART 10: Kamiti’s Iron Walls

David was arrested and charged.

He was held at Kamiti Maximum Security Prison.

15 years.

From privilege to prison.
From son to suspect.
From home to concrete walls.

Ironically, he then started phone scams from inside prison.

Still hustling.

Still choosing shortcuts.

FINAL WORD

David had love.
Support.
Opportunity.

Many people would die for that life.

But bitterness turned him into his own enemy.
He didn’t lose his future.
He destroyed it.
With his own hands.

Sometimes, the greatest danger is not outside.
It sleeps in the same house with you.

Buku Fikih Puasa Terlengkap, Problem Aktual Dan Solusinya Karya Gus M Syihabuddin Dimyathi 

I. Pendahuluan dan Kerangka Penulisan

Bab ini menjelaskan latar belakang penulisan buku, pentingnya membahas fikih puasa secara aplikatif, serta manhaj yang digunakan. Ditekankan bahwa buku ini hadir untuk menjawab problem nyata umat dengan bahasa yang mudah dan solusi yang menenangkan.

II. Hakikat, Tujuan, dan Urgensi Puasa

Bab ini membahas makna puasa secara syar‘i dan ruhani: mengapa kita berpuasa, apa tujuannya, bagaimana puasa membentuk ketakwaan dan betapa pentingnya puasa bagi kita. Pembaca diajak memahami bahwa puasa bukan sekadar menahan lapar, tetapi ibadah yang mendidik jiwa dan akhlak.

III. Niat Puasa dan Permasalahannya

Bab ini mengurai berbagai kegelisahan seputar niat: lupa niat, ragu niat, was-was, niat sebulan penuh, hingga niat membatalkan puasa. Penekanannya bahwa niat itu sederhana dan tidak perlu dibuat rumit, sehingga masyarakat tidak terjebak dalam kecemasan.

IV. Imsak, Subuh, dan Kondisi Awal Puasa

Membahas persoalan waktu mulai puasa: masih boleh makan saat imsak, adzan subuh, ragu masuk waktu, hingga kondisi junub dan haid yang berhenti menjelang subuh. Bab ini memberi kepastian hukum agar tidak muncul kebingungan di awal hari puasa.

V. Masuknya Benda ke Dalam Tubuh

Bab ini mengupas berbagai kasus teknis yang sering menimbulkan was-was: debu, dahak, asap, rokok, suntik, sisa makanan, ludah, muntah, darah, air wudhu, korek telinga, air masuk saat mandi biasa dan lainnya. Disajikan dengan batasan fikih yang jelas agar pembaca tidak membatalkan puasa hanya karena kekhawatiran.

VI. Syahwat, Hubungan Badan, dan Konsekuensi Puasa

Membahas ciuman, pelukan, pacaran, keluar mani, hingga jima‘ dan kafarah. Dijelaskan mana yang membatalkan, mana yang tidak, serta konsekuensinya. Tujuannya agar umat memahami batas syariat tanpa sikap berlebihan atau meremehkan.

VII. Waktu Berbuka dan Hukum-Hukumnya

Bab ini membahas kepastian masuk maghrib, adzan yang keliru, doa berbuka, hingga hukum berbuka karena sangkaan waktu telah masuk. Ditekankan prinsip kehati-hatian tanpa terjatuh pada was-was.

VIII. Puasa Anak-anak dan Orang dengan Kondisi Khusus

Membahas cara mendidik puasa anak kecil, baligh di tengah Ramadhan, orang pikun, pekerja berat, musafir, haid, nifas, istihadhah, dan kasus-kasus sosial seperti teman jarang puasa. Bab ini memberi panduan praktis sesuai kondisi masing-masing tanpa menggeneralisasi hukum.

IX. Puasa dan Akhlak Seorang Muslim

Menegaskan bahwa ruh puasa adalah menjaga lisan dan akhlak. Dibahas bagaimana menyikapi celaan, provokasi, dan maksiat di bulan Ramadhan. Puasa tidak boleh berhenti pada lapar, tetapi harus membentuk kepribadian.

X. Perbedaan Penetapan Awal Ramadhan dan Fenomena Terkait

Mengupas perbedaan hisab–rukyat, pindah daerah, hingga fenomena mimpi bertemu Nabi terkait penetapan Ramadhan. 

XI. Puasa dan Ibadah Malam Ramadhan

Membahas tarawih (4 rakaat sekali salam, 8 atau 20 rakaat), shalat kilat, witir, dan optimalisasi pahala. Tujuannya agar masyarakat beribadah dengan ilmu, bukan sekadar ikut-ikutan atau saling menyalahkan.

XII. Fidyah, Qadha’, dan Tanggung Jawab Puasa

Bab ini menjelaskan siapa yang wajib qadha’, siapa yang wajib fidyah, atau keduanya. Termasuk kasus orang wafat, hutang puasa, detail perhitungan fidyah, serta meluruskan kesalahpahaman “bayar fidyah dulu, qadha’ nanti”. 

XIII. Puasa Syawal dan Melanjutkan Ibadah Setelah Ramadhan

Membahas keutamaan puasa enam hari Syawal, makna “seperti puasa sepanjang masa”, hukum menggabungkan niat, dan prioritas waktunya. Bab ini menjadi penutup yang mendorong kesinambungan ibadah setelah Ramadhan.

Buku ini memberi penegasan bahwa syariat tidak menyulitkan sebagaimana disebutkan dalam Al-Qur'an dan Hadits. Harapannya pembaca dapat beribadah dengan tenang, yakin, dan penuh kesadaran.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
Plateau State, Nigeria.
February 17, 2026.

Plateau Convenes Climate Policy Dialogue to Promote Inclusive and Gender-Responsive Action.

The African Centre for Leadership, Strategy and Development (Centre LSD), in collaboration with the Side-By-Side Movement Nigeria – Plateau Chapter, and with funding support from Christian Aid Nigeria, will convene Key Climate Policy dialogue to promote Inclusive and Gender- Responsive Action from February 18–20, 2026, in Plateau State, Nigeria. 

Plateau State sits at the intersection of climate vulnerability, economic fragility, and communal tensions, where climate-induced resource pressures have exacerbated insecurity and widened socio-economic inequalities. Effective climate governance must therefore bridge environmental sustainability with peacebuilding, gender justice, and inclusive development. 

Ms. Offiong Enang, Women’s Rights Coordinator at Centre LSD, emphasized that the dialogue represents a strategic intervention aimed at ensuring climate budgeting is responsive to the needs of women and vulnerable populations, strengthening the Plateau State Climate Assembly as an effective platform for meaningful citizen engagement, positioning climate action as a driver of social cohesion and sustainable peace, and advancing implementation frameworks that deliver measurable and accountable outcomes beyond policy commitments.

Held under the theme “Building Bridges for People, Peace, and Our Planet,” the three-day multi-stakeholder engagement is designed to deepen public ownership of the Plateau State Climate Change Policy and strengthen pathways for inclusive, gender-responsive, and conflict-sensitive implementation.

The dialogue will bring together government representatives, civil society actors, interfaith and traditional leaders, women’s rights advocates, persons with disabilities (PWDs), youth leaders, media practitioners, and community stakeholders to translate climate policy commitments into practical, community-driven action. Discussions will examine Plateau State’s climate risks and vulnerabilities, clarify the mandate of the Plateau State Climate Assembly (PSCA), and simplify policy provisions into accessible and inclusive action points. 

According to Ms. Enang, high-level panel discussions featuring representatives of the Plateau State Ministry of Environment, PSCA, and the media, participants will interrogate implementation pathways that prioritize gender equality, social inclusion, climate justice, and accountability. 

The final day of the meeting will transition from dialogue to direct engagement, with advocacy visits to the Ministry of Environment and the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the State (SGS). These engagements will provide an opportunity to present community-driven demands and secure commitments for inclusive implementation. High-level stakeholders demonstrating leadership in climate justice will be conferred with the honorary recognition of “Climate Ambassador,” reinforcing partnership, responsibility, and accountability.

The African Centre for Leadership, Strategy and Development reiterates its commitment to advancing evidence-based, people-centred policies that protect both the planet and the most vulnerable communities. 
 
Members of the public are encouraged to follow updates on the meeting via Centre LSD’s social media platforms.

In times like these, when politics feels tense and uncertain, a country naturally reflects on its history and the leaders who helped shape it. For Salva Kiir Mayardit, his journey has never been about comfort or personal gain. It has been about sacrifice, endurance, and commitment to the freedom and sovereignty of South Sudan.

This is the same man some people try to mock today. But leadership is not built on loud criticism or social media noise it is built on years of struggle, survival, and service. President Kiir is one of the few leaders who went through the hardships of the Anyanya I and Anyanya II wars, and later stood firm during the long liberation struggle under the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement/SPLA. He remained committed until the 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement gave the South self-governance, which later led to the historic 2011 referendum that gave us our independence.

He is more than just a politician. He represents a generation that fought for this country to exist. On the international stage, he remains the recognized face of our nation a symbol of the long road that brought South Sudan into the community of nations. Positions can be contested, but history cannot be erased. Sacrifice cannot be faked, and legitimacy cannot simply be claimed.

In this difficult political moment, stability is not optional it is essential. The implementation of the Revitalized Peace Agreement (R-ARCSS) requires experience, patience, and understanding of the complex realities of our country. Transition periods are delicate. They require steady leadership, not risky experiments.

Of course, people may disagree politically. That is normal in any democracy. But changing leadership in the middle of a fragile peace process demands more than frustration  it demands a realistic and unifying alternative that can hold the country together and complete the transition responsibly.

Despite the challenges, many South Sudanese still believe in him and continue to hope for stability under his guidance. Leading during war builds strength; leading during fragile peace requires wisdom, calmness, and vision.

May God grant President Salva Kiir Mayardit wisdom, good health, and strength to guide South Sudan through this difficult chapter toward lasting peace, accountability, and a stable democratic future.

History always remembers those who carried the nation on their shoulders when it mattered most.

Sweden’s Deputy Prime Minister Ebba Busch has sparked an intense and wide-ranging debate across Europe after stating that immigrants must integrate into Swedish values and respect the country’s laws. Her remarks quickly drew strong reactions both domestically and internationally, placing Sweden at the center of a broader Western discussion on identity, security, and social cohesion.

Supporters believe her statement reflects growing public concerns about integration gaps, parallel communities, and the need to safeguard democratic principles. They argue that openness and humanitarian policies must go hand in hand with civic responsibility, respect for the rule of law, and a shared commitment to national values. In their view, integration is not about exclusion—it is about participation, accountability, and protecting the social contract that binds a nation together.

Critics, however, caution that such rhetoric may risk alienating immigrant communities and oversimplifying complex social challenges. They emphasize that integration issues are closely linked to housing, education, employment opportunities, and discrimination. According to them, strong political messaging without balanced policy solutions can deepen divisions rather than bridge them. Their concern is that powerful slogans may overshadow nuanced, long-term strategies.

This debate highlights a larger European challenge: balancing humanitarian responsibilities with cultural integration and the rule of law in a time of high migration and increasing political polarization. Sweden’s experience mirrors similar tensions in countries such as the USA, Canada, the United Kingdom, and beyond—where questions of national identity, inclusion, and public safety are increasingly intersecting. The direction these debates take will likely depend on thoughtful leadership and responsible dialogue, rather than quick or simplistic answers.

An image that people on social media are claiming shows Jeffrey Epstein alive and walking down a street in Tel Aviv, Israel, is fake and was made using AI. It has been shared thousands of times, and many appear to think it’s genuine. But Epstein died by suicide in 2019 while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges.

There’s also another clear red flag: the Hebrew street signs in the image are gibberish.

Always check the source before you share.

MONITORING AND IMPACT ASSESSMENT VISIT
____________________________________________________________

A Remarkable Transformation
Walking through Mogiri yesterday, the atmosphere is unrecognizable from ninety days ago. What was once a flashpoint for road ambushes, revenge killings, and cattle raiding has become a corridor of quiet and communal interaction. The "Success of the Impossible" is visible in the eyes of the youth who have traded their weapons for dialogue through Peace Committees, Women, faith and community leaders engaging the Murle traders, Dinka Bor Youth, host communities and the residence in Mogiri.
Key Impacts Observed:
• Security of Movement: Road ambushes and criminal activities at the Mogiri center have effectively ceased.
• Restored Trust: Youth from the Dinka Bor, Murle traders and host communities are now engaging in peaceful co-existence, breaking the cycle of historical hostilities.
• Community Stability: The cessation of road ambushes, cattle raiding and diverse youth violence in Mogiri and long Juba – Bor road  has allowed local markets and daily life to resume without the constant shadow of fear, children playing games and sports activities at the corners of the centre
The Road Ahead: Protecting the Peace
While the results are inspiring, Peace is a fragile garden that requires constant tending. As the current project phase nears its conclusion, we have identified critical sustainability gaps that must be addressed to ensure this harmony isn't temporary.
"We have already built the bridge with our partners; now we must ensure it is strong enough to weather the storms of tomorrow.
Gratitude and Partnership
This intervention was made possible through the unwavering support of the Canadian Embassy through Canada Fund for Local Initiatives (CFLI). Their commitment to grassroots peacebuilding has saved lives and restored hope to Mogiri residence and the surrounding communities including Bilnyang and Mangalla. 
Special thanks to @Geoffrey LD and the entire team at the Embassy. Your partnership is the engine behind this progress. We look forward to discussing how we can address the remaining gaps and solidify these gains for the long term sustainability.

There are certain kinds of loss that defy comprehension. The death of a young parent is one of them—especially when that parent is serving their country, doing their duty, and leaves behind an infant who will never remember their face except through photographs.

Captain Victoria Pinckney was 27 years old on May 3, 2013. She was a wife, a new mother to a 7-month-old daughter, an Air Force Academy graduate, and a KC-135 Stratotanker pilot. She was supposed to come home from her deployment. She was supposed to watch her daughter grow up, teach her to be strong like her mother, show her what it meant to serve something bigger than yourself.

Instead, on that day in May, her refueling aircraft crashed during a mission in Kyrgyzstan, a mountainous country in Central Asia that serves as a critical transit point for U.S. military operations. In an instant, Captain Pinckney, along with Captain Mark Tyler Voss and Technical Sergeant Herman Mackey III, lost their lives in service to their country.

And a 7-month-old baby girl lost her mother forever.

Let's talk about who Victoria Pinckney was, because she wasn't just a rank and a name on a casualty list. She was a force of nature—the kind of person who attacked life with the same intensity she brought to everything else.

Victoria attended the United States Air Force Academy in Colorado Springs, one of the most demanding undergraduate institutions in America. Getting accepted to a service academy requires not just excellent grades and test scores, but demonstrated leadership, physical fitness, and a commitment to military service. Victoria had all of that and more.

While at the Academy, she didn't just study—she competed. She played rugby, a brutal, physically demanding sport that requires toughness, teamwork, and the willingness to throw your body into situations most people would avoid. Rugby players are a special breed—they play without pads, embrace contact, and finish games covered in mud and bruises with huge smiles on their faces. That was Victoria's style.

As if rugby wasn't enough, she also earned a black belt in karate. Think about what that represents. A black belt isn't something you get by showing up to a few classes—it requires years of dedicated practice, countless hours of training, mastering complex techniques, pushing through pain and frustration, and demonstrating both physical skill and mental discipline. Victoria did that while managing the intense academic workload of the Air Force Academy and competing in rugby.

She was an achiever, a competitor, someone who set high standards for herself and then exceeded them.

After graduating from the Academy, Victoria entered pilot training and earned her wings as a KC-135 Stratotanker pilot. The KC-135 is an aerial refueling aircraft—essentially a flying gas station that extends the range and capabilities of other military aircraft. It's not the glamorous fighter jet that gets featured in movies, but it's absolutely critical to modern air operations. Without aerial refueling, fighters, bombers, and transport aircraft couldn't complete many of their missions.

Flying the KC-135 requires exceptional skill. You're piloting a large aircraft loaded with thousands of pounds of fuel, often at night or in bad weather, meeting up with other aircraft traveling at high speeds, and transferring fuel through a flying boom or drogue system while both aircraft maintain precise formation. One mistake, one moment of inattention, and disaster can occur.

Victoria mastered this complex mission. She became a rated aircraft commander, trusted to lead crews and execute critical refueling operations. And she did all of this while starting a family, balancing the demands of being a new mother with the requirements of being an Air Force officer and pilot.

Imagine that balancing act for a moment. You're a young mother with a baby who's just learning to sit up, to recognize faces, to smile and laugh at the world. Every day brings new milestones you don't want to miss. But you're also an Air Force officer with a duty to fly missions, to deploy when needed, to serve your country even when it means leaving your infant daughter behind for weeks or months at a time.

That's what military families sacrifice—not just the service member's time and safety, but precious moments with children who grow up so fast. First words spoken while mom or dad is deployed. First steps taken while a parent is thousands of miles away. Birthday parties celebrated through video calls instead of in person.

Victoria accepted those sacrifices because she believed in service. She'd taken an oath. She'd trained for years. And she understood that her missions mattered—that every successful refueling operation meant other aircrews could complete their missions, that her work saved lives and accomplished objectives that kept Americans safe.

On May 3, 2013, Victoria was flying a mission in support of operations in Afghanistan when her KC-135 crashed shortly after takeoff from the Transit Center at Manas in Kyrgyzstan. Investigators would later determine the cause, but in that moment, three Air Force members lost their lives: Captain Victoria Pinckney, Captain Mark Tyler Voss, and Technical Sergeant Herman Mackey III.

Three families shattered. Three sets of parents who'd raised children they were proud of, only to receive the knock on the door that every military family dreads. Three circles of friends and fellow service members grieving the loss of people they'd trusted, worked with, and cared about.

And one 7-month-old daughter who would never remember her mother's voice, her laugh, her touch. Who would grow up looking at photographs and videos, hearing stories from family members, trying to understand why everyone else has a mom and she doesn't.

Victoria's grandfather spoke at her memorial service. His words captured something essential about who she was: "Family was everything to Tori. She loved her family, her country, and the Air Force."

That's the order that matters—family first, then country, then service. Victoria didn't serve because she loved flying more than she loved her daughter. She served because she believed that by doing her duty, she was building a safer world for her daughter to grow up in. She was protecting the freedoms her daughter would someday exercise. She was setting an example of courage, dedication, and selfless service that her daughter could be proud of.

But she would have traded all of it—the Academy degree, the black belt, the pilot wings, the missions, the service—for one more day with her baby girl. Any parent would.

That's the cruelty of military service. Sometimes it asks for everything. Sometimes dedicated, skilled, accomplished people like Victoria Pinckney don't come home. Sometimes babies lose parents. Sometimes families are left with memories and medals and a flag, when all they want is their loved one back.

Victoria's daughter is a teenager now, growing up without the mother who gave her life and then gave her life protecting others. She's probably heard countless stories about her mom—the rugby player, the black belt, the pilot, the officer who served with honor. She's probably looked at photos trying to see herself in her mother's face, searching for connections, building a relationship with someone she can't remember.

And somewhere, Victoria's grandfather and the rest of her family carry on, keeping her memory alive, making sure that little girl knows exactly who her mother was and how much she was loved.

To Captain Victoria Pinckney: you were a warrior, an athlete, a leader, and most importantly, a mother. Your daughter will grow up knowing that her mom was someone special—someone who could do anything she set her mind to, who served with courage and skill, who loved her family fiercely, and who made the ultimate sacrifice while serving her country. That's a legacy worth honoring.

To Victoria's daughter: your mother loved you more than anything. Every time she flew, she carried you in her heart. Every mission she completed, she did believing she was building a better world for you. Though you can't remember her, she will always be part of you—in your strength, in your courage, and in the example she set of what it means to live with purpose and serve with honor.

To all who serve in uniform: thank you. And to the families who support them, who wait anxiously for their return, who raise children with one parent deployed—thank you. Your sacrifice matters. Your service, though different, is equally important.

Captain Victoria Pinckney gave everything. May we honor her memory by never forgetting what she and so many others have sacrificed for our freedom.

Rest in peace, Captain. Your watch is over. And may your daughter grow up knowing she had a mother who was truly extraordinary.

Edmund Yakani, Executive Director of Community Empowerment for Progress Organization (CEPO), has welcomed the roadmap adopted by the AUC-5 Plus Summit regarding the situation of South Sudan’s transitional process.

Mr. Yakani stated that the roadmap has met the expectations of civil society and expressed hope that it will be implemented genuinely, effectively, and in a timely manner.

He emphasized that the past experiences of delayed implementation of the Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in the Republic of South Sudan (R-ARCSS) must not be repeated during the execution of the AUC-5 roadmap. According to him, the culture of “dragging feet” in implementing peace agreements has previously undermined public confidence and slowed progress toward stability.

Mr. Yakani further stressed that it is high time for South Sudan’s leaders to demonstrate their primary responsibility and political will by ensuring the full and faithful implementation of the AUC-5 roadmap for the country’s transitional process.

He called upon all stakeholders to prioritize national interest, peace, and democratic transformation over personal and political interests.

This is a deeply sensitive issue, and there isn’t a simple yes-or-no answer. Immigration enforcement affects real people and communities, so opinions often depend on how raids are carried out, who they target, and what safeguards are in place.

Supporters of increased enforcement argue that immigration agencies are responsible for upholding the law regardless of location or religion. They believe consistent enforcement helps maintain the rule of law and discourages illegal activity, stressing that actions should be based on legal status, not faith.

Opponents strongly disagree, especially when raids appear concentrated in Muslim-majority areas. They argue this creates fear, stigmatization, and the perception of religious or ethnic targeting. Critics say such actions can damage trust between communities and authorities, making people less likely to cooperate with law enforcement or seek help when needed.

The broader reflection is about balance. Every country has the right to enforce its laws, but how enforcement is done matters just as much as the law itself. Policies that prioritize fairness, transparency, and human dignity tend to strengthen social cohesion, while those seen as selective or aggressive risk deepening division in an already polarized world.

Khúc Lan và “Sa mạc tình yêu”
Nhà văn Duyên Anh đã viết về nữ nhạc sĩ Khúc Lan, cô em gái của nhạc sĩ Phượng Vũ, tác giả của những ca khúc “Cánh thư mùa hạ”, “Rừng ái ân”, “Áo nhà binh”: “Khúc Lan, thuở sinh viên du học bên Nhật, đã chớm mơ mộng và lãng mạn. Cô gái của thị xã Thủ Dầu Một nên thơ nhất miền Nam, còn mang tên Bình Dương, xa xứ mẹ, mang theo nỗi hoang mang. Năm 1973, quê nhà đang hiu hắt chiến trường, quê người hoa anh đào thi nhau đua nở, rợp kín mọi tủi cực của nhân loại. Những khổ nhục của riêng mình xếp đống lên nhau, canh cánh cõi lòng Khúc Lan. Hoa đào bất lực trong sứ mạng xóa sạch niềm đau đớn của nàng. Lãng mạn và mơ mộng vừa chớm nở quê nhà, đã úa héo quê người. Cơ man nốt nhạc nhảy múa tưng bừng quanh hồn nàng, nhưng chẳng chịu đậu trên khuôn nhạc nàng. Khúc Lan rầu rĩ. Ngày lại ngày, đêm lại đêm, nàng mong tháng năm qua mau. Để nàng về Thủ Dầu Một ươm mơ. Chỉ quê hương của nàng mới giúp đỡ nàng toại nguyện giấc mộng trở thành người soạn ca khúc và người truyền đạt ca khúc của mình tới dân gian.

Năm 1975, Khúc Lan sang Pháp. Bắt đầu một thân phận lưu vong. Nàng miên man sáng tác những ca khúc thương làng cũ, nhớ cảnh xưa. Hai chữ quê hương bàng bạc trong nhạc Khúc Lan. Nó rơi, rơi mãi như nước mắt dân tha hương lưu lạc! Rồi một ngày kia, không thể nghe giọt lệ đổ xuống đời, Khúc Lan đẩy ca khúc của mình qua một khúc rẽ mới. Nàng làm nhạc chiến đấu. Tổng hội sinh viên Paris hoan nghênh nàng nhiệt liệt. Tuổi trẻ gặp tuổi trẻ. 4 tập nhạc liên tiếp xuất bản. Ở Paris, nghệ thuật âm thầm tuyệt vọng, im lặng như tờ. Khúc Lan hát nhạc Khúc Lan, quảng cáo trịnh trọng trên báo chí, áp phích in màu đàng hoàng dán gần nơi Khúc Lan xuất hiện, chỉ có 300 thính giả trẻ tuổi nhiều nhất, 100 thính giả ít nhất, náo nức tới chiêm ngưỡng Khúc Lan và nghe Khúc Lan hát nhạc của nàng. Đằng đẵng 8 năm, Khúc Lan cống hiến tài năng của mình cho Tổng hội sinh viên Việt Nam lưu vong ở Paris. Khi Khúc Lan thất vọng với Paris, một câu hỏi bất chợt hiện ra: Nhạc chiến đấu thôi ư ? Không phải. Nhạc chiến đấu phục vụ một giai đoạn ngắn ngủi nào đó. Nó sẽ chết, chết chẳng ai thương xót vào một giai đoạn ngắn ngủi nào đó. Âm nhạc dùng âm thanh để diễn tả niềm vui và nỗi buồn của con người, không diễn tả những cảnh thù hận, những cảnh giết chóc của loài người... Nói thật đúng, âm nhạc là nghệ thuật siêu đẳng rung lên tình yêu và hạnh phúc nhân sinh. Những ca khúc phản chiến của Trịnh Công Sơn biến đi, chỉ còn những ca khúc thương yêu của Trịnh Công Sơn tồn tại. Khúc Lan đã có câu giải thích và tâm hồn nàng bị cuốn xoáy vào nhạc yêu thương và hạnh phúc. Năm 1983, Khúc Lan quyết định sang Mỹ định cư để sáng tác những ca khúc mới nhất. Nước Mỹ, tiểu bang California ưu ái Khúc Lan lắm. Nàng phơi phới soạn nhạc tình yêu, phơi phới truyền đạt nhạc tình yêu của nàng…” (Khúc Lan, người nghệ sĩ chới với trên giòng nhạc)

Từ khi đặt chân lên quê hương mới trên lục địa Bắc Mỹ, Khúc Lan đã viết được nhiều ca khúc, đặt lời Việt cho nhiều nhạc phẩm nước ngoài, và những giọng ca hàng đầu của cộng đồng người Việt ở hải ngoại đã giúp cho công chúng biết đến tên tuổi của cô. Các album nhạc ngoại lời Việt của những nữ ca sĩ tài danh như Ngọc Lan hay Ý Lan bao giờ cũng có những nhạc phẩm ký tên Khúc Lan và tình yêu cô dành cho nước Nhật của một thời tuổi trẻ đã được thể hiện qua những ca khúc của Nhật được cô đặt lời Việt.
