Funerals in Juba: Reciting Quranic Verses at the Funerals of non-Muslims!

By DENGDIT AYOK 

Today, I want to write honestly about this phenomenon that has infiltrated our funerals and mourning gatherings, where we grieve and are consumed by sorrow for our departed loved ones. 

This occurs amidst an atmosphere of shameful silence, and none of us dares to speak about it, despite the occasional feelings of astonishment or social shock that lead people to remain silent. 

This is because the social customs prevalent in our society do not permit questioning, expressing opinions, or raising respectful, logical objections about anything in a place of grief or mourning, out of respect for the deceased and their family, and also out of fear of hurting the feelings of the bereaved family during these moments of profound pain and deep sorrow.

Between this and that, the phenomenon crept in and imposed its authority on everyone against their will, amidst this gloomy silence; indeed, everyone coexisted with this phenomenon because it is repeated so often in funeral houses, and it became part of the manifestations of grief and mourning in most of the funerals held in Juba, the capital, and I do not know if it is the same situation in the states.

Let me give you some examples upon which we will base our arguments and what should be done.

On Sunday, September 15, 2024, a dear sister and colleague passed away in Juba. She was a Catholic Christian, but I later learned that her husband's family is a Muslim family. According to the information I obtained, her husband is also a Muslim. Although I had known him for some time, I hadn't seen anything in him to indicate that he was a Muslim, perhaps because I wasn't very close to him, and because in South Sudan, we don't care much about asking people about which faith or religion they follow as it was the case in the old Sudan, a practice imported into Sudan from the Arab countries.

On the other hand, I consider him a respectable man who keeps the details of his faith to himself and doesn't reveal them to others, unlike the Pharisees and Sadducees of our time.

In general, we joined the family to console them in their most difficult moments of loss. The funeral rites proceeded as usual in her home, and she was buried in her hometown after her body was transported there. Then prayers were held at Simba Square in front of Giada Aljunubia—the Southern Command Garrison—in Juba on Saturday, October 05, 2024.

As usual, people from all walks of life, both Christians and Muslims, attended the prayers, because occasions of mourning, as is their nature, bring people together regardless of their faith.

The Catholic Church led the prayers for the soul of the deceased, after which condolences were offered to the family. I was a member of the information committee at the time, responsible for introducing the speakers who offered their condolences to the family.

Halfway through the program, some people approached me and asked me to welcome one of the sheikhs who had arrived at the funeral, so I did. The sheikh was a tall man wearing a white robe or jalabiya, a white turban wrapped around his head, a scarf draped over his shoulders, and Sudanese sandals (markoub) on his feet. He had a long beard, and from his features, I could tell he was from the Republic of Sudan—either northern or central Sudan.

A few moments after I welcomed him by name, which had been written down on a piece of paper handed to me, the same people who had approached me the first time and asked me to welcome him again said he wished to recite verses from the Quran.

This request came after the church services had concluded, and I, along with everyone else, thought the services were over. Since our deceased sister was a Christian, we felt there was no need to recite Quranic texts or verses at her funeral, as the church had already come and performed prayer service according to Christian faith.

I felt it was right for us, as Christians who are still alive, to organize prayers for our sister's soul, perform the eulogy, introduce mourners one by one, and observe all the mourning rituals according to her Christian faith and her political affiliation with the Sudan People's Liberation Movement (SPLM), also giving opportunities to her comrades in the SPLM. 

Based on these principles, I decided not to allow the aforementioned sheikh to recite Quranic verses, not to exclude him from any service at the funeral, but to ensure that the funeral rituals followed the deceased sister's faith. Unfortunately, there were signs of unease and silent anger on the faces of those sent to me demanding that I allow the sheikh to recite verses from the Quran. However, I was determined to proceed as planned.

On Sunday, September 27, 2025, a dear friend passed away at the height of his success in a life dedicated to serving humanity, not just in his small homeland, but across the vast expanse of his larger homeland—the African continent. His untimely death deeply saddened us, but we found strength to bear the shock because we know that death knows no age or anything else we, as living beings, consider. When death comes, it comes true and irrevocable, leaving behind only regret and sorrow for the loss of a loved one, and the pain of that loss.

At the funeral held at the deceased's home, we were surprised when the program's host invited one brother to recite verses from the Quran, after one of the church evangelists present had offered Christian prayers. Our deceased brother, as we knew him, was a devout Catholic. Despite his respect for all religions and his social connections and friendships with people of all faiths, including Muslims—a characteristic for which he was known—he never entered a mosque, but church to attend worship service. It was only natural that the funeral rites be conducted according to his Christian faith.

Quranic verses were recited at a funeral for a non-Muslim, and everything proceeded normally, but I didn't approve it. This was due to the funeral committee's courtesy.

Such mistakes or courtesies often occur when funeral committees are composed of both Christian and Muslim members, especially if the committee head happened to be a Muslim. They might prefer to include Quranic recitation in the rituals after the Christian prayer during the mourning period. There's nothing wrong with a Muslim man or woman being chosen to head the funeral committee, as people are related by blood and social ties, but they must adhere to the rituals according to the deceased's faith.

It's noticeable that Muslim brothers insist on reciting the Quran at funerals, even though they know the deceased wasn't a Muslim. They believe that letting non-Muslims hear Quranic recitations is a good deed and brings divine reward. Conversely, I have never seen a Christian insisting on holding a Christian funeral service for a Muslim.

I was chosen as a translator at the funeral. Initially, I didn't like the idea, but I later realized it was necessary because the mourners were diverse. There were guests from the African Union who had accompanied the deceased's body from the country where my dear friend passed away to Juba. They didn't understand Arabic, the language spoken by most South Sudanese, nor did they understand Dinka, the language some of the speakers at the funeral used to address the mourners.

In October 2024, my Christian friend's Muslim wife passed away. He insisted on performing the funeral rites according to Islamic tradition. He brought a sheikh from a nearby mosque, along with several Quran reciters, who recited the Quran in a circle, the air thick with incense smoke. They concluded the recitations with prayers for her soul, asking God the Almighty to accept her into Paradise with the righteous, the martyrs, and the good companions, as Islamic faith dictates.

Another time, last year, I attended a funeral at the home of a dear and highly respected friend, who had lost relatives. I found that most of the prayers had been performed, and people were listening to a sermon by a Christian preacher.

Ironically, the Christian preacher didn't adhere to readings from the Bible alone. Instead, he delivered sermons using both the Bible and the Quran simultaneously, claiming that the person in whose home the prayers were being held was a man living with Christians and Muslims within his family.

This family was in deep mourning, having lost two members in a single day. I listened to the sermon, and the overall impression the preacher left on me was more about showcasing his knowledge of the Bible and the Quran than performing the funeral rites as intended.

There was no need to recite the Quran at a funeral for a non-Muslim. The proper procedure would have been to conduct the rites according to Christian faith, but social niceties dictated otherwise. There is no objection to reciting the Quran if the deceased is a Muslim.

Finally, a memorial service was held for the late Amin Akasha Mohamed Ahmed (may God have mercy on him), a prominent national businessman who passed away in Cairo on Saturday, January 24, 2026. The service took place at Simba Square on Saturday, February 07, 2026, and the usual social customs were observed.

He was a man truly deserving of the memorial service, which highlighted his contributions and role in supporting the political cause of South Sudan, from the Anya Nya Movement to the SPLM/SPLA. We heard firsthand accounts from historical leaders of the SPLM about Amin Akasha's contributions, including Mama Rebecca Nyandeng de Mabior, Vice President, General Aleu Ayieny Aleu, Minister of Interior, and others who spoke at the memorial service.

Amin Akasha was honored as a national leader and social icon by the Red Army's military mudic band in a manner befitting his stature, in the presence of prominent national figures from the SPLM leadership, who recognized his merits. This, in my opinion, was a good thing.

Initially, the rituals proceeded according to our uncle Akasha's faith, as we all know he was a Muslim, and that the living should adhere to the rituals according to his Islamic beliefs. However, I was surprised while watching the memorial service live on Journalist Michael Rial Christopher's Faceook page when Sheikh Juma Saeed invited a Christian Pastor to read passages from the Bible, contrary to my expectations and the norms followed in such a situation, arguing that the deceased was a man who had interacted with all kinds of people. While this is true, mixing different funeral rites is unnecessary. Sheikh Juma Saeed's action was merely a product of the repeated social niceties and the policy of seeking partnership in everything that the members of the Islamic Council follow.

At that moment, I realized that social niceties had reached their peak, with people trying to curry favor and gain approval at any cost, even when it was misplaced. The deceased believed in only one book during his lifetime, so why shouldn't those who pledged to hold a memorial service for him read only that book? Are we to convert our departed Christian loved ones to Islam and Muslims to Christianity just to appease those attending the funeral? This behavior contradicts the reality of the lives the deceased lived before their passing, as witnessed by everyone. I suppose that these are matters that both Christians and Muslims understand perfectly.

In summary, this fabricated phenomenon in Juba confirms that the dead are more truthful than we, the living, because they depart with the faith they chose and practiced during their lives. Yet we, the living, recite books they never believed in during their funeral rites, books whose teachings they never adhered to in life—not to honor them, but to appease the social diversity present at the funeral. Perhaps these deceased held a different view during their lives.

This phenomenon underscores that our funeral rites are sometimes insincere, as social niceties have become publicized and often compromise their authenticity. It suggests that the dead are the true believers, while the living merely pay lip service to others at the expense of the departed.

This phenomenon confirms that honesty is eroding in the face of frequent social niceties, and that these niceties have carved out a niche for themselves in funerals, becoming the accepted reality without question or objection. And if someone objects, they are seen as disrespectful to the dead and their families, and are labeled as deviant and a troublemaker for going against the herd mentality.

But let me tell you, in the words of Christ, “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be pulled up by the roots” (Matthew 15:13). And I also tell you to beware of the leaven that the Pharisees, Sadducees, and social tax collectors sow in funerals.

In conclusion, adhering to the funeral rites of the deceased's faith is essential and it is right for us to do so. It is what the living should offer the dead in return for their sincerity in their faith during their lives. Every society has its own specific funeral rites. So why make mere formalities a reward for those who have passed away sincerely, just to please those attending the funeral? This is undoubtedly hypocrisy. These practices must stop.

When the national leader, John Garang de Mabior, passed away on July 30, 2005, and prayers were held for his soul on August 06, 2005, in Juba prior to the lowering of his casket near the National Parliament, the services were led by Christian clergy: the late Bishop Joseph Marona, the late Bishop Paulino Lukudu Loro, among others.

Muslims were present at the funeral, including the President, Omar Hassan Ahmed al-Bashir, but the Christian clergy did not request a sheikh to recite the Quran, adhering to the deceased's religious beliefs in order to conduct the funeral rites according to his faith, as the late leader and politician was a Christian.

MANDI WAJIB SEBELUM PUASA RAMADHAN 

Menjelang bulan suci ini, banyak umat Islam mulai mempersiapkan diri, bukan hanya secara mental & ibadah, tetapi jg dalam hal kebersihan dan kesucian diri.

Salah satu amalan yang kerap dilakukan adalah mandi wajib sebelum memasuki hari pertama puasa. Tradisi ini sudah lama dikenal di tengah masyarakat, terutama bagi mereka yang ingin memulai Ramadhan dalam keadaan suci dari hadas besar.

Selain menjadi bentuk penghormatan terhadap bulan penuh berkah, mandi wajib juga menjadi langkah penting agar seseorang bisa menjalan
kan ibadh lain seperti shalat, membc Al-Quran, dan aktivitas ibadah lainnya tanpa hambatan.

Namun, perlu dipahami bahwa istilah “Niat Mandi Sebelum Puasa Ramadhan” sering dipakai dalam dua konteks, 
*Mandi sunnah untuk menyambut Ramadhan, "Mandi wajib bagi orang yg memang sedang
 dalam keadaan junub atau hadas besar.

#Adakah Anjuran untuk Mandi Wajib Sebelum Ramadhan?

Pada dasarnya, mandi wajib bukanlah syarat sah puasa. Artinya, seseorang tetap bisa men-
jalankan puasa meskipun ia belum mandi wajib saat malam hari, selama puasanya dimulai sebelum fajar dan ia berniat puasa.

Meski begitu, para ulama menjelaskan bahwa orang yang memiliki hadas besar dianjurkan untuk segera mandi sebelum masuk waktu Subuh.
 
Tujuannya bukan agar puasanya sah, melainkn
agar ia dapat menjalankan ibadah lain seperti shalat Subuh dalam keadaan suci.

Dalam beberapa riwayat hadits, disebutkan bahwa Rasulullah Shalallahu'alaihi Wa Sallam pernah memasuki waktu fajar dalam keadaan junub, lalu beliau mandi dan tetap melanjutkan puasa.

Ini menjadi penegasan bahwa kondisi junub ketika fajar tiba tidak otomatis membatalkan puasa, selama seseorang segera bersuci untuk ibadah lainnya.

Adapun mandi sunnah menjelang Ramadhan lebih dimaknai sebagai bentuk kesiapan me-
nyambut bulan suci, sekaligus menjaga ke -
bersihan tubuh dan ketenangan batin.

#Kondisi yang Mengharuskan Mandi Wajib

Mandi wajib harus dilakukan ketika seseorang mengalami hadas besar. Beberapa keadaan yang mewajibkan mandi besar antara lain:
*Keluar air mani, baik karena mimpi basah
  maupun sebab lainnya
*Melakukan hubungan suami istri
*Selesai haid bagi perempuan
*Selesai nifas setelah melahirkan
*Masuk Islam, menurut sebagian pendapat
  ulama, sebagai bentuk penyucian diri

Pada hakikatnya, melakukan mandi wajib  sebelum puasa hanya untuk membersihkan diri dari hadas besar, bukan sebagai syarat puasa. 

Namun, banyak muslim memilih melakukannya lebih awal agar lebih tenang saat memasuki hari pertama Ramadhan.

#Niat Mandi Wajib Menjelang Puasa
  Ramadhan

Ada dua jenis mandi yang bisa dilakukan menjelang Ramadhan, masing-masing memiliki niat yang berbeda.:
*Niat Mandi Sunnah Sebelum Ramadhan
  Bagi yg ingin mandi sunnah untk menyambut datangnya bulan Ramadhan tanpa sedang ber
hadas besar, berikut bacaannya:

نَوَيْتُ أَدَاءَ اْلغُسْلِ اْلمَسْنُوْنِ لِيْ فِيْ هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ مِنْ رَمَضَانَ لله تَعَالَى

Artinya:
 “Aku berniat menjalankan mandi yg disunnah
kan kepadaku pd malam ini di bulan Ramadhan karena Allah Ta’ala.”

*Niat Mandi Wajib Sebelum Puasa Ramadhan
  (untuk yang berhadas besar)
  Bagi yang sedang berhadas besar dan ingin bersuci sebelum memulai puasa, bacaan niatnya adalah:

نَوَيْتُ الْغُسْلَ لِرَفْعِ اْلحَدَثِ اْلأَكْبَرِ مِنَ اْلِجنَابَةِ فَرْضًا لِلهِ تَعَالَى

Artinya: 
“Aku niat mandi untuk menghilangkan hadats besar dari janabah, fardhu karena Allah ta’ala.”

Niat ini dilafalkan tepat ketika air pertama mulai disiramkan ke tubuh.

#Tata Cara Mandi Sebelum Puasa Ramadhan
  Mandi wajib bukanlah mandi biasa. Ada rang
kaian yang perlu dilakukan secara berurutan agar mandi dianggap sah menurut syariat. 

Berikut langkah-langkahnya :
*Bacakan niat mandi wajib sebelum masuk ke
  kamar mandi atau saat hendak memulai.
*Cuci tangan kanan dan kiri masing-masing
  sebanyak tiga kali.
*Bersihkan bagian dubur, kemaluan, serta area
 yang rentan kotoran seperti ketiak, pusar, dan
 sela-sela jari kaki menggunakan tangan kiri.
*Cuci kembali kedua tangan hingga bersih,
  bisa menggunakan sabun.
*Berwudhu sebagaimana wudhu untuk shalat.
*Basahi rambut dari pangkal hingga ujung
. secara merata.
*Guyur kepala sebanyak tiga kali hingga
 seluruh bagian kepala basah.
*Siramkan air ke sisi tubuh kanan sebanyak
  tiga kali, kemudian lanjutkan ke sisi kiri juga
  tiga kali.
*Pastikan lipatan kulit seperti bagian belakang
  telinga, leher, dan sela-sela tubuh turut
  dibersihkan.
*Lanjutkan mandi seperti biasa hingga seluruh
. tubuh benar-benar bersih.
*Sebelum keluar dari kamar mandi, dianjurkan
  untuk berwudhu sekali lagi sebagaimana
. wudhu sebelum shalat.

#Doa Setelah Mandi Wajib
  Rangkaian mandi wajib akan lebih sempurna jika ditutup dengan doa setelah keluar dari kamar mandi. 

أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لاَ إِلَهَ إِلاَّ اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لاَ شَرِيكَ لَهُ وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا عَبْدُهُ وَرَسُولُهُ اللَّهُمَّ اجْعَلْنِى مِنَ التَّوَّابِينَ وَاجْعَلْنِى مِنَ الْمُتَطَهِّرِينَ

Artinya: 
“Aku bersaksi bahwa tiada Tuhan selain Allah Yang Maha Esa, tiada sekutu bagi-Nya, dan aku bersaksi bahwa Muhammad adalah hamba sekaligus utusan-Nya. Ya Allah, jadikanlah aku bagian dari orang-orang yang senantiasa ber-
tobat, & jadikanlah aku pula termasuk golongan orang yang selalu menjaga kesucian diri.”

Doa ini merupakan penutup yang indah dari seluruh proses penyucian diri. Membacanya bukn sekadar kebiasaan, melainkan pengakuan bahwa kesucian lahir hars seiring dgn kesiapn
an batin menyongsong Ramadhan yang mulia.

Menyambut Ramadhan dengan tubuh dan hati yg bersih adalah cara terbaik untuk membuka lembaran ibadah satu bulan penuh. 

Semoga setiap langkah persiapan yg dilakukan menjadi bagian dari amal yang diterima.

Memo
NPP Coordination Office
Date: 15 Feb 2026
To: All Our Members
Ref: The Announced General Election

Dear Members of the NPP,
We are writing to inform you about the announced general election in the Republic of South Sudan. As we know, the interim government of South Sudan has been discussing elections since the signing of the R-ARCSS in late 2018. However, the ruling coalition has never been ready to conduct the vote. As a result, elections have been postponed several times to date. The reasons that delayed elections in the past have not been resolved. They include the lack of funds, insecurity, and a lack of political will from the various factions of the SPLM to move the country past the current political impasse. 
After careful consultation with other political forces in the country, we have concluded that elections will not proceed as announced by the ruling factions of the SPLM. Hence, the recent government announcement of an election at the end of the year is pure political propaganda by the SPLM and its partners in the government. Their plan is to continue ruling the country for an extended period under the R-ARCSS arrangements. 
Up to this point, there are no preparations for the election. This shows that the country is not ready for an election. It is unlikely to conduct a credible election without voter registration and other necessary measures that facilitate a free and fair election.
If there are new developments concerning the election and other political issues, we will inform you immediately.
Sincerely,
NPP Coordination Office

Ziarah kubur adalah amalan sunnah dalam Islam yang bertujuan untuk menghormati orang yang telah meninggal, berdoa untuk mereka, serta merenungkan kehidupan akhirat. Berikut adalah adab dan tata cara yang perlu diperhatikan:
 
Adab Ziarah Kubur
 
- Niat ikhlas: Lakukan ziarah karena Allah SWT, bukan untuk tujuan duniawi atau mencari berkah mistis.
- Persiapan diri: Berwudhu atau mandi junub jika diperlukan, dan berpakaian sopan serta rapi.
- Menjaga sikap: Bertutur kata dengan tenang dan sopan, tidak bercanda atau berbicara hal yang tidak penting.
- Menghindari larangan: Tidak duduk, menginjak, atau menyandarkan tubuh pada kuburan; tidak menangisi secara berlebihan atau meratap; tidak meminta doa atau pertolongan kepada orang yang telah meninggal; tidak membawa barang-barang yang tidak perlu seperti bunga atau dupa dengan keyakinan mistis.
- Merenungkan kematian: Gunakan kesempatan ini untuk menyadari bahwa kehidupan dunia adalah sementara dan harus bersiap menghadapi akhirat.
 
Tata Cara Ziarah Kubur
 
1. Sebelum berangkat: Berwudhu dan bacakan doa perjalanan (doa safar).
2. Saat tiba di pemakaman: Masuk dengan kaki kanan dan ucapkan salam kepada penghuni kubur, misalnya: "Assalamu 'alaikum ya ahlal qubur" atau bacaan salam yang lebih panjang sesuai sunnah.
3. Ketika berada di depan kuburan:
- Jika mengenal orang yang meninggal, dapat menghadap wajahnya dan menyebut namanya saat mengucapkan salam.
- Bacakan ayat-ayat Al-Qur'an yang pendek seperti Surat Al-Fatihah, Al-Ikhlas, Al-Falaq, dan An-Nas, serta berdoa untuk orang yang meninggal, contohnya: "Allahumma ighfir lahum warhamhum wa 'afi him wa 'fu 'anhum" (Ya Allah, ampunilah mereka, rahmatilah mereka, berikanlah kesejahteraan dan maafkanlah mereka).
- Berdoa juga untuk diri sendiri dan umat muslim secara umum.
4. Setelah ziarah: Boleh memberikan sedekah atas nama orang yang telah meninggal dan kembali dengan hati yang penuh refleksi.
 
Beberapa ulama juga menganjurkan untuk tidak berziarah pada waktu yang makruh seperti setelah Ashar hingga Maghrib atau tengah malam, kecuali ada keperluan khusus.

For many helping professionals, documentation is where institutional expectations most press against our ethics. Notes can easily center problems and locate them inside people.

What might become possible if documentation itself reflected the values, intentions, acts of resistance, and “little gems” that people bring into our conversations?

In this two-day, practice-rich workshop, participants will engage directly with narrative documentation practices — including letter writing, counter documents, collective practices, and “consulting your consultant.” A live participant interview will take place, and attendees will practice writing narrative letters in response, with opportunities to witness and reflect together.

This training is intended for practitioners already familiar with the Narrative Worldview (e.g., those who have taken NTI’s What Is Narrative Therapy? workshop or equivalent training).

Regular registration is open.
Student/senior rate and group discounts available.
We are applying for 8 CEUs for LMFTs and LICSWs/LCSWs.

If this feels resonant, we would love to have you join us.

We were honored to host a powerful engagement at Femnet Secretariat  new offices at Parklands on behalf of #WildFeministNetwork, where we met with the  Director of networks Ms. Deidre from the  Open Society Foundations (OSF USA).The meeting created an important space for dialogue, reflection, and movement strengthening.

As a grassroots feminist organization, we shared how organizing the End Femicide March demonstrated the collective power of movements in Kenya and how being part of movements and networks has enabled us to connect globally, amplify our voices, and build solidarity beyond borders.

We also highlighted the current realities facing activists in Kenya  including the urgent need for sustained support such as healing retreats and wellness spaces for frontline human rights defenders, whose work often comes with burnout, threats, and emotional strain. We shared the impact we continue to make at the centre through community empowerment, advocacy, and movement building, and emphasized the importance of resource mobilization to strengthen feminist organizing.

This engagement provided a meaningful opportunity to pitch our intentions, share our work, and continue building partnerships that sustain grassroots movements and collective action.

We deeply appreciate FEMNET’s Executive Director  Memory Zonde Kachambwa for continuously nurturing the leadership of grassroots women and creating spaces that elevate our voices, strengthen our capacity, and expand our impact.

We continue building stronger, resilient feminist movements.

The Man Called Mzamo
Chapter 52

Mpumi, out of everyone, has given birth to nothing but problematic children. I haven’t seen her other two children in years. Mbali has at least slowed down on giving her more grandchildren, but she still sleeps out and disappears whenever she wants. So for Mpumi to complain about Liwa, it really means my cute brother isn’t as innocent as I thought.
He moved out of his mother’s house. Nodumo is anything but patient with a man she didn’t snatch from another woman. Liwa has been living at home with Mpumi ever since. And Mpumi, conveniently, has forgotten who his mother is. Every complaint is directed to me.
So I decided to take him in while schools are closed. Let me monitor his behaviour myself.
Mpumi was escorting him with his bags like she’s making sure he actually comes here and nowhere else.
“When are we going to report the pregnancy?” she asks loudly from the couch.
I freeze. I’m sure Liwa thought I was just getting fat. Now he knows I’m pregnant.
“There’s no need,” I say quickly, hoping she shuts it down.
“Hhayi bo, his family needs to take responsibility.”
This will get out of hand.
I turn to Liwa. “Please make me a cup of tea.”
I just need him out of this conversation. He gets up immediately, earphones already in his ears. Mpumi watches him leave, then turns back to me.
“So he just listens to you?”
Like I said, Liwa is respectful when he’s around me. I don’t know the other versions of him.
“But you’re the same, that’s why you get along. You’re both disobedient.”
I’m not even offended. They say when you point at someone, the other four fingers point back at you.
She continues, “Anyway, the father’s family needs to pay the damages.”
“They’re not responsible,” I say quickly. I’m not going to demand Gail and Fanele clean up Mzamo’s mess.
“His family is responsible. Are you communicating with them?”
“I was talking to his sister. But she’s fixated on him. She expects me to visit him and look after his properties. I’m trying to distance myself from the whole situation so I can focus on myself.”
“Is it promising though?”
I roll my eyes. “Trial begins soon. I don’t know what the outcome will be.”
“But he can still get out,” she says.
I refuse to build hope just to watch it collapse again. Mzamo pays top lawyers and they’ve already failed to get him bail twice.
“Do you have access to his money?”
“No, I don’t want to.”
She nearly chokes on the Jelly Babies she’s been eating since she walked in. “What???”
“I can take care of myself.”
“You made this baby with another person. No matter where he is, he must take care of you. I will call MaNgobese.”
I frown. “For what?”
“To set a date so we can report the pregnancy. Look how big you already are, like a balloon. And they’re not supporting you?”
I sigh deeply. The Maphumulos are supportive. I went to my first check-up with Fanele. Gail even wanted me to move in with her, which was insane. With everything I’m dealing with, why would I live under her supervision?
I’m distancing myself from them so I can heal and prepare for my baby in peace.
“It’s their responsibility. Just like it’s now ours to pay damages for your father.”
“Huh?” I blink. What is she talking about?”
She chews another sweet and shakes her head. “Do you know how evil that woman is?”
“Nodumo?” I glance toward the passage and lower my voice. She is still Liwa’s mother.
“She’s now demanding that we pay damages.”
“You and who?” I ask slowly.
“Your mother.”
“Uyahlanya!” I forget to whisper. There is no way Nodumo took Vusi from my mother and now wants the same woman to pay damages.
“Your mother wants to pay. For the sake of your brothers, especially Liwa.”
My mother again! Heat and cold rush through me at the same time.
“I didn’t send half of my inheritance to MaNgobese so she can pay damages Vusi never bothered to pay when he was…”
Footsteps!
I stop mid-sentence and clear my throat. I’m fuming.
Liwa places the tray on the table and pulls one earphone out. “Anything else?”
“No, thank you,” I say quickly.
“I’ll go to my room.”
I nod and wait until he disappears down the passage before turning back to Mpumi.
“You agreed? You’re scared of her?”
“Scared? Who is scared?”
“You,” I say bluntly.
“You must have forgotten who you’re talking to. I’m only respecting your mother because she wants to do right by the kids.”
“My mother is a weakling. What next? Nodumo will demand a house and she’ll build it.”
“Don’t call your mother a weakling. She never fell pregnant for a jailbird.”
Now I’m offended. A jailbird? He’s only been there for four months. When I fell pregnant, he was a businessman.
“My advice to you is, don’t fight with your mother. Let her fight her own battles. You have your own battles to fight…the worst ones we have ever seen kwaShezi.”
If I wasn’t pregnant, I would have fought my mother over this. Nodumo is demanding damages simply because I received a bigger share than my brothers.
Mpumi leans back, still munching sweets. “I’m not leaving until we go report the pregnancy.”
She clearly just wanted an excuse to camp in my house. But honestly, I don’t mind. Her big mouth is the only thing keeping my brain from running wild.

Later, Mpumi announces she is in charge of dinner later. I already see potatoes being diced in the kitchen. A stew from hell is definitely loading. I escape to the lounge and sit next to Liwa. He is watching a movie, completely absorbed.
“Can I speak to you for a second?” I ask.
He lowers the volume and turns to me, suddenly tense. I have a soft spot for him. Maybe it is the oldest-sibling connection.
“Everyone is complaining about your behaviour. What’s going on?”
His eyes drop immediately.
I exhale slowly, forcing myself to stay calm.
“Look, I know you are going through physical and mental changes as a teenager. It is confusing. Everything feels confusing and frustrating, and sometimes you don’t even know why you’re angry.”
He keeps his eyes on the TV, but I know he is listening.
“I’m not here to shout at you. I just want you to understand something early. The choices you make now follow you for a long time. Longer than you think.”
He shifts slightly, uncomfortable.
“You don’t have to be perfect. Nobody is. But you do have to be responsible for your behaviour. Respect doesn’t start when you’re older. It starts now.”
He sighs. “Everyone thinks I’m a problem.”
“They don’t think you’re a problem. They think you’re changing. And sometimes adults panic when they don’t understand that change.”
He finally looks at me.
“You’re growing into a man, and being a man is not about doing whatever you want. It’s about discipline and self-control. Making decisions that won’t embarrass you later.”
His shoulders drop a little.
“I don’t want you to learn life the hard way like some of us did. You still have time to build a life that makes you proud. And start with the small things,” I say, nudging his shoulder. “School, respect at home, and listening when people speak to you. Those things seem small now, but they shape everything.”
He nods, but the smile fades. He goes quiet for a moment, then clears his throat. “Sisi…”
I brace myself. “Yeah?”
“You’re really going to have a baby?”
The disappointment in his voice hits me harder than it should. Why do I suddenly feel embarrassed?
“Yes, I’m pregnant.”
“But you live alone. Who’s going to help you with the baby?”
The question is a heavy one. Yes, I live alone. The baby will not have a present father. My mother finally has a life of her own, and I refuse to turn her into the kind of grandmother who raises children from cradle to adulthood. She married young, had children young. It is her time to rest now. 
“I don’t know, Liwa,” I say.
He looks at me for a long moment; his eyes are full of sympathy he is too young to carry. This is not how my love story was supposed to end. Yet here I am, pregnant and alone, the man I wanted to spend my life with is behind bars.
.
.
.

I haven’t spoken to Hlobani in months, so his name lighting up my phone feels unreal. I thought he had disappeared for good. But he’s here, and he wants to see me. Part of me resents the way anything connected to Mzamo keeps pulling me back in. I’m trying to protect my peace now. I need to be mentally stable for the baby I’m carrying.
I leave Mpumi and Liwa in the lounge and step outside.
He’s parked across the street in a silver Polo R-Line. When he sees me, he unlocks the passenger door from inside. I slide into the seat and close the door.
He looks different, even his clothes look unfamiliar. The polished bodyguard aura is softer now. Hlobani in shorts feels illegal.
“Hi,” I say.
He exhales slowly. “I didn’t think you’d come. How are you, stranger?”
“I’m okay,” I answer, and we hold eye contact for a second too long. Something about him has changed.
“Where have you been?” I ask.
“I went to Mpumalanga. I needed to lay low for a while. But now that the trial is getting closer, I have to be back.”
“If you’re here to talk about that, I’d rather not hear it,” I say quickly.
“I understand, I’m not here to drag you back into anything. But I need your help.”
“Okay?”
He clears his throat. “I know you have your job and your own life. But Mzamo’s company is collapsing.”
I turn to him fully. “What do you want from me, Hlobani?”
“The company is bleeding, Mavulane. Investors are nervous, projects are stalling, and the vultures are already circling. They need someone who can manage operations and projects with integrity and skill.”
I stare at him, waiting for the part he’s avoiding.
His eyes finally meet mine. “They need you.”
A short laugh escapes me before I can stop it. “No! Absolutely not.”
“I wouldn’t be here if there was another option.”
“There are many options. People with MBAs. People with experience. People who aren’t pregnant with the owner’s baby.” I shake my head. “I told you, I don’t want to be involved in the case.”
“I’m not asking you to be involved in the case. I’m asking you to protect what he built while he can’t.”
“What about my job, Hlobani? The one thing I have for my baby’s future.”
His brows pull together. “What do you mean? Mzamo will take care of his baby no matter where he is. Even if everything falls apart, he won’t fail his blood. We won’t.”
The certainty in his voice unsettles me because he believes it completely.
Maybe he’s right. Mzamo has investments, properties, streams of income I don’t even fully understand. Money has never been the real problem. Which is exactly why I don’t need to sacrifice my own career and step into his construction company right before maternity leave.
I stare out the window for a minute, then ask, “What do they actually have against him?”
I don’t know why I’m asking because whatever he says next is going to live in my head rent-free and I already know I won’t sleep tonight.
Hlobani rubs his thumb along the steering wheel. “It started with the detective’s murder, right?”
I nod, holding my breath.
“They don’t have enough to pin the murder on him.”
My chest loosens but Hlobani doesn’t look relieved.
“They do have everything the detective found before he died.”
My stomach drops again.
“What does that mean?”
“It means they stopped chasing a murder case and started building an organised crime case.”
Lord, have mercy!
“They’re saying he financed drug distribution. Not just street dealing but big networks, warehouses and transport routes.”
I stare at him, trying to read his face, but it’s shut tight.
“They’ve got phone records, transactions they don’t understand and people who got arrested and suddenly remembered his name. They’re piling everything they can find onto one case and hoping something sticks.”
The car feels smaller by the second.
“Do you think he will win?” I ask hopelessly. I know chances are slim as a needle.
Hlobani doesn’t answer right away. He stares straight ahead with his jaw tight.
“They just need one charge to stick. And right now they have piles of paperwork, witnesses trying to save themselves, and a story that sounds believable enough to a judge.”
My stomach sinks.
“So that’s a no.”
“Mzamo has the best lawyers money can buy. He’s fought harder battles than this.”
“That doesn’t sound convincing. If he’s charged, how many years are we looking at?”
He exhales heavily. “In cases like this, they don’t expect every charge to win. They aim for enough to secure a long sentence.”
I swallow hard. “How long is long?”
“If he’s convicted on the main charges… he could be looking at twenty years. Maybe more.”
That’s not a sentence. That’s a lifetime in slow motion. My baby could graduate from university, get married and start a family of their own without him ever being there.
His hand comes to rest on my shoulder, rubbing gently. “Don’t cry, please.”
How can I not cry? My child will grow up carrying the same father wounds I did. Mzamo won’t be there for first steps, first words, school matches, broken hearts. Twenty years is an entire life.
“He’s worried about you, Mavulane. You’re not the only one breaking. You know he was leaving that life for you. He was changing…”
“It was too late,” I say in a trembling whisper.
“It wasn’t too late. He was already stepping back. Cutting ties and cleaning things up. This case caught him mid-exit.”
“Mid-exit still looks like inside to a judge.”
“He knows that. He knows how it looks. He knows the story they’re telling about him. But he also knows who he was trying to become.”
I shake my head, tears spilling freely. “I can’t do it, Hlobani.”
“What do you mean?”
“I can’t wait that long. I need to be a good mother to my baby. I’m all he or she is going to have.”
He exhales slowly and for once doesn’t rush to fill the silence.
“I don’t know if I will ever heal from this. But such is life,” I whisper.
“Mzamo loves you…”
“That’s not important right now. His love can’t protect me. It can’t keep me warm at night. It can’t raise a child from behind glass.”
“But Mavulane…” he says and pauses for a second. “It just sounds like you’re giving up on everything and closing his chapter in your life.”
I wipe my eyes. “Yeah…that’s what I’m trying to do.”
“Kanjani nje kodwa?”
I wish I knew kanjani. But I don’t. I’m still trying to figure out how I move on from this.
.
.
.

My pillow is soaked. My throat feels tight and dry. I didn’t even bring water to my room, but it’s late now and everyone has gone to bed.
I drag myself to the kitchen, pour a glass of water and head back down the passage, still sniffing back tears.
Liwa appears unexpectedly. He looks straight at me. The kitchen light is still on; my bare, swollen face gives everything away.
“Sisi… are you okay?”
No, I’m not okay. Seeing Hlobani today hollowed me out. I’ve been pretending for months, holding myself together for the innocent soul growing inside me. But seeing Hlobani pulled me back to the reality I was trying to escape.
Liwa takes my hand and I follow without resistance. We sit on the couch. I sip my water and place the glass on the table.
He keeps glancing at me. I never imagined my brother would see me cry like this.
“Who was that man?” he asks, almost stern.
“Mzamo’s friend… the baby’s father’s friend,” I say.
“What did he say?” His tone sharpens, already protective and suspicious.
I shake my head. I’m not crying because Hlobani hurt me. I’m crying because I miss Mzamo.
“Mzamo… he could face up to twenty years in prison.”
Liwa’s eyes widen. “Damn! Did he kill a police officer?”
My heart jumps. How did he know?
“No! It’s not true. He didn’t kill the officer. He did other things, but not that one,” I say quickly.
He looks confused. Maybe he was just guessing.
I inhale shakily. “I can’t believe I’m going to be a single mother.”
He clears his throat. “You didn’t know his history?”
“It’s complicated,” I whisper.
He looks at me again. “I don’t understand how you fell pregnant. You have medical aid.”
“What does that have to do with anything?”
“You didn’t learn about protection in Life Orientation?” he asks.
“Mxm! Liwa, you are the last person to judge me for my mistakes. Your mother kicked you out. Everyone complains about your behaviour.”
He goes quiet.
Exactly!
“It’s not like I’m stupid,” I add.
“No, sisi. I didn’t say you’re stupid.”
I exhale slowly. “Well… maybe I am.”
He shifts closer and wraps his arms around me. He’s still a baby. Why is he the one consoling me?
I want to pull away… but I need the hug.
“My teacher said first heartbreaks are the most painful,” he says.
I almost laugh. “This isn’t my first heartbreak. My first heartbreak was Baba.”
He doesn’t reply. I just feel him sigh and pull me closer.
“I hope it’s a boy…”
I blink. I’m in the middle of an emotional collapse and this child is doing gender predictions?
“I will take care of him when he needs a father,” he continues proudly.
My lips stretch into a small smile despite the tears.
“But only if you give birth after my final matric exams,” he adds.
Huh? This boy just shamed me for not paying attention in Life Orientation and now he thinks pregnancy works on appointment booking.
“I’m not going to be pregnant for two years, Liwa. I’m not an elephant.”
“Then when?”
Oh Lord!
“In August,” I say.
“Oh no, that’s too soon. I’ll be busy.”
Wow! This child really raised my hopes just to hit me with his academic calendar. He literally just promised to be the father figure, now he’s pulling out.
“So I will be alone?” I ask, tearing up again.
“No, no,” he says quickly, holding my hand. “I will be here during school holidays and long weekends.”
Still sounds like a deadbeat uncle to me. But I guess it’s better than a father who’s behind bars. 
.
.
.

The question of whether te reo Māori should be compulsory in schools in New Zealand involves considerations of cultural recognition, educational priorities, and practical implementation. Te reo Māori is an official language of New Zealand and holds significant cultural and historical importance as the language of the Indigenous Māori people. Advocates for compulsory teaching often frame it as part of honoring Treaty relationships and strengthening national identity.

Supporters argue that early exposure can help preserve the language, promote cultural understanding, and foster social cohesion. They may also point to bilingual education research suggesting cognitive and social benefits from learning additional languages. Critics, however, sometimes raise concerns about curriculum overload, teacher availability, and whether mandatory instruction is the most effective way to encourage genuine engagement.

Implementation would require sufficient trained teachers, appropriate resources, and flexibility to accommodate different school contexts. Debates often center on whether compulsion enhances equity and revitalization efforts or whether voluntary pathways better sustain long term interest. As with many education policies, perspectives vary depending on how cultural preservation, parental choice, and academic priorities are balanced.

As part of ongoing efforts to promote peace and freedom of religion or belief in Plateau and Benue,

The Dialogue, Reconciliation & Peace Centre (DREP), in partnership with the Crest Research and Development Institute, CRADI, has commenced a Youth FoRB initiative focused on strengthening and mentoring Interfaith Hubs.

The project recognizes that while many youth-led hubs begin with strong passion and commitment, they often struggle over time due to gaps in governance, leadership, ownership and sustainability. Participants explored how unclear roles, weak communication systems and activities disconnected from real community needs can undermine even well-intentioned peace efforts.

A core component of the engagement emphasized hub self-diagnosis, creating space for youth leaders to critically assess what is working, what is not, and what needs to change. Through guided mentoring sessions, hubs were supported to identify internal gaps, strengthen collaboration, clarify vision and begin building practical systems that ensure continuity and impact.

Key topics covered during the sessions included governance and why it matters, how to build functional organizational structures, the importance of documentation, and the introduction of early warning logic to help hubs detect and respond to emerging community tensions before they escalate.

Facilitators highlighted that strong governance frameworks provide clarity of roles, accountability and shared responsibility, which are essential elements for resilient interfaith spaces.

Participants also engaged in practical discussions on developing simple documentation processes and creating early warning mechanisms that enable proactive peacebuilding at the grassroots level.

By equipping young faith leaders with these tools, the project aims to transform interfaith hubs into sustainable platforms for dialogue, mutual respect and community-led solutions.

When youth are empowered to lead with accountability and inclusion, interfaith spaces become catalysts for freedom of religion or belief and lasting peace.

• Addressing harmful practices such as child marriage and gender-based violence through internal reform and dialogue; 
• Confronting broad “carpet reservations” that risk emptying conventions of their substance.

From the day Mr. "Bill" Abernathy handed me the flyer and we decided to defy Governor George Wallace, I worked to understand conflict and peaceful protest. It was April 4, 1969, in Selma, Alabama, as thousands stood in defiance that I emotionally understood. Forty years later, I concluded my study in the context of teaching back in California, what I first learned in Alabama.
In "Searching for Social Justice: An Examination of the Views of Alternative School Educators in the San Joaquin Valley of California" (2011/2012), I explored social justice through the lens of ethical leadership, drawing on frameworks that examine how educators define justice, care for students, and critique systemic inequities.
Justice (Ethic of Justice): Focuses on fairness, rights, and policies, with educators navigating between principles of equal access and individual rights versus systemic or group-based equity.
Caring (Ethic of Care): Emphasized through the relationships educators build with students, particularly in alternative settings, to foster a supportive environment.
Critique (Ethic of Critique): Involves analyzing who holds power, controls educational policies, and defines legitimate knowledge. Critique aims to question practices that marginalize students. 
My studies highlight a conflict between these ethical approaches and a "culture of silencing" that often inhibits the critique of social justice issues in schools.

STATEMENT ON THE ATTACK BY THE MBORORO MILITIA IN MBAT VILLAGE, NWA SUB-DIVISION, DONGA-MANTUNG DIVISION ON FEBUARY 13-14-2026.

The Centre for Human Rights and Democracy in Africa (CHRDA) is appalled by the burning of houses and destruction of properties by the Mbororo Militia in Mbat village located in Nwa Sub-division, Donga-Mantung Division of the Northwest Region of Cameroon. The incident is reported to have taken place on Friday the 13" and Saturday the 14th of February, 2026 respectively.

This incident registered severe and heavy loss of property and livestock. All inhabitants of Upper Mbat village lost their homes and have sought refuge in the bushes. Estimated damages resulted in about two hundred and five (205) houses burnt, about eight hundred and fifty (850) persons displaced, six (06) motorbikes taken away, one hundred and fifty five (155) maize barns destroyed, thirty eight (38) goats taken away while the buildings of the Government Primary School (GS) Mbat and Baptist church Upper Mbat were all burnt down and fifteen (15) provision stores looted.
In videos and pictures received from sources on ground, several houses could be seen in flames.
Attacks perpetrated by Mbororo Militias has been recurrent in Donga-Mantung Division as evident from local sources. As of now, authorities have not yet commented on the incident.

It should be noted that burning down homes, schools and churches and leaving unarmed civilians homeless is crime against humanity. This act of damage is a blatant violation in international human rights and humanitarian law, including the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) as well as the Criminal law of Cameroon. Targeting this village is illegal, inhumane and criminal.

Considering the magnitude of this act, CHRDA therefore calls on:

• The Government to immediately ensure the protection of civilians in Mbat Village and surrounding communities and provide basic necessities for the new group of internally displaced persons.
• Competent judicial authorities to open prompt, independent, and impartial investigations into the attack, identify all those responsible whether direct perpetrators or accomplices and ensure they are held accountable in accordance with the law.
• All armed actors, including militia groups, to immediately cease attacks on civilians and fully respect international human rights and humanitarian law.
• Traditional authorities and community leaders to engage in dialogue and conflict-prevention efforts aimed at de-escalating tensions and preventing further violence.
• International committee to closely monitor the situation and support protection, accountability, and peace-building initiatives in Donga-Mantung Division.

CHRDA expresses its solidarity with the victims and affected communities of Mbat Village and reiterates its commitment to documenting human rights violations, supporting victims, and advocating for justice, accountability, and lasting peace in Cameroon.

Barrister Nkongho Felix Agbor "Agbor Balla"
President
Centre for Human Rights and Democracy in Africa (CHRDA)

Miejsc dostępnych, całorocznych i atrakcyjnych. Do tego istnieje poczucie, że do młodych ludzi nie docierają informacje o wydarzeniach i inicjatywach, które mogłyby być dla nich ciekawe. This year, I made a covenant with my body. After dropping the boys at school, I would longer drive home like a Lagos aristocrat.

I started doing 6k steps of intentional and measured walking. 

So on Monday, as I was about to begin my holy pilgrimage of cardio, I met a neighbour from the next compound whom I haven't seen in a while. We exchanged pleasantries and she asked where I was headed.

“I’m doing my 6k steps,” I said, with the smug humility of someone who has recently discovered discipline and wants witnesses.

She said she would like to join me and I agreed.

As we were about to begin, she gently suggested that we shouldn't stop at 6k steps. She said we could do 10k or more.

Or more.

Those two words should have triggered an alarm in my spirit.

But I, a woman of optimism and poor discernment responded with “Let’s see how it goes.”

And so we began.

The sun was gentle and the breeze was cooperative.

 Our conversation flowed like chilled zobo because she was such an excellent company. She gisted me about another neighbour who testified that after she made lifestyle changes in addition to walking consistently, her menses returned after four months of cease fire. It was all the encouragement I needed.

By the time we reached the landmark I had earmarked for my respectable 6k steps, I was ready to turn back home. Discipline maintained, mission accomplished.

But what did neighbim do?

She pointed ahead and said “Let’s just get to that pawpaw tree.”

I hesistated and looked at it. It looked back at me.That pawpaw tree was not a tree. It was a portal.

It stood there innocent and sunlit, minding its chlorophyll.

“What is there to lose?” I shrugged.

She inched forward and I followed. 

Every time I gathered the strength to say, “Let’s head back,” she would unlock another topic.

Motherhood. How it swallows you whole.

How reading used to be our oxygen. How we miss the quiet woman we once were before someone started calling us “Mummy!” every seven minutes.

We laughed, bonded and walked.The deeper the conversation, the further we acquired mileage per kilometers.

Six trees became seven forests. Seven forests became seven oceans.
I began to suspect we were approaching Jericho.

Suddenly I looked up.

We were at a major market that takes about forty-five minutes’ drive from my house.

Forty-five!

By this time, my thighs had started speaking in morse code and my knees were vibrating like a faulty generator.

Meanwhile, this woman of uncommon stamina was still glowing like she had plugged herself into national grid.

“Let’s keep going small,” she said.

Small? Madam, I have seen the other side.

By my estimation, we had crossed fifteen thousand steps. Fifteen. My ancestors did not trek this much during migration. Even the Israelites did not suffer like this.

I refused firmly and politely.

And with that, I headed back home already imagining my sofa like Canaan.

Then I heard my name and I turned.
It was neighbim again.

She was waving something and gesturing for me to take. It was a colorful looking magazine.

I took it and looked closer at the sans serif fine print.

And in that moment, everything made sense...the 10k steps suggestion, the supernatural stamina, the relentless energy...

It was an AWAKE! magazine. 

Neighbim was a Jehovah's witness!

She’s home. And I’m still trying to breathe through the emotions.
My graceful Whippet girl, Daisy, made it through surgery this morning—and seeing her like this hurts more than I expected. The shaved patch along her side. The careful line of stitches. The faint bruising beneath that slim, delicate body built for speed and freedom.
Every mark tells a story I wish she never had to carry.
But she’s here.
She’s breathing.
She’s fighting.
When we walked through the door, she didn’t cry. She didn’t panic. She moved slowly on her long, elegant legs, carefully climbing onto the couch before curling into her favorite warm spot.
Her big, soulful eyes were heavy with exhaustion.
And when I sat beside her, she gently rested her narrow head in my lap.
Soft. Sensitive. Trusting.
Like she was saying, I’m safe now.
Whippets don’t understand surgery.
They don’t understand why their body suddenly aches or feels unfamiliar.
But they understand comfort.
They understand quiet presence.
They understand when their person stays close.
Tonight, Daisy is resting—wrapped in her soft blanket, stretched out in the home she feels safe in, surrounded by love.
Healing won’t be instant.
There will be slow steps. Gentle movements. Patient nights.
But she’ll get there.
Because the heart of a Whippet is gentle, resilient, and deeply devoted. She didn’t choose this battle—but she’s facing it the only way she knows how: quietly, bravely, with complete trust.
And I’ll be right here.
Every nap. Every cuddle. Every small victory.
If you have a moment, send her some love.
She’s been so brave—and she deserves every good thought, every prayer, and every bit of healing energy you can send. 🤍🐾

She’s home. And I’m still trying to calm my heart.
My sweet, fluffy Bichon Frise girl, Daisy, made it through surgery this morning—and seeing her like this breaks me in ways I can’t explain. The small shaved patch along her side. The neat row of stitches. The faint bruising hidden beneath that soft, cloud-like white coat.
Every mark tells a story I wish she never had to live.
But she’s here.
She’s breathing.
She’s fighting.
When we walked through the door, she didn’t cry. She didn’t panic. She moved slowly on her tiny paws, carefully climbed onto the couch, and curled into her favorite spot like she always does. Her fluffy head resting gently, her dark eyes heavy with that deep post-surgery tiredness.
And when I sat beside her, she leaned into me softly.
Gentle. Loving. Trusting.
Like she was saying, I’m safe now.
Bichon Frises don’t understand surgery.
They don’t understand why their body suddenly hurts or feels different.
But they understand love.
They understand warmth.
They understand when their person stays close.
Tonight, Daisy is resting—wrapped in her favorite blanket, safe in the home she fills with joy every single day.
Healing won’t be instant.
There will be slow walks. Soft cuddles. Patient nights.
But she’ll get there.
Because the heart of a Bichon Frise is cheerful, resilient, and full of unconditional love. She didn’t choose this battle—but she’s facing it quietly, bravely, with complete trust.
And I’ll be right here.
Every cuddle. Every nap. Every small win.
If you have a moment, send her some love.
She’s been so strong—and she deserves every good thought, every prayer, and every bit of healing energy you can send. 🤍🐾

On 16th February, our Executive Director, Abubakar Abdullahi Suleiman, who also serves as Director of Administration, Network of Civil Society Organizations (NECSOB) Borno State, delivered a presentation on the Humanitarian Reset during the Pre-Congress Meeting.

His presentation emphasized the transition toward strengthened government leadership, increased localization, and greater responsibility for Nigerian CSOs in humanitarian coordination and financing.

He highlighted the urgent need to build stronger national and state systems, channel more resources directly to local actors, and ensure that humanitarian principles and protection remain central throughout the transition process.

The message was clear: the future of humanitarian response in Nigeria must be locally led, sustainable, and aligned with long-term development and durable solutions frameworks.

As civil society actors, this transition calls for stronger collaboration, accountability, institutional strengthening, and readiness to step confidently into leadership roles. It is a defining moment for Nigerian CSOs to move from participation to co-leadership, and from co-leadership to ownership.

The Humanitarian Reset is not just about transition; it is about building a resilient, self-reliant humanitarian system that truly reflects the needs and realities of our communities.

The African Union Ad-Hoc High-Level Committee on South Sudan (C5) was established by the AU Peace and Security Council (AUPSC) on 5 December 2014. Its mandate is to enhance the AU’s support for the mediation efforts of the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD). The Committee was officially launched at the 25th Ordinary Session of the Assembly of Heads of State in Johannesburg on 15 June 2015.

Composition and Leadership

The Committee comprises one representative from each of the continent’s five regions: Algeria, Chad, Nigeria, Rwanda, and South Africa. The C5 is chaired by H.E. Cyril Ramaphosa, President of South Africa. The Chair is tasked with direct diplomacy involving the Government of South Sudan, opposition groups, and stakeholders to foster consensus.

Key Milestones

November 2018: The C5 signed the R-ARCSS as guarantors. This agreement outlines governance structures, security sector reform, the establishment of unified forces, disarmament, demobilisation, and reintegration (DDR), as well as judicial review and constitution-making processes.
30 June 2018: The Committee convened its 7th meeting in Nouakchott, Mauritania, under the chairmanship of President Ramaphosa.

In Como from February 3rd to 5th, I had the privilege of contributing to something that truly matters.

As part of the delegation of the Hungarian Youth Association, I participated in the International Youth for Peace Forum Milano-Cortina 2026 - organised by Collectif pour un service civique européen and Acli Lombardia, held in Como as part of the Gen26 Education Programme of MilanoCortina2026, linked to the upcoming 2026 Winter Olympics and 2026 Winter Paralympics.

What made this experience especially meaningful for me was being part of the working group on “Education as a Means of Preventing Conflict and Promoting Peace.”

We explored a simple yet powerful idea: peace is not built only at negotiation tables — it is built in classrooms, youth programmes, civic initiatives, and cultural exchanges. Education shapes narratives, challenges prejudice, and equips the next generation with the tools to resolve tensions before they escalate into conflict.

Throughout the Forum, I saw how international cooperation moves from theory to practice. With the support of the European Commission and in collaboration with civic and youth organisations across Europe, the discussions connected grassroots initiatives with broader international frameworks. It was a reminder that peacebuilding requires alignment between local engagement and global institutions.

The link with the Olympic and Paralympic spirit added a unique dimension. The values behind Milano Cortina 2026 — solidarity, respect, excellence, inclusion — are not just sporting principles. They are social principles. Sport has the power to unite across borders, and when combined with education, it becomes a powerful platform for dialogue and mutual understanding.

For me personally, this Forum was more than an event. It was a space where youth leadership, international organisations, and the global stage of the Winter Olympics intersected around one shared ambition: making peace hashtag#tangible, hashtag#practical, and hashtag#generational.

Grateful for the conversations, the ideas, and the responsibility that comes with being part of this movement.

Today we pause to honor the life and legacy of Reverend Jesse Jackson — a towering figure in the American civil rights movement whose voice echoed across decades of struggle, progress, and political transformation.
From marching alongside Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. during the height of the Civil Rights Movement to founding the Rainbow PUSH Coalition, Reverend Jackson dedicated his life to expanding economic opportunity, fighting voter suppression, and demanding equity in education, employment, and public policy.
He was more than a preacher.
He was more than a candidate.
He was a movement.
In 1984 and again in 1988, he made history with his presidential campaigns — building one of the most diverse political coalitions the country had ever seen at the time. He challenged the system from within, giving voice to communities that felt ignored and overlooked. His message was clear: everyone deserves a seat at the table.
Through decades of activism, negotiations, protests, and policy advocacy, Reverend Jackson stood at the intersection of faith and politics. Whether you agreed with him or not, his impact on American civic life is undeniable.
He helped shape national conversations about race, poverty, foreign policy, corporate accountability, and human rights. His influence can still be seen in modern grassroots organizing and coalition-building across the political spectrum.
Love him or critique him — his name will forever be etched into the story of American democracy.
Rest in power, Reverend Jesse Jackson.
A voice for the voiceless.
A bridge between generations.
A chapter of history that will not be forgotten.

National Mother Nature Awareness Day to Launch on 21 September 2026
United Kingdom 

A new annual observance, National Mother Nature Awareness Day, will begin on 21 September 2026, aligning with the Autumn Equinox in the Northern Hemisphere. Initiated by Gaynor Williams-Linnecor, founder of Nature’s Healing World and long-time Unity Beacon facilitator, the day is designed as a non-commercial, consciousness-focused pause dedicated to environmental awareness and reconnection.

Positioned deliberately on the Equinox, a point in the year when day and night are held in equal balance, the observance symbolises equilibrium between humanity and the natural world. The date was chosen to emphasise harmony, responsibility, and seasonal awareness.

“Light and dark stand equal at the Equinox,” says Williams-Linnecor. “It is nature’s annual reminder that balance is not abstract, it is observable. I felt this was the most meaningful moment to introduce a day that invites us to reconsider our relationship with the Earth.”

National Mother Nature Awareness Day is not affiliated with political movements or commercial campaigns. Its focus is simple and practical: encouraging individuals, families, schools, and community groups to consciously reconnect with nature for one day each year.

Suggested actions include:
 • Spending intentional time outdoors
 • Reducing personal consumption for 24 hours
 • Planting or tending something living
 • Supporting local conservation initiatives
 • Educating children about ecological respect
 • Reflecting on seasonal change and personal balance

The theme for its inaugural year in 2026 is “Reconnection.”

Williams-Linnecor explains that the initiative emerged from years of seasonal observance work through Nature’s Healing World, including community gatherings aligned with solstices and equinoxes. “We are living in a time of environmental urgency, but also of emotional and social disconnection,” she notes. “Before large-scale change can occur, awareness must deepen. This day is about creating space for that awareness.”

Importantly, the observance is structured to be accessible. It requires no membership, fee, or formal affiliation. Participation can be as simple as lighting a lantern at dusk in gratitude or walking quietly in a local green space.

The founder emphasises that the day is intended to complement existing environmental initiatives rather than compete with them. “There are many excellent environmental campaigns already,” she says. “This is about adding a reflective, seasonal anchor point, a moment of collective pause that recurs annually.”

By launching in 2026, organisers aim to build gradual national recognition over time, encouraging schools, councils, and community organisations to incorporate the observance into their calendars.

National Mother Nature Awareness Day will take place every year on 21 September moving forward.

Further information and participation guidance will be made available through Nature’s Healing World channels in advance of the 2026 launch

In 1965, Singapore was kicked out of Malaysia.

No resources. No military. No hinterland. And one terrifying vulnerability nobody wanted to say out loud.

Water.

Almost all of Singapore's water came from the state of Johor in Malaysia — piped across a causeway under colonial-era agreements.

Malaysia's Prime Minister said it plainly: "If Singapore's foreign policy is prejudicial to Malaysia's interests, we could always bring pressure to bear on them by threatening to turn off the water in Johor."

Not a metaphor. Not a negotiation tactic. A survival threat.

Lee Kuan Yew's response? "Every other policy has to bend at the knees for our water survival."

In 1972, Singapore launched a Water Master Plan. By 1974, they'd built a pilot plant to recycle used water into drinking water.

It failed. The technology was too expensive and too unreliable. They shut it down.

For twenty-four years, the idea sat on a shelf. Singapore kept paying Malaysia for water. And Malaysia kept reminding them who held the tap.

Then in 1998, membrane technology finally caught up. Singapore dusted off the old plan and commissioned a new study. Could they actually turn sewage into water clean enough to drink?

The answer was yes. Not just drinkable — ultra-pure. Cleaner than tap water. Clean enough for semiconductor wafer fabrication.

They called it NEWater.

But here's the problem nobody expected: how do you convince 4 million people to drink recycled sewage?

Singapore's answer was audacious.

At the 2002 National Day Parade, Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong stood in front of 60,000 people and raised a bottle of NEWater in a toast. To Singapore.

The subtext was unmistakable. Patriotic Singaporeans drink their own recycled water.

Not everyone was convinced. Someone wrote a parody of the national song "Count on Me, Singapore." The new version? "Drink Our Pee, Singapore."

PUB didn't flinch. They rebranded sewage plants as "water reclamation factories." They stopped saying "wastewater" and started saying "used water." They built visitor centres to show the process. They invited every grassroots leader and MP to tour the plants.

And they kept building.

Today, NEWater meets 40% of Singapore's water needs. By 2060, it's projected to meet 55%. The water agreement with Malaysia expires in 2061.

That's not a coincidence.

Singapore didn't just solve a water problem. They built an entire industry around it. Over 150 water companies. 26 R&D centres. A water sector contributing over $2 billion to GDP. The country that once begged for water now exports water technology to the world.

Here's the business lesson:

Most people see dependency and try to negotiate better terms. More supply. Lower price. A longer contract.

Singapore looked at its single greatest vulnerability — a neighbour who could turn off the tap at any time — and asked a completely different question: What if we didn't need the tap at all?

They couldn't control the source.

“Help me, Lord, to remember that religion is not to be confined to the church, but must be carried into the home.” - Susannah Wesley 

Susannah Wesley formed this prayer in the ordinary pressure of domestic life rather than in public ministry. In early eighteenth century England, amid poverty, frequent illness, and the daily care of a large household, she understood that faith must be lived where it is most tested. Religion, she believed, does not begin in the meetinghouse and the descend into the home. It is proved in the home first, where patient is required, conscience is trained, and character is shaped before God. 

She held motherhood as a sacred trust. A mother’s first work, in her judgment, was to bring her children to Christ, not merely by instruction but by order of living. She warned that whatever weakens reason, dulls the conscience, obscures the sense of God, or steals delight in spiritual things becomes sin to the one who tolerates it. The will of God, she taught, is both the role of duty and the measure of peace, and time must be redeemed with diligence because spiritual formation does not happened by accident. 

Susannah Wesley valued counsel yet knew how reluctantly it is received. She testified that much of her understanding of God was learned through her children, whose needs exposed both impatience and grace. Education, for her, aimed at shaping a right temper of mind rather than mere accomplishment. She was content to fill a space if God was glorified, finding genuine pleasure in religious exercise not as escape, but as life. 

Her witness remains quiet and demanding. Faith that does not govern the home soon loses the authority elsewhere. True religion carries its weight into daily order, unseen obedience, and the patient work of shaping souls before God.

Puasa tidak menghalangi Rasulullah untuk tetap menunjukkan kasih sayang kepada istrinya.

>

Aisyah menceritakan bahwa Rasulullah selalu melakukan itikaf di masjid pada sepuluh hari terakhir. Terkadang, istri-istri beliau, termasuk Aisyah, juga ikut beritikaf dengan mendirikan tenda kecil di dalam masjid, menunjukkan bahwa semangat mencari rida Allah dilakukan bersama-sama sebagai pasangan.

Hubungan Rasulullah dan Aisyah mengajarkan kita bahwa Ramadhan bukan hanya tentang menahan lapar, tetapi juga tentang mempererat ikatan kasih sayang (mawaddah) melalui ibadah bersama dan saling mendukung dalam kebaikan.

This is a setup sketch for a future painting in my "Well Regulated Militia" series, a portrait of the one and only Nat Turner.

Nat Turner was an enslaved preacher born in Virginia in 1800 who led one of the most significant slave rebellions in American history in 1831. Believing he was divinely called to act against the brutality of slavery, Turner organized an uprising in Southampton County that resulted in the deaths of dozens of enslavers and sent shockwaves through the South. The rebellion was swiftly and violently suppressed; Turner was captured, tried, and executed, and in retaliation hundreds of enslaved and free Black people were killed. In response, Southern states passed even harsher laws banning the education, assembly, and movement of Black people. Turner’s revolt exposed the deep terror beneath the slave system: that those who were denied humanity might one day demand it by force.

There are no known images of Nat Turner, and that absence is the charge. As the "Founding Daddies" are “remembered” with statues, engravings, and school lessons, Turner wasn’t celebrated, he was all but erased. 

In this study, he wears an African continent pin on one lapel, a Black Lives Matter pin on the other, and a gold chain with a Black Power fist as the emblem. He holds a hand cannon because the whole series is asking a question America keeps dodging:

What does the Second Amendment look like in his hands?

Imagine telling Nat Turner, in the middle of a rebellion against bondage, “All lives matter.”

This isn’t a fantasy of violence. It’s an exposure of hypocrisy. It’s a refusal to keep polishing the "Founding Daddies" into saints while pretending the people they oppressed were supposed to stay grateful, obedient, and unarmed.

Nat Turner belongs in the American story, not as a footnote, not as a scare tactic, but as proof that freedom was never handed down. It was contested.

Supporters say the law promotes transparency, security, and social cohesion, while critics argue it infringes on personal freedom and religious expression. The first fine signals that authorities are prepared to actively enforce the rules and sets the stage for ongoing debates about civil liberties in Switzerland.

Ultimately, the debate reflects a broader European challenge—how to remain humanitarian while preserving unity and the rule of law. The discussion shows that integration cannot be solved through slogans alone, but requires nuance, empathy, and long-term dialogue.
