He was so hated that children burned him in effigy. His hair fell out from stress. Then he gave away his fortune—and lived fifty more years. By 1913, John D. Rockefeller was the richest man in the world—worth over $900 million (roughly $400 billion today, more than Bezos or Musk). He controlled 90% of America's oil through Standard Oil, a monopoly so powerful that the Supreme Court ordered it broken up in 1911. He was also the most hated man in America. Newspapers called him a robber baron. Political cartoons showed him as an octopus strangling the nation. Striking workers sang songs about his greed. Children made effigies of him and burned them in the streets. And John D. Rockefeller was dying. At 53, his body was failing. Chronic digestive problems meant he could barely eat—surviving on crackers and milk. Anxiety consumed him. His hair fell out—all of it, including his eyebrows and eyelashes. He wore wigs in public. Insomnia plagued him. His weight dropped to 140 pounds on a six-foot frame. His doctors were blunt: "Slow down or die." But slowing down meant losing control. And losing control was unthinkable to a man who'd spent his life controlling everything—oil prices, competitors, markets, employees, entire state legislatures. Rockefeller had built Standard Oil through ruthless brilliance. He negotiated secret railroad rebates that let him ship oil cheaper than competitors. He bought rival refineries at bankruptcy prices after undercutting them. He created a monopoly so efficient that kerosene prices actually dropped—consumers benefited even as competition died. But his methods were brutal. He destroyed small businesses. He controlled politicians through bribes and campaign donations. When workers demanded better wages and safer conditions, he crushed their unions. In 1913, miners at a Rockefeller-owned coal mine in Ludlow, Colorado went on strike. They wanted safer conditions, an eight-hour workday, and the right to unionize. Rockefeller's company evicted them from company housing. Families lived in tents through the winter. On April 20, 1914, the Colorado National Guard—paid by Rockefeller's company—opened fire on the tent colony. Thirteen people died, including two women and eleven children who suffocated when soldiers set the tents on fire. The Ludlow Massacre made headlines worldwide. Public fury turned violent. Workers rioted. Protesters marched on Rockefeller's New York mansion. He couldn't appear in public without bodyguards. And through it all, his body was eating itself from stress. In 1915, desperate to salvage his reputation, Rockefeller hired Ivy Lee—America's first PR consultant. Lee's advice was revolutionary: "Stop hiding. Start giving. Publicly." So Rockefeller began distributing dimes to children on the street—a calculated image campaign to seem generous and approachable. Photos of the "kindly old man" handing out dimes appeared in newspapers, slowly replacing the octopus cartoons. But something unexpected happened. As Rockefeller started giving money away—first in small amounts, then massive sums—his health improved. His hair didn't grow back. But his appetite returned. He started sleeping. The crushing anxiety that had defined his fifties began to lift. By his sixties, Rockefeller had given away hundreds of millions to: The Rockefeller Foundation (public health, medical research) University of Chicago (transformed American higher education) Spelman College (historically Black women's college) Medical research that led to vaccines, antibiotics, and modern medicine Was it genuine generosity or reputation laundering? Probably both. Rockefeller's philanthropy was strategic—controlled, calculated, designed to create institutions that would outlive him and reshape his legacy. But it also seemed to genuinely bring him peace. "I have always tried to turn every disaster into an opportunity," he said late in life. Giving away his fortune was the ultimate conversion—transforming public hatred into public monuments bearing his name. Here's the paradox: Rockefeller's ruthlessness created the wealth that his philanthropy distributed. Without crushing competitors and exploiting workers, he wouldn't have had billions to give to universities and hospitals. So which John D. Rockefeller was real? The monopolist who ordered violence against strikers? Or the philanthropist who eradicated hookworm in the American South and funded the research that discovered penicillin? Both. He was both. He built his empire through methods we'd now call criminal. Then used that empire's profits to fund institutions that saved millions of lives. The Rockefeller Foundation's public health work in the early 20th century prevented more deaths than Standard Oil's practices caused. Does that balance the ledger? There's no objective answer. But there's a personal one: John D. Rockefeller was expected to die at 53. He lived to 97, dying peacefully in his sleep in 1937. The stress that nearly killed him at 53 lifted when he stopped accumulating and started distributing. Whether that was karma, psychology, or coincidence, we can't know. But the correlation is stark. In his final decades, Rockefeller played golf, spent time with grandchildren, and maintained meticulous control over his philanthropy. He didn't become a saint—he remained calculating, controlling, convinced his wealth gave him the right to reshape society according to his vision. But he found peace. The anxiety that had consumed him, that had literally made his hair fall out, eased when he shifted from defending his fortune to deploying it. Modern billionaires study Rockefeller's playbook—not his monopolistic tactics (those are mostly illegal now), but his philanthropic strategy. Bill Gates, Warren Buffett, MacKenzie Scott—all follow the model Rockefeller pioneered: make a fortune through capitalism, then give it away through foundations that shape society for generations. Some call it generous. Others call it oligarchy with a charitable face. Both are true. John D. Rockefeller was the richest, most hated man in America. His greed nearly killed him at 53. Then he started giving away his fortune—strategically, calculatedly, but genuinely. And he lived fifty more years. His legacy is complicated: the man who crushed competition also funded the institutions that train doctors and discover vaccines. The oligarch who paid guards to shoot strikers also built the modern philanthropic foundation. He was a robber baron and a benefactor. A monopolist and a medical savior. And he lived long enough to see his name on universities instead of burning effigies. Your money or your life? Rockefeller chose both—took all the money, then bought a longer life by giving it away. Whether that's redemption or just excellent PR depends on who you ask. But he died at 97, peacefully, in his bed. The strikers' children died in burning tents at Ludlow. History remembers his foundations. It mostly forgot their names.

Isabella of Aragon lived through one of the most brutal periods in Italian Renaissance history, and her life reads like a tragic opera where every act brings fresh betrayal and loss. Born on October 2, 1470, in Naples, she was the daughter of Alfonso, Duke of Calabria, who would later become King Alfonso II of Naples, and Ippolita Maria Sforza, connecting her by blood to two of the most powerful dynasties in Italy. Her parents' marriage had been orchestrated by her grandfather, King Ferrante of Naples, as the keystone of an alliance between Naples and Milan, and from the moment of Isabella's birth, her life would be shaped entirely by the dynastic politics and power struggles of Renaissance Italy.

Isabella's childhood was spent in the Kingdom of Naples, where she received an excellent education from her mother. But her future had already been decided before she could walk. She was betrothed to her first cousin, Gian Galeazzo Sforza, who would become Duke of Milan, continuing the pattern of strategic marriages between the Aragonese rulers of Naples and the Sforza family of Milan. When Isabella was just 19 years old, she married Gian Galeazzo on February 2, 1490, in Milan. The wedding was one of the most spectacular events of the Italian Renaissance, with celebrations designed by none other than Leonardo da Vinci, who at that time lived at the court of Ludovico Sforza. Leonardo created theatrical performances, mechanical games, and elaborate fountains of light and water that amazed the guests at Castello Sforzesco. It must have seemed like a fairy tale beginning for the young bride.

But Isabella's marriage was doomed from the start, and not because of anything lacking between her and her husband. The problem was Ludovico Sforza, known as "Il Moro" (the Moor) for his dark complexion. Ludovico was Gian Galeazzo's uncle and had been acting as regent since Gian Galeazzo became Duke at age seven following his father's assassination in 1476. By the time Isabella arrived in Milan, Ludovico had been the de facto ruler for years, and he had absolutely no intention of relinquishing power to his nephew, regardless of the fact that Gian Galeazzo was now old enough to rule in his own right. 

Contemporary sources describe Gian Galeazzo as beautiful and delicate, but chronically ill with epilepsy and physical frailty. He lacked the strength and probably the will to stand up to his powerful uncle. Isabella, on the other hand, was described very differently by those who saw her.

Ambassador Giacomo Trotti, known for his frank judgments, wrote to Duke Ercole d'Este describing Isabella as "dark-faced and not very beautiful," though he quickly added that "she has a kind and beautiful personality" and that "the Duke is beautiful and delicious" by comparison. Another courtier, Ambrogio da Corte, was even more brutal, describing Isabella as "ugly, black, cross-eyed, too much made up, and her breath stinks." While he likely exaggerated, contemporary sources agree that Isabella had a dark complexion, a thick and slightly hooked nose, the swollen cheeks typical of the Aragonese family, and possibly inherited a degree of strabismus from her father, Alfonso II, who was called "il Guercio" (the cross-eyed one). In an era when beauty was considered almost as important as political alliances for noblewomen, Isabella's physical appearance became yet another weapon her enemies could use against her.

From the moment Isabella arrived in Milan as the new Duchess, Ludovico made her life miserable. He isolated the young couple from court, eventually moving them out of Milan entirely to the castle in Pavia, effectively exiling them from the center of power. He dismissed Isabella's Neapolitan attendants, cutting her off from anyone who might support her interests. He kept them under guard that prevented them from contacting the outside world freely. Despite their isolation, Isabella and Gian Galeazzo lived in lavish surroundings, but luxury without freedom or power is just a gilded cage. Ludovico's actions had an unintended consequence, however. The isolation brought Isabella and Gian Galeazzo closer together, and despite Gian Galeazzo's chronic poor health, they became genuine partners. Their marriage produced four children between 1491 and 1495, proving that whatever his other weaknesses, Gian Galeazzo was capable of fathering heirs.

On January 30, 1491, Isabella gave birth to their son Francesco, who was immediately nicknamed "il Duchetto" (the little Duke) as the heir to Milan. This should have been a moment of triumph for Isabella, cementing her position and her son's future. Instead, Ludovico barely acknowledged the birth. When Isabella's daughter Ippolita Maria was born on January 26, 1493, the event passed almost without notice because the day before, Ludovico's own son, Ercole Massimiliano, had been born. Ludovico celebrated his son's birth with elaborate pomp and ceremony befitting an heir, making it crystal clear that he considered his own bloodline, not Gian Galeazzo's, to be the future of Milan. Isabella gave birth to another daughter, Bona Maria, on February 2, 1494, in Vigevano. The girl was named after Gian Galeazzo's grandmother, Bona of Savoy, and she would be the only one of Isabella's children to survive her.

By 1494, Ludovico's ambitions had grown beyond simply controlling Milan through his nephew. He wanted to be Duke in his own right, and his anti-Aragonese foreign policy was making Isabella's position increasingly dangerous. In January 1491, Ludovico had married the young and spirited Beatrice d'Este of Ferrara, who was also connected to the Aragonese family. The two women, both intelligent and ambitious, became bitter rivals. Beatrice could not stand hearing Isabella's beauty praised in her presence, according to some accounts, though the reality is that contemporary sources consistently described Beatrice as pretty while calling Isabella unpleasant-looking. The rivalry between the two young duchesses became one of the defining dramas of the Milanese court.

Then Ludovico made a catastrophic decision that would change Italian history. Desperate for allies and determined to neutralize the threat posed by Isabella's Neapolitan family, Ludovico turned to Charles VIII of France and established a mutual defense pact with him in 1492. Charles VIII claimed the throne of Naples in his own right and had become obsessed with establishing a base in Italy for mounting a crusade. Ludovico encouraged Charles to invade Italy and remove Isabella's father from his throne. When the French King arrived in Milan in October 1494 on his way to Naples, he was well received by Ludovico and Beatrice with great ceremony. Isabella, desperate to save her father's kingdom, made a move that showed both her courage and her desperation. She tearfully pleaded with Charles VIII to have mercy on her father. The French King was embarrassed by Isabella's emotional appeal, and historian Philippe de Commines, who was part of Charles's retinue, later described the scene. But Isabella's pleading was in vain. The Italian Wars had begun, and her father would be driven from his throne by the French in 1495.

The crisis in Naples coincided with personal tragedy for Isabella. Her sickly husband Gian Galeazzo, who had been suffering from stomach ailments for years, experienced a severe relapse during the French King's visit. After several days of agony, the young Duke died on October 21, 1494, at just 25 years old. He had been Duke of Milan for 18 years, but had ruled in name only for exactly zero of them. The very next day, with unseemly haste, Ludovico Sforza was proclaimed Duke of Milan by the Milanese nobility. Persistent rumors claimed that Ludovico had poisoned his nephew, though no direct evidence was ever found. Isabella, who was pregnant at the time with her fourth child, was devastated by her husband's death and by Ludovico's immediate usurpation of power. For almost six weeks, she withdrew to the Castello Visconteo in Pavia with her children, avoiding all visitors. On December 6, 1494, Ludovico persuaded her to move with her children to Castello Sforzesco in Milan, where she was kept under even stricter guard. In February 1495, she gave birth to her youngest daughter, Bianca Maria, named after Gian Galeazzo's grandmother. The child would die the following year.

Isabella's suffering was far from over. Within two years of her husband's death, she lost both her father and her brother in quick succession. Her father, King Alfonso II of Naples, abdicated the throne amid the French invasion and died on December 18, 1495, leaving Isabella without her most important source of support. Her brother Ferdinand II briefly reclaimed Naples after initial defeats, but he succumbed to illness on October 7, 1496, accelerating the complete collapse of Aragonese rule in southern Italy. Within the span of two years, Isabella had lost her husband, her father, her brother, and the entire kingdom that was supposed to be her family's legacy. 

She was left alone in Milan, a widow with small children, at the mercy of Ludovico Sforza, the man she considered her deadliest enemy.
Then in 1499, everything changed again when the French King Louis XII invaded Milan and deposed Ludovico. Before fleeing, Louis XII saw that Isabella's young son Francesco was growing popular among the inhabitants of Milan, which posed a threat to French control. The King assured Isabella that he planned to marry Francesco to his daughter, and on that promise, he took the nine-year-old boy to France. It was a lie. Louis XII placed Francesco in a monastery, effectively imprisoning the child. Isabella refused to give up hope and petitioned Maximilian I, King of the Romans, to liberate her son from France, but her efforts were fruitless. She would never see Francesco again. The boy who should have been Duke of Milan lived in French captivity until January 1512, when he died after falling from his horse while hunting in Angoulême. He was just 21 years old.

This betrayal, combined with the destruction of her family's kingdom in Naples, filled Isabella with a deep and lasting hatred for the French. But it also freed her from Ludovico's control. Louis XII granted Isabella the Duchy of Bari as her personal property, along with the titles of Princess of Rossano and Lady of Ostuni. Isabella received a modest income from the French King and traveled south to Naples with her two surviving daughters, Ippolita and Bona. On the way to her hometown, she visited relatives in Mantua and Bologna. In mid-February 1500, she stayed in Rome with her illegitimate half-brother Alfonso of Aragon, Duke of Bisceglie, who was married to Lucrezia Borgia, daughter of Pope Alexander VI. Alfonso would be assassinated later that year, almost certainly on the orders of Lucrezia's brother Cesare Borgia.

In Bari, Isabella finally found the independence and authority that had been denied to her in Milan. She ruled in her own right as Duchess, established her own court, and devoted herself to the education and protection of her remaining daughters. Her experiences in Milan had taught her that political security was essential, so she introduced vigorous surveillance of public officials to combat the notorious corruption that plagued Italian cities. She built up defenses and took administrative matters seriously. During the ongoing wars between Spain and France, she traveled to Naples for safety when necessary but always returned to Bari. After her half-brother Alfonso's murder, Isabella took in his young son Rodrigo of Aragon, Duke of Bisceglie, raising him along with her own daughters. She maintained friendly relations with Lucrezia Borgia, who sent Isabella numerous gifts over the years.

Isabella's court in Bari became a center of Renaissance culture, attracting poets and artists. She took particular care with the education of her daughter Bona, whose tutors included Italian humanists Crisostomo Colonna and Antonio de Ferraris. They taught Bona mathematics, natural science, geography, history, law, Latin, classical literature, theology, and how to play several musical instruments. Isabella was determined that her daughter would be educated to rule. In 1510, tragedy struck again when Isabella's daughter Ippolita, who had been living with her, fell seriously ill. Isabella asked the convent of Santa Maria della Nuova to pray for the sick princess. Ippolita did recover temporarily, and mother and daughter made a pilgrimage to the convent to offer thanksgiving gifts. But Ippolita died in 1501, leaving Bona as Isabella's only surviving child.

Under Isabella's rule, Bari and especially Ostuni experienced an artistic renaissance. The city walls were extended, new squares were built, and the façade of Ostuni's cathedral was designed with direct inspiration from the church of Santa Maria Maggiore in Milan, the burial place of Gian Galeazzo Sforza. Many believe Isabella herself influenced the cathedral's design, including the curved motifs that characterize it. She applied to the city council of Bari in 1513 to raise salaries for public school teachers and exempt them from taxes, showing her commitment to education. When her foster child Rodrigo died in Bari in August 1512, just months after learning of Francesco's death in France, Isabella poured all her remaining energy into raising Bona.

After the House of Sforza was restored to Milan in 1512 following French defeats, Isabella hoped to marry Bona to Duke Maximilian Sforza, thereby providing legitimacy to Maximilian's reign and reclaiming her family's place in Milan. There were other proposals as well, including matches with various Medici princes and even Ferdinand of Austria. But when the French won the Battle of Marignano in 1515 and deposed Maximilian, those plans collapsed. Then Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor, learned that Polish King Sigismund I the Old had been widowed in October 1515. Maximilian didn't want Sigismund to marry another Habsburg opponent, so he promoted Bona Sforza as a candidate. 
Isabella, ever the strategic diplomat, negotiated from her position in Bari. On December 6, 1517, at age 23, Bona married Sigismund I and became Queen of Poland and Grand Duchess of Lithuania.

Bona would prove to be as intelligent, energetic, and ambitious as her mother, becoming heavily involved in Polish political and cultural life and implementing major economic and agricultural reforms. She bore Sigismund six children, including Sigismund II Augustus, who would become King of Poland. Isabella's bloodline, which Ludovico Sforza had tried so hard to eliminate from the succession, ended up on the Polish throne instead. It was perhaps the greatest vindication of Isabella's long struggle to preserve her family's status and power.
Isabella of Aragon died on February 11, 1524, in Bari at the age of 53. She had outlived her husband by 30 years, spending those three decades fighting to protect her children and maintain her dignity in the face of constant political upheaval, betrayal, and personal loss. Of her four children, only Bona survived her, and through Bona, Isabella's descendants continued for generations. She was buried in the Church of San Domenico Maggiore in Naples, returned at last to the city where she had been born.

In 2012, nearly five centuries after her death, anthropologists excavated Isabella's body. The scientific examination revealed that she had suffered from syphilis, and her teeth showed high levels of mercury, which was used (ineffectively) to treat the disease during the Renaissance. The mercury treatments had given her tooth enamel a black color, most of which had been removed by abrasion, probably in an attempt to improve her appearance. The discovery adds a tragic medical dimension to a life already marked by political and personal suffering. Isabella of Aragon lived through one of the most turbulent periods in Italian history, endured a loveless power struggle disguised as a marriage alliance, watched as her husband's uncle stole everything that should have belonged to her son, lost three of her four children, saw her entire family's kingdom destroyed, and spent years fighting to maintain her dignity and protect her surviving daughter. And she did all of this while suffering from a painful, stigmatized disease that Renaissance medicine could do nothing to cure.

What made Isabella of Aragon famous is not that she was particularly beautiful, or that she wielded great military power, or that she was a patron of Leonardo da Vinci, though some historians have speculated about that connection. What makes her remarkable is her resilience. She was dealt perhaps the worst hand any Renaissance noblewoman could receive: unattractive by the standards of her time, married to a weak husband controlled by a ruthless uncle, widowed young under suspicious circumstances, robbed of her children's inheritance, separated from her son who died in captivity, and afflicted with a disease that caused chronic pain and social stigma. And yet she survived, ruled competently in Bari, educated her daughter to become a queen, and maintained her dignity and political relevance for three decades in a world designed to destroy women who lost their male protectors. Isabella of Aragon's fame rests not on what she achieved in spite of her circumstances, but on the fact that she simply refused to disappear when everyone expected her to.
"The longer I live the more beautiful life becomes."

Mon expérience avec les militaires : une leçon de vie et de gratitude
Mon parcours avec les militaires a commencé en 2015, à la radio des forces. À cette époque, je n’avais aucun contact avec eux : je me contentais d’animer mon programme et de repartir, sans imaginer que ma vie allait changer grâce à cette rencontre.
En 2024, Dieu m’a fait la grâce de pouvoir enseigner les militaires. Ce fut une véritable révélation. Enseigner ne consiste pas seulement à transmettre des connaissances ; c’est aussi recevoir, apprendre, et se découvrir soi-même à travers les autres. Depuis ce moment, j’ai énormément appris : le leadership, la discipline, l’importance de la ponctualité, et surtout de réfléchir avant de parler.
Mais la leçon la plus précieuse que j’ai reçue est celle du respect. J’ai appris à respecter chaque personne, quelle que soit sa classe sociale ou son rang. Chaque interaction devient alors une opportunité d’apprendre et de grandir.
Je me souviens d’un moment amusant qui illustre bien cette relation unique. Si un de mes étudiants ne copie pas ses leçons et que je décide de l’emmener chez le RSM (Regimental Sergeant Major), il m’appelle soudainement « marraine » et tout à coup, je finis parfois par changer d’avis. Ce petit rire partagé me rappelle que derrière la discipline et les règles strictes, il y a toujours l’humanité et la bienveillance.
Aujourd’hui, je peux dire avec sincérité que mon expérience avec les militaires est l’une des plus grandes bénédictions que Dieu m’ait offertes. Elle m’a permis de grandir, de comprendre la valeur du respect, de l’écoute et de la patience, et de voir que la vie est faite de leçons inattendues qui nous transforment profondément.
Ce que je vis avec eux n’est pas seulement un travail ou une responsabilité ; c’est une aventure humaine qui m’inspire chaque jour, et que je suis heureuse de partager.

Transparency Calls Grow for Full Review of Clinton Foundation Finances

Debate surrounding the Clinton Foundation has resurfaced, with renewed calls from critics and political commentators for a comprehensive financial audit of the global nonprofit organization.

The foundation, established by former President Bill Clinton and later associated with former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, operates worldwide initiatives focused on public health, economic development, and climate-related programs. As a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit, it is legally required to file annual IRS Form 990 disclosures and undergo independent audits, which are publicly available on the IRS website and the foundation’s own transparency portal.

Supporters of a deeper review argue that any large foundation connected to high-profile political figures should meet the highest possible transparency standards. They say a full forensic audit could strengthen public confidence, address lingering questions about donor influence, foreign contributions, and spending patterns, and reinforce accountability across major charitable institutions—regardless of political affiliation.

Critics, however, note that the foundation has already been subject to extensive regulatory oversight and multiple reviews over the years, including IRS examinations, congressional investigations, and independent audits. No criminal charges related to its primary financial operations have resulted from past examinations. They argue that repeated audit demands often arise during election cycles or politically charged moments and may reflect partisan tensions rather than new, credible evidence of wrongdoing.

Under U.S. law, agencies such as the Internal Revenue Service or state attorneys general have authority to initiate investigations if credible evidence of wrongdoing emerges (e.g., misuse of funds, improper donor influence, or tax-code violations). Absent that, nonprofits remain governed by existing federal and state reporting requirements, including public disclosure of major donors, executive compensation, and program spending.

The broader issue highlights an ongoing national conversation about transparency, accountability, and the standards applied to politically connected charitable organizations. As public scrutiny of major institutions continues, the balance between legitimate oversight and politicization remains central to the debate. Any call for a new, comprehensive review would need to demonstrate specific, evidence-based concerns rather than broad suspicion to avoid perceptions of selective targeting.

QCPD’s MUST SEE 🔍 | Faith in UN Human Rights Treaties (2026 Book Release) 

In January 2026, the book Faith in United Nations Human Rights Treaties, co-edited by Michael Wiener, Ibrahim Salama, and Britta Nicolmann, was released as a pioneering contribution exploring the intersection between faith and the United Nations human rights treaty system. 

Published by the University for Peace, the British University in Egypt, and the Norwegian Centre for Human Rights, the volume gathers an inclusive and impressive blend of contributors, offering valuable historical and normative perspectives on how faith traditions have shaped — and continue to influence — the interpretation and implementation of international human rights instruments, highlighting both opportunities and challenges for rights protection. 📣 

Of particular relevance to QCPD’s work, Chapter IX examines the interplay between faith perspectives and the International Convention on the Protection of the Rights of All Migrant Workers and Members of Their Families, providing important reflections on migration, inclusion, and rights-based policymaking. 

As supporters of the OHCHR Faith for Rights platform, QCPD welcomes this novel contribution, which strengthens dialogue between faith actors, policymakers, and human rights practitioners working toward more inclusive and coherent implementation of international standards.

THE STORY OF THE MOMBASA SHEIKH WHO WAS ASSASSINATED 

In the humid coastal heat of Mombasa, where the call to prayer drifts over coral-stone alleys and the Indian Ocean breathes against the shore, the name Sheikh Aboud Rogo still lingers like gunpowder after a shot.

He was born in 1968, long before his name would echo in courtrooms, intelligence briefings, and whispered conversations in mosque courtyards. As a young man at the Kisauni Islamic Institute, he was not yet the figure who would unsettle governments. He was a student with sharp eyes and restless ambition. When money ran dry and formal education slipped from his grasp, he returned to the streets—selling fish by day, leading prayers by night. But it was never just about prayer.

His mentor, Sheikh Abdul Ra, planted a dangerous seed: religion was not only devotion—it was power. It was resistance. It was governance. For Rogo, faith became something muscular, something that could move crowds and redraw borders.

In 1992, he tried his hand at politics and lost a council seat. The ballot box rejected him. The pulpit did not.

From the mosque, his voice grew louder, heavier, sharpened by grievance and conviction. He spoke of a Muslim-ruled world, of injustice, of enemies lurking behind foreign flags. His sermons did not float—they struck. And people listened.

Soon, his orbit darkened.

He was said to have welcomed dangerous men into Kenya’s shadows. Among them was Fazul Abdullah Mohammed—a ghostly figure later tied to the devastating 1998 bombings of the U.S. embassies in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam. The explosions ripped through East Africa, shattering buildings and lives. In intelligence files, Rogo’s name began appearing in uncomfortable proximity to men who trafficked in destruction.

In 2003, after attacks on the Kikambala Paradise Hotel and an Israeli charter plane, the Kenyan state moved. Rogo was arrested, charged with 13 counts of murder. The courtroom became the stage; the nation watched. For over two years he sat in prison, his supporters calling him persecuted, his critics calling him exposed. But evidence is a stubborn thing. In 2005, the court acquitted him. Insufficient proof. He walked free.

If prison was meant to silence him, it did the opposite.

He returned to preaching with sharpened rhetoric and an air of vindication. He declared the Islam practiced in Kenya diluted, compromised. He denounced America as an enemy of the faith. He accused the Kenyan government of crushing the poor under taxes and corruption. His sermons were no longer merely theological—they were political manifestos.

And then Somalia.

Across the border, the militant group Al-Shabaab was tightening its grip. To Rogo, Somalia was not chaos; it was refuge—a place he described as pure and uncorrupted. He urged young men to go. He dismissed warnings as propaganda. He framed the struggle as sacred.

Authorities accused him of secretly financing the militia. Washington and the United Nations would later sanction him, labeling him an al-Shabaab sympathizer. His name entered international watchlists. The distance between preacher and target grew thinner.

By 2012, he seemed to know the walls were closing in.

In January, police raided his home. They claimed to find grenades and explosives. His supporters cried fabrication; the state insisted it was proof. The tension in Mombasa thickened, like air before a storm.

In his final sermons, there was an edge of prophecy. He warned young men not to follow what he called weak leaders. He spoke as though preparing them—for something. For loss. For martyrdom. For revenge.

On August 27, 2012, the prophecy found him.

He was driving with his family through Mombasa’s streets when gunfire erupted. Bullets tore through metal and glass. His car became a cage of shattering windows and screaming steel. When it stopped, Sheikh Aboud Rogo was dead. His wife survived, wounded. The assassins vanished into the city.

The killing ignited fury. Protests exploded across Mombasa. Supporters clashed with police. Tires burned. Streets filled with smoke and chants. Accusations flew—at the government, at foreign powers, at shadowy operatives. Among the rumors was the name of Samantha Lewthwaite, the so-called “White Widow,” though no evidence ever solidified into charges. No arrests were made. The murder remains officially unsolved.

And so his legacy hardened into two incompatible stories.

To some, he was a fearless imam who refused to bow—to Western influence, to state pressure, to dilution of belief. To others, he was a radical firebrand whose words helped feed a pipeline of violence stretching from Kenya’s coast to Somalia’s battlefields.

In Mombasa, both versions still walk the streets.

His story is not neat. It is not clean. It sits at the uneasy intersection of faith, politics, power, and blood. A preacher who moved from selling fish to shaking governments. A man acquitted by a court but condemned by global powers. A voice that rose from a mosque and ended in a spray of bullets.

And like all unresolved crimes, it leaves behind a question that refuses to die:

Was he silenced because he was guilty—or because he was dangerous?

Today's post is about Dr. Thomas Burton.

Born into slavery on May 4, 1860, near Tates Creek, Burton was the youngest of 15 children. His early years were marked by profound hardship — he lost his father at age five and his mother at age nine. With no access to schooling, he continued working on the plantation simply for room and board. Yet even in those difficult years, a spark was lit. His mother taught him the alphabet before her passing, planting the seed of an education he would not be able to pursue until adulthood.

While still living and laboring in Madison County, Burton heard whispers of Berea College, an interracial institution just miles away. That knowledge ignited something powerful in him — a belief that education could change his life, even if it felt out of reach. At 21 years old, he finally left Richmond to attend Berea College. Burton did not have financial resources, so he worked his way through school. Throughout his educational journey he took on jobs such as waiting tables, working in a lumberyard, and doing domestic work for private families.  

After his time at Berea College, Dr. Burton later attended the Medical College of Indiana and graduated from the Eclectic College of Physicians and Surgeons in 1892, officially becoming a physician. After earning his medical degree, he moved to Springfield, Ohio, where he opened his own medical practice and married Hattie B. Taylor in 1893. He quickly became a respected community leader. 

His service extended beyond medicine: Dr. Burton was commissioned as Assistant Surgeon of the Ninth Battalion Infantry of the Ohio National Guard, where he helped organize a regiment of the state militia during the Spanish–American War. 

Dr. Burton’s life is a powerful reminder of the brilliance, resilience, and leadership that has come from Madison County’s Black community. From enslavement in our own county to becoming a respected doctor, military officer, and author, his journey reflects the strength of those who refused to let circumstance define their future.

Bollywood legend Govinda recently became the center of an online rumor that left fans shocked and his family members fuming. Social media users speculated, “Govinda सड़क पर आ गए?” suggesting financial trouble for the veteran actor. The comment quickly caught attention, sparking a wave of discussions and misinformation.
Responding firmly to the baseless claim, actor Vinay Anand, Govinda’s nephew, took to social media to clarify the situation. He expressed his anger at the false narrative and defended his uncle, stating that Govinda is far from financial distress. Vinay highlighted that the veteran actor owns substantial assets and remains a successful figure in the film industry, emphasizing, “Mera mamu crores ke malik hain, ye galat afwah hai” (My uncle is a millionaire; this rumor is false).
Fans appreciated Vinay Anand for standing up for his uncle and correcting misinformation. The clarification helped quell some of the panic, reminding everyone how easily rumors can spread about celebrities’ personal lives. Many netizens also criticized those spreading unverified claims, noting the harm such false stories can cause.
Govinda, known for his charismatic screen presence and iconic comic timing, has had a long and successful career spanning decades. Despite occasional financial speculations in the media, the actor continues to enjoy respect, admiration, and a loyal fan base across generations.
This episode highlights the importance of fact-checking in the age of social media and the impact of false narratives on public perception, even for legends like Govinda.

Advocacy Efforts and Why It All Matters (2026 Coffee with Council Edition)

Council’s advocacy isn’t a single lane; it’s a whole network, each carrying the same mission forward: to protect rural interests, elevate community needs, and keep life in the MD peaceful, progressive and prosperous.

Below is a picture of the work done and the issues championed.

Intermunicipal and Regional Collaboration
• Strengthened shared service delivery models, including FCSS through the Town of Grimshaw, ensuring smaller communities continue receiving consistent, cost-effective social supports.
• Active collaboration with Grimshaw, Berwyn, and County of Northern Lights on recreation, regional planning, and community services.
• Advocacy through intermunicipal negotiation committees to keep regional relationships resilient and productive.
Impact on residents: Stable funding, lower service delivery costs, stronger regional partnerships, and smoother access to programs.

Family and Community Well-Being
• Advocacy for consistent FCSS funding and support for local preventative social programming.
• Promotion of inclusive, accessible community events that strengthen rural belonging.
• Support for local initiatives such as libraries, Christmas hamper programs, and volunteer-based services.
Committee connections:
• Library Board & Peace Library System (literacy, lifelong learning)
• Peace River Aboriginal Interagency Committee (cultural relationships)
Impact: These are the programs that reduce isolation, strengthen families, and keep our social fabric stitched.

Recreation, Leisure, and Tourism
• Advocacy for recognition and funding of rural recreation assets: campgrounds, trails, river access points, and the MD’s campground on the Peace River.
• Promotion of the Peace River as a regional tourism corridor.
• Engagement with provincial partners to share the economic value of rural recreation.
Committee connections:
• Mighty Peace Tourist Association
• Lac Cardinal Regional Economic Development Board
Impact: Tourism growth, improved recreation infrastructure, and a stronger local economy.

Infrastructure and Essential Services
• Advocacy for sustainable water and wastewater funding and modernization of bacterial water testing methods.
• Ongoing dialogue with Alberta Transportation, including bridge concerns.
• Engagement through the Mutual Aid Committee, Emergency Advisory Committee, and Long Lake Regional Waste Management Commission.
Impact: Reliable water systems, safer transport routes, and strong emergency coordination.

Rural Voice and Capacity Building
• Consistent advocacy in provincial consultations to ensure rural perspectives are not overshadowed by urban priorities.
• Highlighting the disproportionate administrative and financial burdens on small municipalities.
Committee connections:
• Rural Municipalities of Alberta (RMA)
 •Northern Alberta Elected Leaders (NAEL)
• PREDA (economic development and investment attraction)
• Mackenzie Municipal Services Agency (planning and development)
Impact: Policies better shaped for rural realities.

Peace Region Nuclear Power Project
• Participation in community engagement sessions and town halls to ensure residents’ perspectives are heard.
• Membership in the Peace Region Energy Committee to ensure the MD secures a fair position if a nuclear plant proceeds (taxation, infrastructure load, workforce impacts).
Impact: Protection of long-term tax base, planning readiness, and transparent information flow.

MLA & Provincial Ministry Advocacy
• Addressed the financial aftermath of the Shaftesbury wildfire.
• Continued advocacy for the Peace River Airport.
• Engagement on policing needs, including sheriff involvement in real-time operations.
• Responsive engagement with changes to the Municipal Government Act regarding service delivery, contracting, and intermunicipal frameworks.
• Advocacy for regulatory clarity and flexibility recognizing rural realities.
Impact: Improved public safety, infrastructure funding, regional transportation stability, smarter service delivery, and more local control.

Healthcare Advocacy
• Support for Ken Sargent House so families have a place to stay when accessing Grande Prairie Hospital services.
• Advocacy and financial support for Maskwa Medical Centre to improve rural access to primary care.
• Participation through the Grimshaw Healthcare Attraction & Retention Committee and the Peace Regional Healthcare Attraction & Retention Committee.
Impact: More stable healthcare access for MD residents.

Agricultural Advocacy and Disaster Response
• Agricultural Disaster Declaration recognizing drought severity and pest pressures.
• Advocacy for the MD’s inclusion in the federal Livestock Tax Deferral Program.
• Ongoing work through the Agricultural Service Board, VSI Services Board, and Weed/Pest Appeal Committees.
Impact: Financial relief, better pest management, and more robust supports for producers.

Additional Key Advocacy Focus Areas for 2026
Women’s Shelter Support
• Continued financial support, including $10,000 in 2025, for local shelter operations and services.
Unhoused Population & Crime
• Advocacy for integrated policing efforts, including coordination with the sheriff’s real-time operations centre.
Northwest Polytechnic (Fairview Campus) Closure
• Advocacy regarding the economic, educational, and workforce loss caused by the campus closure.
• Emphasis on maintaining rural pathways to post-secondary education.
Impact: Stronger community safety, access to services, and long-term prosperity.

How Committees Multiply Council’s Advocacy Power
Council doesn’t only advocate through letters and meetings; much of the real work happens through committee participation. Each committee is a vantage point, giving Council early information, influence, and the ability to champion local interests.
Below are a few ways committees drive advocacy:
Emergency & Protective Services
• Emergency Advisory Committee
• Mutual Aid Committee
• Rural Crime Watch
• RCMP Community Advisory Committee
These groups ensure preparedness, strengthen relationships with policing partners, and push for rural-appropriate safety solutions.

Health & Social Services
• Health Attraction & Retention Committees
• Regional Mental Health & Addictions Task Force
• Library boards
These shape policies that affect residents’ well-being every day.

Agriculture & Environment
• Agricultural Service Board
• Weed & Pest Appeal Committees
• Grimshaw Gravels Aquifer Management Advisory Association
These committees keep Council close to issues affecting land, water, and local producers.

Land Use, Growth, and Regional Development
• Intermunicipal Negotiation Committees
• MMSA
• Regional Assessment Review Board
• Subdivision & Development Appeal Board
• Economic Development Boards
These influence development, land use, investment attraction, and long-term planning.

Why All This Matters to Residents
• Your water, roads, firefighters, and emergency system are protected because Council is constantly pushing for fair rural funding.
• Your recreation spaces, libraries, campsites, and river access points exist and grow because Council fights for them.
• Your healthcare access improves because Council is at multiple regional tables saying rural families deserve better.
• Your taxes stay stable because Council works regionally to reduce duplication and share services.
• Your safety improves because Council is at the table with police, sheriffs, and emergency planners.
• Your children and grandchildren’s opportunities improve through advocacy on education, economic development, and community services.

Nigeria’s challenges are well known. What we need now is not another narration of our pain, but clear and practical strategies for healing, reconciliation and rebuilding trust.

On February 16, 2026, The Kukah Centre (TKC) convened a Roundtable Conversation to confront the hard questions shaping Nigeria’s future. Scholars, diplomats, faith leaders, policy actors and citizens came together to reflect honestly on the path forward.

The discussion acknowledged the deep fractures in our national life including insecurity, toxic politics, weakened institutions and a growing culture of fear and distrust. Participants were clear that paying ransom and relying on appeasement only deepen the crisis. Real solutions must begin at the grassroots.

A nation is built intentionally over time. It requires a shared identity where Nigerians see themselves as Nigerians first. It demands civic education that prepares the next generation, strong and credible institutions especially a judiciary that does not fail the people, and deliberate processes of reconciliation. We must confront our history with honesty and transform painful memories into meaning and purpose for a better future.

The state must guarantee protection and social security. That is how citizens develop loyalty and a genuine sense of belonging. A true democracy safeguards minority interests and upholds the common good above narrow gains.

The conversation also highlighted Nigeria’s greatest asset, its young people. Many are leaving because they feel excluded from the promise of the nation. Restoring trust, expanding opportunity and ensuring security are essential to renewing their confidence in Nigeria’s future.

There was a strong call for authentic interfaith dialogue. Not symbolic gestures, but honest engagement that builds trust across differences. Citizens were encouraged to build networks across regions, faiths and sectors and to see themselves first as one people with a shared destiny.

Insights from distinguished speakers including Majeed Dahiru, Chris Kwaja, Gloria Ballason, Paddy Harte and Peter Ryan enriched the exchange with lessons drawn from both Nigerian and international peace efforts.

The message was simple and sobering. Nigeria will not be transformed overnight. A nation is something we build every day through justice, shared identity, democratic renewal and commitment to the common good.

At The Kukah Centre (TKC), we remain committed to advancing dialogue, strengthening democratic culture, deepening interfaith engagement and promoting ethical leadership as pillars for a just and peaceful Nigeria.The work continues. 

The nation is still being built.

NURSE THEMBENI 
CHAPTER 19
THEMBENI 

Everyone’s on their knees except my brothers. They are still standing there like idiots, faces twisted in total confusion. They look from the kneeling Hlongwane uncles to Baba who’s actually on his knees, head bowed low, then to this fragile-looking guy leaning on his father and the driver. The Mthunzi people are down too, murmuring “Bayede Ngwane kaNgwadi.”
“What the hell is this? Who is this man? Why are they bowing like he’s Jesus?” Mkhululi complains to Lindani. 
 “I don’t know, bhuti. But look at Ngiyabonga, he’s nervous. Why is he sweating like that?”
I can’t help it, a small, tired laugh runs up in my chest. It’s not loud, but it’s vocal enough to make Mkhululi shoot me a death glare. I don't care about him anymore. 
Mehlo really looks sick. His shoulders are hunched, and his breathing shallow. What happened to him? Why is he here when he looks like he’s scheduled for his own funeral? 
I have so many questions for him, but mostly, I want to touch his face and make sure he’s real. 
I leave Baba’s side and start walking toward him. Mkhululi’s hand clamps around my wrist before I get three steps. 
“Where do you think you’re going?”
“I’m just going to greet him.”
“You’re not going anywhere near that man until we figure out what’s happening.”
I yank my arm. 
“Figure it out from over there then, the truth is right before your eyes but you refuse to see it.”
“You’re easily deceived, Thembeni.” 
Has he taken a look in the mirror? I’m not going to stop because he said so. Ever felt like you’re losing your mind and there is nothing you can do about it? Yep, that’s me right now. I have never in my life spoken to my brothers the way I have been doing since they found me at Qondi’s house, and it’s a real shocker that Mkhululi has not exercised his back-hand on me. I wish Ngcwele was here, he always makes things easy when these two force me to carry burdens I can’t carry. 
“Yey wena, calm down, maan.” That’s Ngiyabonga snapping at someone. 
I check and see him grabbing his son’s arm, Menzi does not look okay. I forgot he was standing there, he’s muttering something under his breath. I can’t make out the words, but his face… yoh. He looks like he’s seen a ghost that came back specifically to haunt him. His eyes are wide with terror, his mouth is moving fast. I can’t hear what he’s saying. 
“Calm down. Calm. Down.” Ngiyabonga keeps whisper yelling, while his wife MaNxumalo tugs at Menzi’s arm. 
“Come son, let’s go to the car. You don’t need to be here.” She says. 
I feel suffocated on his behalf. Why are they hovering over him like that? 
Menzi shoves her hand off, harder than I’ve ever seen him do to his mother. 
“I’m not a child, Ma. Leave me alone.”
That loud shout gets to Ngiyabonga, his face twists in annoyance. He acts like Menzi just embarrassed him in front of important people.
Menzi starts moving, he’s walking straight to Mehlo. I move closer while praying in Hebrew that Menzi does not attack the man who looks like he escaped from the hospital. Seriously, I don’t know what he’s about to do after that virginity revelation. He stands right in front of Mehlo and hugs him like they’re long-lost brothers.
Is that a cease fire? 
Mehlo doesn’t hug him back, his arms stay limp at his sides. His face is cold as ice and unreadable, his eyes meet mine and I see his jaw clench. Menzi keeps whispering apologies into his shoulder. 
“I’m sorry… I’m so sorry… I didn’t mean… forgive me…”
I feel my mouth drop open. What in the actual hell? Is he talking about stealing the throne? Or something else? 
Ngiyabonga has had enough, he marches over, grabs Menzi by the back of the shirt like he’s a naughty toddler, and yanks him away. 
“Enough of this stupidity! Get a hold of yourself, boy!” He snaps.
Menzi stumbles back, and that’s because Mehlo’s driver just threw a punch at him. His mother screams, catching him half way to the ground. Menzi doesn’t even try putting up a fight, he knows what he did.
“How dare you touch royalty. Do you know who he is?” Ngiyabonga roars at the driver, but he doesn’t get close to him. I can smell his fear all the way here. I need to find out out what’s going on. 
I can’t look away from Mehlo. He’s still staring straight ahead, like the hug never happened. But his jaw is tight, something flickers in his eyes, I think it’s anger, or just exhaustion, it’s hard to tell with this one.
“What is going on?” 
Mkhululi finally lets go of my wrist, I rub my wrist and take a step. This time nobody stops me.

I walk right up to Mehlo, close enough to smell the hospital smell still clinging to him, I was right. He’s sick.
“Phakade lami.”  His voice is barely above a whisper. 
“Golide,” I say softly.
His eyes have been on me since he arrived. 
“Is that what you call your king? This is a sign that I should let my cousin keep the throne. Angisho KaMajola?”
I roll my eyes and a tiny, cracked smile pulls at the corner of his mouth. First real thing I’ve seen on his face since he got here. I can’t laugh, not when he looks like he's dying. He's not even breathing normally. 
“Yeah well, you never told me that you’re royalty. It took a dream and all this chaos for me to realize I have been opening my legs for royalty.” I say, crossing my arms to hide how much my hands are shaking. 
“Your royal legs, you mean.” he replies with a challenging smile. 
I want to roll my eyes again, but he’s laughing now. Things really do change. 
“I am not royalty, and what happened to you? You look like death ubered you here and you requested a return.” I say. 
I didn’t realise that he’s touching my hand, his thumb is playing behind the back of my hand. 
“I will tell you about it, after my father sorts this mess out.” His eyes point around us, the noise has become background. But I know for sure Ngiyabonga is complaining, his voice is all I can hear. 
“Next time answer your phone.” I tell Mehlo. 
He exhales something that might be a laugh. 
“Next time I’ll try not to get poisoned first.” he says.
Poisoned?
Ngiyabonga clears his throat loud. 
“This is a private family matter now, we should all go inside and talk properly.”
Mehlo doesn’t even look at him, he just keeps his eyes on me and in that second, with everyone watching, with Menzi looking ready to throw up and my brothers looking lost and the real king standing here half-dead but still standing…
I realise something, I’m the one who’s going to be dragged around in the middle of whatever this is, and I think the middle just found me.
“What is going on? Why is everyone still on their knees for this stranger when the chief is right there?” Mkhululi shouts. 
”They will stay on their knees until the king tells them to rise.” Bab’ Mvula says. 
I can’t believe this is real, Golide is a king.  
“It’s obvious, bhuti. The real king just arrived.” I tell my brother.
He laughs, it’s what he does when he thinks he’s being lied to.
“Impossible.”
“This is the real king of KwaZulu. Mehlokazulu Hlongwane. It was said he was in exile after the fire that killed his parents. Or that he died. But here he is, alive and well.” That came from one of the Hlongwane uncles. 
He just pissed Ngiyabonga off. 
“Shut up! You’re lying! My son Menzi is the real king, this dark-skinned imposter is nothing but a crook!”
I glance at Mehlo just as he winces, hand pressing to his side like it hurts to breathe. 
“Are you okay?” I ask and he nods, it’s a lie. He’s covered in sweat. 

“What are you waiting for? Go get the king a chair! Can’t you see he’s not feeling well?”
It’s my ever-opportunist sister in-law, she’s snapping at Ntando, not me. Ntando jumps like she’s been shocked, runs to the tree, grabs one of the plastic chairs so fast she almost trips over her own feet. Poor girl stumbles on the way back and nearly crashes right into Mehlo. 
The driver throws his arm out, creating a barrier between them, and takes the chair from her. 
“Thank you,” he sets it down and helps Mehlo lower himself into it. Mehlo exhales as if sitting is the hardest thing he’s done all day.
What happened to him? If he was poisoned, what kind of poison is this? 
I catch Philile giving Ntando a big thumbs-up and a proud-mama smile. She’s giving me an opportunity to sigh, but I hold it in. Here we go again. Groomed since birth, ready to serve royalty on a platter.
Oh how quick the tables have shifted from Menzi to Mehlo. She now has her eyes on Mehlo for her precious daughter.  
“This is ridiculous! Why is this imposter getting special treatment? He is a fraud. Menzi is the true king. Get off your black knees, all of you.” Ngiyabonga keeps yelling, he’s really trying to drown everything out. The people don't move. 
But why hasn’t Mehlo told everyone to get up? Is he trying to prove a point. 
“Mehlo, what is going on? Is Menzi related to you? I had a dream about you, you were dressed like a king, but you burnt to ashes.”  
Oh great! I have made the sick man worry. 
“My father will speak to your father, everything will be sorted out. Then we'll talk ” He says. 
I don’t know what he means by everything.

 Mehlo’s father leaves his side and walks straight to Baba. He sits down in front of him on the ground and tells him he can get off his knees, baba sits on his bum.   
“Mpondo, kunjani.” 
My father responds with a nod. Why is he avoiding Bab’ Mvula’s eyes? I thought they were friends. 
“You were the greatest warrior during King Muzingaye’s reign, Mehlokazulu’s father. You know his history better than anyone. Why would you sit there and let these boys believe these lies?”
My father was a what? Hayyi! He looks so thin and old and fragile. I could swear he wouldn’t hurt a fly. How was he a warrior? And why am I hearing about it now? 
“KaMajola’s brothers are doing what’s best for her.” Baba says, not looking up to meet bab’ Mvula’s eyes. 
Why is he avoiding his gaze so much? 
Bab’ Mvula raises an eyebrow, he’s calling this bullshit. 
“By lying, Mpondo?”
“No one is lying here! If he’s the true king of KwaZulu, then where has he been all these years? Why only come now to claim the throne?” Ngiyabonga jumps in. 
Mehlo lifts his head and looks straight at Ngiyabonga. 
“You know why.”
I don’t want him talking anymore, it sounds like he’s running out of breath. Ngiyabonga swallows hard and looks away fast. His hands twitch, I think he wants to punch something or someone.
“We want to do right by your daughter, Mpondo. Accept inkomo for inhlawulo. Then we start lobola negotiations for our queen. The Zulu kingdom cannot function without her, you know the prophesy.” Bab’ Mvula says. 
Is he talking about me? Nurse Themi? A whole queen who is needed in the Zulu kingdom? Nah! This must be one of those lucid dreams. I will wake up anytime now. 
“Let them in.” My father’s shaky voice frees me from my thoughts. 
He just agreed. 
“Baba, no! This is all a lie, you’re making a mistake!” Mkhululi protests. 
Baba looks at him tired, too tired to open his mouth but he still does. 
“I know them, ndodana. That man seated on the chair is inkosi uNgwane KaNgwandi, Mehlokazulu Hlongwane. His father was Muzingaye Hlongwane, a splitting image of him. He died in a fire years ago. Ever since that fire, the ancestors were enraged. They stripped the kingdom of…”
Ngiyabonga cuts him off, screaming. “Mpondo! Mpondo! Stop lying maan, you’re all lying! Guards, arrest them all and sentence them to death.”
“The guards aren’t even here. You’re the one who should be arrested.” One of the uncles says. 
“It’s over, Ngiyabonga. You and your family should turn around and leave.” Bab’Mvula says. 
Ngiyabonga laughs, it sounds fake. He walks to a chair under the tree where everyone else is gathered and sits down, crossing his leg over the other. 
“Nothing is over, my people came here for lobola. Let omnyamana finish with their one cow. My people and I will wait here, I will empty my kraal if I have to. These lobola negotiations are happening today.” Ngiyabonga says. 
“But you can’t continue. KaMajola was chosen for the real heir to the throne, Mehlokazulu, and that is who she is going to marry.” Bab’ Mvula stands his ground. 
Ngiyabonga laughs. “Over my dead body. You people have no idea who you’re dealing with. For years my son has been ruling this town and you’re turning your backs on him because of this dark demon? Please, start with this inhlawulo nonsense so my son can get his wife.”
Ngiyabonga’s screws are missing, I don’t want his kraal. I don’t want him as my father in-law. I look at Menzi, hoping he’d knock some sense into his father’s head. I mean, he does give off alpha-male vibes. But right now he looks like a chicken rained on. 
“The king looks sick, he should rest in the meantime.” That’s Philile mummuring beside me. She taps Ntando on the arm. 
“Go prepare your room, Ntando. Change the bedding and put those new ones I bought last week. King Mehlokazulu will rest in your room.”
Classic Philile. Always betting on the winning horse, even if she has to switch saddles mid-race.
I watch Ntando run off like her life depends on it. Girl moves like she’s auditioning for queen already. 
“KaMajola,” Ngiyabonga calls, I was about to tell Philile I stop. 
“Go get ready, today is your day, ntombi. After inhlawulo from omnyamana, those dark skinned people, it’s your lobola from Menzi. Your father is about to become a rich man. Ithi halala phela, sisi.” Ngiyabonga says. 
Halala for what? Is he going to marry me to his son by force? 
.

GOVERNOR CALEB MUTFWANG REAFFIRMS COMMITMENT TO SUSTAINABLE PEACE AS PLATEAU STATE PEACE BUILDING AGENCY COMMEMORATES 10TH ANNIVERSARY 

The Executive Governor of Plateau State, His Excellency, Barr. Caleb Manasseh Mutfwang, has reaffirmed his administration’s unwavering commitment to peace, social cohesion, and inclusive governance as the Plateau State Peace Building Agency (PPBA) commemorated its 10th Anniversary.

Speaking at the event, Governor Mutfwang described the establishment of the Peace Building Agency a decade ago as a bold and visionary decision that institutionalized peacebuilding in Plateau State, noting that peace is not accidental but must be structured, nurtured, coordinated, and sustained.

Governor Mutfwang, represented by his deputy, Ngo Josephine Chundung Piyo, emphasized that the anniversary marks ten years of intentional and institutionalized peacebuilding, characterized by sustained dialogue facilitation, effective early warning and early response mechanisms, community engagement, and deliberate efforts to build bridges across divides while strengthening trust between communities and the government.

Reflecting on the state’s journey, Governor Mutfwang acknowledged that Plateau has experienced difficult seasons in the past but has continued to chart a path toward stability and reconciliation through resilience, purposeful leadership, and collective effort. 

Governor Mutfwang reiterated that his administration places peace at the centre of governance, stressing that peace remains the foundation upon which sustainable development thrives.

He further stated that peacebuilding is a collective responsibility, calling on traditional institutions, faith leaders, women's groups, youth organizations, civil society, security agencies, and citizens to continue working together to strengthen the state's peace architecture.

Earlier, the Director-General of the Peace Building Agency, Ms Julie Sanda, highlighted that the development of a modern technology and communication strategy marks another significant milestone in the Agency’s peacebuilding efforts, while also underscoring the importance of trauma support and resilience for vulnerable communities.

In his keynote address, the Special Envoy to the Governor on Peace Building, Prof. Chris Kwaja, emphasized the need for proactive measures to ensure peaceful coexistence, stressing the critical role of strong institutions, partnerships, and stakeholder collaboration in achieving lasting peace.

Goodwill messages were delivered by the Acting Chairperson of the Gender and Equal Opportunities Commission, Olivia Dazyem; the President of the Peace Practitioners Network, Mrs Bali Nanmak, security agencies, among others, all of whom commended the Agency’s decade-long impact in promoting dialogue, reconciliation, and peaceful coexistence across Plateau State.

Highlights of the event included the unveiling of the Management Communication Strategy document, the unveiling of the 10th Anniversary logo, and the cutting of the anniversary cake, marking a decade of institutionalized peacebuilding and renewed commitment to a peaceful and prosperous Plateau State.

Today, I had the honour of joining stakeholders, partners, and peace advocates to commemorate the 10th Anniversary of the Plateau State Peace Building Agency, a milestone that speaks to a decade of intentional, structured, and institutionalised peacebuilding in our dear state.

10 years ago, Plateau State took a bold and visionary step by establishing the Peace Building Agency, with the clear understanding that peace is not accidental, it must be nurtured, coordinated, and sustained through deliberate policies and collective action. This anniversary is not only a celebration but also a moment of reflection. Plateau State has experienced challenging periods in the past, yet through resilience, purposeful leadership, and the collective commitment of our people, we have continued to make steady progress towards stability, reconciliation, and peaceful coexistence. The Peace Building Agency has remained a critical pillar in this journey and a model for subnational peace architecture in Nigeria and beyond.

Under the leadership of His Excellency, Governor Caleb Mutfwang, we remain unwavering in our commitment to peace, social cohesion, and inclusive governance. We strongly believe that peace is the foundation upon which sustainable development is built — without peace, there can be no meaningful investment, no thriving youth enterprise, no sustainable agriculture, and no secure future for our children.

However, peacebuilding is not the responsibility of government alone. It is a shared duty that requires the active involvement of traditional institutions, faith leaders, women groups, youth organisations, civil society, security agencies, and every citizen. The architecture provides the framework, but the people provide the spirit that sustains peace.

As we look beyond this first decade, we must deepen community-based conflict prevention mechanisms, strengthen trust-building initiatives, leverage technology for early warning systems, and continue to promote dialogue over division. We must also be more intentional about youth inclusion and women’s leadership in peace processes, because sustainable peace thrives on inclusive participation.

🩻My dog had recently been diagnosed with a bulging disc and also has some arthritis in his hocks and hip.

😱For some people the suggestion of pain investigation can feel like opening Pandora’s box. Are we opening a money pit? A really difficult topic is that many qualified trainers and behaviourists lose clients when it comes to pain and many of us burn out because we don’t want to keep working with dogs showing symptoms of pain with an owner who won’t do anything about it and how many unqualified trainers are ready, waiting like gannets to scoop them up and apply whatever level of pain is needed for a dog to shut down. 

😬Was I scared that I was opening a massive vets bill - Yes! Was it expensive? Yes! But I now have a dog who is calm and able to cope with so much more and his world is so much bigger and he deserves a life as free from pain as possible and happy, bigger world.

💊 The fallout of untreated chronic pain will always be greater than pain management and don’t forget you can ask your vet about contextualised care.

Growing older with grace. 🤍

On my next birthday, I’ll be turning 60 — and I’m learning to embrace it with grace.

I’ve decided I’m done spending hours in a salon chair — and a small fortune — trying to cover up the gray that naturally belongs to me.

Today my stylist began the process of bringing me back to my natural state. I haven’t colored my hair in six months, and it will probably take another six months to a year before the transition is complete.

Yes, this picture was taken today.
No, it’s not AI generated.
And the only makeup I’m wearing is mascara and lipstick.

I’ve never loved the feel of heavy makeup on my skin, so I rarely wear it. For me, this season is about learning to be comfortable in my own skin — and that has been a long journey.

After all, God created us in His image. What could be more beautiful than what He already designed?

This isn’t about judging anyone. We live in a time of fake lashes, fake nails, tattooed eyeliner, tattooed lips, fillers, Botox… and I’m not saying any of that is wrong. I may even try a little Botox someday.

I’m simply asking myself a question:
What happened to just liking ourselves?

In the 60s and 70s, it was long straight hair — whatever color you were born with. A little mascara. Maybe some lip gloss. We weren’t perfect… but we were real.

Somewhere along the way, many of us were taught we weren’t enough as we were.

So this — for me — is about unlearning that lie.

It’s about building self-confidence.
It’s about embracing who God created me to be.
It’s about no longer living under old narratives that whispered I had to fix everything to be worthy.

I’m not saying everyone needs to “go natural.”
I am saying we all deserve to feel comfortable in our own skin.

For me, grace looks like mascara, lipstick, healthy hair returning to its natural color — and letting the rest simply be.

Here’s to growing older gracefully.
Here’s to confidence rooted in Christ.
Here’s to becoming more ourselves with every year. ✨

— Donna Fuller

I agree with Michael Deibert. It’s time for Leon to step down.

post_text_pi:
Today, we had the honor of welcoming Senator Andy Kim to Interfaith Caregivers of Greater Mercer County.

We shared how our Neighbors Helping Neighbors program connects volunteers with older adults and adults with disabilities, providing free rides, grocery shopping, friendly visits, and support that help our neighbors remain independent at home.

We were also proud to highlight New Jersey’s Project Healthy Bones program, an evidence-based education and exercise program we oversee in Mercer County, that helps older adults improve strength, balance, and bone health while reducing the risk of falls and fractures.

The visit concluded in the most meaningful way — Senator Kim joined one of our dedicated Volunteers for a friendly visit with one of our Care Receivers, Maureen.

During their conversation, Maureen and the Senator discovered they shared something deeply personal, as both have walked the road of loving and caring for someone with Alzheimer’s. Maureen spoke about her husband, and the Senator shared about his father. In that moment, the conversation moved beyond programs or politics and instead became about connection and understanding.

Because the heart of what we do isn’t found in statistics… it’s found in relationships.

We are grateful for leaders who take the time to listen, connect, and witness firsthand the relationships that strengthen our community every day.

Thank you, Senator Kim, for spending time with us and the neighbors we serve.

Chairman Al Haj Murad Ebrahim's support for the Bangsamoro women's assumption to power is truly commendable.

Empowering women in leadership roles can bring about significant positive change and promote inclusivity and diversity.

By supporting women's leadership, Chairman Ebrahim is helping to challenge traditional gender roles and stereotypes that may have held women back in the past.

His move can inspire a new generation of women leaders and contribute to a more equitable society. It was a step towards a more inclusive Bangsamoro. 

During his term as the Chief Minister of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), he has taken significant strides towards inclusivity and gender equality.

Chairman Ebrahim's leadership and commitment to empowering women are crucial in building a more just and equitable society for all.

Chairman Ebrahim invested in empowering women which is not a popular decision since Bangsamoro women are often regarded as incapable of leadership.

La Pastoral Social Cáritas Ecuador presentó oficialmente la Campaña Cáritas Múnera 2026, que este año cumple 50 años de vida al servicio de los más necesitados. Bajo el lema “Todos somos hermanos, yo creo en el amor que se comparte”, la iniciativa se desarrollará durante la Cuaresma en parroquias y colegios católicos de todo el país.
 
La campaña sostiene la acción social de la Iglesia y, gracias al aporte solidario de miles de fieles, en el último año permitió acompañar a millones personas en situación de vulnerabilidad, mediante proyectos coordinados desde las jurisdicciones eclesiásticas y articulados a nivel nacional.
 
Durante la rueda de prensa, Mons. David de la Torre, sscc, Obispo Auxiliar de Quito y secretario general de la Conferencia Episcopal Ecuatoriana, recordó que fue el Cardenal Pablo Muñoz Vega quien impulsó esta colecta hace cinco décadas en Quito. Destacó que la fraternidad que la anima ha llevado esperanza concreta —hecha pan, medicina y acogida— a lo largo del país, y subrayó que hoy más que nunca es necesario no vivir de espaldas al dolor del hermano.
 
Mons. Antonio Crameri, SSC, Obispo del Vicariato Apostólico dé Esmeraldas y Presidente de Cáritas Ecuador, señaló que la campaña es una expresión concreta de la conversión cuaresmal, donde la oración, el ayuno y la limosna se traducen en caridad activa. Invitó a toda la Iglesia y a cada familia a preguntarse qué pueden compartir, recordando que ningún aporte es pequeño cuando nace del amor.
 
Por su parte, el Padre Euclides Carrillo, secretario ejecutivo de la Pastoral Cáritas Nacional, informó que en 2025 se recaudaron 414.014 dólares a través de la campaña. El 50% fue destinado a las jurisdicciones eclesiásticas y el otro 50% a Cáritas Nacional; de este último monto, una parte cubrió gastos operativos y el resto se ejecutó directamente en proyectos sociales. Estos recursos sostienen ancianatos, centros médicos, casas de acogida, comedores, apoyo escolar, atención a personas con discapacidad, acompañamiento en movilidad humana, respuesta a emergencias y programas de seguridad alimentaria y pastoral penitenciaria, entre otras acciones. Además, la cooperación internacional aportó más de 3 millones de dólares para fortalecer la labor social en el país.

Dentro de su intervención también motivo a todos los ecuatorianos a ser parte la formación que se realizará los días miércoles a las 20hrs, empezando desde 25 de febrero, con el tema Delexi Te, esta formación que se trabaja en conjunto con el Itpe. será impartida por parte de los Obispos del Ecuador.

Por su parte, el Hno. Guillermo Oñate, SJ, presidente de la CONFEDEC, expresó el compromiso de las instituciones educativas católicas para promover el compartir fraterno desde las aulas y garantizar el apoyo a las obras de Cáritas, formando en valores evangélicos y responsabilidad social.
 
Las contribuciones podrán realizarse en parroquias y colegios desde el 19 de febrero y culminarán con la colecta nacional el Domingo de Ramos, 29 de marzo. También se podrá donar a través de la página web oficial www.caritasecuador.org y la App Deuna.
 
Después de 50 años, la Colecta Cáritas Múnera continúa siendo un signo concreto de fraternidad. Un gesto sencillo puede convertirse en esperanza real para miles de familias en el Ecuador

A lactate test isn’t something you do randomly — you schedule it at key transition points in your training. I did mine at @wa_sportsmed upon recommendation by @_mybestseason 

The best time to test is:
• at the start of a structured training block to set accurate zones
• after a full adaptation phase to measure real physiological change
• when power, heart rate, and RPE stop lining up

Why? Because lactate testing identifies your true metabolic breakpoints (LT1 & LT2) — the intensities where your body shifts from purely aerobic energy production to progressively greater glycolytic contribution.

That means:
✅ precise endurance intensity (no more “fake Z2”)
✅ correctly targeted threshold work
✅ early detection of aerobic improvements — before FTP even moves

In short: you don’t test to get numbers.
You test to make every session count.

The Stono Rebellion was not a spontaneous event. It was catalyzed by a Spanish proclamation offering liberty to enslaved people who reached St. Augustine, Florida—a deliberate act of geopolitical sabotage against British Carolina. The rebellion's leader, often called Jemmy, was likely from the Kingdom of Kongo, a region with a strong Catholic tradition, adding a layer of religious conflict to the struggle. The uprising triggered immediate panic. The colonial militia, led by the Lieutenant Governor himself, caught up with the group by late afternoon. In the ensuing fight, many rebels were killed. The backlash was swift and severe: South Carolina passed the Negro Act of 1740, which further restricted movement, education, and assembly for the enslaved population for decades. Sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, PBS.
