At dinner, my parents logged into my account using a fake ID. I didn’t raise my voice. I didn’t stop them. I just smiled and took a sip of my wine. What they didn’t realize was that the login they’d just completed activated a silent federal flag — one I’d put in place months earlier, the moment I suspected my own family might try something exactly like this.

Game over.
They just didn’t know it yet.

My name is Morgan. I’m thirty-two years old, and I work as a CFO for a mid-sized tech company. My job is straightforward to explain and brutal to execute: I identify risk before it explodes. I assume good intentions until the numbers say otherwise. I plan for worst-case scenarios — because they usually arrive disguised as family.

That night, the data was sitting across from me, passing the bread basket.

I drove to my parents’ house fully aware of what this dinner was really about. They’d called it family business. Loose ends. Helping Bianca get back on her feet.

Translation: access.

I parked my seven-year-old sedan behind Bianca’s brand-new luxury SUV, its paint still gleaming. The contrast didn’t escape me. It never did.

Bianca is my older sister. Thirty-five. Permanently “in transition.” Never quite employed. Always financially insulated.

The golden child.

I was the other one.

The dependable one.
The organized one.
The one whose money was apparently considered communal property.

Before I rang the doorbell, I checked my phone once. The recording app was active. The secondary authentication monitor was live. The compliance trigger — quiet, invisible, devastating — was armed.

Dinner was warm. Candlelit. Carefully staged.

My mother, Sylvia, hugged me a little too tightly. My father, Victor, poured wine as if this were just another pleasant evening. Bianca barely glanced up from her phone.

We ate. We chatted. We performed normalcy.

Then Victor stood and said casually,
“Why don’t we take care of that account issue while we’re all together?”

There it was.

He gestured toward my laptop, already open on the sideboard.

I stayed seated.

“I trust you,” my mother added with a thin smile. “It’s just formalities.”

They sat down.

My father typed.
My mother produced an ID.

It wasn’t mine.

A forgery. My name. My photo. Not my signature.

They logged in.

And at that exact moment — silent, seamless, irreversible — the system did exactly what I’d designed it to do.

No alarms.
No warnings.
Just a timestamp, a location ping, a credential mismatch, and a quiet escalation routed directly into federal financial monitoring.

I lifted my glass and took a slow drink.

They talked about renovations. About Bianca’s “next chapter.” About how proud they were of her resilience.

They had no idea the clock had already started.

To understand why I was prepared, you have to understand my family’s ecosystem.

In nature, there are predators and prey.
In my family, there was Bianca —
and then there was me.

I learned that distinction when I was ten.

It was my birthday. I’d wanted an art set for months — a wooden case, colored pencils, something precious and quiet. When I opened it, something dangerous bloomed in my chest.

Hope.

Then Bianca screamed.

She collapsed onto the carpet, sobbing that it wasn’t fair, that she wanted it, that no one loved her. A performance refined over years of being rewarded for chaos.

My parents didn’t stop her.

My mother looked at me like I’d caused the problem by receiving something.
My father knelt beside me and said gently,
“You don’t want to be the reason your sister is upset, do you?”

I was ten.

I handed it to her.

That was the moment I learned a rule I never forgot:
In this family, my success was inconvenient — and my compliance was expected.

So I adapted.

I learned systems. Controls. Safeguards.
I learned how to smile while documenting everything.
I learned how to let people believe they were winning.

That dinner wasn’t an argument.

It was a test.

And they failed it the instant they thought they could steal from me in plain sight.

When I left that night, I didn’t slam doors.
I didn’t make threats.

I walked out calmly — already knowing that by morning, their phones would start ringing.

And for once, the consequences wouldn’t be something Bianca could cry her way out of.

At a recent “Board of Peace” event in Washington, D.C., Donald Trump offered a glowing assessment of his wife’s documentary and its supposed box-office dominance.

Here is the full quote:

“She has a very successful movie out right now, like number one. Can you believe this? Big movie star, and I always say it’s trouble, because I always say there’s not room in one family for two stars. I told her that we can’t have two stars in one family… The theaters are all packed. Women, especially, they go back, and they see it two or three times, four times.”

Let’s examine that calmly.

He describes a documentary about Melania Trump as “number one.” He claims theaters are “all packed.” He says women are returning to see it three and four times.

That is not how documentaries perform in measurable, verifiable box-office reality.

When a film is actually number one in the United States, the data is public. Industry outlets like Variety and box-office tracking services publish weekend totals, rankings, theater counts, and gross revenue. There is no ambiguity when something leads the national box office.

There is no credible reporting showing a Melania Trump documentary dominating nationwide charts or generating blockbuster-level repeat attendance. Documentaries can succeed — some even break out nationally — but when they do, the numbers are transparent. They don’t rely on vague descriptions of “packed theaters” and unnamed repeat viewers.

But the setting makes this even more revealing.

This statement was delivered at something called the “Board of Peace.” The name itself suggests global seriousness, coalition-building, and diplomatic weight. Yet look at who was not aligned or participating in any meaningful way.

Major democratic allies such as:
 • Germany
 • France
 • United Kingdom
 • Canada
 • Japan
 • Australia
 • New Zealand 

If you are announcing something called a “Board of Peace” and the world’s most stable democratic allies are not meaningfully present or aligned, that absence tells you more than any press release ever could.

Serious international coalitions are measured by participation, legitimacy, and shared commitment. Branding alone does not create credibility.

And that pattern mirrors the documentary claim.

Declare it “number one.”
Declare theaters “packed.”
Declare global leadership.

Then expect people not to ask for evidence.

This isn’t about disliking someone personally. It’s about the recurring substitution of measurable fact with grandiose narrative — whether the subject is box-office performance or global diplomacy.

So here’s the straightforward question:

Do you actually believe that a documentary dominating the national box office somehow escaped every major tracking outlet?
Do you believe a “Board of Peace” carries global weight when the most influential democratic nations aren’t clearly part of it?

If you do, then you’re not evaluating claims against evidence. You’re accepting spectacle in place of substance.

And that — more than any boast about stars or packed theaters — is the real issue.

HATEFUL AND ANGRY PREACHER.
One of the most damaging effects of a hateful and angry preacher is the fracturing of the community and the erosion of social empathy. When a leader uses their platform to preach hostility rather than compassion, the consequences often ripple out far beyond the walls of the church. Here are the primary ways this "toxic oratory" takes its toll:

1. The Normalization of Aggression
When a figure of spiritual authority validates anger, it gives the audience "moral permission" to act on their own prejudices.

 * Dehumanization: By labeling certain groups as "evil" or "other," the preacher makes it psychologically easier for followers to treat those people with cruelty.

 * Validation of Bias: Instead of being challenged to grow, the listener feels that their existing hatred is actually a "divine virtue."

2. Psychological Trauma & Spiritual Abuse
For those within the congregation, particularly the youth or those who don't fit the preacher's "ideal," the impact is deeply internal.

 * Fear-Based Faith: This creates a spiritual environment rooted in terror rather than peace. It can lead to "Religious Trauma Syndrome," where individuals suffer from chronic anxiety and a loss of self-worth.
 * Isolation: Members may feel forced to cut off friends or family members who don't subscribe to the preacher’s narrow views, leading to a profound sense of loneliness.
3. The "Cynicism Loop"
Perhaps the most widespread social effect is the damage done to the institution itself.

 * Loss of Credibility: When "faith" becomes synonymous with "fury" in the public eye, it alienates those who might otherwise seek community or spiritual guidance.

 * Societal Polarization: It turns faith into a political or social weapon, making it much harder for a diverse society to find common ground or work together on shared problems.

The "Peer" Take:  It’s a bit of a paradox, isn’t it? A preacher’s job is usually to offer "the good news," but an angry one sells a "bad news" product. It replaces a sense of belonging with a sense of "us vs. them," which is a much more addictive—and destructive—emotion.

Self-Injurious Behaviours (SIB)

Self-injurious behaviours are one of the most misunderstood — and frankly, quite traumatic — aspects of autism, especially in cases of moderate to profound support needs.

Often abbreviated as SIB, self-injurious behaviours are actions in which a person physically harms their own body, with common examples including:
Head banging
Hitting oneself
Biting oneself
Scratching skin until it breaks
Pulling hair
Excessive skin picking

In autism, these behaviours are most commonly seen during periods of extreme emotional dysregulation.

In my son's case, he forcefully hits himself on the head and joints (elbows, knees, wrists). In the most severe cases, he breaks large glass surfaces (windows, mirrors) and only stops — at this point displaying deep relief — once a deep cut (sometimes multiple) has been sustained and blood is furiously gushing out. That is the only time he will then calm down and allow me to touch him.

Other children bite themselves until they bleed. One of the more severe cases I have heard of was a young boy who used to bang his head against the wall so hard that he sustained head injuries, including blindness.

Why Do SIB Happen?

Self-injury is usually a nervous system event — not a character flaw.

Clinical research points to four primary drivers:

Overwhelm (Sensory or Emotional)

As we now know, the autistic nervous system processes the world differently (refer to the sensory processing topic).
When stimulation exceeds what the body can tolerate in that moment — sound, light, demand, confusion, etc. — the body may go into fight-or-flight, and self-injury can become a release valve.

In that moment, self-injury can:
Discharge unbearable tension
Interrupt internal chaos
Create a sensation that “grounds” the body

Other explanations suggest that, for some individuals, physical pain feels more manageable than invisible emotional pain.

Communication Breakdown
When language fails, the body speaks — this is often the case for non-speaking individuals who cannot express:
“This is too much.”
“I am scared.”
“I am confused.”
“Stop.”
In that moment, the body may escalate until it is heard.
The injury becomes the amplifier.

Anxiety and Loss of Control
In high-anxiety states, some autistic individuals experience internal pressure that builds rapidly. In those cases, self-injury can:
Restore a sense of control
Provide predictability in a chaotic moment
Act as a coping mechanism
It may not look logical — but neurologically, it often is.

Sensory Seeking
In some cases, self-injury is sensory-based, meaning the individual may be:
Under-stimulated
Seeking deep pressure
Trying to regulate through impact
This means the body is not trying to self- destruct — it is trying to make itself feel better.

What SIB Is Not
It's important to separate autism-related self-injury from other contexts.
In autistic dysregulation:
The act is often impulsive
It happens during overwhelm
It reduces once regulation returns
It is not rooted in self-hatred
As such, it is different from non-autistic self-harm that may be tied to depression, shame, or suicidal ideation.
Both require compassion, however, the causes are not always the same.

What Makes It Worse?
Certain responses can unintentionally escalate self-injury, such as:
Shouting
Threatening punishment
Restraining without calm containment
Shaming
Ignoring underlying triggers
When the nervous system is already on fire, confrontation adds fuel.

What Helps?
There is no single solution. But there are patterns that help.

Reduce Triggers
Track:  Time of day, environmental stressors, transitions and unmet needs
Patterns always exist.

Co-Regulation
Before self-regulation comes co-regulation — what you, as a parent or caregiver, can do to try and de-escalate the situation:
Calm presence, lowered voice, slow breathing and fewer words. 
The nervous system borrows safety from another nervous system.

Sensory Alternatives
Offer:  Deep pressure (weighted items, firm hugs if welcomed), safe objects to squeeze or hit, chewable items and cushions for impact. 

During this time, the goal is not suppression, but to offer or redirect the child toward safer regulation.

Anxiety Support

In cases where anxiety is chronic and severe, professional evaluation may be necessary. Therapy, environmental changes, and/or medical support may be helpful.

For the Parent
Watching your child hurt themselves can trigger panic, guilt, helplessness, and trauma. It can activate your own nervous system. And when two nervous systems are dysregulated at once, the cycle intensifies.

So, in moments of self-injurious behaviour, it is very important to remember:

The child is not being manipulative.
The child is not being naughty.
This is not bad behaviour.
This is communication.
The child is trying to regulate themselves.
They are actively trying to stop the internal turmoil — fighting to settle into their bodies and feel better.

Please share your child's self injurious behaviour and how you are managing or managed to redirect regulation.

This week, we are featuring Clement Wani Konga in our 𝐃𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐲 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐩𝐨𝐭𝐥𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 program, recognizing a leader whose journey reflects resilience, discipline, and principled public service.

Clement Wani Konga is a prominent leader from Mundari community, senior military officer, and former Governor of Central Equatoria State, whose public life spans liberation struggle, national military service, and civilian governance in South Sudan.

𝐄𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐄𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧

Clement Wani Konga was born around 1950 in Terekeka, Equatoria. He began his early education in Okaru in the early 1960s before proceeding to Uganda, where he completed his secondary education at Mvara Secondary School. His formative years unfolded alongside the rise of southern Sudan’s resistance movements, shaping his political awareness and leadership orientation from an early age.

𝐋𝐢𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐠𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐲 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐫

In 1969, Konga joined the Anyanya Movement during the first southern Sudanese civil war. After military training, he was commissioned as a lieutenant and actively participated in operations across Equatoria and the Lakes area of Bahr El Ghazal, contributing to efforts aimed at southern self-determination.

Following the Addis Ababa Agreement of 1972, he was integrated into the Sudanese national army. He rose steadily through the ranks, eventually attaining the rank of Major General. 
Alongside his military career, he held key administrative roles, including Commissioner of Terekeka, and later became a minister in the Coordinating Council of Southern States in 2003.

𝐆𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐨𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐥 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩

In 2004, Major General Konga was appointed Governor of Central Equatoria State, with his administration based in Juba. His appointment coincided with a notable improvement in security in the state capital, reflecting his command experience and emphasis on order and discipline. In July 2005, he was confirmed as caretaker governor by the late Dr. John Garang.

Konga was subsequently elected governor on the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement ticket in April 2010. His tenure prioritized the rule of law, inter-communal dialogue, and infrastructure development, including proposed power generation projects intended to support economic growth in Greater Yei. 
In August 2015, he was dismissed from office by President Salva Kiir Mayardit.

𝐋𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩

After leaving office, Clement Wani Konga remained active in public and community life. As Chairperson of the Mundari Community, he has continued to advocate for peace, reconciliation, and dialogue during periods of local and national tension, maintaining influence beyond formal government roles.

𝐋𝐞𝐠𝐚𝐜𝐲

Clement Wani Konga’s life reflects the complex transition of South Sudanese leadership from armed struggle to state governance. 
His legacy is defined by decades of military service, a central role in the administration of Central Equatoria State, and sustained engagement in community leadership and peacebuilding in South Sudan.

VIETNAM TODAY
A Return, A Reckoning
By Đặng Hiền
____________
I only began to breathe easier when the plane touched down in California.
Not because America is perfect.
But because I had just left a place that weighed heavily on my chest.
One month traveling through Ho Chi Minh City, Nha Trang, Đà Nẵng, and Hà Nội was enough to feel the pulse of a country growing fast—
yet growing like a child who has never been asked what it wants to become.
________________________________________
1. A NATION OF TOURISM AND UNCERTAIN WORK
From north to south, tourism appears to be the safest industry. Hotels multiply. Resorts stretch along the coastline. Every city wants to become a “must-see” destination.
Behind the sunset photos, however, lies a quieter truth: young people driving for ride-hailing platforms, juggling short-term gigs, surviving on fragmented income. Many hold degrees. Many have ambition. What they lack are stable pathways.
An economy that leans heavily on tourism resembles a crowded café without a real kitchen—busy, vibrant, but structurally fragile. Growth numbers may look impressive, yet depth and resilience remain uncertain.
Vietnam today has speed.
It is less clear whether it has direction.
________________________________________
2. THE ENVELOPE SOCIETY
“Envelopes” have become less of a secret and more of a ritual.
Journalists receive envelopes.
Judges receive envelopes.
Administrative procedures move smoothly—if accompanied by envelopes.
Nothing is spoken explicitly. Everything is understood.
The tragedy is not merely that corruption exists. The tragedy is its normalization. When wrongdoing becomes procedure, society slowly loses its sense of justice.
A system does not collapse because it lacks laws. It collapses when good laws are unevenly enforced.
________________________________________
3. EDUCATION AND MANUFACTURED REVERENCE
In families with financial means, children study eight to ten hours a day. Their schedules resemble those of corporate executives. Achievement is relentless.
Alongside this intensity runs another curriculum: reverence. Leaders are presented not simply as historical figures, but as near-sacred icons. History is often streamlined into a singular narrative. Complexity is softened; doubt is discouraged.
A society that does not teach children how to question may one day produce adults who no longer know how.
Meanwhile, social stratification grows sharper. Wealth purchases better schools, cleaner environments, greater protection. Those without wealth learn adaptation and acceptance.
Vietnam once criticized capitalism for inequality. Yet contemporary class distinctions often feel equally—if not more—visible in daily life.
________________________________________
4. LITERATURE AS ORNAMENT
Independent journalism and environmental advocacy are sometimes dismissed as naïve idealism.
Much official literature functions as ornamentation—polished language in service of stability rather than scrutiny. It decorates power instead of challenging it.
Meanwhile, environmental degradation is tangible. The air in major cities hangs thick. Rivers darken. Coastal ecosystems show strain.
Nature does not participate in propaganda. It records governance with ruthless honesty.
________________________________________
5. TRAFFIC AS METAPHOR
Few systems capture Vietnam’s paradox as vividly as its traffic.
Motorbikes swarm like a living hive.
Each rider negotiates survival in real time.
Formal order seems absent, yet an instinctive choreography emerges.
In that swarm, one is simultaneously vulnerable and dangerous.
The constant honking is more than noise—it is the heartbeat of urgency, impatience, improvisation. It is the sound of a society always in motion, rarely at rest.
Returning to California, the silence felt almost unreal. I had forgotten what a lower decibel of existence feels like.
________________________________________
6. THE PARADOX OF PARADISE
And yet there is Cam Ranh.
The sea remains luminous.
The sand remains soft.
Nha Trang – Cam Ranh can still rank among the most beautiful destinations in the world.
If one arrives purely as a tourist.
If one does not have to navigate the bureaucracy, the structural inequalities, the environmental compromises. If one sees only the surface.
Vietnam today resembles a carefully filtered photograph—radiant, saturated, appealing. Beneath the surface lies a far more complex negotiation between growth, governance, and identity.
________________________________________
7. LEAVING, WITHOUT INDIFFERENCE
This reflection is not a rejection of Vietnam. Nor is it a celebration of America. Every nation carries contradictions.
What unsettles me is the sense of trade-offs accumulating quietly:
Truth traded for convenience.
Accountability traded for stability.
Environmental health traded for short-term expansion.
Vietnam is undeniably rising.
The question is: toward what model of adulthood?
A country needs more than GDP.
It needs trust.
It needs more than resorts.
It needs transparent institutions.
It needs more than slogans.
It needs space for truth.
Perhaps I am overly sensitive.
Perhaps distance sharpens criticism.
But as long as someone still feels unease, still writes, still questions—
hope has not entirely vanished.
California Feb. 19, 2026

In today’s modern India, a widening gap has emerged between ‘Personal Liberty’ and ‘Family Responsibility’, shaking the very foundation of social structure. Increasingly, cases surface where children, upon turning 18, leave home due to relationships or personal choices and stand before authorities claiming, “We are in danger from our parents.” At the same time, a massive counter-narrative is gaining momentum across social media and public platforms. A tough question now echoes loudly: Does the 18 years of sacrifice made by parents carry no monetary value at all?

A deeper analysis of this moral crisis reveals a striking and controversial suggestion that is rapidly going viral. Many argue that young adults are legally free to live life on their own terms — the law grants them that right — but before leaving home, they should compensate their parents for 18 years of upbringing, school fees, medical bills, and daily expenses. Supporters of this idea see it as a response to what they describe as emotional abandonment, where parents are reduced to mere “service providers” once children achieve independence.

From a psychological perspective, this debate reflects a clash between duty and rights. A mother who sacrifices her own happiness to raise a child, and a father who postpones his needs to secure the child’s future, may feel deeply wounded when they are portrayed as adversaries. Experts emphasize that freedom does not mean freedom from responsibility. While many young people strongly assert their right to live independently, critics argue that gratitude as a value is gradually fading.

Legally, the matter is complex. Under Indian law, parents are obligated to provide for their children, but there is no formal legal “debt” that children owe in return for their upbringing. Laws such as the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act apply primarily when elderly parents require support later in life. There is no statutory provision allowing recovery of the financial “investment” made during the first 18 years. This legal gap is why some sections of society are now calling for what they describe as a moral contract rather than a legal one.

This evolving debate suggests that the generation gap is transforming into an emotional conflict. While many young adults describe their choices as an assertion of independence, others interpret the trend as a decline in cultural values. The core question is not whether an adult has the right to make personal decisions — that right is clear — but whether such decisions should come without acknowledgment of parental sacrifice.

This conversation is unlikely to fade anytime soon. It serves as a mirror to society, prompting reflection on what values are being passed to the next generation. Are we nurturing responsible individuals, or merely cultivating a culture centered solely on rights without equal emphasis on responsibility?

من يحكم جنوب السودان فعلياً؟ أمة تطالب بالشفافية
كلارا مارتن  | مقال رأي 

أثار مقطع مصوَّر حديث للرئيس سلفا كير خلال قمة إقليمية في أديس أبابا تساؤلات ملحّة بشأن القيادة والحكم في جنوب السودان.

وتُظهر التسجيلات المصوّرة الرئيس وهو يواجه صعوبة في المشي ويلقي خطاباً بدا متعثراً وغير واضح. وفي بلد يمرّ بانتخابات مؤجّلة، وأزمات اقتصادية، وتنفيذ هشّ لاتفاق السلام، وتحديات أمنية مستمرة، فإن الأمر يتجاوز كونه لحظة رمزية؛ بل يشكّل اختباراً لمتانة المؤسسات.

هذه ليست انتقادات شخصية، بل مسألة تتعلق بالمساءلة الوطنية.

فإذا كان الرئيس يمارس مهامه بكامل قدرته، فإن من حق الشعب الحصول على تطمينات واضحة. أما إذا كانت هناك تحديات صحية، فإن الاتفاق المُنشّط لحل النزاع في جمهورية جنوب السودان لعام 2018 (R-ARCSS) يوفر إطاراً دستورياً يضمن استمرارية القيادة.

لقد أرسى الاتفاق المُنشّط تقاسماً للسلطة وضمانات مؤسسية صُمِّمت لمنع هشاشة الحكم في أوقات عدم اليقين. وهذه الضمانات وُجدت لحماية الدولة، لا لحماية الأشخاص.

القيادة المقرّبة من الرئاسة

تشغل أدوت سلفا كير منصباً رفيعاً داخل المكتب الرئاسي. وفي وقت تتعرض فيه صورة الرئاسة لتحديات، فإن دورها يكتسب مسؤولية مضاعفة.

أين صوتها في حماية كرامة المنصب وسمعة الدولة؟
هل تقدّم النصح للرئيس، وتطمئن الرأي العام، أم تلتزم الصمت بينما تتزايد الشكوك بشأن القيادة؟

إن الروابط الأسرية بالسلطة لا ينبغي أن تحل محل المساءلة المؤسسية. فالرئاسة تمثل جمهورية جنوب السودان، لا أسرة بعينها.

نواب الرئيس الخمسة

أنشأ إطار السلام في جنوب السودان خمسة مناصب لنواب الرئيس لتقاسم السلطة التنفيذية وضمان الاستقرار.

وفي لحظة تُثار فيها تساؤلات حول قدرة الرئيس، يُفترض بهؤلاء المسؤولين أن يقدّموا تطمينات ويعزّزوا هياكل الحكم. غير أن صمتهم يثير تساؤلات جوهرية: هل يمارسون دورهم التنفيذي بفاعلية؟ هل هم مستعدون لتحمّل المسؤولية إذا اقتضت الحاجة؟ أم أن القرارات تُتخذ خلف أبواب مغلقة بطريقة تتجاوز مقتضيات المساءلة؟

لماذا تكتسب وضوح القيادة أهمية إقليمية؟

يقع جنوب السودان في قلب منطقة القرن الأفريقي. وأي ضعف في الحوكمة ينعكس على الأمن، وحركة اللاجئين، والتنسيق الإنساني، والدبلوماسية الإقليمية. يحتاج الشركاء الدوليون والإقليميون إلى الثقة في مؤسسات جوبا. إن مظاهر الغموض في السلطة التنفيذية تُضعف الثقة الداخلية والمصداقية الخارجية على حد سواء.

من حكم قائم على الأشخاص إلى مؤسسات قوية

يعتمد الاستقرار طويل الأمد في جنوب السودان على قوة المؤسسات لا على الأفراد. ويتطلب ذلك إصلاح وتعزيز منظومة الحكم عبر:
 • وضع إجراءات واضحة لانتقال السلطة
 • ضمان الشفافية بشأن الحالة الصحية للقادة أثناء توليهم المنصب
 • الحد من تركّز السلطة التنفيذية
 • الفصل بين النفوذ الأسري والمنصب الرسمي

إن الشفافية المؤسسية تعزّز الحكم الرشيد، بينما يضعفه الغموض. ويجب أن تخدم القيادة الوطن أولاً.

دعوة إلى الإصلاح

لا يمكن للجمهورية أن تواصل الاعتماد على الأشخاص بدلاً من المؤسسات. ينبغي أن تُحدِّد الضمانات الدستورية آليات واضحة لانتقال السلطة، وتقرّ شفافية إلزامية بشأن الحالة الصحية للقادة، وتحمي الصلاحيات التنفيذية من التركّز غير الرسمي. فالدستور، لا الأفراد، هو الذي ينبغي أن يصون الاستقرار وكرامة جنوب السودان.

ويبقى السؤال الجوهري قائماً: من يحكم جنوب السودان فعلياً اليوم — وبأي سلطة؟

إلى أن يُجاب عن هذا السؤال بشفافية، ستظل الثقة العامة والمصداقية الإقليمية عرضة للاهتزاز.

Founded in 2001 by Jakka Srinivasulu Reddy (JS Reddy), the IRCS Cancer Hospital, Nellore began as a modest cancer detection centre driven by a strong commitment to help patients lacking timely diagnosis and treatment. Through dedication, vision and sustained effort, it has grown into a comprehensive and trusted cancer care institution serving the region for over 25 years.

The hospital provides Medical Oncology, Gynaec Oncology, Radiation Oncology and Surgical Oncology services with 105 approved beds. Nearly 90% of patients receive treatment under the Dr. NTR Vaidya Seva Scheme, ensuring affordable and accessible care, especially for economically weaker sections.

Accredited with Entry-Level NABH certification, the hospital continues to upgrade its infrastructure and adopt advanced technologies while maintaining patient-centred, compassionate care.

Supported by philanthropists, medical professionals and donors, IRCS Cancer Hospital stands as a beacon of hope for thousands of families, delivering ethical, affordable and comprehensive cancer treatment with dignity and humanity.

نيروبي – عمق الحدث 

اتهم القائم بأعمال رئيس الحركة الشعبية لتحرير السودان – في المعارضة (SPLM-IO)، ناثانيال أويت بيرينو، حكومة الرئيس سلفا كير ميارديت بـ«تفكيك» الاتفاق المُنشّط لحل النزاع في جنوب السودان (R-ARCSS)، وبـ«إضعاف» الجهود الدبلوماسية الرامية إلى معالجة الخلافات السياسية.

وجاءت تصريحات أويت في منشور على صفحته الشخصية، في وقت تشهد فيه البلاد توترات سياسية وأمنية متزايدة، وسط نقاش محتدم حول مسار تنفيذ الاتفاق وترتيبات المرحلة الانتقالية.

مسار الدستور الفيدرالي محور الاتهامات

وقال أويت إن ما وصفه بإجراءات الحكومة يضع البلاد على مسار “الفناء والتفكك”، مشيراً إلى إنهاء/تعطيل عملية إعداد الدستور الفيدرالي. واعتبر أن هذا التطور يعيد إلى الأذهان تجربة اتفاقية أديس أبابا لعام 1972 وما انتهت إليه لاحقاً، وفق تعبيره.

تحذيرات من تصاعد سياسات الهوية وتبدّل «العقد الاجتماعي»

وحذّر القيادي المعارض من أن سياسات الحكومة—بحسب رؤيته—تعزز “سياسات الهوية” وتدفع نحو إعادة صياغة “العقد الاجتماعي” في جنوب السودان، مؤكداً أن استمرار هذا النهج من شأنه رفع مستوى الاحتقان وتعميق دائرة الصراع، لا سيما في ظل ما وصفه بتواصل سياسات “التهميش والإقصاء” وتداعياتها على الاستقرار.

خلفية سياسية متوترة

وتأتي هذه التصريحات بينما تواصل الحركة الشعبية–المعارضة انتقاد أداء الحكومة، متهمةً إياها بالتلاعب ببنود اتفاق السلام وإضعاف دور المعارضة داخل مؤسسات الفترة الانتقالية. وفي المقابل، تتزايد التحذيرات المحلية والدولية بشأن استمرار العنف وتدهور أوضاع الحقوق والحريات في البلاد.

सीधी में हॉस्पिटल भवन निर्माण हेतु भूमिपूजन कार्यक्रम हुआ सम्पन्न .....................................................। 

सीधी जिले के जमोड़ी सेगरान में रेडक्रॉस सोसाइटी, सीधी शाखा द्वारा रेडक्रॉस हॉस्पिटल भवन निर्माण हेतु भूमिपूजन कार्यक्रम आयोजित किया गया। कार्यक्रम में सीधी सांसद डॉ. राजेश मिश्र मुख्य अतिथि के रूप में शामिल हुए। इस अवसर पर उन्होंने कहा कि क्षेत्र में स्वास्थ्य सुविधाओं का विस्तार जनहित की दृष्टि से अत्यंत आवश्यक है और रेडक्रॉस हॉस्पिटल का निर्माण आमजन को बेहतर एवं सुलभ चिकित्सा सुविधा उपलब्ध कराने की दिशा में महत्वपूर्ण पहल है।

कार्यक्रम की अध्यक्षता इंडियन रेड क्रॉस सोसाइटी मध्य प्रदेश के अध्यक्ष एवं सेवानिवृत्त आईएएस अधिकारी डॉ. श्याम सिंह कुमरे ने की, वहीं वरिष्ठ समाजसेवी श्रीमती मंजू सिंह सेंगर विशेष रूप से उपस्थित रहीं।

जानकारी के अनुसार रेडक्रॉस हॉस्पिटल का निर्माण लोक निर्माण विभाग (PWD) के माध्यम से कराया जा रहा है। इस परियोजना की टेंडर राशि 227.29 लाख रुपये तथा प्रशासनिक स्वीकृति 268.20 लाख रुपये की है। अस्पताल का निर्माण एनटीपीसी के सीएसआर मद से किया जा रहा है। इस अस्पताल में सस्ती चिकित्सा सुविधाओं के साथ ब्लड बैंक की व्यवस्था तथा जरूरतमंदों के लिए कई विशेष सेवाओं में निःशुल्क उपचार की सुविधा उपलब्ध कराई जाएगी।

सांसद डॉ. राजेश मिश्र ने रेडक्रॉस सोसाइटी की पूरी टीम को इस जनहितकारी पहल के लिए बधाई देते हुए विश्वास जताया कि अस्पताल निर्माण से क्षेत्रवासियों को समय पर उपचार की सुविधा मिलेगी और स्वास्थ्य सेवाएं और अधिक सुदृढ़ होंगी। कार्यक्रम में बड़ी संख्या में स्थानीय नागरिक एवं गणमान्यजन उपस्थित रहे।

Sakeena Itoo advocates collective efforts to combat drug abuse across J&K
Minister for Health and Medical Education Sakeena Itoo today emphasized the crucial and collective role of legislators, senior citizens, intellectuals, community members and religious leaders in combating the menace of drug abuse across Jammu and Kashmir.
The Minister said this while replying in the House today to a clubbed question of Legislators Pirzada Farooq Ahmad Shah, Surjeet Singh Slathia, Ali Mohammad Sagar (raised by Legislator Mubarik Gul on his behalf) and Ghulam Mohi Ud Din Mir on the issues relating to drug Abuse.
She added that the department has taken various steps like mandatory CCTV installation and computerized billing of medical shops training counselors at village level as well as CCTV installation in and around schools and colleges. She also said that teachers are being trained in schools to counsel students showing some early signs of drug addiction.
The Minister informed the House that Drug De-addiction services are being strengthened across the Union Territory under the Health and Medical Education Department and the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyan. She added that Addiction Treatment Facilities (ATFs) are functional in all the districts of Kashmir Division and nine districts of Jammu Division, with dedicated IPD beds and OPD services available to ensure comprehensive treatment and rehabilitation.
The Health Minister said that in Kashmir Division ATFs are functional in SKIMS, GMC Bemina Srinagar, GMC Anantnag, GMC Baramulla, GMC Handwara, District Hospital Kulgam, District Hospital Shopian, District Hospital Pulwama, District Hospital Budgam, District Hospital Ganderbal and District Hospital Bandipora. In Jammu division, ATFs are functional in GMC Doda, GMC Jammu, GMC Kathua, GMC AH Rajouri, GMC AH Udhampur, District Hospital Kishtwar, District Hospital Poonch, District Hospital Ramban, District Hospital Reasi and DH Samba (functional on OPD Basis), she added.
The Minister said that OPD services are being ensured in all the districts, IPD services in all the GMCs besides the psychiatrists are also available. Efforts are underway to bolster de-addiction counselling and treatment services, particularly in rural and vulnerable areas, by strengthening OPD-based counselling, improving access to essential medicines, and enhancing follow-up and outreach programmes, she added.
“Health and Medical Education Department is regularly organizing awareness campaigns through field functionaries as well as via print media, encouraging the drug abuse victims to seek treatment and counselling to get rid of this evil addiction”, she said.
The Minister said that 32517 patients have been registered in ATFs in J&K, with 16759 in Kashmir division and 15758 in Jammu division. She added that there is no proposal to establish Drug De-addiction and Rehabilitation Centre in Pulwama district of Kashmir division and Samba district of Jammu division, saying that a Drug De-Addiction and Rehabilitation Centre at Village Bajwani, Tral district Pulwama is functional and catering to patients from across the district.
The Health Minister said that an addiction treatment facility has been established at District Hospital Samba since February 2024 sponsored by NDDTC (AIIMS New Delhi) under MoSJE. “The centre is staffed with a psychiatrist and other trained staff to provide treatment and rehabilitation services”, she said. She added that the centre is presently working on OPD basis and providing services like OPD by Psychiatric, counseling, Addiction Treatment Facility and de-addiction medicines are also provided free of cost to the patients.

Health & Wellness Friday

Let me say something that might feel uncomfortable…

I know keeping the grudge makes sense.
I know hating the person who hurt you feels justified.
I know replaying what they did feels like protection.

But listen to me for a moment — from a health and wellness perspective.

Your body does not know the difference between a current threat and a remembered one.

Every time you rehearse the hurt, your nervous system activates as if it’s happening again. Your heart rate shifts. Cortisol rises. Muscles tighten. Digestion slows. Inflammation increases. Sleep becomes fragmented.

You think you’re holding a grudge…

But your body is holding a stress response.

And the nervous system was never designed to stay activated long-term. It was designed to mobilize… and then settle.

When we don’t settle, it shows up as:
 • Chronic fatigue
 • Gut issues
 • Headaches and muscle tension
 • Hormonal imbalance
 • Anxiety that “comes out of nowhere”
 • Emotional reactivity in unrelated situations

This is not about excusing what happened.
This is not about pretending it didn’t hurt.
This is not about bypassing accountability.

This is about biology.

Grudges feel like strength.
But physiologically, they are sustained survival mode.

From a trauma-healing lens, unresolved resentment keeps the nervous system in hypervigilance.
From a shadow-work lens, hatred often protects unprocessed grief.
From an emotional fitness lens, the body carries what the mouth refuses to release.

Forgiveness is not spiritual politeness.

It is nervous system regulation.

It is saying:
“I will not allow your behavior to live inside my body.”

Healing does not mean reconciliation.
It does not mean access.
It does not mean trust.

It means your internal environment returns to safety.

And here’s the deeper truth:

You don’t get sick from what happened.
You get sick from what stays activated.

So today, ask yourself gently:

What am I still reliving?
What is my body still bracing against?
What would it feel like to lay it down — not for them, but for me?

Health is not only about food and exercise.

Health is about what you refuse to carry any longer.

Happy Health & Wellness Friday. 💛

Who Really Governs South Sudan? A Nation Demands Transparency
 
By: Clara Martin 

Recent footage of Salva Kiir during a regional summit in Addis Ababa has sparked urgent questions about leadership and governance in South Sudan.

Videos show the president struggling to walk and delivering a speech that appeared difficult and unclear. In a country dealing with postponed elections, economic difficulties, fragile peace implementation, and security challenges, this is more than a symbolic moment — it is a test of institutional strength.

This is not personal criticism. It is about national accountability.

If the president is fully capable of governing, the public deserves clear reassurance. If there are health challenges, the 2018 Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in the Republic of South Sudan (R-ARCSS) provides a constitutional framework to ensure leadership continuity.
Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in the Republic of South Sudan established power-sharing and institutional safeguards designed to prevent governance fragility during uncertainty. These safeguards exist to protect the nation — not personalities.

Leadership Close to the Presidency

Adut Salva Kiir holds a senior position within the presidential office. At a time when the presidency’s public image is challenged, her role carries responsibility.

Where is her voice in protecting the dignity of the office and the country?
Is she advising the president, reassuring the public, or remaining silent while doubts about leadership grow?

Family ties to power must not replace institutional accountability. The presidency represents the Republic of South Sudan, not a household.

The Five Vice Presidents

South Sudan’s peace framework created five vice presidents to share executive authority and ensure stability.

At a moment when questions about the president’s capacity arise, these officeholders should provide reassurance and uphold governance structures. Their silence raises critical questions: Are they actively governing? Are they prepared to assume responsibility if needed? Or are decisions being made behind closed doors in ways that bypass accountability?

Why Leadership Clarity Matters Regionally

South Sudan sits at the heart of the Horn of Africa. Weak governance affects security, refugees, humanitarian coordination, and regional diplomacy. International and regional partners need confidence in Juba’s institutions. Visibility of executive uncertainty undermines both domestic trust and international credibility.

From Personality-Centered Rule to Institutional Strength

South Sudan’s long-term stability depends on institutions, not personalities. The country must reform and strengthen governance by:
 • Establishing clear succession procedures
 • Ensuring transparency regarding the health of sitting leaders
 • Limiting concentration of executive power
 • Separating family influence from formal office

Institutional transparency strengthens governance. Secrecy weakens it. Leadership must serve the nation first.

A Call for Reform

The Republic cannot continue to rely on personalities over institutions. Constitutional safeguards must clearly define succession, provide mandatory transparency on health, and protect executive powers from informal concentration. The Constitution, not individuals, must safeguard stability and the dignity of South Sudan.

The fundamental question remains: Who is truly governing South Sudan today — and under what authority?

Until this question is answered transparently, public confidence and regional trust will remain at risk.

Family Political Views: Despite his parents supporting Spanish rule, Guerrero was strongly influenced by his uncle, Diego Guerrero, a member of the Spanish militia who held, or led him toward, independentist ideas.

MORAL CONSISTENCY, HISTORICAL MEMORY AND THE QUESTION OF JUSTICE IN SOUTH SUDAN: A RESPONSE TO DR. SUNDAY DE JOHN WITH Sixty 4 Tribes Press Watchdog Press, Hon. Bol Joseph Agau Adhil Emmanuel Sunday de John Gai Mayen Luk Cde Gai Nyadeang Bol Agau Daniel Chol Mading

BY JUOL NHOMNGEK DANIEL

In recent days, Dr. Emmanuel Sunday de John, Chairman of the South Sudan United Front-Progressive (SSUF-P), published an opinion article titled “Nigeria is wrong on South Sudan, and the continent should say so.” The article criticizes Nigeria’s diplomatic call for the unconditional release of South Sudan’s detained First Vice President, Riek Machar, arguing that such a demand rewards rebellion and undermines state sovereignty. While the piece attempts to frame itself as a principled defense of African stability, it raises deeper questions about moral consistency, historical memory, and the ethical obligations of professionals who engage in public discourse.

Historical Irony and Selective Memory

The central claim advanced by Dr. Sunday de John, that rebellion must never be rewarded, reveals a striking historical irony. South Sudan itself emerged from a prolonged armed struggle led by the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement (SPLM), under the leadership of John Garang. The independence of South Sudan in 2011 was not a diplomatic gift; it was the culmination of decades of resistance against systemic marginalization. To argue today that any armed movement must automatically be delegitimized ignores the historical foundations upon which the South Sudanese state stands. It also overlooks the reality that many contemporary African governments, including those in the Horn of Africa, owe their legitimacy to liberation movements that were once labelled insurgent or rebellious. This is not to romanticize armed struggle, but to highlight that political legitimacy is historically contingent. Rebellion, in itself, is neither inherently virtuous nor inherently criminal. It must be assessed in the context of justice, representation, and the political environment in which it arises.

Diplomatic Recognition and International Practice

Dr. Sunday de John’s critique also appears to misunderstand the nature of international diplomacy. The recognition of political actors, whether governments or armed movements, is governed not by rigid legal standards but by political discretion. States operate under doctrines such as international comity and sovereign freedom in foreign policy. For example, Nigeria’s call for dialogue and release does not constitute recognition of rebellion. Rather, it reflects the pragmatic approach commonly adopted in conflict resolution across the continent. From West Africa to the Horn, mediation often requires engaging armed actors in order to prevent escalation and protect civilians. This approach is not unique to Nigeria or to the current government under Bola Tinubu. It has been applied in conflicts in Liberia, Sierra Leone, Sudan, and elsewhere. Diplomacy seeks to stop violence before accountability mechanisms can function effectively. In this regard, Nigeria’s position reflects a peace-first strategy, not an endorsement of armed confrontation.

The Question of Moral Consistency

Perhaps the most troubling dimension of Dr. Sunday de John’s intervention is the inconsistency between his current argument and his previous public positions. In earlier analyses, he characterized the legal proceedings against Dr. Riek Machar as politically motivated and highlighted serious procedural flaws in the charges filed. He warned that inaccuracies in the indictment undermined judicial credibility and risked national embarrassment.
Today, however, he appears to frame the same process as a legitimate criminal proceeding that must run its course without external interference. Such a shift invites legitimate scrutiny. Intellectual integrity demands that public commentators maintain coherence or explain the basis for changing their views. Without this, analysis risks becoming political opportunism rather than principled reasoning. Consistency is not stubbornness; it is accountability. When positions change, transparency is necessary to maintain public trust.

Professional Ethics and Public Responsibility

Dr. Sunday de John occupies a unique space as a medical doctor, journalist, and political actor. Each of these professions is grounded in ethical principles that converge around integrity, truthfulness, and public trust. Physicians are bound by non-maleficence, the duty to do no harm. Journalists are bound by accuracy and independence. Politicians, ideally, are bound by accountability and service to the public. The intersection of these roles places an even greater burden on ethical consistency. When a public figure moves between professions while advancing shifting political narratives, the credibility of all three domains may be compromised. The public begins to question whether the guiding motivation is truth or expediency. This concern is not merely personal. In fragile states such as South Sudan, public trust in institutions is already low. When prominent figures appear inconsistent, it deepens cynicism and weakens confidence in governance, justice, and national dialogue.

The SPLM-IO and the Question of Legitimacy

The Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-In Opposition (SPLM-IO) cannot simply be dismissed as a terrorist organization. It is a political movement that signed the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement (R-ARCSS), a document recognized regionally and internationally. Its participation in government institutions was intended to stabilize the country and prevent a return to war.
Whether one agrees with its methods or not, the SPLM-IO remains a political actor whose grievances must be addressed through dialogue. Labeling it purely in criminal terms risks collapsing the fragile peace framework and returning the country to full-scale conflict.
History shows that sustainable peace rarely emerges from exclusion. It emerges from negotiated settlements that integrate political, legal, and security concerns.

Nigeria’s Role and African Solidarity

Nigeria remains one of Africa’s most influential diplomatic actors. Its engagement in South Sudan should be welcomed rather than dismissed. Constructive diplomacy, when balanced, can help stabilize fragile states and prevent regional spillovers. African solidarity must not be reduced to defending governments or opposition movements uncritically. Instead, it should promote accountability on all sides, ceasefires, and credible political processes. A balanced approach would encourage both the government in Juba and the opposition to recommit to dialogue and electoral preparations.

Conclusion: Beyond Opportunism Toward Principle

The debate sparked by Dr. Sunday de John’s article is valuable because it exposes deeper tensions within South Sudanese political discourse. However, it also demonstrates the danger of selective reasoning and moral inconsistency. South Sudan does not need polarizing rhetoric that delegitimizes dialogue or oversimplifies complex conflicts. It needs principled leadership grounded in historical awareness, ethical integrity, and strategic realism.

The country’s future depends not on who wins the argument today, but on whether its leaders, government, opposition, and commentators alike, can rise above opportunism and work toward a sustainable political settlement. True patriotism is not measured by loyalty to power or rebellion. It is measured by commitment to justice, peace, and the dignity of the South Sudanese people.

The writer, Juol Nhomngek Daniel, is a lawyer, politician, lecturer, and member of the SPLM-IO. His area of interest is constitutional, administrative, and human rights law. He can be reached via email: nhomngekjuol@gmail.com.

Today we have the second day of Ramadan, the fasting month, and I went to the shelter for the first time in Ramadan. We had desperately tried to take all the possible measures to free the dogs and the shelter grounds of the bloody ticks, and we made a huge effort, to finish it before start of Ramadan. So, today, I was checking out the result of our fight. It was a beautiful day with Egypt's signature blue sky. The workers had decorated the shelter entrance with streamers of glittering coloured paper, it looked lovely, the glittering strips reflecting the sunlight and rustling in the soft  breeze. The dogs were completely relaxed, resting peacefully, and not bothered by the terrible blood suckers any more. I examined the grounds, the sand, the walls of the buildings, the sun shades, the wooden huts, all the places, which had been crawling from ticks before. I stood barefoot in the sand of the big playground, where before, I would have collected countless tick bites, and nothing happened. I brushed dead ticks out of the fur of many dogs, and only rarely picked a tick, which was still active but already dying, discovered very, very few intact ticks. I am not kidding myself: I don't know, how long this positive status will hold, and we will be super watchful for any tick development. But for the time being, and, hopefully, for the month of Ramadan, we have a "cease fire" in our fight against the disgusting pests. Special thanks and respect is owed to Waleed, our head worker, and his whole team, who were meeting this huge challenge in addition to their already strenuous routine work. We wish a happy and peaceful Ramadan to everybody, and to all of Egypt's animals.

CHAIRMAN’S ORDER NO.01/2025 FOR THE REMOVAL AND DISMISSAL OF MR. HUSSEIN ABDELBAGI AKOL FROM THE SOUTH SUDAN PATRIOTIC MOVEMENT (SSPM)

Title and Commencement: -

This Order shall be cited as Chairman’s Order No.01/2025 for the removal and dismissal of Mr. Hussein Abdelbagi Akol, the suspended acting Deputy Chairman of the South Sudan Patriotic Movement. It shall come into force on the date of its signature by the Chairman.

The Order: -

WHEREAS, the South Sudan Patriotic Movement (SSPM) is governed by its Constitution, which upholds discipline, integrity, and adherence to democratic principles among its members;

WHEREAS, Article 38 (i, ii, viii, x, xi, and xv) of the SSPM Constitution mandates all members to abide by party rules and procedures, and Article 39 (iv, vi, and vi) prohibits acts that undermine the party’s unity, integrity, and objectives;

Signed

Shalat Tahajud Lagi Setelah Shalat Tarawih
Muhammad Abduh Tuasikal, MSc  Follow on XSend an emailJune 19, 201510 366,296 4 minutes read
Apakah kita boleh mengerjakan shalat tahajud lagi padahal sudah mengerjakan shalat tarawih yang ditutup dengan witir?

Jawabannya dibolehkan.

Ketahuilah bahwa shalat tahajud merupakan bagian dari shalat malam yang di mana shalat tahajud dikerjakan setelah bangun tidur. Demikian pendapat Imam Nawawi dalam Syarh Al-Muhaddzab. Oleh karenanya tidaklah bertentangan antara niat shalat malam dan shalat tahajud. Siapa yang mengerjakan shalat malam setelah bangun tidur, ia disebut sebagai orang yang bertahajud dan shalatnya dianggap pula sebagai shalat malam.

Kalau seseorang sudah mengerjakan shalat tarawih dan ditutup witir, maka ia boleh menambah shalat tahajud lagi di malam harinya dengan beberapa tinjauan sebagai berikut:

1- Perintah mengerjakan shalat malam bersama imam hingga imam selesai

Dari Abu Dzar radhiyallahu ‘anhu, ia berkata bahwa Rasulullah shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam bersabda,

إِنَّهُ مَنْ قَامَ مَعَ الإِمَامِ حَتَّى يَنْصَرِفَ كُتِبَ لَهُ قِيَامُ لَيْلَةٍ

“Sesungguhnya siapa saja yang shalat bersama imam hingga imam itu selesai, maka ia dicatat telah mengerjakan shalat semalam suntuk (semalam penuh).” (HR. Tirmidzi no. 806. Abu Isa Tirmidzi mengatakan bahwa hadits ini hasan shahih)

Dalam riwayat lain dalam Musnad Imam Ahmad, disebutkan dari Abu Dzar, Rasulullah shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam bersabda,

إِنَّ الرَّجُلَ إِذَا قَامَ مَعَ الإِمَامِ حَتَّى يَنْصَرِفَ حُسِبَ لَهُ بَقِيَّةُ لَيْلَتِهِ

“Sesungguhnya jika seseorang shalat bersama imam hingga imam selesai, maka ia dihitung mendapatkan pahala shalat di sisa malamnya.” (HR. Ahmad 5: 163. Syaikh Syu’aib Al-Arnauth menyatakan bahwa sanad hadits ini shahih sesuai syarat Muslim)

Kalau seseorang keluar dari shalat tarawih karena ingin menambah shalat tahajud dan witirnya di malam hari, maka ia tidak mendapatkan pahala shalat semalam suntuk. Walaupun dari sisi kesahan tetaplah sah.

2- Masih boleh menambah shalat malam setelah tarawih karena jumlah raka’at shalat malam tidak ada batasannya.

Ibnu ‘Abdil Barr mengatakan,

فَلاَ خِلاَفَ بَيْنَ المسْلِمِيْنَ أَنَّ صَلاَةَ اللَّيْلِ لَيْسَ فِيْهَا حَدٌّ مَحْدُوْدٌ وَأَنَّهَا نَافِلَةٌ وَفِعْلٌ خَيْرٌ وَعَمَلٌ بِرٌّ فَمَنْ شَاءَ اِسْتَقَلَّ وَمَنْ شَاءَ اِسْتَكْثَرَ

“Tidak ada khilaf di antara kaum muslimin bahwa shalat malam tidak ada batasan raka’atnya. Shalat malam adalah shalat nafilah (shalat sunnah) dan termasuk amalan kebaikan. Seseorang boleh mengerjakan dengan jumlah raka’at yang sedikit atau pun banyak.”(At-Tamhid, Ibnu ‘Abdil Barr, 21: 69-70, Wizaroh Umum Al Awqof, 1387 dan Al-Istidzkar, Ibnu ‘Abdil Barr, 2: 98, Dar Al-Kutub Al ‘Ilmiyyah, 1421 H)

Adapun dalil yang menunjukkan bahwa shalat malam tidak dibatasi jumlah raka’atnya, yaitu ketika Nabi shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam ditanya mengenai shalat malam, beliau menjawab,

صَلاَةُ اللَّيْلِ مَثْنَى مَثْنَى ، فَإِذَا خَشِىَ أَحَدُكُمُ الصُّبْحَ صَلَّى رَكْعَةً وَاحِدَةً ، تُوتِرُ لَهُ مَا قَدْ صَلَّى

“Shalat malam itu dua raka’at salam, dua raka’at salam. Jika salah seorang di antara kalian takut masuk waktu shubuh, maka kerjakanlah satu raka’at. Dengan itu berarti kalian menutup shalat tadi dengan witir.” (HR. Bukhari no. 990 dan Muslim no. 749, dari Ibnu ‘Umar). Padahal ini dalam konteks pertanyaan. Seandainya shalat malam itu ada batasannya, tentu Nabi shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam akan menjelaskannya.

3- Kita memang diperintah menutup shalat malam dengan shalat witir sebagaimana disebutkan dalam hadits dari Ibnu ‘Umar, Nabi shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam bersabda,

اجْعَلُوا آخِرَ صَلاَتِكُمْ بِاللَّيْلِ وِتْرًا

“Jadikanlah akhir shalat kalian di malam hari adalah shalat witir.” (HR. Bukhari no. 998 dan Muslim no. 751).

Pengertian menutup shalat malam dengan shalat witir, hukumnya adalah sunnah, bukan wajib. Sehingga setelah shalat witir masih boleh menambah lagi shalat sunnah. Alasannya adalah praktik Nabi shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam yang sesudah shalat witir masih menambah lagi dengan dua raka’at yang lain.

‘Aisyah menceritakan mengenai shalat malam Nabi shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam,

كَانَ يُصَلِّى ثَلاَثَ عَشْرَةَ رَكْعَةً يُصَلِّى ثَمَانَ رَكَعَاتٍ ثُمَّ يُوتِرُ ثُمَّ يُصَلِّى رَكْعَتَيْنِ وَهُوَ جَالِسٌ فَإِذَا أَرَادَ أَنْ يَرْكَعَ قَامَ فَرَكَعَ ثُمَّ يُصَلِّى رَكْعَتَيْنِ بَيْنَ النِّدَاءِ وَالإِقَامَةِ مِنْ صَلاَةِ الصُّبْحِ.

“Nabi shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam biasa melaksanakan shalat 13 raka’at (dalam semalam). Beliau melaksanakan shalat 8 raka’at kemudian beliau berwitir (dengan 1 raka’at). Kemudian setelah berwitir, beliau melaksanakan shalat dua raka’at sambil duduk. Jika ingin melakukan ruku’, beliau berdiri dari ruku’nya dan beliau membungkukkan badan untuk ruku’. Setelah itu di antara waktu adzan shubuh dan iqomahnya, beliau melakukan shalat dua raka’at.” (HR. Muslim no. 738)

Ibnul Qayyim rahimahullah menjelaskan, “Dua raka’at setelah witir itu tanda bahwa masih bolehnya dua raka’at setelah witir dan jika seseorang telah mengerjakan shalat witir bukan berarti tidak boleh lagi mengerjakan shalat sunnah sesudahnya. Adapun hadits di atas “Jadikanlah akhir shalat kalian di malam hari adalah shalat witir“, yang dimaksud menjadikan shalat witir sebagai penutup shalat malam hanyalah sunnah (bukan wajib). Artinya, dua raka’at sesudah witir masih boleh dikerjakan.” (Zaad Al-Ma’ad, 1: 322-323). Lihat penjelasan: Dua Raka’at Sesudah Shalat Witir.

Yang jelas bagi yang sudah melaksanakan tarawih lalu menutupnya dengan witir tidak lagi melakukan witir yang kedua setelah melakukan shalat tahajud di malam hari. Dari Thalq bin ‘Ali, ia mendengar Rasulullah shallallahu ‘alaihi wa sallam bersabda,

لاَ وِتْرَانِ فِى لَيْلَةٍ

“Tidak boleh ada dua witir dalam satu malam.” (HR. Tirmidzi no. 470, Abu Daud no. 1439, An Nasa-i no. 1679. Syaikh Al Albani mengatakan bahwa hadits ini shahih)

Kesimpulan, boleh melaksanakan shalat tahajud walaupun sudah mengerjakan shalat tarawih dan ditutup dengan witir. Namun di malam hari ketika melakukan shalat tahajud tidak lagi ditutup dengan witir. Jumlah raka’at shalat tahajud yang dilakukan bebas, tidak dibatasi jumlah raka’atnya.

Baca artikel lain di web ini: Setelah Shalat Witir, Bolehkah Shalat Sunnah Lagi?

Semoga bermanfaat. Wallahu waliyyut taufiq.

—

Last week, CENSCOPE, alongside other Mine Action partners, participated in a two-day workshop organized by UNMAS to strengthen community safety and reduce the risks posed by explosive ordnance across the BAY States.

The workshop reviewed findings from the 2025 Knowledge, Attitudes, Practices, and Behaviour (KAPB) survey to assess Mine Action interventions and supported the development of an annual work plan to enhance responses. 
Key discussions also focused on mainstreaming Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE) into broader humanitarian programming, improving coordination across sectors, and reviewing IEC materials to better address the specific vulnerabilities of at-risk groups.

On 29 November 1993, four months after APLA fighters stormed St James Church in Cape Town with grenades and automatic weapons, a man named Khallid Abdul Muhammad stood in front of roughly a hundred and forty students at Kean College in New Jersey and delivered a three-hour speech that would be condemned by both chambers of the United States Congress. In that speech, broadcast nationally and transcribed in full, Muhammad turned to the subject of South Africa and said this:

"We give them 24 hours in South Africa to get out of town by sundown. I say, if they don't get out of town, we kill the men, we kill the women, we kill the children, we kill the babies, we kill the blind, we kill the cripple, we kill the crazy, we kill the faggots, we kill the lesbians, I say god dammit we kill them all...Why kill the women in South Africa? I say kill the women because the women are the military manufacturing center. And every nine months they lay down on their backs and reinforcement rolls out from between their legs, so shut down the military manufacturing center by killing the white woman...Why kill the older crackers? The old crippled crackers in South Africa. How in the hell you think they got old? They got old oppressing and killing black people" 

 (Khallid Abdul Muhammad, Kean College, 29 November 1993)

https://www.rhodesia.nl/mission.jpg

The United States Senate voted 97 to 0 to censure the speech. The House of Representatives passed its own resolution condemning it as outrageous hatemongering of the most vicious and vile kind. Louis Farrakhan, leader of the Nation of Islam, eventually repudiated the speech's manner but not, as he put it, its truths.
Consider the timing. Khallid Muhammad delivered this call for the extermination of white South Africans in November 1993. Four months earlier, in July, APLA operatives had murdered eleven people at St James Church. That same year, APLA's commander Sabelo Phama had declared the Year of the Great Storm. On New Year's Eve 1993, just weeks after Muhammad's speech, APLA fighters used the same weapons from St James to kill four more people at the Heidelberg Tavern in Cape Town. The language on the podium at Kean College and the violence on the ground in South Africa were not coincidences. They were expressions of the same ideology, spoken in different accents, on different continents, in the same calendar year.

This is the story of the thread. The ideological thread that connects a Pentecostal mission in the Vumba mountains of Rhodesia to a church in Kenilworth, a college auditorium in New Jersey, a kosher market in Jersey City, and a real estate empire in Los Angeles. It is a thread that has been documented, named, and traced by scholars, journalists, and federal investigators, yet never drawn in a single line for the public to see. That is what this second instalment attempts to do.

Khallid Abdul Muhammad was not a fringe figure. He was, at the time of the Kean College speech, the national spokesman for the Nation of Islam, the oldest black nationalist organisation in the United States. He had been appointed to that role by Louis Farrakhan himself. He addressed audiences at more than a hundred universities across America, Africa, and Europe. He appeared on albums by Ice Cube and Public Enemy. He was, as the Chicago Tribune described him, the hottest commodity on the African-American lecture circuit.

After Farrakhan demoted him from the Nation of Islam, Muhammad did not disappear. He became the national chairman of the New Black Panther Party for Self-Defence, an organisation the Anti-Defamation League and the Southern Poverty Law Center both classify as a hate group. The NBPP's radio programming continued to play recordings of Muhammad's Kean College speech as its opening segment years after his death in 2001. His call to kill white men, women, babies, the blind, the crippled, and then dig them up and kill them again was not an embarrassment to the organisation. It was liturgy.
And notice where Muhammad's eliminationist fantasy was directed: South Africa. Not America. Not Europe. South Africa. The same country where APLA was carrying out precisely the kind of racial warfare Muhammad was calling for. The same country whose Pan Africanist Congress would, three years later, host Louis Farrakhan's visit to Johannesburg.

In January 1996, Louis Farrakhan arrived in South Africa as part of a twenty-three-nation tour of Africa and the Middle East that included stops in Libya, Iran, Nigeria, and Sudan, several of which were on the US State Department's list of state sponsors of terrorism. The Washington Post reported that his three-day visit to South Africa was hosted by the Pan Africanist Congress. Not the ANC. The PAC. The same organisation whose military wing had massacred churchgoers at St James, hacked families to death at Bashee River, and declared that there was no role in the new South Africa for any one of the race that invented apartheid.

Farrakhan met President Nelson Mandela at the presidential residence in Johannesburg's Houghton district, a meeting that Mandela publicly insisted did not signify an embrace of Farrakhan's views. Fair enough. Mandela met with many people. But the PAC's decision to serve as Farrakhan's host was not diplomatic courtesy. It was ideological kinship. The PAC's founding principle, Africa for the Africans, mirrored the Nation of Islam's core doctrine of racial separation. Both organisations rejected integration. Both framed their struggle in terms of land, blood, and spiritual destiny. And both, by the mid-1990s, had produced operatives who had killed people in the name of that vision.

Two years later, in January 1998, Farrakhan returned to South Africa. This time he was received by Winnie Madikizela-Mandela at her home in Orlando West, Soweto. She introduced him as my dearest brother. Farrakhan used the visit to attack the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which was at that moment investigating Madikizela-Mandela's links to at least eighteen gross human rights violations, including the murder of fourteen-year-old Stompie Seipei. The leader of the Nation of Islam flew to South Africa to defend a woman credibly accused of involvement in the murder of a child, and to undermine the process that was trying to establish accountability.

The connection between the Pan Africanist Congress and the Nation of Islam was not incidental. It was structural. Both organisations drew from the same ideological well: a vision of the world divided into oppressor races and oppressed races, in which land, wealth, and spiritual legitimacy belonged exclusively to people of African descent. The PAC's founding slogan, Africa for the Africans, and the Nation of Islam's theology of Yakub, which teaches that white people were created by a rogue scientist as a race of devils, arrive at the same destination through different routes. One is political nationalism. The other is religious mythology. Both conclude that coexistence is impossible and that the presence of white people on African soil, whether in Johannesburg or Chicago, is an ongoing act of occupation.
Elijah Muhammad, the Nation of Islam's founder, taught that white civilisation was inherently temporary and that its destruction was divinely ordained. Louis Farrakhan has maintained this doctrine while softening its public expression. But the doctrine itself has not changed. And when Khallid Abdul Muhammad stood at Kean College and described the extermination of white South Africans, he was not freelancing. He was applying the theology to a specific geography. South Africa, with its visible white minority and its recent political transition, was the test case. If the ideology could be normalised there, it could be normalised anywhere.

There is a name that connects the 1960s revolutionary underground in America to the financial infrastructure of the largest racial justice movement of the twenty-first century. That name is Susan Rosenberg.
Rosenberg was born into a middle-class Jewish family on Manhattan's Upper West Side. By her late twenties she was on the FBI's Most Wanted List. She was a member of the May 19th Communist Organisation, a far-left militant group named after the shared birthday of Malcolm X and Ho Chi Minh. The organisation provided operational support to the Black Liberation Army, itself an offshoot of the Black Panther Party, and carried out a series of bombings targeting government buildings. In 1983, the group bombed the United States Capitol. In 1984, Rosenberg was arrested in New Jersey while unloading 740 pounds of stolen dynamite and an arsenal of weapons from a car. She was also wanted in connection with the 1981 Brink's armoured car robbery in Nyack, New York, in which two police officers and a security guard were killed. She was sentenced to fifty-eight years in federal prison.
On 20 January 2001, his last day in office, President Bill Clinton commuted Rosenberg's sentence to time served. The commutation produced bipartisan criticism. Republican Mayor Rudy Giuliani and Democratic Senator Chuck Schumer both condemned it. During a 2008 presidential primary debate, Barack Obama criticised Clinton's decision.

After her release, Rosenberg became the vice chair of the board of directors of Thousand Currents, a California-based nonprofit that served as the fiscal sponsor of the Black Lives Matter Global Network Foundation from 2016 to 2020. This meant that Thousand Currents handled the intake of donations, financial management, and institutional support for the central BLM organisation during the period of its explosive growth. The Capital Research Center first reported the connection in June 2020. Within days, Thousand Currents removed its entire board of directors page from its website. Snopes confirmed the connection, noting that Rosenberg had been listed as vice chair since at least 2017.

Trace the line. The Black Liberation Army, active in the 1970s and 1980s, carried out armed robberies and assassinations of police officers. The May 19th Communist Organisation provided support to the BLA and bombed the US Capitol. Susan Rosenberg, a convicted member of the M19CO, served sixteen years in federal prison before a presidential commutation, and then sat on the board of the organisation that handled the money for Black Lives Matter. This is not a conspiracy theory. It is a chain of custody, documented in court records, tax filings, and archived web pages.

The co-founders of Black Lives Matter have been transparent about their ideological orientation, at least to interviewers who bothered to ask. In a 2015 interview, Patrisse Cullors, one of BLM's three co-founders, described herself and co-founder Alicia Garza as trained Marxists who were super-versed in ideological theories. The interview was with Jared Ball of The Real News Network. It was not hidden. It was not a leak. It was a statement of identity. Cullors credited her political formation to Eric Mann, a former member of the Weather Underground, the same radical organisation that had bombed government buildings in the 1970s and whose alumni overlapped with the May 19th Communist Organisation. The Weather Underground, the Black Liberation Army, M19CO, Thousand Currents, Black Lives Matter: the thread does not break. It transfers.
Alicia Garza, BLM's other principal co-founder, has repeatedly cited Assata Shakur as one of her primary inspirations. Shakur, born Joanne Chesimard, was a member of the Black Liberation Army convicted of murdering New Jersey State Trooper Werner Foerster during a 1973 traffic stop. She was sentenced to life imprisonment but escaped from prison in 1979 and fled to Cuba, where she received political asylum from Fidel Castro. She remains on the FBI's Most Wanted Terrorists List with a one million dollar reward. When Garza invokes Shakur's words at the opening of BLM gatherings, she is not making a casual cultural reference. She is drawing from a specific lineage: one that includes armed robbery, cop killing, and international flight, and that connects directly to the same Black Liberation Army whose support network produced Susan Rosenberg.

In December 2019, two supporters of the Black Hebrew Israelites, David Anderson and Francine Graham, opened fire on a kosher market in Jersey City, New Jersey, killing three people inside after previously shooting and killing a police detective. The attack was classified as domestic terrorism motivated by antisemitism and anti-police sentiment. The Black Hebrew Israelites, like the Nation of Islam, are classified by the SPLC as a black nationalist hate group. They share the Nation of Islam's antisemitic theology and its framing of white people as fundamentally illegitimate. And they were, by 2018, part of the fastest-growing category on the SPLC's hate group list: the 264 black nationalist chapters that outnumbered every other category, including white nationalists and neo-Nazis.

The SPLC's response to the Jersey City shooting was revealing. In comments to the Forward, the organisation attributed the growth in black nationalist movements to the rise of white nationalism. The shooting itself, which targeted a kosher market and killed Jewish Americans, was framed as a downstream consequence of Donald Trump. The ideological framework that had produced the attack, one that classifies Jews as impostors and white people as devils, was treated not as a self-generating belief system with its own theology, literature, and organisational infrastructure, but as a reaction. A backlash. Something that would presumably disappear if the provocation were removed.

Apply that logic to any other extremist movement and its absurdity becomes obvious. Nobody describes jihadist terrorism as a backlash against Western foreign policy and then suggests the solution is simply to change the foreign policy. Nobody treats white supremacist violence as a reaction to demographic change and then concludes the real problem is the demographics. But for black nationalist extremism, the framing holds. The ideology is never the subject. It is always the object. Acted upon, never acting.

Now draw the map.
In South Africa, the Pan Africanist Congress was founded in 1959 on the principle of exclusive African ownership of the continent. Its military wing killed white civilians with axes, grenades, and automatic weapons from the 1960s through the 1990s. Its ideology classified Christianity as a colonial weapon and churches as legitimate targets.

In the United States, the Nation of Islam was founded in the 1930s on a theology of racial separation that teaches white people are a race of devils. Its national spokesman called for the genocide of white South Africans in 1993, the same year APLA was doing it. Its leader visited South Africa as a guest of the PAC. After being expelled from the Nation of Islam, the spokesman who called for genocide founded the New Black Panther Party, which continues to broadcast his speeches as its organisational liturgy.

In the United States, the Black Liberation Army carried out assassinations and armed robberies in the 1970s and 1980s. Its support network, the May 19th Communist Organisation, bombed the US Capitol. A convicted member of that bombing network, Susan Rosenberg, served on the board of the nonprofit that handled Black Lives Matter's money during its period of maximum growth and influence. BLM's co-founders describe themselves as trained Marxists and cite a convicted cop killer on the FBI's Most Wanted Terrorists List as their inspiration.
In December 2019, adherents of the Black Hebrew Israelites, another black nationalist movement on the SPLC's list, attacked a kosher market in Jersey City. The SPLC attributed the growth of such movements to white nationalism.

In Zimbabwe, ZANU's fighters killed missionaries and babies in the Vumba mountains. In South Africa, APLA's fighters killed worshippers at St James Church. In America, a Nation of Islam official called for the killing of white babies in South Africa. In New Jersey, a convicted terrorist who supported the Black Liberation Army sat on the board of BLM's fiscal sponsor. The thread does not break. It crosses oceans, it changes accents, it updates its language, but it does not break.

There is a moment, in the study of any network, when the individual nodes stop mattering as much as the connections between them. You stop asking who and start asking how. How does an ideology born in the Transkei bases of APLA show up in the rhetoric of a New Jersey college lecture? How does a theology developed by the Nation of Islam in Chicago find a host organisation in the Pan Africanist Congress of South Africa? How does a bombing network from the 1980s produce a board member of the largest racial justice organisation of the 2020s?

The answer is not conspiracy. It is something more durable: convergence. These movements share a common intellectual ancestor in Marxist-Leninist theory, filtered through Fanon's doctrine of redemptive violence and Cone's Black Liberation Theology. They share a common enemy: Western civilisation, its Christian foundations, its institutions of property and law, and the white populations who built them. They share a common method: the framing of all inequality as evidence of ongoing oppression, all Western institutions as instruments of that oppression, and all resistance to that framing as proof of the oppressor's guilt. They do not need a central command. They need only a shared analysis. The analysis provides the targeting. The targeting provides the solidarity. The solidarity provides the infrastructure.

And the infrastructure, as Part III will show, has gardeners. People who cultivated it, funded it, and protected it from scrutiny, not from the revolutionary underground but from the most respectable institutions in the Western world: its universities, its foundations, its cultural industries, and its governments.

The killings in Part I happened because an ideology permitted them. The connections in Part II show that the ideology was never local. It was always transnational, always networked, always moving between continents and adapting to new hosts.
Part III asks the question that neither the SPLC, nor the World Council of Churches, nor any mainstream watchdog has ever been willing to answer: who let it grow?
